title: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s terrifying and acutely moving prison drama is set in a young offender institute – and the reality it depicts needs national attention
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s terrifying and acutely moving prison drama is set in a young offender institute – and the reality it depicts needs national attention
Content: ‘McGovern at his finest’ … David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreen‘McGovern at his finest’ … David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewTime review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as AdolescenceThe third series of Jimmy McGovern’s terrifying and acutely moving prison drama is set in a young offender institute – and the reality it depicts needs national attentionLucy ManganSun 11 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJimmy McGovern has said that this new, third instalment of hisprison anthology dramaTime will be the last. For the sake of audiences’ emotional equilibrium, you have to hope so. For the sake of scripted drama, for the sake of art that has a hope of stirring the conscience of authorities and effecting change, you have to hope not.This time, Time is inside a young offender institution. It is crammed with under-18-year-old males, locked up often for 23 hours a day, all subject to the relatively new “keep apart” system whereby prisoners deemed likely to be violent towards each other are not allowed out of their cells at the same time. Naturally, this leads to a lot more boys being banged up for a lot more of the day and suits the officers a lot better. It is a facet of modern YOIs that McGovern and his co-writer Sam Bailey, a man evidently cut from the same socially conscious cloth, are clearly intent on bringing to wider attention. Their script, and the direction by Paul Whittington, do a wonderful, terrifying job of conveying the kinetic energy pent up and desperate for release, and the seething fury ever threatening to erupt, in every scene.And what scenes. This is McGovern (and Bailey) at his finest – stripped of sentimentality, always furious and driven by an agenda but never descending into agitprop, and giving us stories of suffering, of moral struggle, of the damage and the glory that people are capable of, the burdens they bear and the gifts they can give.View image in fullscreenHope of redemption … Siobhan Finneran with Tennant.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyA restrainedDavid Tennant, in one of his best ever performances, plays corrections officer Bobby Bailey, wearied by the job but not entirely devoid of compassion for the lads in his care. Alongside him is his colleague Freddie Jennings (Daniel Ryan), of whom much the same can be said. At least until we see him gut-punch James (Louis McCartney), a mouthy smart alec, suddenly gasping for breath on the floor after one wisecrack too many.Into the prison comes chaplain Marie-Louise (the inimitableSiobhan Finneran), who has been in all parts of the triptych and is – blissfully – given more to do here. She has lost her faith, after a relationship ending and a marked lack of Christian charity from expected sources in its wake. She expects to be fired from the new post when she confesses it, but the elder chaplain tells her they need her now more than ever. So they do, but she is a straw in the howling wind of need within the system. And she knows it. But she keeps on and keeps on and this, in McGovern’s theology, is where all hope of redemption resides.We get to know the boys – or young men, but the drama limns them so clearly as boys within, inarticulate, insecure, capable of sweetness and softness but hardening by the minute – gradually. McGovern and Bailey don’t shy away from the fact that offenders are (unlike the women in the second series, say, the pettiness of whose crimes was part of the point) incarcerated for “proper” reasons. James has killed his brother, a group of Liverpudlian boys murdered a man in the street, and the sense is that the rest of them have all committed, or been involved with, similar levels of violence. Most of the actors – including Ollie McNulty as Peter, the conscience-stricken part of the murderous gang, and Chukwubuikem Molokwu as Christopher/Ushindi, whose avoidable tragedy powers much of the narrative – are making their debuts, and the quality of their performances (and Molokwu must also navigate his character’s painful stammer, which he does without losing a moment’s focus) is just astonishing. Kudos to them all and to the woman who found them, casting director Amy Hubbard.All of McGovern’s customary concerns are on display as Bobby’s sins, major and minor, accumulate, temptations encourage straying from the path of righteousness, and guilt becomes a prison of its own. The boys show us how grief, abuse and a lack of language with which to express any of it manifest in simple violence and how little a gut punch – actual, from an individual, or metaphorical from the state – will do to quash let alone solve it.Love is offered, slightly more overtly than elsewhere in the series, as an answer. Not a panacea, just … an opportunity. To be better, feel better, live better. Eventually, after three of the most harrowing and acutely moving hours, we are allowed some hope.For myriad reasons, including its very complexity and the dreadfulness of the truths it holds, this portrait of masculinity and the misery it brings probably won’t garner the attention and momentum that Jack Thorne’s Adolescence did. But it should. Our boys need it.Time aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now in the UK. An Australian broadcast has yet to be confirmed.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionDavid TennantreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Yes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politics | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: We must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitism, says Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales
Author: Zack Polanski
Headline: We must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitism, says Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales
Content: Delegates gather around the Young Greens booth during the first day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelegates gather around the Young Greens booth during the first day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesOpinionGreen partyYes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politicsZack PolanskiWe must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitismSun 11 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTShareWhen Istood for leaderof the Greens in 2025, our party was at a crossroads. The transformative leadership of Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay had taken us to an electoral success we’d never seen before. I knew we had even greater potential – and that the country was crying out for the bold politics we could offer.We have seen unprecedented wins this year – from our first everparliamentary byelection winto our landslide council and mayoral victories in former Labour strongholds.Those victories have moved Labour. Our electoral successes helped topple Keir Starmer, seeing him replaced by a prime minister unarguably to his left. They forced a change in tone in the government’srelations with Israel. The government has evenrowed back onsome of its cruel anti-migrant policies.Our work isn’t done. But the next phase for our party takes place in a landscape that is clearly more challenging for us. Andy Burnham is enjoying a honeymoon phase, and hasn’t yet had to make the “difficult decisions” that will reveal exactly who will lose out under his government – unpopular choices he will probably start making at his fast-approaching first budget.Of course I wanted to win theHolborn and St Pancras byelection. But our result shows, as the polling expert John Curtice has said, that our party represents agreater threat to Labourin places like this than ever before. Wetripled our vote sharein a seat that Labour has comfortably held since 1983 and forced it to campaign hard in a constituency it would once have taken for granted.We have transformed the electoral landscape and, as the first nationwide serious threat toLabouron its left in modern political history, we are here to stay.The result also came at a difficult moment for our party. A motion voted through at our conference, “Zionism is racism”, hasstirred up strong feelingsamong many members and the wider public too. And I know there have been questions about my approach to the motion.I’m a Jewish man who grew up in a Zionist household. The story I was told about Israel was one of destiny and safety: a land without a people for a people without a land. But since then I have learned about the people whodidlive on that land – and what has happened to them. The Palestinians driven from their homes; slaughtered en masse; and those who remain, living underan apartheid systemthat denies them fundamental rights, including that of self-determination.It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up withidentity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with – such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone theGreen party– to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.Before the vote, I made it clear thatthere were amendmentsI would like to see made, and I am disappointed that those did not pass.I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party. I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John HarrisRead moreMy responsibility now is to bring our party together to achieve our full potential. This starts with an assurance from me: under my leadership, I will not tolerate antisemitism. No one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith or where they worship. I will meet any group within our party that fears victimisation to understand exactly what they need in order to feel safe and welcome.Second, our party has grown to a size none of us could have anticipated when I became leader. Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible.Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better. This government is on course to preside over theworst parliament for living standardsin modern times. Energy bills are expected to rise again this winter; rent increases are forecast to speed up. Meanwhile, Burnham is offering no concrete support for bills and ruling out any controls on rents, and Reform UK is still using cost of living pressures to stir up division in our communities.The Green party’s bold, principled ideas have never been more needed. From an emergency brake on rents to full public ownership of water companies, we are offering solutions that this government won’t go near unless we force it to. We have work to do – and I will bring my party together to get it done.Zack Polanski is the leader of the Green party of England and Wales and a member of the London assemblyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘I want to do everything I can to head off dementia’: why demand for the shingles vaccine is soaring | Dementia | The Guardian
description: Could a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabs
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Could a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabs
Content: Illustration: Grace Russell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Grace Russell/The GuardianDementia‘I want to do everything I can to head off dementia’: why demand for the shingles vaccine is soaringCould a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabsIan SampleScience editorSun 11 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Jenny, a 50-year-old marketing and branding professional from Cambridge, went for her shingles vaccine last year, an entirely different disease was on her mind. Having witnessed three of her four grandparents succumb to dementia, with all the distress that brought, she wants to avoid the same fate. She hopes the shingles vaccine might help.Jenny is far from alone. Britain’s high street chemists have reported a rise in demand for the shingles vaccine, at least some of which is driven by people more worried about dementia than shingles. And while the vaccine is free forsome on the NHS, most under-65s pay around £450 for the full two doses.The trend follows a flurry of studies that suggest, but do not prove, that the shingles vaccination might offer some protection against dementia. How much protection? It depends on how the study is done, but scientists have reported as much as a 20% reduction in risk, with the strongest effects in women. On a brutal disease that has no cure, the impact could be profound. “Imagine a vaccine that became a medicine for dementia,” says John Todd, professor of precision medicine at the University of Oxford and one of the scientists involved. “Wow. Wouldn’t that be amazing?”Recent figures from Boots show that bookings for its shingles vaccination service more than doubled over the past year, after rising 30% in the year before. A similar trend has played out at Superdrug, where bookings are up 41% year on year.Of course, many who go for their shots simply want to avoid shingles. It’s a painful rash, triggered by reactivation of the chickenpox virus which lies dormant in the nervous system after a childhood infection. The vaccine is not approved for any other condition. But dozens of people who contacted the Guardian said preventing dementia was at least part of their reason for getting the shots.“I want to feel as if I’ve done everything I can to try to head it off, in terms of risk factors and preventive measures that are available to me now,” says Jenny. “If there’s a potential for this to give me more time without the onset of dementia in 20 years’ time, then God, I’ll take it.”Nearly 60 million people live with dementia globally, but the figure is set to rise with population growth and ageing. By 2040, more than 100 million people are projected to have the disease. In England and Wales, it’s expected dementia could affect 1.7 million people that year, with the annual cost reaching £90bn.View image in fullscreenNearly 60 million people live with dementia globally, but the figure is set to rise.Photograph: Posed by models; Jessie Casson/Getty ImagesThe most common form of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, is associated with the abnormal buildup of proteins in the brain. Plaques (clusters) of amyloid accumulate between neurons, and tangles of another protein, tau, form inside the nerve cells. New drugs can clear amyloid plaques and slow the disease, but so far the impact on patients appears small and the side-effects can be serious.The wave of work on the shingles vaccine was spurred by suspicions that the virus that causes chickenpox and shingles, varicella zoster virus or VZV, might somehow contribute to dementia. After a chickenpox infection, some virus remains in the body, lying dormant in neurons. As the immune system weakens with age, or is suppressed through medications or stress, the virus can reactivate and travel down nerve cells to the skin where it causes shingles. In the brain, the virus can drive inflammation, nerve cell stress and the accumulation of amyloid and tau.In aninfluential paperin Nature last year, researchers at Stanford University in California focused on a natural experiment that arose in Wales during a shingles vaccination programme. The vaccine on offer, Zostavax, was a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning it contained a weakened version of the varicella zoster virus. It was made available from 1 September 2013, but anyone who was 80 or older on that day was ineligible, because it becomes less effective the older a person gets.The age-related cutoff split the older population into two groups: those who could get the vaccine and those who could not. This allowed scientists to compare dementia rates in thousands of people born on different sides of the eligibility line.When the Stanford team ran the numbers, they found that dementia rates were 8.5% lower in the vaccine-eligible group over seven years, in women, but not in men (the gender disparity in this experiment remains unexplained). Since only about half of the group went along for their shots, the researchers concluded that the vaccine lowered dementia risk by nearly 20%. They have since reported similar effects inAustraliaandOntario, Canada.“We have a really compelling body of data from these studies,” says Pascal Geldsetzer, an epidemiologist on the Stanford studies. “We’re much more confident that what we’re looking at is cause and effect rather than just correlation.”More evidence came in 2024 from the University of Oxford, when Todd teamed up with psychiatrists Maxime Taquet and Paul Harrison to study Shingrix, a newer and more potent shingles vaccine that has largely replaced Zostavax. Shingrix is not a live-attenuated vaccine but contains viral proteins and an adjuvant – an additive designed to strengthen the body’s immune response and so make the vaccine more effective. In this case, the adjuvant is made of tiny fat-based particles called liposomes that are filled with various compounds that stimulate different parts of the immune response.View image in fullscreenShingles is triggered by reactivation of the chickenpox virus which lies dormant in the nervous system after a childhood infection.Photograph: Posed by models; Milan_Jovic/Getty ImagesThe Oxford team analysed health records for more than 200,000 US citizens who were vaccinated for shingles. About half had Shingrix and half Zostavax. Over the next six years, dementia cases were17% lower in those who had Shingrixcompared with Zostavax, amounting to an extra 164 days lived without the condition. Women fared better, with a 22% lower risk compared with 13% for men. (Womenhave a higherdementia risk, which seems mostly down to them living longer.) One benefit of the study was that it compared Zostavax v Shingrix rather than vaccinated v unvaccinated people. That reduced the risk of the results being skewed by the “health vaccinee” bias, whereby people who get vaccinated are generally more health conscious and do more to reduce their risk of dementia in other ways.“I thought wow, I’ll just book the vaccine online,” says Todd. “If by chance it does lower the risk of dementia, I’m 68 – why wouldn’t I take that? And also, it’s really effective against shingles.” Todd is a consultant for GSK, the manufacturer of Shingrix, but the company had no involvement in any of the studies.More recent work hints at other potential benefits of the vaccine. In August, the Oxford team publisheda papershowing a reduced risk of heart attacks and stroke after the Shingrix vaccination. The effect is small, but across the population it could prevent thousands of deaths per year. Separate work at Kaiser Permanente, the US healthcare giant,found a similar effect.The results are exciting, but none of this is proof. Critical questions remain. In July, researchers at the University of Bristol, and others including Geldsetzer, foundno evidencein much larger English hospital records that Zostavax protects against dementia. That may be due to quirks in the data or how it is analysed, or a sign that the old Zostavax vaccine does not protect against dementia after all. Geldsetzer suspects hospital data is not the best for studying dementia, as most patients are managed in primary care.Precisely how the vaccine might protect against dementia is still a puzzle. By stimulating the immune system to attack VZV, the vaccine might help to reduce inflammation and cellular damage in the brain.There may be knock-on effects whereby inflammationreactivates another dormant virus, the cold sore-causing HSV1, which in turn drives Alzheimer’s-like damage. The vaccine may also have broader effects, boosting ailing immune systems so they are better at clearing harmful waste from the brain.One avenue scientists are exploring is whether the adjuvant, which is in Shingrix but not Zostavax, is important for protection against dementia. The Oxford team suspect that might explain why a vaccine for respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, which contains the same adjuvant as Shingrix, also appears toprotect against dementia. The adjuvant specifically stimulates T-cells that are central to the immune response to the virus. “You want a really healthy immune system to do the garbage collection of damaged neurons,” says Todd.The lack of hard proof hasn’t stopped people taking action. Jenny had already had a bout of shingles – “It looked like I’d been slapped across the face by a zombie,” she says – but it was the fear of dementia that prompted her to get vaccinated. She made the decision after reading the research for herself, wary that the press might have hyped it.View image in fullscreenPrecisely how the vaccine might protect against dementia is still a puzzle.Photograph: Andrew Brookes/Getty Images/Connect ImagesSally, a 68-year-old former headteacher in Telford, Shropshire, cared for her mother with dementia for five years. “It does bring you up very sharply when you’re considering your own future,” she says. Sally runs marathons, watches her nutrition carefully and does all she can to protect herself from the disease. “I was going to have the shingles jab anyway, but when I saw the research saying there may be a protective effect against dementia, I jumped at it. The experience of caring for someone who developed dementia was pivotal in my decision.” She got the jabs on the NHS.It could be a while before we have clear answers. Todd and colleagues want to do a mechanistic study to understand at the deepest level what happens to the immune system when people have the shingles vaccination. Meanwhile, two major clinical trials are under way in Finland and Denmark to see whether Shingrix genuinely protects against dementia, but they won’t report for years.What should people do in the meantime? Geldsetzer says that while vaccine recommendations are a matter for government advisory bodies, he wouldn’t discourage people who want to get the shingles vaccine for dementia protection. Todd says: “I have been suggesting to friends and colleagues to get the vaccine if they are 50 or over – it’s safe.”Alzheimer’s Research UK does not advise people to have the shingles vaccine specifically to prevent dementia. Instead, it recommends all the healthy habits we know promote brain health: exercise, a good diet and challenging the brain throughout life. Michael Jones, evidence manager at the charity, says: “While new studies finding these links are promising and growing in number, there isn’t enough data to demonstrate a direct cause-and-effect relationship.”Dominic, a 61-year-old engineer in Christchurch, Dorset, paid for the Shingrix vaccine last year. His father had shingles, the classic rash around the torso, which lasted for months. His eldest sister had shingles, too. It affected her eye and caused minor damage. A cousin also developed the condition. Dominic planned to get the shot, but only acted after reading the dementia research. “I really don’t want to get shingles,” he says. “That could strike at anytime. And when does dementia start? We just don’t know, do we?”Explore more on these topicsDementiaHealthVaccines and immunisationHealth & wellbeingAlzheimer'sMedical researchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war | Primatology | The Guardian
description: John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world
Content: Primatologist John Mitani, who co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project in Kibale national park, Uganda.Photograph:  Lauren SarringhausView image in fullscreenPrimatologist John Mitani, who co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project in Kibale national park, Uganda.Photograph:  Lauren SarringhausNature heroesPrimatology‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil warJohn Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific worldSupported byAbout this contentGloria DickieSun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Mitani can still remember the first time he set foot in Uganda’s Kibale national park. The old-growth east African rainforest enveloped him, its canopy stretching to heights of 40 metres. Fruit trees bowed under the weight of African star apples and bountifulFicus mucusofigs. And then there were the chimpanzees. Furry black blobs darted through the jungle, their raucous calls often deafening.It was the summer of 1995, and Mitani, a primatologist from northern California, had just come from working with the chimps living in theMahale mountainsof Tanzania. At the time, Mahale was home to the largest known population of chimps, with about 100 individuals. But there were rumours that this section of Kibale – only accessible via a 12-hour drive from the capital, Kampala – might host an even more unusual abundance of apes.“It only took a few days to realise that something weird was going on at this place,” Mitani, now 72, recalls. “There were chimps everywhere.”He was then a professor at the University of Michigan, and with his colleagues would eventually count nearly 200 chimpanzees living together peacefully in the forests of Ngogo, aresearch areain thecentral section of Kibale first established in the 1970s for the study of red colobus monkeys. Such a large chimp troop was then unheard of in primatology.View image in fullscreenChimpanzees groom each other at Ngogo in Kibale national park.Photograph: Ngogo Chimpanzees ProjectLater that year, Mitani co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project with the Yale university primatologistDavid Watts, using a $500,000 (£380,000) award from the US National Science Foundation. Three decades on, the project is one of just 12 long-term studies worldwide of chimpanzees in their natural environment, and has transformed what we know about one of our closest relatives.It took years to build trust with the population, Mitani says. The chimps were not accustomed to human presence and were quick to run away whenever researchers approached. Days were spent chasing them over hills and down valleys. “It was fun, exciting and exhilarating. It was also a challenge.”The first ape to break the ice was a 25-year-old male with an easily identifiable cleft palate that Mitani would latername Hare. During his second year at Ngogo, Mitani was observing chimpanzees in a massive fig tree when Hare descended. Mitani assumed he would run away as he had done in the past. Instead, the chimp walked slowly toward the next fruit tree, permitting Mitani to follow.View image in fullscreenHare, the male chimp that was the first to establish trust with Mitani at Ngogo.Photograph: John Mitani“When I realised what was happening, I almost started to cry. After working so hard for so long, it was tremendously gratifying to have gained Hare’s trust,” Mitani wrote in the 2022 anthology Chimpanzee Memoirs.Mitani estimates he has spent 85 months of his life hiking the forests of Ngogo, or approximately seven years. What began as a few basic structures and tents has grown into a large – albeit rustic – research camp that has housed the nearly 90 researchers who have worked with the Ngogo project over three decades.The findingsthat have emerged from Ngogo over the years have stunned the scientific world, similar to the discoveries first made atGombein Tanzania byJane Goodallin the 1960s and 1970s. Mitani and his colleagues documented the lowest mortality ever recorded for a wild chimp population, suggesting that good habitat conditions couldlengthen life expectancyto close to that of human hunter-gatherers.They found that unrelated males couldform strong alliances and cooperate, moving beyond the accepted paradigm that only close kin would work together.Hunting and meat-eating(particularly munching on the red colobus monkeys) were found to be important for male social bonding, not just nutrition.View image in fullscreenAdult male chimpanzees of one group attack a male chimpanzee of another group at Kibale.Photograph: Aaron Sandel/ReutersBut the most notable – and disturbing – finding of Ngogo began on a June day in 2015. Mitani and his fellow researchers were observing a cluster of the group when the chimps began to display nervous behaviour and scattered at the sounds of approaching group members. “All of a sudden, the individuals I was following just ran down the hill for no apparent reason,” Mitani says. “Chaos erupted. They started to run around and chase each other.”Wild chimpanzees recorded waging ‘civil war’ with coordinated attacks between two groupsRead moreThat moment, in retrospect, was the first sign of what would become a years-long bloody conflict – chronicled in the 2023 Netflix seriesChimp Empire–between a once close-knit group of chimps. Ina studypublished this April in the journal Science, Mitani and his colleagues describe what may be the first “civil war” among wild chimps.By 2018, two distinct chimp groups had formed in Ngogo. Nine males and 19 infants have been killed during the conflict. Scientists later found that the unexpected result of this lethal aggression was thatfemale fertility doubledand offspring survival increased substantially at Ngogo.But for Mitani, who has spent much of his life among the Ngogo chimps, witnessing the split was far more personal. “I was in denial. I was still in this mindset that they were doing so well together as a big group,” he recalls.“It’s been hard to watch. In the first 20 years, going back to see the chimps was fun. I always looked forward to these visits. But it’s gotten to be increasingly difficult to go back and see this, to see these killings continue.”View image in fullscreenJackson, the former alpha male of the central group of chimpanzees at Ngogo.Photograph: John MitaniSo much so, he adds, that it took him more than a decade to write the paper on the dark events they had borne witness to in the forests of Ngogo. “I think I was dragging my heels because maybe I didn’t really want to write about this.”Still, Mitani pushes back against the takeaway that the civil war says anything about humans’ evolutionary propensity for violence and in-fighting. This behaviour, he adds, has not been witnessed among bonobos, with whom we also share a common ancestor dating back approximately 8m years.“Many of us who study chimpsemphasise the similarities, and for good reason,” Mitani says. “But when it comes to the behavioural similarities, sometimes I think my colleagues stretch things a bit too much. If there is one thing I’ve learned from studying chimps all these years, it is that they are not us.”View image in fullscreenJohn Mitani says the Ngogo chimps have many more important stories to tell us.Photograph: Ewan DryburghThough the greatest threat the Ngogo chimps now face is, in a way, themselves, Mitani says the presence of researchers on the ground over many decades has helped toconservethese populations. Researchers work with the wildlife authority to remove snares for other wild game that occasionally trap a chimp by mistake, for example.But Mitani, who now lives between Michigan and Arizona, worries for the future of research at Ngogo. The project has received the bulk of its funding from the US National Science Foundation’s behavioural and cognitive sciences division. Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget, that funding is due to be eliminated.“The chimps there have many more important stories to tell us,” Mitani says. “This is one of the reasons I am so concerned about the war on science and truth in this country.”He will return again to Ngogo this month – and for as long as he is able. “The funny thing is that the hills at Ngogo get increasingly steeper every year. And the distance between the trails seems to get longer. But I feel blessed that I still can do it.”If there is any legacy to his life’s work, he hopes that being able to impart some knowledge of the complex lives of these animals will give people a better appreciation of the chimpanzees. That maybe that will inspire people to ensure we continue living on a planet alongside them. “That would be the grand, big hope.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldon the app for all the latest news and features.Explore more on these topicsPrimatologyNature heroesAnimal behaviourWildlifeConservationUgandaAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brink | Devon | The Guardian
description: A dry summer has left the Bristol Channel island critically short of water, forcing visitor caps and talk of evacuating its 28 residents
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: A dry summer has left the Bristol Channel island critically short of water, forcing visitor caps and talk of evacuating its 28 residents
Content: Matt Scantlebury, Lundy’s manager, stands in shallow water at Pondsbury pond, one of the island’s freshwater pools.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMatt Scantlebury, Lundy’s manager, stands in shallow water at Pondsbury pond, one of the island’s freshwater pools.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianDevonRapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brinkA dry summer has left the Bristol Channel island critically short of water, forcing visitor caps and talk of evacuating its 28 residentsSteven MorrisSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Carr was peering up at the clouds scudding around the island ofLundy, 10 miles off the coast of north Devon. “That one’s definitely got rain in it,” he said. “The mainland will be wet at the moment. And look over at Wales – it’s getting a real soaking just now.”But aboveLundythe sky was, stubbornly, blue. No significant rain has fallen here since the start of May, leading to perilously low water levels. Restrictions have been put in place, visitor numbers limited and there has been talk of the island – home to 28 people – being evacuated.“It’s been a challenge,” said Carr, a conservation farmer who looks after sheep, cattle and ponies. He has been here more than 20 years and reckons the combination of the climate emergency and the topography of the granite outcrop, which soars out of the Bristol Channel, is the problem.View image in fullscreenEngineer Tristan Howes inspects a water tank.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“Climate change is here, it’s happening. We’re having hotter, drier summers. And when the rain clouds do come in, they tend to split as the approach the island and we stay dry.”The three-mile long island, famed for its puffins and its pirate past, relies on rainwater and five boreholes. The biggest rain catchment area is in the south. From there – when it does rain – water tumbles down to a collection tank near the harbour. It is then pumped up to an array of tanks and a purification plant near the old lighthouse.View image in fullscreenA tractor pulls water containers on Lundy.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianThe island manager, Matt Scantlebury, said a fortnight ago the tanks were at 13% capacity – only enough water to keep the island going for about a week. Tonnes of water was being brought over in 1,000 litre containers on the island boat, the MS Oldenburg, to top up the supply.The campsite, which is popular with climbers once the cliff-nesting seabirds have gone, was shut. The toilets at the island pub, the Marisco Tavern, were closed. Bath plugs in holiday lets – up to 110 people can stay here – were taken away and people were asked to think twice before flushing toilets.Happily, on the day the water reached its low point, the island received confirmation that the water in one of its freshwater pools – called Pondsbury – was of a good enough quality to be used.View image in fullscreenVisitors arriving at Lundy, which is owned by the National Trust. Tourist numbers have been limited because of the water shortage.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianAbout 12,000 litres of water has been taken from there every day since and the levels are back up to 22.5%. But now the pond is starting to run dry. “And still no proper rain is forecast,” said Scantlebury. “We know we have to find ways of future proofing ourselves.”To that end, a new 300,000-litre water tank has been ordered. The idea of a desalination plant – seawater is one thing the island is not short of – has been suggested but Scantlebury said it would be expensive and would probably need more energy than the island was capable of producing.Tristan Howes, the island’s engineer, said finding ways of conserving the little water Lundy had was crucial. “A dripping tap can lose a lot of water,” he said. A broken pipe would be a disaster.View image in fullscreenDepleted water levels at Pondsbury pond.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianStaff have got used not only to having a rapid shower but catching the water they use in a bucket and using it to flush the toilet. “It’s about being as efficient as we can.”Luckily, visitors to Lundy, which is owned by the National Trust and managed by the Landmark Trust, tend to be the sort who don’t mind a little bit of hardship.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMichelle Phillips, an animal lover keen to see the island’s ponies, and her husband, Fred Bullinaria, arrived for a day trip with 1.6 litres of water, four Lucozades and a tube of hydration tablets in their backpacks. “I think that will keep us going,” she said.Vick and Ed Crane were staying on Lundy for a few days to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary. They had bought wet wipes to limit their water usage. “We don’t mind roughing it,” said Vick. “That’s part of the Lundy experience. It’s an adventure.”View image in fullscreen1,000-litre containers have been used to replenish water supplies on the island, which usually relies on rainwater and five boreholes.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianThe residents are positive, always looking for the bright side.Tara McEvoy-Wilding, assistant warden on the island, said some creatures had done well from the hot summer. “It’s been a good year for butterflies and moths.”And it has also been a good summer for the Lundy cabbage, a primitive brassica that grows only on the island. “It’s quite a pioneering species and likes dry bare ground where there isn’t much vegetation,” said McEvoy-Wilding. “Hundreds of tiny cabbage plants have started to establish in areas where they wouldn’t normally. So that’s positive, at least.”View image in fullscreenWorkers top up a water tank.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianMcEvoy-Wilding said residents had become accustomed to using less water. “You’re more mindful – you only have a short shower and you don’t always flush the toilet. In a way it’s not a bad thing. It makes you think about how much water you could be saving every day by just making very small changes.”But that doesn’t mean that McEvoy-Wilding is not hoping for rain. “It’s amazing how little rain we’ve had. We had one day in August when it rained for an hour. Absolutely torrential. I was caught in it and got drenched but the ground was so dry it just poured off the island.“I’ve got an allotment and it’s been hard to keep my vegetables alive. The pumpkins aren’t anywhere near as big as normal. Some nice, steady rain would be perfect.”Explore more on these topicsDevonDroughtWaterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashes | Rachael Stirling | The Guardian
description: When the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us all
Content: Rachael Stirling with a portrait of her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachael Stirling with a portrait of her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianRachael Stirling‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashesWhen the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us allRachael StirlingSun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been headlines of late that make me out to be an ash-guzzling savage nightly devouring her mother’s charred remains. “Rachael Stirling eats mother Diana Rigg’s ashes before going on stage” declared a dozen news outlets last month, while others referred to the “strange habit only she really understands” and “Dame Diana’s daughter admits eating her ashes in bizarre tribute”. I’ve written a book about our relationship, All About My Mother, in which I do confess to nibbling a grain or two, but I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a matricidal cannibal by the press.My mother wasDiana Rigg, an iconic actor with a 60-year career. Young ’uns will know her as the Queen of Thorns from Game of Thrones, be-wimpled spouter of the best verbal roasts on television: “I’ve known a great number of clever men. I’ve outlived them all. You know how? I ignored them.” Old ’uns, meanwhile, go dewy-eyed at the memory of her leather-catsuited telly triumph as Emma Peel in The Avengers from the 60s, the first woman to perform kung fu on western television. She was also the only woman ever to marry James Bond. She appeared in The Great Muppet Caper because I was profoundly in love with Miss Piggy, and her child-murdering Medea was the toast of Broadway. She won an Emmy and a Tony, and had countless honours bestowed upon her for her many stage performances. She was a complete original and very witty to boot.I missed her so intensely, I wrote the book to bring her back to life. Mum never wanted a biography in her lifetime, having been put off by a couple of limp jobs that managed to make her seem a bit dull or, worst of all crimes, earnest. My mother was not earnest. She was honest, sometimes eye-bleedingly so.View image in fullscreenStirling as a baby with her mother.Photograph: Chris Barham/Daily Mail/ REX/ ShutterstockI was her only child, and followed her into the acting profession. She strongly disapproved of my career choice, and this caused some rumpuses, I can tell you. We ran the gamut of emotions from A to Z and eventually we made our way back to the love we’d had in the early years. In the end, the love bits between us did conquer all the awful bits, though there are some joyful and some jaw-dropping stories to share.Which brings us neatly back to the subject of ashes and my ingesting of them.Groucho Marx wished to be cremated, with one tenth of his ashes to be “given to my agent, as written in my contract”. Dying in the Covid lockdown, my mother wished to be cremated, too, but with no ceremony, and scattered in places she loved. Pragmatic to the last, she even made sure we’d paid for the cremation on her bank card before she died. However, we never thought to decide what receptacle her remains would be returned in, so it wasn’t until after her death that I found myself browsing the selection of “scatter tubes” on offer.Scatter tubes are cardboard containers of varying sizes. Some are plain, others have images printed on them. These are pretty unoriginal, pictures of doves and sunsets – or was it a sunrise – and images that felt to me a bitsurle nez.It turns out most things are quite on the nose when it comes to death. There isn’t much of a market for irony. Not many skull and crossbones, or red stilettos, or tubes with “I told you I was ill” written on them. In the end I settled for a variety of receptacles in a variety of sizes, with the least offensive floral decorations on them. I needed quantity, as my mother had many places to go. She was to be scattered from the air across the green fields of England from a biplane by her aviator friend Tracey Curtis-Taylor; she was to be scattered in her garden in France and mine in London; and on the site of the actors’ church in Covent Garden.double quotation markI did not expect human ashes to be so heavy. But they are very heavy. I discovered this when my mother’s mortal remains were returned to me one bright September morningI did not expect human ashes to be so heavy. But they areveryheavy. I discovered this when my mother’s mortal remains were returned to me one bright September morning. The cremation company had told me, when organising delivery, that taking receipt of the ashes could be an emotional event. Certainly, the carbonised corpse of my beloved Ma was the strangest delivery I’d ever expected, and not one to be left on the porch or with a neighbour. So I sat waiting, like an obedient dog awaiting her mistress by the front door.My mother was delivered to me by the gentlest of gentlemen from the cremation firm in Yorkshire, where my mother was born. He pulled her out of the boot in a box wrapped in plain cloth. With kind eyes searching my face, presumably to see if I was going to start bawling and drop her, he handed her to me with the tenderness with which one might hand over a newborn babe.While cremation frees the family to celebrate the life of a loved one in the great outdoors and away from the stuffy formality of funerals, things don’t always go to plan. Everyone has seen a movie where the ashes are scattered and the wind picks up and blows them into the faces of the grieving party. The best story of an ashes mishap took place at a scattering of my father-in-law, Donald Garvey, Dad to seven glorious children, the sixth of whom is my husband, Guy Garvey. There we were to celebrate the greatly missed Don with his huge family at the Great Orme in Llandudno, the site of many a Garvey family holiday. Don had stated he wanted the day to emulate a painting by Jack Vettriano where a woman in a red dress dances with her partner in tails on a stormy day at the beach. Words were spoken on the clifftop, and an intrepid few descended to the shore. Granddaughter Lucie, in a scarlet off-the-shoulder dress, hoicked up her skirts and waded into the unusually clear and calm blue sea to scatter her beloved grandad, as per his specific wishes, in the Welsh tide. Job done, as Lucie solemnly made her way back to her family on shore, she piped up with the now immortal line, “I think I’ve got some of Grandad in mi’ knickers.”The tiniest tube containing my mother was about three inches tall. I’d like to point out that I think scatter tubes are really badly designed. They open exactly the opposite way to the direction they look like they should, so you can easily scatter a loved one’s ashes by mistake. The contents of this tube had – mostly – gone where they were supposed to go, though it still contained the odd grain or 20 of my mother, so I couldn’t possibly throw it away. Plus it was conveniently pocket-size, so I took to carrying what was left of her with me everywhere I went. So far, so normal.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianThe next play I did was at the same theatre I had last performed at pre-Covid. It was the last show my mother ever saw, Love, Love, Love at the Lyric in Hammersmith. The new show, Scandaltown, was by the same writer, Mike Bartlett, and also at the Lyric. Everything felt eerily similar, yet between the two plays Ma had died and the whole world had turned on its arse. Now, here I was going to rehearsals in the same room, with some of the same people, but without Ma to chat to about how the play was going at the end of the day. Strange new world.As I placed her tube in my rucksack on the first day working on the show, I remember thinking how thrilled she’d be, back in a rehearsal room once more. Nearer opening night, I decided she’d enjoy a permanent stint in my dressing room. My mother had used this same dressing room in 1985, when she was performing in Little Eyolf, a grim Nordic drama from 1894 by Henrik Ibsen. It is the “Number One” dressing room, the room nearest the stage, and here she was once again, sitting in front of a Hollywood mirror with its necklace of blazing bulbs, although this time in a tube. The only thing she missed out on was actually going on stage with me. That was her happiest place, after all, but I could not hide the tube anywhere in my tight-fitting gold lamé suit without having a very peculiar lump in my costume. So there she stayed, in her dressing room, waiting for the call to the stage that never came.double quotation markI licked my finger, picked up the few spilt cinders, and popped her on my tongue. Grainy, in case you were wondering, but it didn’t feel wrong, it felt completely rightActors are an emotional tribe at the best of times and come opening night I was a wreck. My maiden first night with no mother in the crowd made me sad, but this was a high-energy Restoration-style comedy so I had to pull myself together quick-smart. I looked at the small tube containing mama residue, and I don’t know what I was thinking, but I found myself opening it. The wrong way round. A few grains fell on to my dressing table and as I panicked and tried to put them back one by one with varying degrees of success, the PA system blared, “Miss Stirling, this is your call to stage.” It was time to make my entrance. The adrenaline started kicking in and now my heart was pounding. It was time to go.In a panic, like a cocaine addict from a movie who can’t bear to waste a grain of the good stuff, I licked my finger, picked up the few spilt cinders, and popped her on my tongue. Grainy, in case you were wondering, but it didn’t feel wrong, it felt completely right. I laughed out loud at myself and the ludicrous situation. And then, just like that, my nerves disappeared.I know this sounds batshit, but it made complete sense to me. After all, quite a lot of people think they are eating the body of Christ on a weekly basis, and at least this way I really could say I took herwith meon stage that night, back on the boards where she belonged.When I told a widow at the party afterwards what I had done, her eyes widened in recognition and she whispered urgently, “I do that, too!”View image in fullscreenRigg in The Avengers circa 1965.Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyThe difference is, she didn’t talk about it.No one talks about it.It’s secret animal behaviour and, let’s face it, most people do a lot worse in private. It’s just they keep shtumm. But it felt much more important to tell the truth – and I love feeling that some of her is on stage with me. She had refused to retire, after all, and this was my way of enabling her to keep on trucking.I have done the same on every first night since then. As the five-minute call hits the PA before every press night, I open the tube – which I have become adept at – stick my finger in and whatever is collected goes in my gob. Some people listen to music before going on; some do press-ups. I eat the last vestiges of my mother. She was on stage with me on the opening night of Noël Coward’s Private Lives in 2023. Just knowing she was there gave me the confidence to play the part that night, to be joyful, to “Go Fly My Girl”, as she used to write in my first-night cards.double quotation markShe’d have adored going on to the Hampstead theatre stage with me. She’s even been back to Broadway, babyShe’d have adored going on to the Hampstead theatre stage with me when I played Sarah Siddons in The Divine Mrs S, a play about the 18th-century actor whose revolutionary realism in performance caused her audiences to scream and faint. Ma used to quote Siddons to me. She’d say, “If it can be found in nature, I know it can be played” so of course she’d want to be with me under the spotlights as I said those exact words. Before the opening night of Giant at the Royal Court in 2024, the smash hit show about Roald Dahl’s antisemitism in which I played his wife, Felicity Crosland, to John Lithgow’s Roald, once more I nibbled on a crumb. I can’t not do it these days, even though there is hardly anything left; it’s the thought that counts.She’s even been back to Broadway, baby. When Giant transferred to New York in March this year, my mother came with me. Oh, there’s no business like show business, and there was one terrible night when I returned to my dressing room post-show to find there had been a huge leak in the roof above my chair and everything was sopping wet. My first thought was,Oh no,Mother’s gone mushy!But in fact the outside of the tube was only a little damp and inside was bone dry.Love is animal, and grief is certainly so. Dogs sniff bums by way of greeting; my mum bit mine on a regular basis and said as much on national television. “I sink my teeth into her flesh! I bury my nose in her stomach!” she declared to a bemused Michael Parkinson. Isn’t that sort of the same thing, and is it really so strange of me to put my mother, whence I came, back in the same mouth she formed in utero? It is my own act of faith. “Ashes to ashes, funk to funky,” as Bowie wrote. “I’ve loved all I’ve needed, love. Sordid details following … ”Love made cannibals of us both. Despite a widow seeing the sense in my actions, judging by the looks on the faces of most people I tell, few others are in agreement. Reactions vary from sour lemon-sucking grimaces to downright disgust. Despite this, I will not be persuaded to give up the habit. I will die on the hill of my ash-eating, and to any who question my sanity, I reply, “It is natural! I’m sure it is, really! I promise I’m not going mad. It’s what she would havewanted!”All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsRachael StirlingDiana RiggBereavementCelebrityShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Content: Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/ReutersView image in fullscreenAftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/ReutersUkraineTrump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructureLuke HardingSun 11 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consultingVolodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia andUkraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it ifVladimir Putindid the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath on Sunday of a Russian strike on Kharkiv that hit residential homes.Photograph: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy/ReutersThere was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he waslifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraineneeded a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.Map of Ukraine with Russian advances and territoryResponding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, whenTrump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.The Financial Times, citing officials inEurope, reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.The New York Timeshas reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors,the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.View image in fullscreenMedics help a woman injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine on Saturday after overnight strikes.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAOn Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered dronesRead moreThe head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee,Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by theTrump administration– would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official toldthe Kyiv Independent newspaper.On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing StreetsaidBurnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.Luke Harding’sBetrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquestis published by Guardian FaberExplore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyyVladimir PutinJared KushnerUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict
Author: William Christou
Headline: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict
Content: Dust and debris inside King Khalid international airport after Saturday’s attack.Photograph: Social media/ReutersView image in fullscreenDust and debris inside King Khalid international airport after Saturday’s attack.Photograph: Social media/ReutersSaudi ArabiaRiyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities sayUnidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflictAnalysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategyWilliam Christouin JerusalemSun 11 Oct 2026 18.28 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.In a post on X, the British embassy inSaudi Arabiaadvised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”The Iran-allied Houthisclaimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300–the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.Regional mapIn response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.Aftermath of strike on Riyadh’s international airportThe Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.View image in fullscreenPeople outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday.Photograph: APIt would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.View image in fullscreenHouthi supporters rally in Sana’a on Friday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAThe Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum | Brexit | The Guardian
description: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled
Content: Andy Burnham: ‘We haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham: ‘We haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesBrexitAndy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendumPM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddledAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum fromRussia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote.The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week.
