Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.”He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”The UK is developing a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt hostile state information campaigns aimed at undermining British democracy. Downing Street said it was working with Germany on a new partnership to counter hybrid threats, including hostile activities that threaten both countries’ security and prosperity.A spokesperson said: “National security is the first duty of any government – we are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.“We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies.“We will continue to leave no stone unturned in our efforts to protect the UK from harm.”Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourRussiaEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Failure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report finds | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: In first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisis
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: In first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisis
Content: The report said the tagging system was ‘performing poorly and failing to meet demand’.Photograph: Stocksolutions/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe report said the tagging system was ‘performing poorly and failing to meet demand’.Photograph: Stocksolutions/AlamyPrisons and probationFailure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report findsIn first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisisJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 5,000 offenders went unmonitored in the first half of the year because probation staff failed to install electronic tags, while 1,600 tags had no signal for more than two weeks due to faults, a report has found.The Institute for Government (IfG) has revealed the full scale of the crisis in the probation system inEnglandand Wales, concluding that “rationing probation supervision” due to a lack of staff meant sentences imposed by the court had become “essentially a fiction” for most offenders.Once the 2026SentencingAct – which reduces the release point for many sentences – is fully implemented, most offenders will spend the final third of their sentence on licence without any active supervision, the report said.“This risks further undermining public trust in the criminal justice system and making sentences even more convoluted and opaque, including to victims,” the report by the independent thinktank found.UK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been taggedRead moreCassia Rowland, the associate director at the institute and author of the report, said: “It’s hard to set out just how demoralised and unhappy a lot of probation staff are. They feel everything is really chaotic, all of these changes are being flung on to them, they’re worried about their personal safety and the public protection risk of the people they’re managing.”She added: “The sentences courts are imposing are having less and less relevance to the time people are actually serving. The situation we’ve reached now is if you get given a six-year sentence, you’re most likely going to be spending two years in prison, two years on probation and then two years with conditions that no one is monitoring or enforcing. That’s just not a six-year sentence.”The report’s most scathing criticisms of the Probation Service included the electronic tagging of offenders, which the report found was “performing poorly and failing to meet demand”.Between January and April, more than 5,000 people who should have been monitored were not tagged, equating to 15% of all people with an electronic tagging order.Almost 1,600 people were wearing a tag that did not send a signal to the monitoring system for two weeks due to technical faults or the device not being charged.The report highlighted how issues of this kind meant that not a single probation delivery unit inspected in 2024 or 2025 received a rating above “requires improvement”, and two-thirds were rated “inadequate”.View image in fullscreenOffenders leaving HMP Brixton as part of the early release scheme on 1 October.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesThe report, based on public data and interviews with frontline staff, found as well as the increased risk to public safety, prisoners were also being let down, with little action taken to reduce reoffending rates.“People have told me stories of referring prisoners on to substance misuse programmes and their sentence ends before they reach the front of the waiting list. The system is not functioning to try to help people,” Rowland said.The report urged the government to increase the number of probation workers at a steady pace, and reintroduce home detention to help manage the prison population.It also called for a sentencing model that is “transparent and understandable”, and which explicitly sets out time in prison and time supervised in the community, with no licence periods without supervision.The report praised Keir Starmer’s government for taking steps to stabilise the prison population, but said this work may have been “undone” by Andy Burnham, whoannounced a number of exemptions to the early release schemeafter public backlash.At the start of October,the first 700 of an expected 4,500 criminals were released early from prisonas part of emergency measures brought in with facilities just months away from reaching maximum capacity.Some said they expected to quickly return to prison as they had nowhere to live and would breach their licence conditions. The IfG report said administrative recalls for issues not relating to a new offence had “skyrocketed” in recent years.The government said all released offenders would be subject to strict monitoring, including the expansion of electronic tagging, but significant concerns have been raised about whether the overstretched Probation Service will be able to cope.“Tagging more people is also likely to substantially increase the workload for probation practitioners, when they are already short-staffed and struggling,” the report found.Rowland said: “This absolutely raises alarm bells. It’s very frustrating because victims are being made promises which potentially the system can’t meet.”A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a justice system in crisis after years of underinvestment and are taking the steps needed to fix it. This government is overseeing the biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring in British history, making record investment into the Probation Service and community punishment, and recruiting thousands of new probation officers.“We are pulling every lever to better protect victims and tagging is just one tool we use to keep the public safe. Offenders can face being housed in approved premises, curfews, mandatory meeting with probation officers, no contact orders, requirements on where to live and the threat of immediate recall to prison.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceSentencingCrimeEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece
Content: US secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conductSenior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to GreeceAssociated PressSun 11 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.Trump donor accuses ‘grifter’ Kimberly Guilfoyle of $100,000 quid pro quoRead moreThe official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsDonald TrumpMarco RubioUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote  | Green party | The Guardian
description: Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article
Content: Polanski also questions whether parties should seek to define what members believe.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolanski also questions whether parties should seek to define what members believe.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockGreen partyZack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism voteRapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian articleZack Polanski: How we’re transforming British politicsAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism.TheGreen partyleader has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation.Writing for the Guardianafter his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion.Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week.He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.”Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction.“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes.His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members.Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged.The controversy intensified last weekend when 1,022 members representing about 0.4% of the party’s total membership voted in favour of a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state.The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution.Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the party must not become vulnerable tocapture by extremists and racists, arguing the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise its policymaking structures.Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.“This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.15:19Did the Zionism row lose it for Zack Polanski? | Politics Weekly“At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up withidentity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.“There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel andPalestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.”The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future.The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership.The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiByelectionsJudaismPalestineIsraelGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City  | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling
Content: Andy Burnham said last month he would be ‘really concerned’ if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said last month he would be ‘really concerned’ if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester CityMove comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach rulingPress AssociationSun 11 Oct 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings withManchester Cityin his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, had urged the prime minister to publish everything related to his work with the club asGreater Manchestermayor and the Liberal Democrats wrote to him asking him to release minutes of meetings and declare all hospitality gifts received from owners of Manchester City.City has been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club has maintained its innocence and appealed against the verdict.Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment was serious and that where wrongdoing was established, those responsible should face the consequences.Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday.He said “the football issues are different from the investment issues”.“But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do.“I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.“None of it is recent … in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting … and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there.“But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.”The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd, which owned the club.The shadow sports minister, Louie French, called for Burnham to also “come clean” about any meetings since becoming prime minister and urged Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, to respond to questions.“The prime minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into No 10, the prime minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamManchester CityManchesterLabourGreater ManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Content: Liquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety effortsKanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangersRobert BoothandDan MilmoSun 11 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCompanies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs anAI safety research body, has warned there is a“50% chance”of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has beensignedby leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.View image in fullscreenThe UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesIn one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Fridayrevealedthat when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturdaycalled forAI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Kanishka NarayanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wildlife park confirms tiger will not be euthanised after man mauled to death | Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband, whose constituency includes the park, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on Saturday
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Ed Miliband, whose constituency includes the park, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on Saturday
Content: The park confirmed the tiger, named Altai, was ‘safe and well and will not be euthanised’ after the incident.Photograph: Yorkshire Wildlife Park/SWNSView image in fullscreenThe park confirmed the tiger, named Altai, was ‘safe and well and will not be euthanised’ after the incident.Photograph: Yorkshire Wildlife Park/SWNSYorkshireWildlife park confirms tiger will not be euthanised after man mauled to deathEd Miliband, whose constituency includes the park, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on SaturdayNeha GohilSun 11 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA wildlife park in Yorkshire has confirmed the tiger thatmauled to death a man who entered its enclosurewill not be euthanised.A man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, located nearDoncaster, before police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday.South Yorkshire police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury” and despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the “tragic incident” and said their “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” remained with the family of the man who lost his life.“The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” the statement read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised” after the incident.View image in fullscreenYorkshire Wildlife Park was closed on Sunday.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSThe foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North,Ed Miliband, said he was “deeply saddened” and sent his “thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died”.“I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,” Miliband added.One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was “happily enjoying” his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him.“The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,” the post read.“He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.”Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was “frightening and confusing” when the park was evacuated after the incident.She said: “At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go.“The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.”The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. “As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,” she said. “We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.”SouthYorkshirepolice said the man’s family was made aware of the incident on Saturday and were being supported by specialist officers. The force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online.Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.Explore more on these topicsYorkshireEd MilibandDoncasterSouth YorkshireZoosnewsShareReuse this content

title: People smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis? | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
Content: People run away from teargas fired by police as they try to cross the Channel from Petit-Fort-Philippe in Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople run away from teargas fired by police as they try to cross the Channel from Petit-Fort-Philippe in Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersImmigration and asylumPeople smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis?As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomesDiane TaylorSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time.“I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.”The wind has dropped, the waves are flat and there are no French police in sight. The conditions are perfect as the smuggler rushes everyone into the dinghy as it moves away from the shore.Amad is one of several asylum speakers who spoke to the Guardian this week from the area of northernFranceknown as the Jungle. They were hoping to cross the Channel to the UK in the next few days.“This place is busier than ever,” says another asylum seeker, Omar, from Yemen. “So many refugees and so many smugglers are here. Everyone wants to cross.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers stand guard on the beach in Petit-Fort-Philippe, Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersSome who have already been forcibly removed from the UK are hoping to return. They were sent to France under the“one in, one out” scheme, where one small-boat arrival is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK.Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?Read moreNow, after moving approximately 1,500 people in both directions across the Channel, the scheme has been brought to an end. Beset with problems, itcould not be effectively scaled up, the British government concluded.NGOs working on the ground with asylum seekers in northern France were unsurprised by the outcome and say the end of “one in, one out” must prompt a wider discussion about how to deal with the crisis in the Channel.The UK government has shown little sign it is contemplating a radical shift in attitude. A Home Office spokesperson pointed the Guardian to anannouncementabout a refugee resettlement scheme that is likely to assist only a few hundred refugees a year and is highly unlikely to stop people crossing the Channel in small boats.The spokesperson said: “Just last week, the home secretary announced the reopening of the UK resettlement scheme for new referrals, providing genuine refugees with a safe and legal route to the UK.”The agencies calling for a different approach hope at least to expand the parameters of the debate.View image in fullscreenPeople sit inside a bus at the port of Calais after three people including a child died while attempting to cross the Channel on 28 September.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersAccording to workers in the Jungle, living conditions there are appalling. Those at Utopia 56, which witnesses police interventions on French beaches where asylum seekers try to board dinghies, say that since the UK increased its funding to France earlier this year on a payment-by-results basis, police violence against migrants has increased significantly.Utopia 56 estimates a 40% increase in police violence from April to August 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. That coincided with an agreement for the UK to pay France£660mover three years to ramp up “stop the boats” initiatives.Sophie McCann, of Médecins Sans Frontières UK, said: “The government’s increasingly brutal efforts to stop people trying to reach the UK by boat are failing. MSF’s medical and mental health teams in Calais and Dunkirk witness the serious physical and psychological harm caused by violence and harassment meted out by French police, largely funded by the UK, on people who have already fled war, persecution and extreme hardship.“People will continue to risk their lives crossing the Channel in search of safety in the UK until the government provides safe and accessible routes.”The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union, which has manyHome Officestaff among its members, has worked with the refugee charity Care4Calais to draw up a blueprint to introduce a refugee visa-to-travel scheme for asylum seekers to travel legally to the UK.The plan would still require asylum claims to be considered on merit and for those whose claims are rejected to be removed from the UK. But they say it would eliminate people smugglers from the equation and save lives. According to the UN’s International Organization forMigration(IMO), at least 225 people have died while trying to cross the Channel since 2018.View image in fullscreenPeople gather after disembarking from a French rescue ship after their boat was caught in the Channel at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 4 August.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/GettyThe scheme would be unlikely to halt irregular arrivals entirely, but Care4Calais says it could dent the smugglers’ business in a way that other initiatives have failed to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCharlotte Khan, of Care4Calais, said: “Consecutive governments have focused on border security measures that have only made Channel crossings more dangerous, resulting in a shocking number of lives lost, while completely ignoring the only solution that will work – safe routes.”The PCS general secretary, Fran Heathcote, called for safe routes to be significantly scaled up. “Our members deal with the human impact of the asylum system on a daily basis and their voices must be heard. The only way to truly undermine criminal smuggling gangs is to remove the demand through a Ukrainian-style visa system, allowing people fleeing war and persecution to travel safely and legally to claim asylum.”The Labour government has arguably made more efforts than any other to try to prevent asylum seekers from reaching the UK in small boats.Previously, people travelled less visibly, in the backs of lorries or on planes, and so attracted less public attention. Images of black dinghies overcrowded with people in orange lifejackets, monetised for social media clicks by far-right agitators, have generated mounting hostility from some who say they are evidence that the government has lost control of its borders.View image in fullscreenA group of people thought to be migrants are brought to a marina in Gosport by the RNLI after a small boat incident in the Channel.Photograph: Trevor Adams/PABut desperate people continue to clamber into dinghies. In the six days between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 peoplearrivedin 23 boats. Along with the now terminated “one in, one out” pilot, which government trumpeted as“groundbreaking”when it announced it in July 2025, the Home Office and the National Crime Agency make regular announcements about smugglers being intercepted and dinghies seized “upstream”.There has been a reduction of more than 40% in small boat arrivals so far this year compared with the same period last year, probably due to a combination of UK government initiatives, windy weather and a drop in irregular migration to Europe overall. According to data published by the IMO, there has beena 39% reductionthis year in these arrivals to Europe – from 98,040 during the same period last year to approximately 60,000.Despite the reduction in arrivals, far-right agitators wearing masks and black paramilitary clothing continue to protest on the streets and try to block small boat arrivals.View image in fullscreenPeople protest against small boats arriving in Gosport near Portsmouth.Photograph: Solent NewsNone of the policy roadblocks appear to have dented the resolve of asylum seekers who want to reach the UK.Two people die trying to cross Channel as anti-migrant protesters clash with police in GosportRead moreSohrab, from Afghanistan, has been sleeping on the streets of Paris and is making his way to the Jungle. “I want to live and I will do anything to save my life from death,” he says. “I have already spent a bad day in jail in France after police caught me trying to get into a lorry heading for the UK. The smugglers are very violent, but there is no other way for me to reach the UK apart than to go to the Jungle.”Despite the failure of “one in, one out” to deter small boat crossings, Emily Graham, of the Future Governance Forum, believes it is the way forward.“The ‘one-in, one-out’ pilot proved cooperation based on responsibility-sharing is right in principle and has the potential to deliver results,” she said. “To reduce the number of people arriving by small boat, the government should build on the previous pilot and seek a new ‘routes for returns’ deal with European partners.”Amad has another idea. “We would much prefer to give our money to the UK government if they allowed us to come here legally, rather than to the smugglers,” he says. “No asylum seeker would pay smugglers who beat and exploit them, or risk our lives on a dinghy, if there was another way.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceMigrationRefugeesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security | UK news | The Guardian
description: Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains
Content: Jamie Burrows, the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union, says there are multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.Photograph: National Farmers' UnionView image in fullscreenJamie Burrows, the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union, says there are multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.Photograph: National Farmers' UnionUK news‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food securityFood producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chainsJoanna PartridgeSun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says.Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop.But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel –has almost doubledsince theconflict in Iranbegan in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period.British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’Read more“Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.”These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during theUK’s hottest summer on record, which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according toofficial production estimates.Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply.Food experts, academics, businesses and thepublic spending watchdog, the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient.The climate crisis, this year’shuge El Niño weather pattern, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks areall considered threatsto food chain security.View image in fullscreenFarmers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesAmid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply.MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment,Foodand Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses.Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours.Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously.The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’sPreparewebsite outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking.Britons kept in dark about scale of climate crisis, say viewers of ‘first-of-its-kind’ emergency briefingRead moreDespite this,a recent warningfrom more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency.“Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter.These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa.Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPALang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway.The UK governmentwound up the strategic food stockpilethat had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”.He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand. They’re looking at their own local production and some countries have strategic stores of grain.”Mother of one Ana, 42, is one of asmall but growing number of citizenswho have been preparing for possible future emergencies for some time. Now living in south Wales, she is originally from eastern Europe and grew up in a family that grew food and preserved it for the colder months. She now shares tips on herYouTube channel, advising other households on resilience and how to build an emergency stockpile.View image in fullscreenAna shares tips on her YouTube channel, advising other households on building resilience and creating an emergency stockpile.Photograph: supplied“It’s just a normal way of life, basically safeguarding yourself and your family,” she says. Ana describes herself as a “prepper”, but wants to move away from its negative connotations, such as panic buying or being a survivalist.“The stereotype was … that preparedness is American, really weird, all camo and blokes in the bushes, hunting and eating squirrels and mushrooms,” she says. Instead she wants to help other citizens learn how they could cope for a few hours, days or even weeks without power, water or being able to get to the shops.“If the stereotype had been dispersed originally by the government, then people would look at preparedness as an everyday thing,” she says.Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic vegetable box delivery company Riverford, believes the UK’s food supply chain needs a “very complicated rethink and a different vision for future security”.Devon-based Riverford distributes about 65,000 boxes a week to customers and about 70% of the produce it sells is grown in the UK, although it also has long-term relationships with growers in Spain and Italy.While the UK is always going to import fruit such as bananas, which cannot be grown in large volumes domestically, Haward believes consumers can also play a role by returning to eating more seasonally.Haward says longer-term contracts can help farmers, giving them confidence to invest in their land and what they grow. He adds: “There are different ways we can try to create a food and farming sector different to now and much more resilient to the future world,” such as working to restore soils to better withstand the changing climate. He also wants government to “pull levers” such as offering lower business rates to greengrocers.Explore more on these topicsUK newsFood & drink industryFarmingRural affairsFoodSupply chain crisisEmergency planningfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Enough of this suffering!’ Joana Vasconcelos on why she is fed up with women’s art defined by pain | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The Portuguese artist is famous for her monumental ceramic wedding cakes and gigantic chandeliers made of tampons. So why is a new show in Lisbon pairing her with Valentino’s size-zero catwalk dresses?
Author: Dale Berning Sawa
Headline: The Portuguese artist is famous for her monumental ceramic wedding cakes and gigantic chandeliers made of tampons. So why is a new show in Lisbon pairing her with Valentino’s size-zero catwalk dresses?
Content: ‘I work at a level of detail that resonates with the fashion world’ … Venus – Valentino Garavani Through the Eyes of Joana Vasconcelos.Photograph: Bruno Lopes/Courtesy EDP Foundation/ MAATView image in fullscreen‘I work at a level of detail that resonates with the fashion world’ … Venus – Valentino Garavani Through the Eyes of Joana Vasconcelos.Photograph: Bruno Lopes/Courtesy EDP Foundation/ MAATArt and design‘Enough of this suffering!’ Joana Vasconcelos on why she is fed up with women’s art defined by painThe Portuguese artist is famous for her monumental ceramic wedding cakes and gigantic chandeliers made of tampons. So why is a new show in Lisbon pairing her with Valentino’s size-zero catwalk dresses?Dale Berning SawaSun 11 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo interview the Portuguese artist Joana Vasconcelos is to jump on to a moving train. She is telling me why she uses needlework to make huge things: 15-metre doilies, say, or a tree 13.5 metres tall rustling with 150,000 hand-sewn leaves. “One day, I said to myself,” she says, “why not bring domestic detail into monumental sculpture? What do we know of works like this? OK, there’s Louise Bourgeois. But it wasn’t enormous. She worked in detail but on small things. There’s the beauty of Niki de Saint Phalle. But it’s always papier mache – a technique that’s very simple, very practical, but not chic.”It takes a certain something to compare yourself to these two French giantesses of art. It takes something else to castigate Bourgeois and de Saint Phalle for not being big, bold and beautiful enough. But if there’s one female contemporary artist who can do it without coming across as delusional, it’s Vasconcelos. Born in Paris in 1971 into an artistic Portuguese family, Vasconcelos has established herself as one of her country’s leading contemporary artists – and one of the world’s most ambitious.View image in fullscreen‘Why not bring domestic detail into monumental sculpture’ … Joana Vasconcelos on her larger-than-life artwork.Photograph: Kenton ThatcherIn dimension and scale, her work recalls male monumentalists like Jeff Koons, Christo or Takashi Murakami. Representing Portugal at the 2005 Venice Biennale, she showed, among other works, The Bride, a six-metre-tall chandelier made of 14,000 tampons. On Valentine’s Day 2019, the city of Paris installed her Coeur de Paris at the Porte de Clignancourt: a giant revolving heart on a pole nine metres tall, tiled red and blinking with thousands of LEDs. Elsewhere, she’s made a 12-metre high ceramic wedding cake with a built-in water feature (currently on view at Waddesdon Manor in Aylesbury), an eight-metre tall engagement ring of 110 golden car rims and 1,450 crystal whisky glasses (recently installed in Atlético FC’s home stadium), and three-metre tall stilettos, of stainless steel pots, called Marilyn.“I work on the macro with the micro,” she says. Her greatest strength, says João Pinharanda, the director of Lisbon’s Museum ofArt, Architecture and Technology (MAAT), is the way her work speaks “very simply” but also “very loudly”.I have come to MAAT because Vasconcelos is installing Venus, a two-person exhibition that puts her creations in dialogue with Italian fashion legend Valentino, as part of the museum’s 10th anniversary celebrations. Each of her works on show is absolutely OTT: riotous in colour, quite preposterously decorative, the size not of a person but a room. Older pieces include Marilyn, Garden of Eden (an immersive Chartres-inspired maze of plastic flowers) and Independent Heart #3 (another giant version of a traditional Heart of Viana, made of red plastic cutlery). Venus Valkyrie, one of the newer works, stems from her long-running series of giddily abstract hanging installations named after the Norse warrior goddesses that, she insists, “fly over the battlefield together”. “Wagner got it wrong,” she says, “making them so militaristic and macho. I decided I’d make them the way they’re supposed to be made: grandiose, monumental, but also soft and refined and beautiful.”View image in fullscreenMarilyn is made up of stainless steel pans and lids.Photograph: © DMF/Atelier Joana VasconcelosOne of the things that irks her in the work of her female predecessors and contemporaries is their focus on pain. She recalls going to see the Tracey Emin show at Tate Modern earlier this year. “I thought, ‘Damn, you’re in pain, all the time!’ Speaking with a collector friend afterwards I said, ‘It’s good, but enough of this suffering!’“I’ve had enough. For women to be able to express themselves, does it have to be through suffering? We’re not depressed all the time! All these generations before us rightly fought for women’s freedoms, but always through criticism. It’s important to show it can be done in another way, through joie de vivre,” she says dressed head to toe in Issey Miyake in grey-blue with a yellow squiggle, an orange Miu Miu on her shoulder, silvery tabi trainers on her feet, double earrings, chunky beads, big rings, bigger smile.“One day, in time, I too will fall into art history, I too will be a reference as all these artists are, but at least people will look at this era with a certain joy.”View image in fullscreenMacro with the micro: Vasconcelos’ Solitaire ring at MAAT LisbonPhotograph: Vitor Miranda/AlamyThe fact that Vasconcelos so frequently expresses her joy through partnerships with big corporations and luxe fashion houses (Dior, Marina Rinaldi) has, for many, uncomfortably blurred lines. In 2012, as the first woman to be invited to do a solo show at the Palace of Versailles, Vasconcelos covered a Bell 47 helicopter in gold leaf, Swarowski crystals and blush, plush ostrich feathers, decking out the interior with gilding, wood carving and embroidered upholstery. When art critic Bárbara Borges de Campos saw it in 2019, she decried its materials list as “indefensible,” and Vasconcelos herself, as “the symbol of a disengaged generation”.Such criticism risks overlooking how much of Vasconcelos’s work is grounded in the value of women’s labour. She made the Valkyrie Venus with her own team, by hand. Journalists visiting her 3,400-sq metre dockside studio often describe it as the biggest they can think of, but it is also one of the most populous, staffed by 60 people. Some seamstresses have been with her since the early 1990s. Their section has floor-to-ceiling storage for every kind of wool, thread, button, bead, marker, fabric and cotton, and a big open-floor section reaching up two storeys so that the largest hanging pieces can be worked on from the top.“When Valentino came to visit my studio, he really appreciated what I’m doing because he understood I’m as crazy as he is – because he could see I work at a level of detail that resonates with the fashion world,” she says. The work itself shows where their paths diverge. The Valkyrie Venus frames multiple catwalk dresses, their size-zero dimensions as inescapably highlighted as if Vasconcelos had circled them in fluorescent strip lighting. “These are small dresses, made in small spaces for small bodies. It’s quite practical. If this were for someone like me, you see,” she laughs, “it would take a lot more time … ”View image in fullscreen‘He understood I’m as crazy as he is’: Vasconcelos next to a Valentino dress at VenusPhotograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesVasconcelos’s work knowingly bulges over the line between refined and cheap. She makes fake flowers glow, dresses ceramic animals in crocheted skins, turns car lights into jewels, and some works feel more edgy than others. In MAAT’s permanent collection, her 2005 piece, Passerelle, features mass-produced ceramic dogs (of the kind you see in suburban gardens) hanging by their leashes from a conveyor belt. Each time a visitor sets it in motion, the dogs clank against each other and slowly break apart, the shards accumulating in a pile on the floor.Early in her career, Vasconcelos decided that to liberate women from the domestic, the beauty and skill of that space needed to be taken out of drawers and shown to be as strong as the industrial. At one point during our interview, three older ladies walk up, with a kind of blushing in their voices, and Vasconcelos, who has been talking to me in French, instantly switches to Italian. “Ciao! Come va? Bene?” she asks. They nod, “Bellissimo! Spettacolare! Complimenti, complimenti.” This isn’t just fawning. If anyone recognises where Vasconcelos got specific motifs and techniques from in this particular Valkyrie, it’s them: they are some of Valentino’s so-calledpetites mains, the seamstresses and master needleworkers who labour in haute-couture ateliers crafting by hand the wearables designers dream up.“They travelled here with the dresses,” she says of the women after they’ve left. “You see, from them to me, there is a change. Women before were like that – imprisoned behind men, doing extraordinary things without being highlighted. I say, enough of being held back. We’re going to do like Richard Serra, bam! Huge! Monumental!”Venus – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelosis at Lisbon’s Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology until 22 February 2027Explore more on these topicsArt and designExhibitionsArtSculpturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino’s West End play The Popinjay Cavalier | Stage | The Guardian
description: The production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage, which he will also direct
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage, which he will also direct
Content: Director Quentin Tarantino and actor Sacha Baron Cohen, who will star in the film-maker’s stage debut, The Popinjay Cavalier, on the West End.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenDirector Quentin Tarantino and actor Sacha Baron Cohen, who will star in the film-maker’s stage debut, The Popinjay Cavalier, on the West End.Photograph: APStageSacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino’s West End play The Popinjay CavalierThe production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage,  which he will also directPress AssociationSun 11 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSacha Baron Cohen will headlineQuentin Tarantino’s play The Popinjay Cavalierwhen it premieres on the West End in London in March 2027.The production marks the Hollywood director’s first work written for the stage – which he will also direct.Premiering at the Phoenix theatre in London’sWest Endon 18 March 2027, tickets go on sale on Monday.Tarantino, 63, who is best known for films including Reservoir Dogs, Pulp Fiction and Once Upon A Time In Hollywood, said he was “keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out”.Please take your seats, the carnage is about to begin: what will Quentin Tarantino’s West End debut look like?Read moreA popinjay is defined as “a vain, foppish or conceited person”, while a cavalier is a cavalryman or courteous gentleman.Baron Cohen added: “Quentin called, I said yes before he even got to say his first ‘motherfucker’. When the best director in the world calls, you don’t ask questions. I am beyond delighted that we will be losing our West End virginity together. I have made him promise not to be gentle.”Set in 1830s Europe, The Popinjay Cavalier has been billed as a “rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen”.It was inspired by the classic swashbuckler genre of old Hollywood, including the writings of George Bruce, Ernst Vajda and Jesse Lasky Jr.Full casting will be announced at a later date.Sony Pictures Entertainment and Sonia Friedman Productions are producing the play.Tom Rothman, the chairman and chief executive of Sony Pictures Entertainment’s Motion Picture Group, and Friedman, said: “It is a joy and an honour to be developing this play with Quentin – and obviously quite an adventure. How lucky we are that one of the great storytellers of our time has chosen to make his theatrical debut.“To see Quentin in action in a rehearsal room is extraordinary. His delight in working with actors, fencers, acrobats, musicians and our creative team is infectious, and there is such pleasure in hearing his delicious language come alive and discovering what his world can become on stage.“And now we haveSacha Baron Cohenat the heart of it all: a fearless, brilliantly inventive actor with the wit, mischief and daring this role demands. We feel immensely fortunate to be producing this show. Audiences are in for a tremendous treat.”Tarantino made his directorial debut in 1992 with Reservoir Dogs, before co-writing, directing and acting in Pulp Fiction, which saw him pick up his first Oscar for best screenplay.He went on to direct Jackie Brown, Kill Bill Volume 1 and Volume 2, Death Proof, Inglourious Basterds, Django Unchained, The Hateful Eight, and Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood.Throughout his career he has won two Academy Awards, two Baftas and four Golden Globes. He has also been nominated for an Emmy and five Grammys.Meanwhile Baron Cohen is best known for creating and playing comic characters including Ali G, Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard.The 54-year-old has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys. He has not yet had a leading role in a major stage production. He trained with the French clown guru Philippe Gaulier.Tarantino first revealed his plans to stage a play in 2025, saying on the Church of Tarantino podcast it was “all written”.“I’m preparing for it to be a success. If it’s a flop, I’ll be done very quickly,” he said.Tickets for The Popinjay Cavalier are on sale from 9am BST on Monday to those who signed up for priority access, with a public sale from 12pm.Tickets start at £25, with more than 16,000 tickets priced at under £50 across the run.Explore more on these topicsStageSacha Baron CohenQuentin TarantinoTheatreWest EndLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Party review – this pacey, perfectly cast thriller is enormous fun | Television | The Guardian
description: Sarah Soleman’s adaptation of Elizabeth Day’s bestseller is hugely moreish – it leaves you absolutely desperate to find out more about the mystery at its heart
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Sarah Soleman’s adaptation of Elizabeth Day’s bestseller is hugely moreish – it leaves you absolutely desperate to find out more about the mystery at its heart
Content: Betrayals major and minor … Lucy (Sarah Solemani) and Martin (Luke Evans) in The Party.Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsView image in fullscreenBetrayals major and minor … Lucy (Sarah Solemani) and Martin (Luke Evans) in The Party.Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Party review – this pacey, perfectly cast thriller is enormous funSarah Soleman’s adaptation of Elizabeth Day’s bestseller is hugely moreish – it leaves you absolutely desperate to find out more about the mystery at its heartLucy ManganSun 11 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImagine going to a huge party in a country pile stuffed with posh Tory MPs. Now imagine being massively pregnant and unable to drink. Now imagine that the party is “Victorian freak show” themed, because the hostess thought that would be even more fun. Such is the situation Lucy Gilmour (Sarah Solemani) finds herself in at the beginning of The Party, Solemani’s adaptation ofElizabeth Day’s 2017 bestsellerof the same name.When you learn that a gun has gone off, your first thought may well be that this can only improve matters. At the very least, the circus troupe will probably decline to perform further, and I believe even posh people have to stop conga-ing to 80s hits once the police show up. Like most of us, I’d be tempted to fire the gun into the air myself.But this is a five-part thriller, so Lucy does not shoot out the nearest chandelier and go home to bed with a packet of Hobnobs. Instead, we get a lavishly and lovingly constructed millefeuille of gloriously hateful characters, flashbacks to various points in their histories, youthful mistakes, betrayals major and minor, outright skulduggery, the odd bag of cocaine, a spot of sexual assault, some simmering class resentment, some homosexuality, some eating disorders, loyalties fraying and Douglas Hodge. His role is to occasionally march on as a bloated paterfamilias in the 1990s flashbacks, take his guests round the gun-stuffed Stable of Foreshadowing and teach them how to kill pheasants.View image in fullscreenGloriously hateful … hosts Ben (Tom Cullen) and Serena (Lydia Leonard).Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsWe open with political journalist Martin (Luke Evans), husband of Lucy and best friend of charismatic host Ben Fitzmaurice (Tom Cullen), being interviewed in a bloodstained shirt by the police. The trained eye can tell Martin has been heavily involved in whatever went down.We then spool back to the party to begin unravelling the mystery. Characters and relationships are swiftly established, plot seeds are sown with a lavish hand and a multitude of secrets are briskly hinted at. Within a very few minutes, the audience is baited on about 30 hooks and going nowhere.The leader of the Tory party resigns. News reaches the revellers, who immediately start hiving off into factions and plotting their next moves. Martin and Ben take a brief break to indulge in some homoerotic wrestling, which ends when Ben gives Martin a lock of Phoebe’s hair. Who Phoebe? Why hair? Phoebe dead? Phoebe when? Whoever she is, it breaks the mood and the men go back to working out how Ben can best take advantage of the coming leadership contest.Their old schoolfriend-slash-mortal-enemy, Jarvis, is said to be preparing to run. But! He has a property scandal about to blow. Could Martin possibly have a word with him and suggest that now is perhaps not the time? It would be so bad for the Tories. Ben is thinking only of the party (political, not house, though he is eager to get back to the latter due to his chronic extroversion, for which modern medicine has alas yet to find a cure).View image in fullscreenLittle Shadow … Jonathan Houlston as the young Martin Gilmour.Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsOff Martin dutifully goes. Martin dutifully going off to do Ben’s bidding is, we will learn, very much the pattern of their relationship. At school he was even nicknamed Little Shadow by Ben’s sister, Phoebe – aha! – and has been known, slightly effortfully, as LS by them all ever since. He must be the world’s most compromised political journalist. I hope no one ever finds out.There is an investigative journalist called Amara Baines at the party (house), which is what happens when you don’t vet people’s plus-ones properly. But I’m sure she won’t be so rude as to take advantage of the situation while she’s here.The Party is enormous fun: pacey, moreish, perfectly cast.Lindsay Duncanas Ben’s calmly furious grieving mother is a standout, but everyone is great – and the scene in which the women verbally eviscerate Jarvis’s fragile wife to help scupper his plans, like lions in beaded gowns gutting a gazelle, is exquisitely awful.There are a few moments when you think it’s about to go completely off the rails (the hologram of Phoebe singing in the family pile’s basement, created by her art college friends, foremost among them), but it never quite does, despite the enormous speed it builds up. There’s no one to root for, no one to invest in – they’re all absolutely awful, and you can just go along for the ride. (Lucy, the exception, remains a cipher.) Whose blood is on Martin’s shirt? Why is he in such thrall to the Fitzmaurices? Don’t know, don’t care, but just desperately want toknow. The story’s the thing and it’s a doozy.The Party is on ITVXExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewLindsay DuncanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Do we really ‘hold tension’ in our hips?  | Well actually | The Guardian
description: The idea is popular in wellness circles, but experts say there’s no evidence that trauma uniquely affects the hips. Here’s what causes hip tightness and what can help
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: The idea is popular in wellness circles, but experts say there’s no evidence that trauma uniquely affects the hips. Here’s what causes hip tightness and what can help
Content: Should tight hips make you question your mental health? Here’s what the experts say.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShould tight hips make you question your mental health? Here’s what the experts say.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyDo we really ‘hold tension’ in our hips?The idea is popular in wellness circles, but experts say there’s no evidence that trauma uniquely affects the hips. Here’s what causes hip tightness and what can helpKeren LandmanSun 11 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn yoga classes, on TikTok and throughout other wellness spaces, you’ve probably heard the saying: your hips hold tension. These joints have a reputation of being emotional storage units of sorts – but is it true that they are affected by old traumas and painful memories?Pain and muscle tension hit harder when you’re going through a difficult time. But should tight hips make you question your mental health? And what can you do to reduce hip tightness? Here’s what you need to know.Is there a connection between stress and hip tension?When you sense muscle tension in your body, it’s probably caused by one of two things.The first possibility is not clearly related to stress and involves muscles resisting stretch even when they’re relaxed. Stiffness like this is a mechanical property that reflects how your tissues are built and used.The other possibility is that your muscles and nerves are engaged in some low-level activity more often than they need to be; this does often happen when people are under psychological stress.Neither of these causes map cleanly on to what people actually feel, nor the anatomical location of the problem. For instance, when people refer to “tight hips”, they may be feeling pain, an unwanted pulling sensation or stiffness – and the sensation may be coming from the buttocks or the back rather than the hip.But there is no particular predisposition for a stress-tightness link in the hips. In fact, the evidence linking mental strain with musculoskeletal tension is strongest for the muscles of theshoulders,jawandpelvic floor. “There’s nothing special about the hip,” says Greg Lehman, a physiotherapist, chiropractor and biomechanics expert who teaches clinicians about pain science.People who have experienced trauma, especially in childhood, aremore likely to have chronic painand tend to be more sensitive to pain in lab tests. But again, there’s no evidence this is more true for the hips.What else can cause hip discomfort?Unpleasant sensations in the joint can arise from anatomical issues. For example, people withvery shallowor very deephip sockets tend to have more pain, says Abby Cheng, a sports medicine doctor who specializes in hip disorders at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis.Another anatomical cause is irritation in the tendons or their fluid-filled cushions on the outside the hip, called tendinitis or bursitis. It’s especially common inmiddle-aged and older women.Other causes are harder to pinpoint. Cheng and other clinicians believe that hip and back pain can be caused by muscles in the front of the hip that are shortened by sitting, as well as other imbalances in muscle strength and length. Having said that, studies haven’t conclusively linked short hip muscles to pain, and many other factors that accompany a sedentary lifestyle may contribute to hip discomfort in desk workers, says Lehman.View image in fullscreenMan with hip, back, spine and sciatica pain at home.Photograph: m-gucci/Getty ImagesOverall health may factor into hip discomfort. An anatomical problem can “nudge up your chance of having pain”, says Lehman, but stress, poor sleep, inactivity and anxiety often tip it over.Furthermore, how tight your muscles feeldoesn’treliablypredict how tight they actually are. Lehman sees it in the clinic: dancers complain of tight hamstrings, “and their foot is behind their head”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat can you do about tight hips?Start by moving more. If walking, gentle stretching and other exercise eases the tightness; it’s probably muscular and nothing dangerous, says Cheng. In these situations, she says, “motion is lotion”.Don’t stretch too aggressively, though. It’s possible to stretch too much, says Cheng, and going beyond the gentle range can hurt more than it helps, especially if your hip discomfort is related to hip socket depth. In that scenario, she says, “you’re really just banging two bones into each other.”Get regular aerobic exercise, and strength-train at least twice a week. For people with hip discomfort, Cheng focuses on glute-strengthening moves like clamshells and “monster walks”.
