These may help by increasing your hips’ ability to tolerate use, and they may also help you age better: in older adults, strength trainingincreases bone density in the hip, which lowers the risk of a dangerous hip fracture.Take steps to improve your health more broadly, which Lehman says can reduce your sensitivity to pain. Anything that makes you healthier helps, includingmeaningful activitiesandtime with friends, he says.When should you see a clinician?Get help if hip tightness doesn’t improve with more movement or gets worse the more you move, says Cheng. Look for a clinician who examines your whole body and asks about your stress and sleep.X-rays and MRIs can occasionally clarify the cause of your symptoms, but both experts said imaging typically doesn’t indicate where you hurt or point to the source of your discomfort. Structure is “not irrelevant, but it’s not destiny”, says Lehman.If discomfort lingers despite your best efforts, try to make peace with it. “It’s OK to look for a fix, but sometimes accepting some pain is easier,” says Lehman. “And then the irony is, it helps.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorMental healthHealthHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gareth Malone looks back: ‘After the Christmas No 1, I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The choir leader and presenter on not fitting in at his all-boys grammar, how synthesisers changed everything, and his ‘dithering’ start on TV
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The choir leader and presenter on not fitting in at his all-boys grammar, how synthesisers changed everything, and his ‘dithering’ start on TV
Content: FlashbackFamilyGareth Malone looks back: ‘After the Christmas No 1, I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber’The choir leader and presenter on not fitting in at his all-boys grammar, how synthesisers changed everything, and his ‘dithering’ start on TVHarriet GibsoneSun 11 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGareth Malone in 1990, and recreating the image in 2026Gareth Malone in 1990 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Grooming: Neusa Neves at Arlington Artists using Vieve. Archive image: courtesy of gareth maloneBorn in London in 1975,Gareth Maloneis a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence, as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude.For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace.I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours.Mum worked forAbbey LifeAssuranceand for the civil service.Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible.In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers.After graduating, Iwent back to Bournemouth.I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from.I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself.My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen you’re recognised it can be a great gift,but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. WhenMilitary Wives got to No 1, I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. People and community are.When I was 15 I had a clear vision of what I wanted with my adult life. It involved a music studio with lots of instruments in it. The teenage me would be overjoyed to know that at the end of my garden is a little den with a piano, drums, shakers, maracas, guitars, bongos, synthesisers, a computer and speakers – that there’s never a day when I’m not doing music, half of it tinkering alone, the rest making music with other people. He’d probably be confused about the amount of hot yoga I currently do. But glad to know I still like a denim shirt.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackGareth MaloneChoral musicClassical musicEducational TVTelevisionYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: Why are national anthems almost always orchestral? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Photograph: Hybrid Images/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hybrid Images/Getty Images/Image SourceNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: Why are national anthems almost always orchestral?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsThis week’s question: Why is a child saying ‘Na-na, na-na-na!’ so annoying?Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy are national anthems almost always orchestral? When – and by whom – was it decided that brass and strings best represent a country’s identity? Where are the power-pop or folk varieties?Ross Gomes, by emailSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyLongstanding national anthems were mostly written before recorded and amplified music existed. They were often played outdoors, or in large halls. Those requirements are practically demanding large assemblies of portable instruments to play them. If it couldn’t be played by a military band, heavily staffed with brass players, a national anthem would not have lasted long.leadballoonAnthems typically pre-date the electronic and digital eras, which meant playing them on traditional woodwind, stringed and drummed instruments. Most of them also have words, so they can be sung by the faithful and the callow. Consequently, most national anthems sound awful to modern ears, quite aside from questions over suitability in an internationalist, secular and increasingly postcolonial world.If you’re in the mood, though, Niger’sL’Honneur de la Patrie(2023) would not be entirely out of place as the theme tune of a grand movie sci-fi. Meanwhile, Syria’s still-unofficialFī Sabīli al-Majd(2024) is perky and evokes the feeling of a whimsical late-1800s western caper movie; they should definitely use that in place of Ḥumāt ad-Diyār, in my opinion.DorkaliciousJust the weight of convention. Monkey see, monkey do.unclestinkyRather than orchestral, they are usually harmonically choral, with the four parts for soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Melodically, Britain’s own is deliberately as simple as it can get, for the untrained masses to join in in unison. The simple monosyllabic words God Save the King are biblical, from the King James version. The first modern one is La Marseillaise, dating from the French Revolution.Keith BarnesMore to the point, why are some of them so dire? There’s no comparison between God Save the King andLa Marseillaise; one’s a dirge, the other makes me want to march to the barricades.GoldgreenEven if they’re originally written for strings or brass, it doesn’t mean that they’re limited to performances by those instruments. Jimi Hendrix’s version of The Star Spangled Banner, for instance, was a better representation of the US at the time than any orchestral recital (and perhaps would be even more so now).superspartanO say, can you see …They’re no more orchestral than, say, Greensleeves, the Londonderry Air or Abide With Me. Many have military origins, which suits mobile groups with acoustic brass, pipes and drums. Others have origins in folk song, court dances and religious hymns (most European languages use a version of the word “hymn”, meaning song of praise, for anthem). The American anthem was a drinking song, the Chinese one a film theme.alexitoFlower of Scotlandwas written in the 1960s and narrowly failed to become the Scottish anthem in a vote of Holyrood. It’s usually performed by a pipe band, or by a large ensemble choir of football fans. Not sure I ever heard an orchestral version.Randomusername222Billy Connolly suggested the Archers theme tune would make a great national anthem. Now, that’s what I hear in my head whenever the UK’s dirge is played. After all, a national anthem is basically a country’s theme tune. So for me, the lyrics to Whatever Happened to the Likely Lads? are perfect.Not only is our national anthem an awful dirge, it fails to even mention the country, its features, its people (unless you include hammering the Scots). It just drones on about the current super-rich welfare claimant with poorly diversified genes.walpole6Explore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesClassical musicCommunitiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Finally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: There is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t work, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: There is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t work, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionMental healthFinally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy?John HarrisThere is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t workSun 11 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTShareBack in late 2025, when Keir Starmer’s grip on the Labour party was loosening and Reform UK was still in its pomp, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, commissioned what the government called its “Independent reviewinto prevalence and support for mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”.Here, it seemed, was not just an inquiry into England’sever-extending waiting listsfor the diagnosis of mental illness and neurodevelopmental conditions, and the dire lack of support for people who experience one or both of them. The review would also dovetail with two other huge issues: mounting claims of “overdiagnosis”, which Streeting hadappeared to partly endorse, and the government’s drive for the reform of so-called welfare. An apparentlywell-briefed piece in the Timesseemed to speak volumes: work led by the renowned psychologist Peter Fonagy, it said, was commencing just “as Labour seeks a fresh crackdown on welfare spending” amid diagnoses “which have become the most common reason for a sickness benefit claim”.Last Friday saw the publication of the600-page final reportFonagy had co-authored with Gillian Baird – a specialist in paediatric neurodisability – and the psychiatrist Simon Wessely. And, as so often happens with such inquiries, its interpretation suggested the media’s equivalent of a Rorschach blot. One of theGuardian’s headlineswas “No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real”. The Mail, by contrast, yelled out arather different message– “Rush to diagnose ADHD and autism can damage children” – while theTelegraph went for“ADHD surge fuelled by benefits, report warns”.Such are the perils of producing a very nuanced mixture of analysis and recommendations. When he appeared on Radio 4’s Today programme,Fonagy saidthat Streeting had been “completely wrong” to agree with suggestions of the common overdiagnosis of mental health disorders. When it comes to autism and ADHD, he and his colleagues’ report says that “if present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing, from previous merited concerns with under-recognition and underdiagnosis towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis”. But it also insists that right now, “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”, and points out that any data that might settle this festering argument “largely do not exist”. This is not the kind of stuff that suits a world that craves simple binaries and polarised shouting, but it speaks an undeniable truth.For the most part, in fact, it is hard to disagree with what the review points out. But among its conclusions lies one troubling proposal – that provision for both mental illness and so-called neurodivergence can and should often be led by observations of need rather than formal diagnosis. In making that suggestion, I have no doubt that Fonagy and his colleagues’ intentions are benign. But our systems of power and politics and the government’s increasingly anxious view of public spending could yet make it very dangerous indeed.First, though, the undeniable positives. In a very elegantly written and often moving introduction, Fonagy – who is 74 – completely rejects the popular idea of a new generation of wilting wimps falsely claiming to be suffering from mental ill-health. “The cacophony of voices now available to a young person – most of them digital, many of them confident, few of them accountable – has made the ordinary developmental process of understanding oneself far harder than it was for me,” he says. He goes on: “Young people today are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”These are mental health issues. When it comes to autism and ADHD, Fonagy and his two colleagues’ insistence that overdiagnosis is currently not happening “at scale” and that “the evidence does not show that people presenting today are less impaired than those presenting previously” is very important indeed. When Streeting commissioned the review, among the most in-vogue books was The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist and epilepsy specialist Suzanne O’Sullivan, whichmade the absurd suggestionthat the overdiagnosis of autism might have reached the point where it was partly to blame for rising rates of anxiety and depression among the young, linked to her claim that “the stigma of autism has been associated with low self esteem among children”. (If autism is still stigmatised, O’Sullivan publicly calling it an “illness” is hardly helpful.)The review, by contrast, is altogether more calm and evidence-based: for a bundle of reasons, it says that overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis may well be a future risk, but we can guard against those dangers by more closely regulating private diagnostic clinics (which are often partly NHS-funded) and stop them advertising their services. These are proposals that many autism and ADHD insiders agree with.On a different subject, Fonagy and his co-authors also do us all a favour by emphasising the correct meaning of the ubiquitous term “neurodiversity”: whereas O’Sullivan says that it “has a biologising, pathologising effect”, the report rightly understands that the word means the complete opposite: it crystallises the plain fact that “variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour is part of natural human diversity rather than pathology or disorder”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Read moreBut what do we do when faced with genuinely diagnosable conditions that are debilitating and entail intensive support? One bit of first-person testimony in the report is heartbreaking. “When she was 12,” says an unnamed parent, “our daughter was put on ADHD medication, which lowered her mood, leading her to self-harm. She was referred to CAMHS [child and adolescent mental health services] who turned her down. Within the next month we ended up in A&E due to taking an overdose. She was then finally accepted by CAMHS, who suggested an autism assessment.“Two years later, after receiving an autism diagnosis, little changed. School would not make any adjustments until an EHCP (education, health and care plan) was accepted, and social care said she did not meet their threshold for support because she did not have a learning disability. Our daughter was broken and unsupported and was admitted to inpatients at 15 years old.”Herein lies one of the review’s few dangers. By way of lessening an increasingly frightening crisis that is partly centred on pitifully long waits for formal diagnoses that can easily be ignored, it suggests moving towards a more “needs-based” approach, which echoes the government’s plans for special needs education. “There should be a fundamental shift from a diagnosis-dependent system to a needs-led plus diagnosis system,” it says. Such a change, the report says, would require “increased capacity, transformation through digitally enabled care, clearer national standards andsustained investment”.They are my italics, with very good reason. The governmentresponded to the reportby saying that the health and social care secretary, Yvette Cooper, “has asked NHS leaders to urgently examine how people can access advice, assessments and treatment more easily”. But without sufficient money, “needs-based” help is likely to amount to very little at all. Coincidentally, the Fonagy review arrivedon the same day as reportsthat the prime minister and the chancellor had rebuffed Cooper’s requests for money to fund a pay rise for NHS staff including nurses, porters and midwives. So what chance of a huge cash injection to tackle what the report so starkly highlights?Meanwhile, the Department for Work and Pensions still has a culture built around crackdowns and pushing people into work. Councils repeatedlyfail to meettheir responsibilities for the care and education of neurodivergent people. And, in the absence of properly funded change, both they and people suffering mental illness only stand even a faint chance of pushing their way through an almost impossible mess of bureaucracy and obstruction if they have pieces of paper confirming that their condition – or conditions – are real and true.This is what makes politicians whotalk of “overdiagnosis”look so crass, and the likely fate of such a definitive and in-depth report so tragic. It is an all too familiar story, indicative of our current defining national predicament: the government simply cannot afford what it proposes, so one of our cruellest modern crises looks set to grind on.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMental healthOpinionAutismHealthNHSAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderNeurodiversityYoung peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNuclear weaponsFixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilationSimon TisdallThis is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the daySun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTShareHumankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.Donald Trump’sblanket denialsof the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some asthe latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity –existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating,global proliferation of advanced nuclear weaponsis bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima,how much longer can our luck hold?Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putinrecently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time,Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacksdeep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US isupgrading its nuclear arsenalof 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing alucrative dealwith Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’sstatus as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim,whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit,is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow– which, at this rate, there may not be.Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spendingreached nearly $3tnlast year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paperpublished by the non-partisan Arms Control Association(ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too,is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and othersadvances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSimon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsNuclear weaponsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart in Bangkok | The Guardian
description: Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries
Content: High debt-servicing costs for developing nations crowd out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHigh debt-servicing costs for developing nations crowd out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesEconomics viewpointDebt reliefLabour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoilHeather Stewartin BangkokJust as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countriesDeveloping nations face triple shock, UN warnsSun 11 Oct 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.17 EDTShareFrom Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and theWorld Bankmay be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.The next global economic emergency? Deepening debt in the developing worldRead moreThere have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including fromAfrican Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.TheG20– the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, andLabourhas made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond,securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another sixsmall island developing statesthat do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.Explore more on these topicsDebt reliefEconomics viewpointGlobal economyEconomicsG20International Monetary Fund (IMF)World BankBondscommentShareReuse this content

title: ​I’ve seen what Amazon thinks about me – and it revealed a depressing truth | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: From ‘has flat buttocks’ to ‘likes brunettes with muscles’, the retailer’s About You pages offer some remarkable insights into customers’ lives and tastes. Naturally, I rushed to check out mine …
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: From ‘has flat buttocks’ to ‘likes brunettes with muscles’, the retailer’s About You pages offer some remarkable insights into customers’ lives and tastes. Naturally, I rushed to check out mine …
Content: ‘Maintains premium coffee brewing setup.’Photograph: agrobacter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Maintains premium coffee brewing setup.’Photograph: agrobacter/Getty ImagesOpinionAmazon​I’ve seen what Amazon thinks about me – and it revealed a depressing truthEmma BeddingtonFrom ‘has flat buttocks’ to ‘likes brunettes with muscles’, the retailer’s About You pages offer some remarkable insights into customers’ lives and tastes. Naturally, I rushed to check out mine …Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTShareThere’s been a disturbing development in the surveillance capitalism space for me and other Amazon users: we can now find out exactly what the site thinks about us. The tax-agnostic shopping behemoth launched an “About You” function, which allows shoppers to see what assumptions and beliefs it has gathered from our purchases, in May, but last week things got interesting.Threads user Megan Montgomeryfound her“About You” page, and discovered Amazon thinks she “has flat buttocks”, prompting other shoppers to post the implacably devastating verdicts they uncovered: “husband has skinny legs”; “likes brunettes with muscles”; “cusses when scared”; “cannot keep real plants alive”; “too short to reach into a 40in-deep box” and “treats cats as biological children”. A TikTok user says hers includes “has a bad father”.By their fruits shall ye know them, if by “fruits” you mean compression socks, shapewear, cat carriers and self-help guides. Obviously, this is bad, but it’s a well-deserved kind of bad – we’ve sacrificed privacy for convenience and this is the result. It’s also bleakly funny, so just as obviously, I was over there like a ferret up a trouser leg to find out what the stuff Amazon has delivered here over the years has caused it to deduce about my household. The results were disappointing. You don’t need a particularly sophisticated algorithm to deduce “likely lives in York”; “feeds wild birds consistently” (not in summer! I followRSPB guidance!) and “cycles recreationally” (absolutely not, but I live with a multi-bike-owning MAMNILYBOROD – that’s “middle-aged man not in Lycra yet because of risk of divorce”).There’s a lot our About You page hasn’t noticed or doesn’t consider important either. What about the sprays, mosses and soils that keep the houseplants I inherited from my son alive? I definitely treat the variegated monstera and temperamental calathea “like biological children”. The multipacks of cuttlefish bones and other tortoise ephemera don’t merit a mention and I’m surprised, too, that my husband’s frequent DIY-related purchases don’t feature. He sources enough widgets, pipes and sealant to open a mid-sized B&Q and I feel obscurely insulted on his behalf that all that hitting things with hammers while swearing (sorry, “cussing”) hasn’t made the cut. It would be nice, too, if my many years of Kindle purchases counted for something – I would have enjoyed a complimentary nod to all the dry histories of ideas and dense Russian classics I optimistically download, fancying myself An Intellectual (glossing over the easy novels about relationships I actually read).Our page isn’t lacking in pretentiousness though:Amazoncomments include “values specialized fitness nutrition products”; “maintains premium coffee brewing setup” and “prefers Japanese stationery brands”. If this portrait of our collective purchases were one real person, you could imagine him – it’s definitely a him – mansplaining David Foster Wallace or how, actually, you should eat nigiri sushi with your hands, on a date. Is this who we are, as a household? I hate us.Really, the thing I hate most about us is that we’re shopping like this at all. What’s the point of taking recycled containers to the organic market, puffed up with my own virtue, when I’m coming home and buying phone chargers and creatine gummies on my phone? Driving, recently, through the vast logistical and petrochemical sprawl that is Rotterdam port after three days clearing my mother-in-law’s flat made me think this more urgently. We accumulate so much stuff over a lifetime, at such heavy environmental cost, only to have to work out how to get rid of it again. Buying from Amazon makes it worse: the company isestimated to have cost the UK £575m in lost tax revenue in 2024, is accused ofunsafeandunethicalemploymentpracticesand is helmed by a man seemingly intent on spending his obscene wealth onsending a flying penis into space.The most damning thing Amazon knows about me is the simplest: I’m too lazy and disorganised to do without it – it’s the ubiquitous, inevitable, depressing answer for so many little “needs” (wants, really). I resolved to print out and put up a picture of Bezos’s rocket to shame myself into shopping around, but I’m already facing my first challenge: where the hell do I get our weird printer cartridges?Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: What’s my first decision as CEO? I’m giving myself the day off | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: A life coach has helpfully pointed out that we’re all chief executives of our own existence. So let’s start enjoying the perks, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: A life coach has helpfully pointed out that we’re all chief executives of our own existence. So let’s start enjoying the perks, writes Polly Hudson
Content: What a to-do! Ditch that list …Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhat a to-do! Ditch that list …Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleWhat’s my first decision as CEO? I’m giving myself the day offPolly HudsonA life coach has helpfully pointed out that we’re all chief executives of our own existence. So let’s start enjoying the perksSun 11 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareTo-do lists are done, apparently: the latest tactic to motivate and galvanise yourself is a “CEO hour”. The rationale for this method, courtesy of career and life coachEva Katzler, is that you arethe chief executive officer of your own existence, so you should routinely sit down and check in, just as they do in other businesses, reflecting on the past week and setting intentions for the next. Regularly having a formal meeting with yourself may be the kind of behaviour that makes people start worrying about you, particularly if you power dress for the occasion, but at least you can be sure you’ll get all the best biscuits.Katzler is against the to-do list because she sees it as “our fast track to feeling like we’re completely out of control, because we can never get through it. When you never get that sense of achievement, what you’re left with is a feeling of failure.”Instead she suggests asking yourself what your wins were from the last week, which tasks you’ve been avoiding, and how you’re managing your energy, time and workload. Also, noting any eureka moments you had, how well you took care of yourself, and what support you need.Scoff all you like, but for me even the idea of a CEO hour was impactful, because I noticed that my immediate instincts were to wonder how low the bar was for what constituted a win of the week (does “lived to tell the tale” count?) and worry about a boardroom coup. My company felt much more unfortunate Apprentice candidate than Fortune 500.But then came one of those eureka moments I’m meant to be looking out for: I don’t have to do this well. In fact, there’s absolutely no point making any effort at all. I’m already the CEO, baby! There’s no position higher – I’ve already climbed to the top of the ladder. Ah, the sweet smell of success. I think I’ll give myself the rest of the day off, and if I’ve got a problem with that, I’ll have to take it up with me.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsLife and styleOpinionHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Pumpkin-spiced latte is a con. It’s time to put an end to Big Autumn  | Chloë Hamilton | The Guardian
description: The aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter days, says journalist Chloë Hamilton
Author: Chloë Hamilton
Headline: The aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter days, says journalist Chloë Hamilton
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onAutumnThe hill I will die on: Pumpkin-spiced latte is a con. It’s time to put an end to Big AutumnChloë HamiltonThe aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter daysSun 11 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s getting earlier every year, that first meme about golden leaves and pumpkin-spiced lattes. This year, I swear, I spotted one in early August, while we were still sweltering under our fourth heatwave of the summer.Because, of course, for those that like crisp mornings, Halloween and glasses of red wine in front of roaring fires, the arrival of autumn brings with it something else: the incessant need to tell everyone just how much they love this perfectly pleasant, if perpetually damp, season.I call it BigAutumn. The idea that liking autumn is enough to sustain an entire personality. I don’t know when it first happened but my instinct is that it’s been driven by an almost entirely brown-and-orange aesthetic pushed out via Pinterest and Instagram, and not by the often grim realities: grey drizzle, shorter days, the sense of impending Christmas.It’s not that I have an issue with the season itself. Sure, my partner and I refer to it as “mud season” because we have a spaniel and two young children, and our house won’t feel truly clean again until the end of March. But I’m partial to a roast dinner and a fairy light, I like oversized jumpers and, although I avoid Halloween, I find Bonfire Night quite magical, even if I do always over-layer and end up sweaty and overstimulated.No, it’s not the season I take issue with but rather our need to define ourselves by our preferences. It’s a trend that has been perpetuated by social media. See also: being a cat person or a boy mum. It smacks of Christian Girl Autumn, a viralmemefrom 2019 that emerged as an antidote – one in knee-high leather boots and an oversized scarf – to Hot Girl Summer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it all | Elle HuntRead moreTo me, it merely highlights our modern-day compulsion to construct and curate personalities rather than simply inhabit them. It’s as though the internet has encouraged – nay, forced – us to paint ourselves with broad brush strokes rather than with the nuance and intricacy that a human life calls for. It demonstrates a terminal lack of imagination, although perhaps lives spent juggling always-on jobs, constantly popping WhatsApp groups and the astronomicalcost of literally living have left us so burned out we haven’t the time or the energy to add more detail.I suspect my irritation lies in the fact that liking autumn has not only become a personality, but – because spending and social media go hand in hand – a way of getting us to part with money we don’t have. A pumpkin-spiced chai latte doesn’t come for free and, go on, you definitely need that new-season chocolate-brown knit. Autumn has become a lifestyle, a commodity, not just the passing of the baton from one season to the next.Maybe my frustration with the people for whom a love of this meteorological phenomenon becomes their defining characteristic is that I fear they are unknowingly playing into the hands of Big Autumn. Or maybe I really do just hate drizzle.Chloë Hamilton is freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsAutumnThe hill I will die oncommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on mental health: overdiagnosis is not the problem facing young people | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Parity of esteem with physical healthcare remains a distant prospect. Ministers must do more to tackle rising distress
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Parity of esteem with physical healthcare remains a distant prospect. Ministers must do more to tackle rising distress
Content: ‘Rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes.’Photograph: Antonio Guillem/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes.’Photograph: Antonio Guillem/AlamyOpinionMental healthThe Guardian view on mental health: overdiagnosis is not the problem facing young peopleEditorialParity of esteem with physical healthcare remains a distant prospect. Ministers must do more to tackle rising distressSun 11 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePerhaps the single most important finding of theindependent reviewinto mental health, ADHD and autism in England, published last Friday, is that mental distress across the population, and particularly young people, hassubstantially worsened. Its chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, told the BBC that the former health secretary Wes Streeting had been “completely wrong” to suggest that conditions and disorders were being overdiagnosed.Mr Streetingacknowledgedhis mistake. But some rightwing politicians and commentators have leapt on the notion that medicalisation of ordinary states of mind is behind the huge rise in young people seeking help. This review should bury that idea. Instead, this should be a moment to face facts. First, that therises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes. Second, that current services are not up to what is being asked of them.Fifteen years after the phrase “parity of esteem” gained prominence – the idea being that people with mental ill health have equivalent entitlements to those with physical illnesses – it is along way from being realised. Years-long queues for mental health care and neurodevelopmental support are not even included in official waiting-list figures.The difficulty comes in deciding what to do about this, particularly given the fiscal rules under which the government has chosen to operate. One proposal already accepted by ministers is for stronger regulation of ADHD and autism assessments. Currently, many of these are delivered by private providers, with no common standards in a market with low barriers to entry; such a situation should never have been allowed, though long waiting lists have driven the demand for their services.There is no straightforward fix to the wider set of problems. The experts are right to say that access to services should be based on need, not labels. It is reasonable to challenge the way that a diagnosis has become a “door to support”, both in mental health and special educational needs contexts. But the more important question is how this situation came about. The answer is that demand overwhelmed services, and diagnosis-based thresholds became a form of triage. On the critical question of resources, the report has less to say.It recommendsstronger accountability for mental health in the Department of Health and Social Care – an excellent idea, and probably a precondition of improvement – and suggests that this and other proposals should be incorporated in the upcoming mental health strategy. Beyond that, it argues for a 10-year plan, one aim of which would be to roll mental health and neurodevelopmental support into one service.This is an ambitious agenda, which deserves a serious response. But while Prof Fonagy may be right that some reordering of waiting lists could be managed at relatively little cost, it is inconceivable that broader reforms can be achieved without new funds. And while the report refers repeatedly, and rightly, to the need for investment, it does not explicitly state that budgets should increase as a proportion of overall health spending; nor does it make the case for waiting list targets.Did the authors fear that such demands would be ignored? So far, Yvette Cooper has followed her predecessor as health secretary in saying relatively little about mental health and young people. Now is the time to show that she is listening.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is right
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is right
Content: ‘Donald Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal.’ The site of a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, 10 October 2026.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal.’ The site of a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, 10 October 2026.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAOpinionInternational criminal courtThe Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifiesEditorialA fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is rightSun 11 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareOn Friday, Donald Trump drove home his belief that might is right and the rule of law is an obstacle rather than an essential foundation stone of international order. First came the escalatedassault on the international criminal court (ICC), sanctioning the body itself. Then he announceda deal with Russiato buy diesel.The US has long chafed at the notion of being bound by the rule of law that it espoused publicly. That hypocrisy now appears as a lesser vice. The president hasdeclaredthat “my own morality” is all that constrains him. His brazen flouting of the law, embrace of dictators and rhetorical attacks all undermine global standards.Weeks before the midterms, Mr Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities for high diesel costs. It is his own unlawful war on Iran that has raised prices.The weekend’s attackson Riyadh’s international airport, suspected as the work of Tehran-backed Houthis from Yemen, underscored that he cannot simply park that conflict when it suits him.The Moscow deal is unlikely to produce significant shipments; the Russian military runs on diesel. But Ukraine is supposed to heed its message to make life easier on Vladimir Putin. It is Mr Putin (for whom the ICC has issued a warrant) who launched the illegal war, and whose troops launched lethal attacks on civilians this weekend. But in a world turned upside down, Mr Trump blamesVolodymyr Zelenskyyfor failing to cut a peace deal and says the democratically elected leader should go.View image in fullscreenNavi Pillay.Photograph: Davide Elias/EPAIt is similarly perverse to wield measures designed to target human rights abusers and war criminals against those who seek to defend their victims. Mr Trump’s attack on the ICC was fuelled first by its Afghanistan investigation – though it has suspended consideration of US actions there – and then the issuing of arrest warrants for Israel’sBenjamin Netanyahuand its former defence minister Yoav Gallant. The court hasbeen preparingfor these  measures. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state,saidthat companies have six months to wind down ties and that US allies must rein in the court: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”In stark (and intentional) contrast, the Nobel committee on the same day announced that this year’s peace laureate is Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and chair of the UN commission which last yearconcludedthat Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. It was not only a recognition of a remarkable career that began in apartheid‑era South Africa, but a reminder that institutions defending universal principles are under increasing pressure, and must be defended. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said.As the ICC says, it cannot stand alone. The UK, EU and others too were right tocriticisethe US decision and declare their commitment to the court; invoking blocking statutes against sanctions would add heft to the rhetoric. They must show similar resolve in standing with Ukraine.The nakedness of Mr Trump’s hostility to the rule of law has one benefit: no one can explain it away, or assume it is narrowly bounded. The war on Iran, kidnapping of Venezuela’s president,extrajudicial killingsof alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and threats over Greenland and Canada have shown how far he will go, and overturned assumptions that allies will be safe. It is clear that the problem is not a “rogue court”, as Mr Rubio has claimed, but a rogue superpower.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Why plan for judge-only trials in fraud cases is wrong | Trial by jury | The Guardian
description: Letters: Nic Madge and David Lindsay respond to the government’s proposals to reform the criminal justice system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Nic Madge and David Lindsay respond to the government’s proposals to reform the criminal justice system
Content: The jury hears a fictional case in the 2017 Channel 4 series The Trial: A Murder in the Family.Photograph: Joss Barratt/Channel 4View image in fullscreenThe jury hears a fictional case in the 2017 Channel 4 series The Trial: A Murder in the Family.Photograph: Joss Barratt/Channel 4Trial by juryLettersWhy plan for judge-only trials in fraud cases is wrongNic MadgeandDavid Lindsayrespond to the government’s proposals to reform the criminal justice systemSun 11 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTShareThe government is right to abandon David Lammy’s main proposal to replace some jury trials with judges sitting alone (Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry, 4 October). There are other ways to reduce the appalling backlog of criminal cases and to protect victims. However, the government is wrong to proceed with its plan for judge-only trials in some fraud cases. As a circuit judge, I presided over fraud trials with juries, including a Ponzi fraud worth £48m and a Russian identity fraud with more than 40,000 documents. The juries were totally on top of both trials and delivered sensible, rational verdicts – in both cases guilty on some charges and not guilty on others. My experience is that the key issue in fraud cases is frequently whether the defendant acted dishonestly. That is not a technical question. It is something that juries are much better able to decide than judges.Nic MadgeSt AlbansAlthough the government has shelved its plan to abolish most jury trials, it still intends to double the sentencing power of magistrates to two years, to introduce judge-only trials in “lengthy and technical” fraud cases, and to abolish the right to elect trial by jury in “either way” cases, thereby greatly restricting access to legal aid. It is not clear whether or not the government still intended to abolish the automatic right of appeal to the crown court from the magistrates court. Every one of those measures must be resisted without compromise.David LindsayLanchester, County DurhamExplore more on these topicsTrial by juryUK criminal justiceEnglandWaleslettersShareReuse this content

title: A two-tier food system for people living in poverty | Food poverty | The Guardian
description: Letters: Jane Middleton says the question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity to eat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Jane Middleton says the question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity to eat
Content: Waste vegetables discarded after processing for retail sale at a farm in Lancashire.Photograph: EnVogue_Photo/AlamyView image in fullscreenWaste vegetables discarded after processing for retail sale at a farm in Lancashire.Photograph: EnVogue_Photo/AlamyFood povertyLettersA two-tier food system for people living in povertyJane Middletonsays the question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity to eatSun 11 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTShareCharlotte Hill (While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution, 6 October) conflates two separate problems. One is food waste; the other is domestic food insecurity. If, as she suggests, we use the former to address the latter, we are simply creating a two-tier food system where people living in poverty do not have the dignity of making their own choices.While the work of food-waste charities such as the that one Hill heads is commendable as a sticking plaster, in the long term it entrenches poverty and removes any incentive for large corporations to tackle the food waste they create.The right to food, established in the United Nations charter, includes the right of individuals to acquire food by socially acceptable means – in effect, having enough income to buy it in the same way as everyone else. The question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity in order to eat.People on low incomes are not there to make large corporations feel good about themselves via charitable donations. Hill says that “unavoidable surplus food” is generated in our farming system. If this is the case, then consider coming to an arrangement with schools, hospitals and prisons, but please don’t view people struggling to make ends meet as a repository for your waste products.In a country with food surpluses, we should be battling against the institutionalisation of food aid, not encouraging it.Jane MiddletonBathHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: How to tackle serious safeguarding gaps in nurseries  | Child protection | The Guardian
description: Letter: Tulip Siddiq and a parent urge the government to take a number of steps to keep children safe, in response to an editorial
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Tulip Siddiq and a parent urge the government to take a number of steps to keep children safe, in response to an editorial
Content: ‘CCTV should be mandatory in nurseries.’Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘CCTV should be mandatory in nurseries.’Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesChild protectionLettersHow to tackle serious safeguarding gaps in nurseriesTulip Siddiqand a parent urge the government to take a number of steps to keep children safe, in response to an editorialSun 11 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTShareYour editorial on early years provision (The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives, 4 October) ends by referring to the horrifying case ofVincent Chan, who worked at Bright Horizons nursery in north-west London. We write as the MP representing the constituency in which the nursery is situated and as the parent of children who attended the nursery and were victims of Chan. We believe his case exposed serious gaps in the safeguarding system that urgently need addressing by government.First, CCTV should be mandatory in nurseries. When used with appropriate safeguards, it can provide both a deterrent and an important source of evidence when allegations are made.Second, implementing a “flare” system that goes beyond Disclosure and Barring Service checks, allowing parents, carers and nurseries to report safeguarding concerns, and connecting allegations and relevant employment information across early years settings and over time.Third, the law governing sexual and exploitative images of children needs examination. One family affected by this case has discovered that photographs of their child found on Chan’s devices did not meet the existing legal threshold for an indecent image. We should ask whether current legislation adequately protects children from exploitative or sexualised imagery that falls short of this threshold.Finally, early years settings need clear, enforceable standards governing electronic devices, backed by Ofsted inspection. Nurseries hold large quantities of photographs and other sensitive digital information about vulnerable children. The rules governing how devices are used should reflect that responsibility. Had this been in place, Chan could have been caught sooner.We urge the urgent attention of the prime minister and the government on these matters.Tulip Siddiq MPLabour, Hampstead and Highgate,Parent AParent of children who attended Bright Horizons, Finchley Road,LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘We make our own noise’: Maresca hails Manchester City after Liverpool triumph | Premier League | The Guardian
description: The head coach said after the 3-0 win at Liverpool, the first game since City’s guilty verdict: ‘You cannot imagine how happy I am. I’m here to win’
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The head coach said after the 3-0 win at Liverpool, the first game since City’s guilty verdict: ‘You cannot imagine how happy I am. I’m here to win’
Content: Enzo Maresca said: ‘My message to the players has been clear: the noise will always be there so it’s about how we deal with it.’Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca said: ‘My message to the players has been clear: the noise will always be there so it’s about how we deal with it.’Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesPremier League‘We make our own noise’: Maresca hails Manchester City after Liverpool triumph‘You cannot imagine how happy I am … I’m here to win’City win 3-0 at Anfield in first game since guilty verdictAndy Hunterat AnfieldSun 11 Oct 2026 15.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca praised Manchester City for “making their own noise” at Liverpool as they brushed aside the controversy and threats surrounding the club with acomprehensive 3-0 winat Anfield.City, intheir first outingsince the club were found guilty on 114 charges relating to Premier League financial rules, maintained their 100% start to the season courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland, the excellent Jérémy Doku and Rayan Cherki. A sixth successive league win ensured Maresca equalled the best start to a managerial reign in Premier League history and kept City at the top of the table.Premier League returns in shadow of Manchester City’s judgment day | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThe City head coach said: “My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear: guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy. It was our fans making the noise at the end of the game today.”Maresca smiled when asked whether he needed City’s appeal to be heard as quickly as possible in order to celebrate such an impressive win. “You cannot imagine how happy I am,” he replied. “I don’t care. I’m here to try and prepare games and to win games. Hopefully I can speak about this situation when we win the appeal.”City’s chief executive Ferran Soriano was present at Anfield as the fallout from the club’s guilty verdict continues. Maresca reflected: “We were all together. For the importance of the game,Liverpoolaway, Anfield away, it was a good idea from the club to be all together. That togetherness is what we need.”The game turned on the 62nd-minute dismissal of Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch for a second bookable offence. Haaland opened the scoring one minute later and City then ran riot.Andoni Iraola, the Liverpool head coach, said: “We played two different games: one until the red card, and one from the red card until the end. I think we were the better team until the red card and they were better than us, obviously, after the red card. But I think the players deserve credit today because they’ve given everything.”Iraola insisted Gravenberch’s red card was harsh. “I think the first foul of Ryan is never a yellow card, never,” he added. “The referee doesn’t even call the foul straight away. He lets it go, Elliot Anderson does a couple of steps and then decides to go down. I don’t know why he shows the yellow card after that because it’s not a situation where it leaves an advantage.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueEnzo MarescaManchester CityLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spectre of ghost football hangs over Manchester City win of unknown significance | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Football felt secondary on the first weekend of action since club were found guilty of breaking financial rules
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Football felt secondary on the first weekend of action since club were found guilty of breaking financial rules
Content: Manchester City fans wave inflatable bananas after Erling Haaland had given their side the lead at Anfield.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City fans wave inflatable bananas after Erling Haaland had given their side the lead at Anfield.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersPremier LeagueAnalysisSpectre of ghost football hangs over Manchester City win of unknown significanceJonathan WilsonFootball felt secondary on the first weekend of action since club were found guilty of breaking financial rulesSun 11 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareThe Cimbri are heading menacingly south, but in Rome life goes on. The asteroid is definitely coming this way, but people go to work, eat, drink, plan as usual. The White Walkers are approaching the Wall, but the squabbles between the great houses go on. Everyone in thePremier Leagueknows the crisis is approaching, thinks – hopes, fears? – it may be apocalyptic, but until it arrives, what can you do but carry on?After any break, there’s always an awkward moment while everybody resets. What was the cliffhanger we left the soap opera on? What new plotline had just been seeded? This is one of the reasons international weeks are so disruptive. It’s not just that the Premier League story slows for a while, it’s that we are reminded that these entities are not eternal but alliances of convenience between paid employees who have a life outside the soap opera.Cherki cracker caps Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield tauntsRead moreBut there has never before been an international break so disruptive as this, never such a sense of unreality about a weekend of Premier League football. It’s not that, the 2022 World Cup aside, this has been the longest international break in history. Nor can anyone, surely, be unaware of the dominant narrative of this window: between 2009 and 2018,Manchester Citycheated. Perhaps an away game at Anfield for City is not quite the event it was when Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp were at their peak, but it should still be a great footballing occasion. Yet this was an afternoon when the football felt secondary.City continue to protest their innocence, clinging to the now-familiar formula that they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that will somehow clear their name, if only people wouldn’t keep refuting it. They havelaunched an appeal, but if that fails the sanction is likely to be unprecedentedly severe. Do their games matter? Will they be annulled before the season’s end? Was this victory just the difference between finishing the season on -100 points and -97? Could they be expelled from the league? Until sentence is announced, there will an air of provisionality about everything they do. It’s the seconds after an incident that everybody knows VAR will check, the ghost football that might be cancelled, but extended for weeks.This, though, is not only an issue of the present; it’s an issue of the past. The sanction may or may not strip City of their titles. Many City fans will ignore such a punishment, continue to claim those honours, will point out that memories cannot be so easily extinguished. But even if City’s appeal is successful, or even if the sanction does not relitigate the past, there will be asterisks there in the minds of those who are not City fans, and perhaps also in the minds of some of those who are. Add inChelsea’s offences, and the Premier League is coming to the end of an 18-year period in which very little was quite as it seemed.View image in fullscreenManchester City fans remain defiant despite the guilty verdict against the club they support.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesTheinflatable bananas brandished by City’s supportat Anfield on Sunday may have harked back to an earlier, more innocent era, but there is no going back. City are not the club of Imre Varadi any more; as it stands they are the clubguilty of the greatest act of cheatingin English football history.
