Their fans can do the Poznan in a spirit of resistance, but they cannot turn their back on the shame their leaders have brought upon them.What that means for the longer-term credibility of the league can only be guessed at. The basis of sport is faith. Incredible finishes mean little if nothing can be believed. Why go through the emotional agonies if a result might be struck off a decade later for offences committed in the air-conditioned offices of a distant state? Will the City decision undermine faith, or reaffirm it, come as proof that cheats do not prosper, that they will – eventually – be exposed, that the Premier League, almost alone in this grubby world of compromise with and abasement before the mega-rich, is prepared to do what is right?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity were booed, there were some chants of “going down” and there were a handful of banners, but Anfield was not the seething pit of disgust many had anticipated. Nor was there much City-related fury at other grounds, although Manchester United fans, erasing all the silverware of the past 15 years, reinstituted their counter on the Stretford End recording the length of time since City last won a trophy. The general sense is of bafflement and bewilderment; what does this mean? What might happen?It is as though the scale of City’s offences have not yet been fully grasped, that no one quite knows what might happen next. City fans, similarly, seem set on a policy of defiance, as though the scandal is something that has been done to them, rather than the result of the actions of their own directors. To an extent, that is understandable. Until the sanctions are announced, until the result of the appeal is known, the sense of unreality, the phoney war, will go on. The crisis is coming, but its impact has not yet been felt.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityFootball politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Impervious Manchester City shrug off chaos and controversy to silence Anfield | Premier League | The Guardian
description: What had been billed as a day of reckoning for the embattled Premier League champions turned into a Sunday afternoon stroll
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: What had been billed as a day of reckoning for the embattled Premier League champions turned into a Sunday afternoon stroll
Content: Banners underlining the level of feeling among Liverpool fans towards Manchester City were dotted around Anfield.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBanners underlining the level of feeling among Liverpool fans towards Manchester City were dotted around Anfield.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueAnalysisImpervious Manchester City shrug off chaos and controversy to silence AnfieldAndy Hunterat AnfieldWhat had been billed as a day of reckoning for the Premier League champions turned into a Sunday afternoon strollSun 11 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTShareAnfield welcomed Manchester City to their new reality, a sullied place where every touch is accompanied by cries of “cheat”, any favourable decision is considered proof of further conspiracy and every victory hollow. But Welcome to Hell this was not. The only body of irrefutable evidence in City’s favoursince the guilty verdicts landedis that Enzo Maresca’s league leaders appear immune to prosecution and persecution.That may well change depending on the outcome of City’s appeal and any punishment that eventually arises, likewise the merits and value of acommanding 3-0 winon Liverpool soil. The sight of Erling Haaland savouring a statement victory in front of City’s supporters after the final whistle, while chants of “going down” echoed around the rest of the stadium, captured the schism at the heart of this Premier League season.Liverpool 0-3 Manchester City: Premier League – as it happenedRead moreCity were transformed by the introduction of Jérémy Doku and the dismissal of the Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch. They were never intimidated, always composed and look a genuine threat to Arsenal’s defence of the title. And yet this could prove their lastPremier Leagueappearance at Anfield for the foreseeable future.It may be difficult, nigh on impossible, to sustain this level of motivation and desire knowing that relegation beckons. Knowing that no one outside City will give them credit for another title triumph did not affect them here, however.In the 17 days since news of City’s guilt first emerged, and the gestation period of a prolonged international break, their return to action in a Premier League undermined and distorted by their 114 breaches had been built up as a chastening day of reckoning for Maresca’s side. It proved nothing of the sort.Anfield can still make its voice heard to seismic effect and in the frantic start whenLiverpoolflew at City, with a fired-up Ronald Araújo whipping up the crowd after winning a challenge against Antoine Semenyo, the collective sense of injustice at a club pipped three times to the title by those in sky blue inspired Andoni Iraola’s players. But bear pits rarely feature in the corporate packaged world of Premier League entertainment 2026.The “reception committee” for the City team coach before the game was populated by fans carrying selfie-sticks and club shop carrier bags, not an incensed brooding mob. At half-time the Kop was asked to cheer on corporate guests of the club sponsor Standard Chartered as they took part in a penalty shootout, many clearly kicking a ball for the first time in their lives.There were incessant chants of “you cheating bastards” and various banners of damning judgement, many with an Oasis twist that may have been appreciated by Noel Gallagher in the away end. “And after all you really robbed us all” read one. “All of your stars are fading away,” read another. “A generation of supporters cheated,” cut to the heart of the issue confronting not only Liverpool but the Premier League itself.View image in fullscreenLiverpool supporters point out that their side finished second to Manchester City three times in the space of eight years.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAThe City support responded in kind. “In Khaldoon we trust – we’ve won it all!” proclaimed the away flags. The visitors, while performing the Poznan before kick-off, also reclaimed one of the “Cheat” flags that had been doing a healthy trade outside the ground before the game. The inflatable bananas that were once part of the City fanscape also made a comeback, a throwback to more innocent days when their club was not in the dock for inflating sponsorship deals. There was more bickering than tangible animosity. The four men who walked on to the pitch carrying the Premier League hoardings before kick-off received a more hostile reception than City’s players when they appeared for the warm-up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe decision for City’s team coach to arrive by a different route ensured a tame reception for the visitors. All eyes were on the usual entrance on Anfield Road as City were ushered in from the opposite side of the stadium. It meant even the referees’ chief Howard Webb could walk in almost unnoticed. The hostility cranked up as soon as the contest started and City, using their vast experience to telling effect, gradually drained the venom from the atmosphere and the threat from a depleted Liverpool team. But it was the 62nd-minute dismissal of Gravenberch that had the greater bearing on the outcome.Doku proved a devastating substitute for Iliman Ndiaye and tormented Liverpool from the left, being involved not only in the red card but all three City goals. The hosts, minus their two most potent attacking players this season in Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak, plus a hamstrung Dominik Szoboszlai, had no answer with Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola largely anonymous.The Kop made no calls to be handed the trophies lost to City – and what would that really mean now anyway? – but took solace in demanding that punishment be served in the form of relegation this season. “No trophies for 50 years, que será, será,” the home crowd chanted. But there was no immediate retribution for Liverpool here. City dealt with the chaos and the controversy serenely.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityLiverpoolanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s when I begin to scream’: Mick Fanning on punching a great white shark | Mick Fanning | The Guardian
description: The Australian surfing champion was monstered by a great white shark in 2015 in the middle of a competition in South Africa. Here, he relives the encounter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Australian surfing champion was monstered by a great white shark in 2015 in the middle of a competition in South Africa. Here, he relives the encounter
Content: Australian surfer Mick Fanning moments before he fought off a shark during the J-Bay Open competition in Jeffreys Bay, South Africa, on 19 July 2015. The attack is recounted in his new memoir, All Heart.Photograph: WSL/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralian surfer Mick Fanning moments before he fought off a shark during the J-Bay Open competition in Jeffreys Bay, South Africa, on 19 July 2015. The attack is recounted in his new memoir, All Heart.Photograph: WSL/AFP/Getty ImagesMick Fanning‘That’s when I begin to scream’: Mick Fanning on punching a great white sharkThe Australian surfing champion was monstered by a great white shark while competing against fellow Aussie Julian Wilson in the 2015 world tour event final at Jeffreys Bay in South Africa. The attack was broadcast live on TV. Here, in an extract from his memoir, All Heart, he relives the encounterMick FanningSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m locked in on my take-off spot in the J-Bay lineup, scanning the horizon, biding my time. Assessing my position against the rippling lines of the oncoming set, I decide to move slightly further inside.As I move, there’s a big splash behind me. Glancing over my left shoulder, I catch a glimpse of a huge dark shape in the water. A jolt of fear grips me. What the hell is that?Instinct kicks in and I haul myself up on to my board to shield my body. There’s a violent lurch directly beneath me. Suddenly, I’m yanked off by a wild tug on my leg rope. I quickly scramble to get back on my board and that’s when I see it. The unmistakable fin of a shark.There’s a split second of full-body panic. Then: THWACK! The shark’s tail whips out and wallops my left cheek. My head jerks back as a white flash of pain explodes in my skull. Then I’m being dragged down into the churning water, the force almost tearing my leg from its socket. Consumed with terror, I’m suddenly released and break through to the surface, gasping for breath. Has the shark got tangled in my leg rope and bitten through it?Suddenly, the shark jackknifes around. It’s like a torpedo hurtling straight towards me. That’s when I begin to scream.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a split second of full-body panic. Then: THWACK!’Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe shark crashes into me from the side and I blindly lash out with my fists, yelling, punching, kicking. It shrugs me off like a leaf. I fall backwards into the waves again and as my head surfaces, I see it swimming away from me towards the horizon.Flailing in the water, head on a swivel, I swim away hard. I can see Jules about 25 metres away now.In my years of spearfishing, I’ve never encountered more sharks than now. But I know where I stand in the underwater pecking order | Clarke GayfordRead moreGot to warn him. Now. “Shark! Shark! Go in! Go! GO!”Jules keeps paddling towards me. “Go in!” I yell.“There’s a bloody shark.” He keeps coming.Just then, I imagine the shark circling back around. If it comes for me now, it’ll get me from behind. I’ve got no board, it’ll go at my legs first. There’s no way to defend myself. Fuck that.There’s no way I’m going to let that happen. I stop swimming. Force myself to turn. Fists clenched, I tread water breathing hard, trying to get as high as I can, scouring the water for the shark’s return. The world goes mute and I’m so focused that I don’t notice the jetski until it’s right by my side.“Mick! Mick! Get up here!”Surfer Mick Fanning fights off shark attack at J-Bay OpenGuardianI scramble up on to the sled it’s towing, looking around for Jules. “Jules? Where is he?”“On the other jetski. He’s fine. You OK?”Wait, am I OK? Hastily, I scan my limbs. Check my hands and fingers, feet and toes. I seem to be alright. I just need to stop hyperventilating.“Yeah, I’m OK. But what the fuck?”Seconds later, the jetski pulls up by the bigger boat. Jules is on board. His eyes are wild. “You right?” he stammers.“Yeah, you? I was telling you to go in! You crazy bastard.”He shrugs and then gripping each other by the shoulders, we both start laughing manically, shit-faced on adrenaline and pure relief. “That was so gnarly. So fucking gnarly.”“Whoah! I can’t believe that actually happened.” And it’s like we’ve survived the biggest scare of all time. Like we’ve won a war, cheated death, escaped the jaws of a great white! Somehow, we’ve got away scot-free. There are high fives and backslaps. Hoots and howls. Everyone on the boat is talking a mile a minute, pumped up with a mix of exhilaration and hysteria.“If you’re both OK, we’re going to get you in now,” says Peter Mel, the field commentator who’s been calling heats from the water.“We can probably just surf in, yeah?”Peter stares at me as if I’m insane, then he speaks to me with the sort of soft tone you’d use to address a small child.“No, Mick, that was a big shark. We’re going to escort you in.”Whatever. I turn to Jules. “I can’t believe you fucking swum towards me. You’re fucking crazy!”“What was I gonna do? Watch my mate get eaten by a shark?”On the shore, we’re bustled straight into a white Volkswagen van and continue our postmortem. When Jules hears that I punched the shark, he convulses in giggles. I laugh too, because it’s all so crazy. Jules still looks utterly wired, his pupils dilated like two black holes.“Mate, that was wild!” he says shaking his head.View image in fullscreenMick Fanning, left, embraces fellow surfer Julian Wilson after the shark attack.Photograph: Kirstin Scholtz/AFP/Getty ImagesI start laughing again. It’s like my nervous system has got whiplash. Then the doors of the van open.Standing outside are Jarrad and Fletch, plus my mates: Otto, Ace and a bunch of other touring surfers. I’m expecting more high fives and wild-eyed grins. Instead, they’re deathly quiet. They look shell-shocked and upset. In fact, most of them are in tears.double quotation markSuddenly, I don’t feel invincible any more. I just feel very, very luckyMick FanningOK, maybe I’ve misread the situation here …I’m engulfed in a tearful hug from Ace[Australian world tour surfer Adrian Buchan]. He’s more distraught than I am. Then Fletch embraces me [Rip Curl team manager Ryan Fletcher]. Then Jarrad[former tour surfer and Mick’s coach at the event]. Immediately, I start explaining what happened. How the shark grabbed my leg rope. Bit through it. How I landed a punch or two.“Someone was looking after us,” I say.Jules and I are led up to the commissioner’s office. Inside, they’re all completely rattled too. I get hugged by more people. I agree to an interview with Ronnie who is there in his role as an event commentator for the WSL broadcast. It hadn’t occurred to me yet that this whole thing has been beamed live all around the world. As Fletch suggests: it’s the easiest way to let everyone back home know I’m OK.Before the interview I’m asked by the tour commissioner, Kieren Perrow, if I’d like to see the footage.“Yeah, I think I’ve got to,” I tell him. “Cause I don’t think I’m processing this the same as everyone else.”Shark attack on surfer Mick Fanning: I punched it a couple of timesGuardianIn Kieren’s office, a bunch of us gather around a big-screen TV. And then, I watch the replay.There I am waiting for a wave, oblivious. Then the splash behind me, the shark’s fin, the flurry of whitewater as I try to scramble away. The next moment, a wave obscures the camera. For eight long seconds no one can see the frantic tussle that almost cost me my life. The camera even pans back as if wanting to protect the viewer from the worst-case scenario.“We all thought you were gone,” Jarrad says. “The last thing we saw was you being knocked off your board, then that set rolled in. Next thing we saw was your board heading out to sea … ”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Simon & SchusterWatching the footage, what’s most terrifying is the size of the shark. It must’ve been at least three-and-a-half metres long, with the girth of a submarine. Suddenly, I don’t feel invincible any more. I just feel very, very lucky. A shark that big can do whatever the hell it wants.“Oh fuck,” I stammer.And suddenly it dawns on me that Mum was watching the final live back home.“Can someone please call Mum? Let her know I’m OK.”Then I realise the quickest way to let her know is to jump on the broadcast, which is still going. I do the interview with Ronnie. The adrenaline is starting to wear off now, the cold horror of what happened is kicking in. The conversation is a blur. I’m just about holding it together, wiping away the odd tear.“The commissioner’s office has decided that there’ll be no final run today,” Ronnie says.“Is that even a concern for you at this stage?”“Mate, I’m happy to not ever compete again. I just want to let all my family and friends know that I’m OK. Right now, I’m just tripping out.”The interview finishes, and as I walk off camera, standing there is Kelly Slater. He’s my arch rival, the man I’ve battled against so hard on so many occasions. He walks towards me and just embraces me in a giant hug.View image in fullscreenMick Fanning, left, hugs US surfer Kelly Slater after the shark scare.Photograph: Kirstin Scholtz/AFP/Getty ImagesI walk downstairs surrounded by security. Parko is standing at the bottom with Ace and Bec, his wife. Bec’s emotional – she knows how bad it could’ve been. She hugs me and my legs just buckle. That’s when it all sinks in and I’m overcome. I burst into tears as reality hits like a tsunami.Ronnie notices me crumble. “Righto mate, we better get you out of here now.”This is an edited extract from All Heart byMick Fanning(A$36.99, Simon & Schuster)Explore more on these topicsMick FanningSharksSurfingAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli admits he can taste F1 glory after Verstappen wins Singapore GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli could seal the drivers’ title in the next race in Texas after Max Verstappen won the F1 Singapore Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli could seal the drivers’ title in the next race in Texas after Max Verstappen won the F1 Singapore Grand Prix
Content: Kimi Antonelli pours champagne over his head on the podium after the Singapore GP.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli pours champagne over his head on the podium after the Singapore GP.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli admits he can taste F1 glory after Verstappen wins Singapore GPItalian can win the title in Texas in late OctoberVerstappen led race at Marina Bay from start to finishGiles RichardsSun 11 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKimi Antonelli said he can finally dare to dream about winning his first Formula One world championship after he finished in third place at the Singapore Grand Prix and put himself in a position where he could secure the title at the next round in Austin.Max Verstappen won with a dominant driveat the Marina Bay circuit but behind him, Antonelli’s podium means he could become F1’s youngest champion at the age of 20, in two weeks’ time. Antonelli leads his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, by 102 points and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton by 111. With six meetings remaining and 25 points for the winner of each race, the Italian will take the title if he wins in Austin and Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower.Resurgent Verstappen holds off Leclerc to seal dominant F1 Singapore GP winRead moreWhen asked if he dared to dream that his childhood ambition of becoming champion was within reach, he acknowledged he did with a smile. “For sure,” he said. “I know it’s very close, I know it’s there but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can. The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can.”Mercedes were outpaced by Red Bull in Singapore, with the silver arrows still striving to exploit recent upgrades but Antonelli feels he and the team will have more to come in Texas.“This weekend I haven’t particularly driven that well,” he added. “I felt like I could have done a better job but I feel confident that a week to reset and I’m really looking forward to being back in Austin. But at the end of the day, if I don’t do my job well, then the result won’t come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that.”Hamilton, who finished sixth, issued an apology to his Ferrari team after his call to not pit under the virtual safety car proved costly, leaving him vulnerable on worn tyres at the death, where he was passed by three rivals. He was unwell after the race and given leave to miss his media duties but Ferrari issued a comment from the British driver. “A painful lesson today but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made,” the 41-year-old said. “Not every call will work out and I can accept getting it wrong but I’m sorry for the team for the points we lost today.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, made it clear the team had not been at fault. “We were P2, P3 on track, we called two of our guys to pit behind the VSC, one of our guys said: ‘No I prefer to stay on track’, or he missed pit entry. Don’t blame the team,” he noted.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL roundup: Daniels’ overtime blunder costs Commanders as Giants salvage wild 27-27 tie | NFL | The Guardian
description: Jayden Daniels runs out the clock with Washington in field-goal range as Giants escape with a 27-27 tie and Patriots cruise past Raiders and Jets stun Cleveland
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jayden Daniels runs out the clock with Washington in field-goal range as Giants escape with a 27-27 tie and Patriots cruise past Raiders and Jets stun Cleveland
Content: Malik Nabers scores a fourth-quarter touchdown against Commanders cornerback Rasul Douglas as the Giants rallied from 14 points down to earn a 27-27 tie on Sunday in Landover, Maryland.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMalik Nabers scores a fourth-quarter touchdown against Commanders cornerback Rasul Douglas as the Giants rallied from 14 points down to earn a 27-27 tie on Sunday in Landover, Maryland.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesNFLNFL roundup: Daniels’ overtime blunder costs Commanders as Giants salvage wild 27-27 tieDaniels’ late scramble leaves Washington unable to kickGiants rally from 14 down but settle for 27-27 drawMaye throws four TDs as Patriots rout Raiders 45-17Jaguars stun Eagles in London with one second leftAgenciesSun 11 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJayden Daniels took off on an ill-advised scramble in the closing seconds of overtime with the Commanders in field-goal range, and Washington were unable to stop the clock before time expired, settling for a 27-27 tie with theNew York Giantson Sunday after both teams made critical mistakes in the extra period.Washington (1-3-1) got the ball with two minutes left in overtime when Daron Payne stripped the ball from Cam Skattebo with the Giants in range for a game-winning field goal. Daniels quickly moved the Commanders to the Giants’ 24-yard line, but with 12 seconds left and Washington out of timeouts, he held on to the ball and went down for no gain. Washington lined up to spike the ball, but the clock ticked down to zero and coach Dan Quinn ripped off his headset in disgust.The Commanders had led by two touchdowns in the fourth quarter before Jameis Winston led a furious comeback for the NFC East-leading Giants (3-1-1). He connected with Isaiah Likely for a 17-yard touchdown midway through the fourth quarter – Likely’s second touchdown catch of the game – and then found Malik Nabers for the tying score, also from 17 yards, with 1:43 remaining.Jaguars stun Eagles in London as Cam Little hits 57-yard winner with one second leftRead moreWinston finished with 326 passing yards and three touchdowns. Daniels threw for 199 yards and rushed for 103 yards and two touchdowns while wearing a brace on his left elbow in his first game back since dislocating it for the second time in Week 2.On a dreary, rainy day at Northwest Stadium, the Giants struggled offensively in the first half but found their rhythm late as Winston led New York to scores on four consecutive possessions.But the Giants also made too many mistakes to come away with the victory. New York’s kicking problems proved costly, with Dominic Zvada converting only two of his five field-goal attempts.Meanwhile, the Giants’ defense struggled to contain Daniels, who rushed for two second-half touchdowns – a 38-yard run in the third quarter that made it 19-6 and a 26-yard score in the fourth that gave the Commanders a seemingly comfortable 27-13 lead.But the Giants rallied behind Winston and his two leading targets, Nabers (11 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown) and Likely (11 receptions for 94 yards and two touchdowns). On his second score, Likely had the ball punched out just after crossing the goal line, but the touchdown was upheld after a replay review.After Nabers’ tying touchdown, the Commanders had one last chance to win in regulation, but their drive stalled at midfield.Las Vegas Raiders 17-45 New England PatriotsDrake Maye threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score as theNew England Patriotsrolled past the Las Vegas Raiders 45-17 on Sunday.Maye completed 26 of 34 passes for 374 yards in the second 300-yard game of his career. Two touchdowns went to Pop Douglas and one each to Hunter Henry and Kyle Williams. Rhamondre Stevenson added a touchdown run.Maye became the first New England quarterback to throw at least three touchdown passes in consecutive games since Tom Brady in 2018. It was also his first turnover-free game of the season. He scored on a three-yard run.The Patriots (3-2) finished with a season-high 536 yards and forced a fumble despite playing without injured receiver Mack Hollins and cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III.Kirk Cousins completed 19 of 28 passes for 243 yards, including a touchdown to Brock Bowers that briefly pulled the Raiders (3-2) level. But Las Vegas did not reach the end zone again until the fourth quarter after scoring at least 26 points in each of their first four games.View image in fullscreenDrake Maye throws a pass under pressure from Raiders defenders during the Patriots’ victory at Gillette Stadium on Sunday in Foxborough, Massachusetts.Photograph: Charles Krupa/APNew York Jets 17-12 Cleveland BrownsBraelon Allen ran 22 yards for the go-ahead touchdown late in the fourth quarter after New York recovered a fumbled punt snap, and the Jets ended a three-game skid with a 17-12 victory over the Cleveland Browns on a rain-soaked Sunday.Rookie David Bailey had three of New York’s eight sacks of Deshaun Watson, and Geno Smith threw a touchdown pass to Garrett Wilson on the Jets’ opening drive, helping snap the Browns’ three-game winning streak.The Browns had a final chance when they got the ball with 1:41 left and no timeouts. But New York’s defense, as they had all game, stiffened and sealed the victory when Will McDonald strip-sacked Watson on fourth down and recovered the fumble.Smith completed 17 of 30 passes for 182 yards and the touchdown to Wilson, who had seven catches for 104 yards. Allen ran for 116 yards and the winning touchdown on 24 carries.It wasn’t pretty, with steady rain falling throughout the game as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias blew through the north-east. But the struggling Jets (2-3) were able to bounce back after surrendering a fourth-quarter lead.Pittsburgh Steelers 34-22 Indianapolis ColtsJaylen Warren piled up 188 total yards and two long touchdowns – one rushing and one receiving – to lead the Pittsburgh Steelers past the Indianapolis Colts 34-22 on Sunday.The Steelers (3-2) shook off a loss at Cleveland by relying on Warren and a defense that frequently bent but rarely broke.Warren caught six passes for 87 yards, including an 80-yard catch-and-run touchdown in the first quarter, and added 101 yards on the ground, highlighted by a 50-yard sprint to the end zone in the third quarter. The typically low-key former undrafted free agent celebrated by hurdling across the goal line.Aaron Rodgers completed 22 of 31 passes for 235 yards and three touchdowns. While Warren did most of the work on their 80-yard connection, the 42-year-old Rodgers absorbed a crushing hit from 314lb Colts defensive tackle Grover Stewart as he released the ball.Pat Freiermuth caught five passes for 44 yards and two touchdowns for Pittsburgh, the second a 17-yard pass from Rodgers with 6:40 remaining that gave the Steelers enough breathing room to beat the Colts for the 10th time in 12 meetings.Houston Texans 26-3 Tennessee TitansCJ Stroud threw for 261 yards and a touchdown and ran for another score as the Houston Texans snapped their winless start to the season by routing the Tennessee Titans 26-3 on Sunday.It was the second straight season Houston (1-4) ended an opening winless skid by beating Tennessee. This time, the Texans forced two turnovers and Will Anderson Jr had three of Houston’s four sacks. Ka’imi Fairbairn kicked four field goals as the Texans took a 12-3 halftime lead.Houston dominated the second and third quarters, outgaining the Titans 225-49 and outscoring them 16-0. The Texans held Tennessee to a season-low 187 total yards.The Titans (0-5) have now lost 11 straight games in the AFC South and six straight overall dating back to the end of last season.Tennessee led only after opening the game with a drive that ended in a 30-yard field goal by Joey Slye. Cam Ward finished with 170 passing yards.The Texans then forced a three-and-out before safety Jalen Pitre recovered a Tyjae Spears fumble on Tennessee’s next possession. Jake Hansen intercepted Ward on the ensuing drive, and Houston followed by forcing another three-and-out.View image in fullscreenTexans wide receiver Jaylin Noel catches a touchdown pass in front of Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor during the second half of Sunday’s game in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APMinnesota Vikings 23-13 New Orleans SaintsJustin Jefferson marked his return to Minnesota’s lineup with a leaping touchdown catch, Aaron Jones made up for an early fumble with a pivotal fourth-quarter score and the Vikings remained unbeaten with a 23-13 victory over the slumping New Orleans Saints on Sunday.Will Reichard made all three of his field-goal attempts from 40 yards or more for the Vikings (5-0), including a 55-yarder that put Minnesota ahead by 10 in the fourth quarter and all but condemned the Saints (1-4) to a third straight loss, all at the Superdome.Jones finished with 113 rushing yards on 25 carries. Jefferson, who sat out Week 4 with an ankle injury, caught six passes for 79 yards from Kyler Murray, who threw for 229 yards and a touchdown without a turnover and rushed for 51 yards.The Vikings, who entered the game allowing an NFL-low 12.8 points per game, surrendered only one offensive touchdown and held New Orleans to 142 yards.Safety Jonas Sanker returned a fumble 87 yards for the Saints’ other touchdown.Cincinnati Bengals 31-24 Miami DolphinsJoe Burrow threw four touchdown passes, safety Jordan Battle had two interceptions and the Cincinnati Bengals beat the Miami Dolphins 31-24 on Sunday.Ja’Marr Chase, who had been questionable after suffering a concussion last week against Jacksonville, caught six passes for 77 yards, including a spectacular one-handed, 45-yard touchdown catch that made it 28-10.Burrow completed 23 of 32 passes for 190 yards and also threw touchdowns to tight ends Mike Gesicki and Tanner Hudson and running back Samaje Perine. The Bengals quarterback exploited the Dolphins’ young secondary, completing passes to nine different receivers.Battle intercepted Malik Willis on consecutive drives in the second quarter. The safety had said earlier in the week that he had spotted a tell in Willis’s throwing motion, pointing out that the Dolphins quarterback appeared to tap the ball before releasing it.The Dolphins (0-5) pulled within seven points with 45 seconds remaining on Willis’s one-yard touchdown run, set up by a 23-yard catch by rookie Kevin Coleman Jr, who had also caught a touchdown earlier in the fourth quarter. Riley Patterson struck the left upright with the extra-point attempt, and the ensuing onside kick went out of bounds as Cincinnati snapped their two-game skid.Green Bay Packers 31-7 Chicago BearsChristian Watson caught two long touchdown passes from Jordan Love, MarShawn Lloyd also scored twice and the Green Bay Packers exacted a measure of revenge against the Chicago Bears with a 31-7 rout on Sunday.Love completed 25 of 31 passes for 367 yards, the most by a Packers quarterback against the Bears at Lambeau Field. He connected with Watson on a 42-yard touchdown in the first quarter and a 53-yarder in the third.Green Bay had lost three of their previous four meetings with Chicago and squandered a 21-3 halftime lead in a 31-27 NFC wild-card playoff defeat last season. Caleb Williams celebrated that comeback victory by grating cheese on the field, mocking Green Bay’s Cheesehead fanbase.Williams missed a third straight game on Sunday with a hamstring injury, leaving Tyson Bagent to start in his place. Xavier McKinney intercepted two of Bagent’s passes as the Packers forced five turnovers.View image in fullscreenPackers running back MarShawn Lloyd celebrates a rushing touchdown with fans at Lambeau Field during Sunday’s 31-7 victory over the Bears in Green Bay, Wisconsin.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesDetroit Lions 45-21 Arizona CardinalsJared Goff threw three touchdown passes, Jahmyr Gibbs added 151 yards rushing and two more scores, and the Detroit Lions shook off a slow start by scoring 31 unanswered points to roll past the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday.Gibbs barreled into the end zone on a one-yard run in the second quarter and added a three-yard touchdown run in the fourth, bouncing off the offensive line before reversing field and finding room to run. The three-time Pro Bowl selection has scored an NFL-record 58 touchdowns before his 25th birthday, surpassing Lions great Barry Sanders, who had 57.Jameson Williams had his first game with multiple touchdown receptions, catching scoring passes of eight and 39 yards for Detroit (3-2).Arizona (1-4) have lost nine straight home games, a streak stretching back more than a year.It was a disappointing, bizarre afternoon for the Cardinals, who finalized a trade to send receiver Marvin Harrison Jr to the Houston Texans midway through the first quarter. Harrison was one of the team’s five inactive players against the Lions and was not seen at the stadium.Denver Broncos 23-17 Los Angeles ChargersWil Lutz kicked a go-ahead 19-yard field goal with 5:07 remaining, lifting the Denver Broncos to a 23-17 victory over the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday.Lutz’s 36-yarder with 1:08 left extended the lead and capped a run of 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter for the Broncos (3-2).Denver earned their first division win and first victory at SoFi Stadium since 2023, with coach Sean Payton calling the plays. He took those duties away from offensive coordinator Davis Webb earlier in the week. The Broncos won without injured cornerbacks Pat Surtain II (ankle) and Riley Moss (ribs).The Chargers also started 0-5 in 2023, the year before coach Jim Harbaugh took over. They came in with a decimated offensive line featuring four rookies trying to protect quarterback Justin Herbert, who completed 14 of 24 passes for 121 yards, a touchdown and an interception while being sacked five times.Courtland Sutton caught a five-yard touchdown pass from Bo Nix, tying the score at 17 midway through the fourth quarter. The Broncos got the ball back after Herbert came up short on fourth-and-one, and the Chargers sputtered the rest of the way.San Francisco 49ers 32-29 Seattle SeahawksBrock Purdy engineered two scoring drives in the fourth quarter as the San Francisco 49ers rallied to beat the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 on Sunday, with Eddy Piñeiro kicking a 43-yard field goal with 1:56 remaining.The win for the 49ers (5-0) offered a measure of revenge for their two late-season losses to Seattle (3-2) last season, including a 41-6 defeat in the divisional round of the playoffs with a short-handed roster.San Francisco were healthier for the first meeting this season, and Purdy delivered late as the 49ers opened with five straight wins for the third time in eight seasons.The game featured an NFL season-high seven combined turnovers, the ejection of 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw and no touchdown drives of more than 25 yards before San Francisco took over trailing 26-21 late in the third quarter.Purdy responded with an impressive drive against Seattle’s vaunted defense, including a 28-yard pass to Mike Evans after an intentional grounding penalty left the 49ers facing second-and-21.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsNew England PatriotsLas Vegas RaidersNew York GiantsDallas CowboysShareReuse this content

title: Exeter finally find first win despite Christian Wade’s hat-trick for Newcastle | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Exeter register first Prem win of the season by beating Newcastle 34-28 while Wade becomes only the second player to score 100 top-tier tries
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Exeter register first Prem win of the season by beating Newcastle 34-28 while Wade becomes only the second player to score 100 top-tier tries
Content: Bachuki Tchumbadze celebrates scoring Exeter’s fifth try in their win against Newcastle.Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBachuki Tchumbadze celebrates scoring Exeter’s fifth try in their win against Newcastle.Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty ImagesPrem RugbyExeter finally find first win despite Christian Wade’s hat-trick for NewcastlePrem Rugby: Exeter 34-28 NewcastleWade becomes second player to score 100 top-tier triesRobert Kitsonat Sandy ParkSun 11 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the current gushing torrent of Prem tries here was a reminder that winning still trumps all else. Exeter finally have their first, relieving, victory of the campaign but there were times when it seemedNewcastlemight conceivably secure a first away league success in almost four years. In the event the Red Bulls fell just short despite Christian Wade running in a hat-trick to become only the second player to score 100 top-tier tries.Exeter will be suitably relieved to have edged a curate’s egg of a contest, ultimately made safe by a late try from their Georgian prop Bachuki Tchumbadze. The Chiefs’ Italian international back-rower Ross Vintcent also contributed two ­first-quarter tries to steal some of the prolific Wade’s thunder. The 35-year-old retains a poacher’s instinct and is now closing in fast – in every sense – on Chris Ashton’s all-time Prem career haul of 101.Sleightholme hat-trick fires up Northampton in 11-try blast of BathRead moreA game of nine tries, slightly below average for this season, was also notable for a promising debut display from 18-year-old Jake Dalziel, the youngest player to represent Newcastle in the Prem and the premature departure of England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso with a tweaked hamstring. “I don’t think it’s a catastrophe but he said he doesn’t feel right,” said Rob Baxter, Exeter’s director of rugby. “It’s more of a concern than a long-term worry.”The same, for now, applies to the meagre attendance of 7,071 on a grey but relatively mild afternoon. This week Exeter slashed ticket prices in most categories between now and Christmas and still there were ­thousands of empty seats around the ground. The quality of the product matters but so, increasingly, does value for money in these difficult economic days.For the first time in recent years for a league fixture here there was not a soul on the North Terrace behind the posts, a real sign of the times. Just 8,682 showed up for Exeter’s opening weekendWest Country derby against Gloucesterand here a stadium with a maximum capacity of 15,000 was more than half empty.View image in fullscreenNewcastle Red Bulls’ Christian Wade evades Henry Slade to score the second of this three tries against Exeter.Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty ImagesThere are plenty of other outdoor activities available in Devon at this time of year but, otherwise, people are either preferring to watch from the comfort of their own sofas, save up for Christmas or they’re not overly bothered. Which, given Chiefsmade the Prem final in June, it is a concerning state of affairs for all involved in marketing and selling the professional game.Those who did turn up, however, were treated to an eventful tussle with five tries in the opening quarter alone. The eager Vintcent collected two of them, the first inside 40 seconds after a chargedown with the help of a (legal) headed assist. Wade was also productively busy, running in an easy first and then unselfishly releasing Max Hicks for a second in the same right corner.Quick GuideGilmore happy despite Harlequins' defeat by SaleShowJason Gilmore claimed his Harlequinsside restored pride despite a third successive loss of the Prem campaign against Sale in Salford.The Sharks snatched a 28-24 win with a 73rd-minute penalty try after they had been outplayed for long periods by a Quins side smarting from last weekend’s 48-0 humiliation against Gloucester.“It’s disappointing. We probably created three chances in the first half which we didn’t take which came back to bite us,” said the Harlequins head coach. “Fair play to Sale. They got themselves back into the game with their set piece but I’m really proud of the boys’ efforts up here.“Two bonus points on the road up here is, I wouldn’t say pleasing, but I’m just happy for the boys that they got some reward out of their work. If you’re prepared to go to dark places for us and win those collisions, then you’re going to get selected. If you’re dipping your toe in one week and then not the next, then we can’t tolerate that.“You can’t be up one week and then down the next week like we had last week. Performance will dictate the shirts.”Marcus Smith impressed with two tries on his return after injury and Harlequins hooker Sam Riley also touched down twice.But Sale, who trailed 17-14 at the break, fought back with Ben Bamber adding to first-half tries from Elia Canakaivata and Gus Warr before the decisive late penalty try.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Hicks is an interesting arrival in the Prem, having grown up near Ethan Roots in New Zealand and even worked on the same building site as his opposite number. He is also English qualified as is the Red Bulls No 8 Hoskins Sotutu, which helps explain why the national head coach Steve Borthwick made the trip to Devon.With the autumn block of the Nations Championship just around the corner this was a timely moment, therefore, for Henry Slade to slice through a big gap behind Werner Kok and score from 40 metres out. The centre also converted his own score from wide out but it was still the visitors who led at the interval.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving lost Roots to the sin-bin for a no-arms tackle on Harrison ­Obatoyinbo, the Red Bulls now had the youthful Dalziel pulling the strings and the teenager’s beautiful offload outside to Sammy Arnold created the platform for Wade to accelerate away for his second. Dalziel, the son of the British & Irish Lions assistant coach John Dalziel, is highly rated in Scotland and looks to have an extremely promising top-level future.View image in fullscreenRed Bulls’ 18-year-old Jake Dalziel marked his debut as the youngest player to represent Newcastle in the Prem.Photograph: Phil Mingo/PPAUK/ShutterstockAfter a stern half-time lecture from Baxter about their lack of defensive energy, Exeter appeared to revive slightly and the former Bath full-back Sam Harris, on his Chiefs Prem debut, finished off a sharp blindside break from Stephen Varney. ­Unfortunately for the hosts, two misjudgments from Slade then muddied the waters, a loose offload allowing Wade to pounce for a third time and a midfield forward pass causing a potential try for Varney to be scrubbed out by the television match official.Instead it required a fine long-range penalty into the wind with 16 minutes remaining by Slade to nudge the Chiefs back in front before Tchumbadze rumbled over from close range. Those who had paid to attend were suitably grateful, though whether this performance frightens their next opponents Toulouse, the French Top 14 champions, is another matter. The likely unavailability of Feyi-Waboso will make it an even tougher assignment although Chiefs do now have their forceful Wallaby back-row forward Tom Hooper back for this weekend’s opening round of the Champions Cup.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyExeterNewcastleRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Record-breaking quartet put Australia in full control against South Africa | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon shared nine wickets as Australia dismissed South Africa for 284 in the first Test in Durban
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon shared nine wickets as Australia dismissed South Africa for 284 in the first Test in Durban
Content: Pat Cummins punches the air after dismissing Tristan Stubbs for the second of his three wickets.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPat Cummins punches the air after dismissing Tristan Stubbs for the second of his three wickets.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesCricketRecord-breaking quartet put Australia in full control against South AfricaAustralia 390 & 33-0; South Africa 284Starc, Hazlewood, Cummins and Lyon share nine wicketsGeoff LemonSun 11 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a fractured news environment demonstrates, observations can be made from just about any perspective. One view of Australia’s Test team could focus on age, with the principal bowlers all having more than 33 years to their names. Another could focus on them all having more than 300 wickets.At the first Test in Durban, an unprecedented achievement by Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon is continuing, one that they began in Mackay two months ago: being the only quartet in history to walk on to Test fields as members of the 300 club. By the end of day three they had taken another nine, South Africa bowled out for 284,trailing by 139 runsby the time bad light stopped play with Australia 33 without loss.South Africa v Australia: first men’s cricket Test, day three – as it happenedRead moreBeyond individual feats, those players are defined by the work they have done together: 38 Tests and counting as a group blitzes the previous record, however you define frontline bowlers. So it went through the first session of the third day. Hazlewood had already taken out Ryan Rickelton with a trademark dismissal the previous evening, but the morning looked set to be South Africa’s. A nice breeze, a snoozing surface, and a bushel of boundaries for Aiden Markram and David Bedingham, the latter taking three in a row from Starc.But Starc was the one to flip the story, the left-armer around the wicket to draw Markram’s edge from a big drive on 37, the ball lifting to cause the error. Temba Bavuma followed cheaply, caught at slip reverse-sweeping Lyon, then Bedingham went for 49, Cummins now the bowler getting lift to tease another nick. The scorecard reflected team effort: Cummins one for 18, Lyon one for 14, Starc one for 37, Hazlewood one for 35.That was the 31st over, before Wiaan Mulder bedded in with Tristan Stubbs. The match looked to be drifting by the 46th, as Australia turned to Travis Head, and Mulder immediately belted the part-time spinner for six and four. But at the other end was Cummins playing the middle-overs enforcer, as he so often does, finding a way when batting difficulty softens with the ball.The breakthrough bouncer was the wrong line, outside off-stump, but the length and the sense of threat initially made Mulder shape to play. The pace and sharpness of bounce meant his attempt to bail out was too late, frozen in the first half of his shot when the ball lobbed up for a catch. In Cummins’ next over, the bouncer ploy snared Stubbs, mindlessly hooking to fine leg. A 55-run stand had fizzled out with both participants gone in the 30s.The story of Australia’s four bowlers is also a story of Steve Smith’s catching. This innings took him back to the top of the Test catching list, in the game of statistical nip and tuck that he will continue to have with Joe Root for as long as they both play. Of Smith’s 223 catches so far, 150 have come from the current bowling quartet. His first three on this day were spectacular.View image in fullscreenSteve Smith takes the plaudits from his teammates after holding a superb catch to get rid of Kyle Verreynne.Photograph: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images/Getty ImagesFor the Bedingham dismissal he dived across from second slip, instinctively poaching a ball heading to first. When Bavuma shaped for the reverse hit, Smith had the fleetness of thought and foot to sidestep a couple of metres, putting himself in the path of a ball that would have flown by. At six down, Kyle Verreynne hit the same shot more sweetly, but Smith moved early again, this time putting himself in range for a full dive to his right and a one-hander. It was beyond the norm, Smith’s victory lap showing that even he rated the effort among his best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarco Jansen’s free swinging was fun but futile, his 26 from 20 balls far less useful for his team than Lyon’s 27 from 91 the day before, leaving South Africa 197 for eight after Jansen bashed Hazlewood to mid-off. The last three did emulate their Australian counterparts for a time, Simon Harmer adding 52 with Keshav Maharaj and 35 with Anrich Nortje, but Maharaj was caught at cover off Starc after tea, and Smith finally got a straightforward slip catch from Nortje.All out 284, trailing by 106, with only Beau Webster’s burgling of the No 11 to ruin the share of wickets, Australia’s big four ended with three for Cummins and two each for Starc, Lyon, and Hazlewood, taking their collective 1,641 wickets before this match to a round 1650. That number could only get so high because the age of the players is high enough to allow it. While their quality remains, the positive perspective wins out.Explore more on these topicsCricketAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamAustralia sportmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Taylor Knibb wins Ironman world title after leader collapses in dramatic Kona finish | Triathlon | The Guardian
description: American triathlete claims first Hawaiian Ironman crown after defending champion Solveig Løvseth collapses within sight of finish
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: American triathlete claims first Hawaiian Ironman crown after defending champion Solveig Løvseth collapses within sight of finish
Content: Taylor Knibb celebrates after winning the women’s Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, on Saturday.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty Images for IRONMANView image in fullscreenTaylor Knibb celebrates after winning the women’s Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, on Saturday.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty Images for IRONMANTriathlonTaylor Knibb wins Ironman world title after leader collapses in dramatic Kona finishKnibb overtakes Norwegian rival in final kilometerDefending champion Løvseth collapses while leadingFrance’s Vincent Luis wins men’s title on Kona debutRoger VaughanSun 11 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican triathlete Taylor Knibb has won her first Hawaiian Ironman world title after one of the most dramatic finishes in race history.With a mile left, Norwegian defending champion Solveig Løvseth led Knibb by more than a minute and looked rock-solid, having taken the lead from her inside the final 10km of the 42.2km marathon run.But then Løvseth quickly developed a dramatic case of the wobbles and collapsed. Knibb passed her about a kilometre from the finish and the Norwegian eventually recovered from the meltdown to finish eighth.It recalled the 1995 race, when Paula Newby-Fraser collapsed within just 500m of her seventh win and was passed by Karen Smyers.In a twist of history, Smyers helped hold the winner’s tape for Knibb.Vincent Luis of France won the men’s race aged 37, on his debut. It was just his third Ironman-distance race after Luis won Olympic bronze at Tokyo in the mixed team relay and claimed the 2019 and 2020 world championship series titles.View image in fullscreenTaylor Knibb competes during the marathon leg of the Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, on Saturday.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty Images for IRONMANGrace Thek was the best-placed Australian, rallying in the marathon to finish 10th on her debut at Kona. Nick Thompson finished 11th among the professional men.Essendon’s David Zaharakis joined a select group of former AFL players to finish Hawaii as an age-group competitor.Knibb had to pull out of the race a year ago with only a couple of kilometres left, while in the lead.But on Sunday (AEST), the American showed she had learned her painful lessons, staying composed when Løvseth passed her.Knibb won the 3.8km swim, 180km cycle and 42.2km run event – triathlon’s most famous race – in eight hours, 36 minutes and 29 seconds. Germany’s Laura Philipp was three minutes back in second.Løvseth was able to walk to the finish, smiling and high-fiving fans. Always a tough race, Hawaii this year was marked by particularly high humidity, and several contenders either did not finish or hit the wall.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“Last year played a huge part because ... I made a big decision and it was just, ‘take care of yourself’, because it was getting really hard,” Knibb said.“Then when Solveig came back, I thought I can’t fight because if I fight, I’m going to lose, so I had to learn from last year to just get to the finish line, get to the finish line, get to the finish line.”Luis had said before his Kona debut that he would also retire afterwards. He will now reconsider.The Frenchman held off hard-charging Norwegian Gustav Iden, the 2022 winner, to claim the world title in 7hr 47min 27sec. Iden finished runner-up in 7:49:03.“I said if I win, I will maybe not continue, but I went through some dark places in the last 3-4km – but 100% worth it,” Luis said.“Let’s see, I have a few nights out to decide what to do with my life now.”Explore more on these topicsTriathlonAthleticsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti | Djibouti | The Guardian
description: Eighty-four others still missing from vessel heading to Yemen with 305 people onboard, UN migration agency says
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Eighty-four others still missing from vessel heading to Yemen with 305 people onboard, UN migration agency says
Content: A member of the International Organization for Migration inspects the abandoned wreckage of a boat near Obock in April.Photograph: Luis Tato/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA member of the International Organization for Migration inspects the abandoned wreckage of a boat near Obock in April.Photograph: Luis Tato/AFP/Getty ImagesDjiboutiAt least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off DjiboutiEighty-four others still missing from vessel heading to Yemen with 305 people onboard, UN migration agency saysCarlos Mureithiin NairobiSun 11 Oct 2026 09.56 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization forMigration(IOM) said.Another 84 people are still missing after the incident, which, according to survivors, happened near Guhere, north of the fishing town of Obock, during the night of 8-9 October when the boat was travelling fromDjiboutito Yemen.Eighty-two people, all Ethiopian nationals, survived the capsizing, the UN agency said.It described the incident as one of the deadliest boat disasters recorded on a migration corridor between the Horn ofAfricaand the Arab peninsula known as the eastern route.“This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” said Alexandre Coissac, the IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti.The organisation is providing healthcare, psychosocial, food and other assistance to 64 survivors at its Obock migrant response centre.The IOM is working with local authorities to provide emergency assistance. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, and local authorities are providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for those who died.The eastern route is one of the busiest migration paths in the world.Hundreds of thousands of peoplea year, mostly Ethiopians and Somalis, use it to reach Gulf countries, mainly Saudi Arabia. Some have been forced out of their communities by conflict and natural disasters, and others move to seek work and other economic opportunities.The route accounts for most of the migratory movement from the Horn ofAfrica. The other main ones are the northern route to north Africa and Europe, and the southern route to southern Africa.The eastern route is also one of the most dangerous globally, with some people dying from walking long distances in searing heat and others from the capsizing of boats that smugglers have crammed them on to in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA 2019 photo shows Ethiopians, led by a people smuggler, walking to an embarking point outside Obock.Photograph: Nariman El-Mofty/APCoissac said: “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”In 2025, more than 900 people died or went missing along the route, according to the IOM’s missing migrants project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%. In March, nine people died and 45 went missing after a migrant boat capsized.This week’s tragedy shows the movement is happening despitefightingbetween the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group and Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast.The violence has forced more than 3,800 people to cross to Djibouti to seek protection, according to the country’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims (Onars).Explore more on these topicsDjiboutiMigrationAfricaRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricaShareReuse this content

title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad | Pennsylvania | The Guardian
description: Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary
Content: Julius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenJulius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APPennsylvaniaPennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dadFather of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinaryCoral Murphy Marcosand agenciesSun 11 Oct 2026 19.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in amassshooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, theAssociated Press reports.“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in PennsylvaniaRead moreThe 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend toldCleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.View image in fullscreenFirefighters work outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in a mass shooting on Saturday in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty ImagesResponding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at anews conference.“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a1982 massacrein Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in aposton X on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsPennsylvaniaUS crimeGun crimeUS gun controlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo to have surgery to remove nodule on his lung | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Pontiff says it was detected at an early stage and procedure will take place in the coming days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pontiff says it was detected at an early stage and procedure will take place in the coming days
Content: Leo made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing at the Vatican.Photograph: Elisabetta Trevisan/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeo made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing at the Vatican.Photograph: Elisabetta Trevisan/ReutersPope Leo XIVPope Leo to have surgery to remove nodule on his lungPontiff says it was detected at an early stage and procedure will take place in the coming daysAssociated PressSun 11 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo XIV has said he will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a nodular lesion on his lung that was recently discovered during medical checks.The 71-year-old said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or well localised. The Vatican later said Leo would undergo surgery in the first days of this week, with an expected recovery time of a week.The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3cm (1in) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.Leo has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.The pope has an extensive trip planned to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November. It is unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery will affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks on Sunday that he planned to go.In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check “doctors found a small, localised nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it.“The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis,died on 21 April 2025of a stroke after a long hospitalisation brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs.The Italian premier, Giorgia Meloni, who was among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalisation, expressed her support and that of the Italian government to Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days”. In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyCatholicismReligionItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism | Chile | The Guardian
description: In the Atacama desert, the extraction of lithium – so crucial to addressing the climate crisis – comes with escalating social and environmental costs
Author: Thea Riofrancos
Headline: In the Atacama desert, the extraction of lithium – so crucial to addressing the climate crisis – comes with escalating social and environmental costs
Content: Andean flamingos. All three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline.Photograph: Santiago Urquijo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndean flamingos. All three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline.Photograph: Santiago Urquijo/Getty ImagesChileWhy a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalismIn the Atacama desert, the extraction of lithium – so crucial to addressing the climate crisis – comes with escalating social and environmental costsThea RiofrancosSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhigh-altitude desert plateau traverses Argentina, Bolivia andChile. I am on the Chilean side, sitting in a Jeep along with two other researchers. The afternoon air is thin and brisk but the sun is piercing – a combination I am familiar with from years of living and travelling in South America’s Andean range.The landscape is a study in contrasts and contours: broad basins suddenly cut off by sweeping curves; flat expanses sliced by near vertical ascents. The Licancabur volcano looms large above us. Vegetation and humidity levels change rapidly with the rising altitude, bringing cooler temperatures, wetter air and denser plant life.We are driving to the Salar de Atacama–the Atacama salt flats – the largest of several dozen salt flats in northern Chile, and the third largest in the world. The brilliant white flat lies in a high basin 7,500ft above sea level, enclosed by the even higher Andean mountains to the east and the Domeyko mountains to the west.View image in fullscreenLagunas Baltinache in the Atacama desert.Photograph: Kanawa_Studio/Getty ImagesThis striking landscape–the salt flat, the flamingos, and the neighbouring Indigenous communities–is under threat from a counterintuitive source: our efforts to save the planet from catastrophic climate change. Just beneath my feet is nearly one-quarter of the world’s lithium reserves, suspended in water saltier than the ocean.Lithium is essential to addressing the climate crisis. It is a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries that play a starring role in eliminating carbon emissions from transportation and energy – the two highest emitting sectors. But extracting this lithium will come at escalating social and environmental costs. It is this dilemma that has brought me to the salt flat.When it does rain in the Atacama, it’s hard to overstate the intensity of the floods. I once found myself caught in what is calledinvierno boliviano, or Bolivian winter, a paradoxical name for a weather phenomenon that occurs during the southern hemisphere’s summer months. These rainy fronts originate in the Amazon and travel up the steep slopes of the Andean mountains, where Bolivia’s high-altitude winds then drive them up and over the ridges, until their torrents drench the Chilean high plateau.View image in fullscreenFlamingos in Laguna Chaxa in the Atacama desert.Photograph: mFlower/Getty ImagesThe scientific term for closed basins like the Atacama is “endorheic” (etymologically, “inside” and “flow”), for water can flow down into the Atacama basin but it cannot leave – except by evaporation. And this is the key to Atacama’s extraordinary lithium brine.After deluges like the one I experienced, water pours down the surrounding mountains; during the long dry spells between storms, it trickles down ravines from the precious mountain springs. As it flows, the water leeches lithium from the volcanic rock, picks up wind-scoured lithium dust, and carries it down to the nucleus, or centre, of thesalar. This pooled surface water can only escape through evaporation, and with every drop of water that evaporates, the concentration of lithium in the remaining brine increases. Without the parched and sun-blasted Atacama’s extraordinarily high evaporation rate, lithium concentrations would not reach the “economical” levels prized by mining companies.Yet further lithium enrichment takes place out of sight. Remaining water gradually seeps into the ground, creating underground wells of lithium-rich brine. These wells are linked to complex hydrothermal systems. Then the heat of magma, especially near the Andes’ active fault lines, drives circulations of subsurface brine through fissures and porous geological strata, dissolving even more lithium out of the subsurface rock.View image in fullscreenThe Piedras Rojas, or red rocks, of the Atacama desertPhotograph: Tatsuya Ohinata/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe resulting brine deposits anywhere from four to 200 feet below the Atacama’s salty crust represent a potential bonanza to corporations. The Atacama’s singular coincidence of climactic, geological, geothermal and hydrological conditions makes it one of the least expensive places on Earth to mine lithium.And at each step, the process of “mining water” is intimately related to the very environmental conditions that formed the valuable deposits in the first place: miners pump the underground brine to vast evaporation ponds on the surface, where natural evaporation concentrates the brine yet again, increasing its lithium levels 40-fold, from approximately 0.15% to a whopping 6%. One cycle of the process can take 10 to 24 months, depending on brine quality and weather conditions.But this relatively low-cost, low-tech and supposedly low-impact extractive process nonetheless imperils the species and communities that call the Atacama desert home. And it is a microcosm of a planetary phenomenon: the expanding extractive frontiers of green capitalism. Everywhere that mines are dug up to provide raw materials for the energy transition, global climate action comes into conflict with local environmental protection.View image in fullscreenThe expanse of the Atacama salt flat.Photograph: Atlantide Phototravel/Getty ImagesMining always transforms, in many ways irrevocably, the landscapes in which it occurs. In remaking the earth in the image of extractive capital, physically and chemically separating what is deemed valuable from often toxic waste, mining evokes the image of terraforming so central to science fiction.But if terraforming is supposed to make a lifeless planet as verdant as Earth, mining, to the contrary, often leaves parts of Earth itself uninhabitable. While the environmental impacts of mining brine are less obvious to the naked eye than, say, mountaintop removal, extracting the lithium-rich liquid does in fact threaten a fragile, desert water system, along with the ecosystems and people that depend on it.The world’s oldest, driest desert may appear bereft of life. Ecologists call it a “polyextreme” environment, given its altitude and high direct solar radiation, its intense aridity, its huge diurnal temperature swings and its densely saline lakes. Those who study such polyextreme environments alternately describe them as low-diversity, with relatively simple webs of life, or astonishing in their biodiversity. It all depends on perspective. Plants and animals have evolved to make do with less and saltier water and, above all, the abundant energy of relentless sun. Extremity stimulates nature’s creativity.Artemia,or brine shrimp, thrive in hypersaline lakes that would be intolerable to most species. These tiny creatures are a key node in the plateau’s food chain. The brine shrimp eat bacteria and phytoplankton (microscopic plants) and are, in turn, food for Chilean flamingos. The flamingos, too, have adapted to the saline lagoons, evolving a filter in their bills akin to the lamellar membranes of oysters or whales to strain the microscopic plants and animals from the brine.View image in fullscreenFlamingos at Laguna Chaxa park in the Atacama desert.Photograph: DoraDalton/Getty ImagesThe flamingos are a barometer of wetland health. As the birds travel the salt flats in search of food and mates (attracted through a courtship ritual of synchronised dancing), they link together the saline lakes into a web of habitats. And as these habitats suffer, so do flamingo populations: all three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline.The distinct drivers of this population loss reveal the compounding harms afflicting this fragile environment. Warmer average temperatures due to climate change evaporate surface water faster, reducing the blue-green algae essential to flamingo andArtemiadiets.
