And the noise and traffic associated with mining operations appear to directly disrupt the flamingos’ breeding.‘The source of all life is here’: plan to mine lithium in Chilean salt flat sparks fears of water scarcityRead moreResearchers are struggling to predict the overall direction of the multiple processes changing the Atacama. Science can only play catchup, documenting the impacts long after the harm has occurred. Lithium extraction’s threat to the liquid supporting its ecosystem is a slow-motion disaster, with planetary causes and consequences.This fact raises existential questions for the planet’s zero-carbon future.In the Atacama, global supply chains intersect with local food chains, webs of economic production undermine webs of life, and colonisation and postcolonial state-building erase ancient histories of continuous Indigenous settlement. And these unexpected entanglements are just the beginning of the story. In more ways than I could have imagined when I first stepped foot on the Atacama salt flat on that blustery day, this extractive frontier is a portal into our planetary future.The task of achieving a globally just energy transition is daunting. But it is possible. Achieving it requires understanding supply chains in reverse, starting from what we produce and consume and working backwards to their material inputs and, further still, to the relentless scramble for new extractive frontiers. Policies that promote alternatives to car use, reduce sprawl, encourage more compact batteries and require recycling would all reduce the scale of mining needed for carbon-free transportation.We can start by demanding supply chains organised around justice for everyone they touch, rather than profits for just a few. Just as any workplace is simultaneously a site of exploitation and locus of worker power, and any mine is at once a setting for extraction and a potential scene of community resistance, the supply chains of green technologies are both a means of domination – of people and of nature – and fertile ground for making the world anew.This is an edited extract from Extraction: The Frontiers of Green Capitalismby Thea Riofrancos, published by Icon Books at £20 in the UK. To support the Guardian,order your copyatguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsChileMiningCritical mineralsAmericasDesertsEndangered habitatsConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action | Politics | The Guardian
description: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold
Content: Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard a central plank of her bid to become the next prime minister in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard a central plank of her bid to become the next prime minister in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAPoliticsAnalysis‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate actionFiona HarveyEnvironment editorTories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on holdSun 11 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTShareNew homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election.Kemi Badenoch madescrapping the future homes standard(FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week.The announcement gained little attention compared to herinheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households tohigher bills for decades to come.Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet errorRead moreThe Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulationcosts about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building– a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to savemore than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000.Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.”View image in fullscreenConstruction workers install solar panels on a house in the north-east of England.Photograph: Washington Imaging/AlamyHousebuilders have beenamong the biggest donors to the Conservative party, though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit.Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.”Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England.The party’s U-turn on environmental issues andnet zerowas contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression.“Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.”While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, whichresolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power.View image in fullscreenZack Polanski at the party conference in Bournemouth. The Greens will still prioritise renewable energy but MPs will now support new nuclear reactors.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsAlthough the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGreen party drops longstanding opposition to nuclear powerRead morePaul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “TheGreen partyhas taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes.“With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.”The battle between the Green party and theLabourparty in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds.Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.”At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced apublicly owned body to invest in the energy grid, alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades. There was also a nod towards localised support for nature with acommunity fund for planting 500,000 trees across England.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature at the Labour conference.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAMcCarthy said: “Voters will be comparing Labour with other parties that have a clear plan to lower energy bills and tackle the climate crisis rather than with the fantasies of theConservativesand Reform. Labour has a clear plan but needs to deliver it – starting with a full-throated rejection of any scramble for fossil fuels in the North Sea.”Thedecision on the future of the Rosebank and Jackdaw drilling siteswas reportedly postponed for the byelection, and McCarthy said it would “truly define this government’s legacy on climate”.Failure to recognise and tackle the damage caused to the UK by a summer of record heat and drought would prove costly, campaigners warned. Arecord El Niño weather system is brewing, super-charged by global heating and likely to bring heatwaves, droughts and floods to key agricultural areas, pushing millions into hunger and raising food prices globally.Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “With El Niño bringing a wetter and stormier winter season to the UK, we desperately need to see some parties getting back in touch with reality. The government must translate its words into action that delivers for people and the planet.”Explore more on these topicsPoliticsConservativesGreen partyLabourKemi BadenochZack PolanskiAndy BurnhamanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader | Schools | The Guardian
description: NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers
Content: Pupils line up with their water bottles at a school in Essex during the heatwave in June.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenPupils line up with their water bottles at a school in Essex during the heatwave in June.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersSchoolsRetrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leaderNEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachersMatthew TaylorSun 11 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had adevastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.Speaking to the Guardian, Kebede called on the government to roll out a mass retrofitting programme to ensure schools – which he said had been built “for a different climate” – were better equipped to deal with extreme heat ahead of next summer’sEl Niño-charged temperatures.And he said it was time for a national conversation about other measures that could help schools adapt to the reality of a rapidly warming climate.“There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate,” he said. “You might want to consider moving the school year around, or having a longer summer holiday – in hot countries they tend to have a longer summer holiday. You might consider an earlier start and earlier finish … and perhaps we don’t want exams to be happening in the hottest part of the year.”Kebede said he had been inundated with messages from teachers during this summer’s heatwaves urging the union to help.“The last time I felt that level of panic in the profession was during the Covid pandemic,” he said. “I was being routinely contacted by members in distress … they felt there was a real risk and danger to themselves and to their pupils.”View image in fullscreenDaniel Kebede: ‘There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate.’Photograph: PA/AlamyAt least760,000 schoolchildrenin England and Wales missed lessons owing to school closures during this summer’s June heatwave – one in five in the UK in the space of a few months – with pupils missing more than 15m hours of lesson time.School staff told the Guardian that learning was almost impossible as temperature records were broken, with pupil behaviour and attention deteriorating rapidly.One primary school teacher said: “Everyone was lying or sitting on the floor with their water bottles, sweating, moaning and feeling tired, [complaining of] headaches and nausea. The adults barely coped and most of the children were calling for their mummies and daddies. There was no learning, just surviving the best we could.”‘Children were calling for their mummies’: UK pupils struggle in 40C-plus classroomsRead moreThis summer’s severe heat was not confined to the UK: brutal temperatures and devastating wildfires hit countries across Europe. One of thekey demands of the student protestersthat have taken to the streets in France this week has been action to make classrooms bearable during extreme heat.Kebede warned that in the UK the impact of these bouts of extreme weather was falling hardest on more disadvantaged communities. He said children were often being sent home to flats that were unsuited to extreme heat, and to parents and carers who were unable to work from home or take time off.“It is having a really uneven impact and it’s particularly impacting children who live in deprived urban areas … you will have a two-tier system where schools in more affluent areas are able to cope with extreme heat.”Kebede said many of the UK’s schools were housed in either old Victorian-era buildings or those built in the 1960s and 1970s, and neither style was equipped to cope with the extreme heat that is expected to become a feature of UK summers.He said a major capital building programme could transform schools, making them “fit for the century we are living in” and also creating good unionised apprenticeships and jobs, revitalising local communities.“We really need plans in place now because [what we experienced this summer] is going to be the norm,” Kebede said.Explore more on these topicsSchoolsTeachingTrade unionsEducation policyExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: There’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayor | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space
Content: Liam Gallagher and Noel Gallagher of Oasis on stage in Chicago in 2025.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher and Noel Gallagher of Oasis on stage in Chicago in 2025.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesGreater ManchesterThere’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayorBev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production spaceHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheManchestermayor, Bev Craig, has said the city’s music scene is about more than just Oasis, as she announced funding to nurture a diverse range of local artists, be they “guitar bands or not”.Craig pledged the £2m investment funding inGreater Manchester, as the city region hosted a conference for the creative industries at MediaCity in Salford.She said there was a “real intentionality” to what Manchester was doing, in terms of growing its own music industry and attracting international events.Earlier this year, Manchester’s Co-op Live arena hosted the Brit awards and the Mobos, Europe’s biggest and most influential celebration of Black music and culture.“I wanted to have a major event that celebrated black music, culture and creativity,” Craig said, “and so that’s why we said, just after the Brits, we’d host their 30th anniversary, because we knew it would be the last one that theMobos founder Kanyawould be able to come to.”“I think there’s a real intentionality around what we’re doing with our music scene,” she added. “We’re known, I think, over the world for the influence that some of our indie guitar bands have had on Greater Manchester music, but there’s more to Greater Manchester’s music scene than justOasis.”View image in fullscreenBev Craig was addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit.Photograph: Marieke Macklon/The Guardian“I’m struck by the diversity, the creativity, the talent that we see,” Craig said. “And the job, as I see it, is making sure that that next generation of talent in an industry that’s becoming more and more middle-class, more and more London-centric, and a world where it’s more and more expensive to be able to break through, that we’re giving our local artists the hand up that they need to be able to be the next big thing, guitar band or not.”Addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit on Friday, Craig set out her plan for diversifying opportunities in the music industry. She also outlined commitments to support AI literacy for music professionals, and to monitor the impact of new technologies on employment, income and diversity in Greater Manchester’s music sector.The festival that accompanied the summit featured performances from up-and-coming black and minority ethnic artists including Bawo, JayaHadADream and Alt Blk Era.The final day of the conference was convened by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, whose love of Manchester guitar bands is well known.The culture minister Ian Murray told the conference: “With a prime minister who picks up his guitar to murder Smiths tracks, we have a passion from the very top.He added, joking: “That’s probably a career-limiting sentence for me.”“We’re living and working at a time of considerable change, particularly with technology,” Murray said, “but the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by the choices we make today, and how we support talent, how we reward creativity and how we embrace that innovation.”The £2m of funding Craig has set out is in addition to the £4m Culture Fund investment announced earlier this month, which will fund music projects from grassroots venues to world-renowned institutions.The additional funding is aimed at improving access to rehearsal and production space across the city region, providing practical support and ensuring there are jobs for musicians in their communities.Although the Manchester music scene may be about more than Oasis, the newly elected Manchester mayor did say she would be going to see the band on their sellout tour next year, which includes 11 nights at Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium.“I will, and thankfully the price of pints are much too expensive and the clientele have aged [which] means that you’re not as cautious as to what’s travelling through the air as historically you once would [be],” she said.But she added that “as somebody who loves all forms of music” she was “as excited about seeing [Merseyside band] the Ks at Beyond the Music as I am about seeing Oasis”.“I’m a little bit more into my dance music than the previous mayor as well,” Craig added. “So maybe a bit more varied in my tastes, shall we say.”Explore more on these topicsGreater ManchesterBev CraigManchesterSalfordOasisArts fundingArts policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’ | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the series
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the series
Content: Richard E Grant: ‘I can only imagine the faces of the producers.’Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenRichard E Grant: ‘I can only imagine the faces of the producers.’Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe TraitorsRichard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the seriesMatthew WeaverSun 11 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard E Grant has said his early exit from The Celebrity Traitors was due to his failure to realise his fellow contestants would take him seriously.The Withnail and I actor was voted off as a traitor after brazenly admitting his status to other contestants.Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Grant said revealing his true identity so early was a mistake. “I never thought they would take me seriously,” he said.“It was a completely catastrophically idiotic thing to do. I can only imagine the faces of the producers looking at each other and mouthing ‘he said what?!’. The strategy of no strategy is the strategy, clearly.”He revealed that his daughter told him before filming that he would be “slaughtered” as he was “incapable of hiding what you feel about people or anything”.During the first episode, Grant appeared to be thrilled to be selected as a traitor. His enthusiasm for the role appeared to get the better of him when he was asked by his fellow contestant Joe Lycett which side he was on.When Grant confessed to being a traitor, Lycett said: “I think you’ve done something that’s never been done in the game. It’s a bold strategy.”View image in fullscreenGrant (right) with Rob Beckett on The Celebrity Traitors. The actor says he has chosen not to watch the series.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAGrant said he now realised he should have made a joke of his admission. He said: “What I should have done in retrospect is go round everybody and say ‘are you a traitor? Yeah. I am a traitor, I am Spartacus. I am a traitor,’ to try and make light of it, but that may have dug my grave even deeper.”Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic | Stuart HeritageRead moreExplaining the context, he suggested contestants were treated like children and prisoners. He said: “You are so institutionalised in that thing within 24 hours, because you are isolated, kept in a room, there is a guard outside your door, your food is delivered and there’s no internet access, so you are kind of shut down.“You are also not told what time it is and are also prescribed on a daily basis what you are going to wear. So, you are kind of infantilised and institutionalised at the same time.”He said he had chosen to avoid watching the series. “It’s a weird thing because as an actor it is very uncomfortable to watch yourself, and if you watch yourself unscripted – which Traitors is – there’s no place to hide. That is unequivocally you.”Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsRichard E GrantnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flu cases higher than usual in England during September, experts say | Flu | The Guardian
description: UK Health Security Agency notes above-average activity and urges at-risk groups to get vaccinated
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: UK Health Security Agency notes above-average activity and urges at-risk groups to get vaccinated
Content: A private flu vaccination costs about £20 at most high street pharmacies, and some retailers offer them for under £10 as part of membership schemes.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA private flu vaccination costs about £20 at most high street pharmacies, and some retailers offer them for under £10 as part of membership schemes.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesFluFlu cases higher than usual in England during September, experts sayUK Health Security Agency notes above-average activity and urges at-risk groups to get vaccinatedNicola DavisScience correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlu is striking earlier than usual inEngland, experts have said, insisting that vaccination is the best way to blunt its impact.According to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), flu is at low levels, butvarious metrics, such as the proportion of positive tests and GP consultations for influenza-like illness, suggest it is on the rise, with the number of emergency-department attendances for influenza-like illness above seasonally expected levels.“Flu activity throughout September has been higher than in the same period during all past four winter seasons,” UKHSA reported, adding that flu trends had been rising since August.Prof Sir Andrew Pollard, the director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, said: “There is one simple action for all those who are at risk because of age or their underlying health conditions, which is to get vaccinated as soon as possible and before we reach the peak of transmission.“Everyone can benefit from being vaccinated but free vaccines are only available for children and those in higher-risk groups.”He added that those who were not eligible for a free flu vaccine via the NHS might be able to access them for free through their workplace, while vaccines were also available privately for anybody able to pay for them.A private flu vaccination costs about £20 at most high street pharmacies, and some retailers offer them for under £10 as part of membership schemes.Pollard said an earlier flu season did not necessarily mean a worse flu season. “We don’t know for certain why the timing varies each year.” He believed an early rise was due to a combination of factors, including the weather, the particular strain of the virus that is around and its ability to spread, the immunity of the population to the circulating strain, and aspects of behaviour – for example, the number of close contacts people have.Antonia Ho, a professor of infectious diseases at the University of Glasgow’s Centre for Virus Research, said it was important to get vaccinated as soon as possible as it took a few weeks for the vaccine to provide full protection.“An early rise in influenza cases may indicate a more intense influenza season overall, because earlier onset is associated with a longer period of community transmission and higher cumulative case numbers,” she said. “However, onset timing alone doesn’t determine severity.”Data from UKHSA has suggested the increase in flu is being driven by cases among young people aged 18 to 24, and that a mix of two flu A subtypes – H1N1 and H3N2 – is circulating in England. “The flu vaccine covers both subtypes and also influenza B,” said Ho.WhileUKHSA has noted that the H1N1 subtype of flu Aappears to have changed or “drifted” a little from the strain that was used to make this year’s flu vaccine, Ho said it was too soon to say if that would affect how well the vaccine worked.According to data from UKHSA, the vaccination programme in England last winter is estimated to have prevented about 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths, despite the flu season again starting earlier than usual.John Tregoning, a professor of vaccine immunology at Imperial College London and author of the book Infectious: Pathogens and How We Fight Them, said: “Last year is a good example where [we] also had an early start to the flu season, and then because of that, probably people slightly changed their behaviours and went and got vaccinated, and then it comes down again.”Experts have urged those eligible for a Covid jab to get vaccinated, with UKHSA data suggesting levels of Covid are rising. Tregoning also emphasised the importance of vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).Ho said that while vaccination against respiratory diseases was important, there were additional measures people could take if they started to feel unwell.“If you have flu-like symptoms, ideally stay at home, practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with others,” she said.Explore more on these topicsFluVaccines and immunisationHealthEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Surgeon faces deportation as Home Office revokes refugee status for Syrians | Home Office | The Guardian
description: UK classifies Syria as safe to return to despite UN refugee body’s advice
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: UK classifies Syria as safe to return to despite UN refugee body’s advice
Content: Syrians gathered in Trafalgar Square, London, in December 2024 to celebrate the ousting of the Assad regime. Thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected by the Home Office decision.Photograph: Mina Kim/ReutersView image in fullscreenSyrians gathered in Trafalgar Square, London, in December 2024 to celebrate the ousting of the Assad regime. Thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected by the Home Office decision.Photograph: Mina Kim/ReutersHome OfficeSurgeon faces deportation as Home Office revokes refugee status for SyriansUK classifies Syria as safe to return to despite UN refugee body’s adviceDiane TaylorSun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Syrian plastic surgeon is facing deportation from the UK after theHome Officerevoked his refugee status, declaring it is now safe for him and his family to return to their home country.Despite Foreign Office guidance advising against all travel toSyriabecause of the “volatile” security situation, the government has classified it as a safe place for refugees to return to.Although some European countries are strongly promotingvoluntary returnto Syria, the Home Office’s decision to actively remove refugee status for Syrians is thought to be the first of its kind in Europe since the fall of the Assad regime.The surgeon, who fled the Assad regime and arrived in the UK in 2016, now lives inLondonwith his wife and six children, three of whom are studying at university. He is understood to be one of the first Syrian refugees in the UK to have his refugee protection cancelled.The move is believed to be the first time the Home Office has cancelled refugee protection for a particular nationality, and thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected.View image in fullscreenPeople gather in Trafalgar Square in December 2024 after rebels announced that they had ousted Bashar al-Assad in Syria.Photograph: Mina Kim/Reuters“I am so shocked by the Home Office’s decision to withdraw refugee protection,” the surgeon said. “I brought my family to what I considered to be a safe place. We have integrated well but now my refugee status has been cancelled.“I worked as a plastic surgeon in Syria, converted my medical qualifications here so that I am registered with the General Medical Council to work as a doctor here. I am currently working in a GP surgery but am hoping I will be able to continue my practice as a plastic surgeon soon.“I don’t believe Syria will be a safe place for me to return to. I was targeted by certain radical groups in Syria who are still operating there. They are capable of doing many things to me. And I don’t believe that the current Syrian government would be able to protect me from these groups.“I have heard of a few other families who have also had their refugee status taken away from them on the same basis as me – the Home Office says Syria is now a safe country for us to return to.“After I received the letter from the Home Office I delayed telling my family because I wanted to protect them from sadness for a few more days. But now I have given them the news. Like me, they are all in shock and are only just starting to absorb this. My three older children are all studying at university: one is doing neuroscience, another cybersecurity and a third pharmacy.“It’s unsafe for all of us to go back to Syria. By revoking our refugee status the Home Office is depriving us of the right to live our lives.”View image in fullscreen‘Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger,’ a Home Office spokesperson said.Photograph: Alex Segre/UCG/Universal Images/Getty ImagesThe Home Office letter states: “Your refugee status has been ceased. Although officials accept that the situation in Syria remains ‘complex’ they consider that changes in Syria are so significant that your fear of persecution and serious harm can no longer be regarded as well founded.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe technical term is “cessation” of refugee status. The UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, in its most recent guidance about the safety of Syria, found that governments should not be returning refugees there.It said: “UNHCR calls on states to refrain from implementing cessation exercises until such time as the situation in Syria has seen significant improvements in overall stability.”Foreign Office guidancestates that the security situation in Syria “remains volatile” and adds: “Fighting and violence may occur around the country and is highly unpredictable. This includes artillery and airstrikes.” The guidance also states that there is a humanitarian crisis in Syria including lack of infrastructure, water, sanitation and health services.The family’s solicitor, Manini Menon of Duncan Lewis, said: “It is regrettable that the home secretary has seen fit to target Syrian refugees and their families as part of her pledge to reduce net migration figures. This is a cynical and unprecedented step which will have devastating consequences for a group of people who have rebuilt their lives in the UK with considerable effort, contributing to their communities and putting down roots here.“The evidence in relation to Syria is clear: the circumstances in the country do not allow the home secretary to lawfully conclude that they have stabilised to the extent that refugees can be safely returned there.”The Home Office said: “Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger. When it is safe for someone to return to their home country, they will be expected to do so. We continue to work closely with governments around the world to develop and maintain returns agreements, including with Syria.”Explore more on these topicsHome OfficeImmigration and asylumRefugeesSyriaLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Oliver Blume says Made in Europe rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Oliver Blume says Made in Europe rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
Content: VW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGView image in fullscreenVW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industryOliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’Jasper Jollyin ParisSun 11 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.The rules are aimed at countering therapid rise of Chinese brands in Europein the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launcheda brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocketRead moreThe proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition fromChina.On Friday,the EU said it had reached a landmark dealwith China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGBlume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryChinese economyEuropean UnionChinaAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detained | Poland | The Guardian
description: Polish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Polish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealed
Content: Donald Tusk was told about the threat first thing on Sunday morning.Photograph: Albert Zawada/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Tusk was told about the threat first thing on Sunday morning.Photograph: Albert Zawada/EPAPolandDonald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detainedPolish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealedAgence France-Presse in WarsawSun 11 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Polish prime minister,Donald Tusk, said on Sunday that a man accused of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister had been detained.“The man threatening an attack has been detained,” Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their “swift and decisive action”.The arrest was also confirmed by the country’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński.The interior ministry had earlier said that Tusk and the defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been targeted.It ordered authorities to take action “in connection with the information received by the police concerning a possible assassination attempt on the prime minister... as well as the deputy prime minister”, who is also defence minister, spokesperson Karolina Gałecka wrote on X.Members of the police, state protection service (SOP) and internal security agency were present at Sunday’s meeting.“We are treating this matter as deadly serious,” a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzyński, told journalists afterwards.“Month by month, year by year, more and more various threats and menacing messages reach the police, SOP, and the services concerningPolandand Poles,” he said. In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out.”Poland, a Nato and EU member, has been on high alert after a series of stabbings in the last week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a “cult of violence”.Explore more on these topicsPolandDonald TuskEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day | India | The Guardian
description: CJP leaders say Modi’s government is creating ‘atmosphere of fear’ after they were among thousands detained on Saturday
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: CJP leaders say Modi’s government is creating ‘atmosphere of fear’ after they were among thousands detained on Saturday
Content: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka at a press conference on Sunday, where they asked why Narendra Modi, the prime minister, and Amit Shah, the home minister, were protecting Gyanesh Kumar, India’s election commssioner.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersView image in fullscreenSaurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka at a press conference on Sunday, where they asked why Narendra Modi, the prime minister, and Amit Shah, the home minister, were protecting Gyanesh Kumar, India’s election commssioner.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersIndia‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second dayCJP leaders say Modi’s government is creating ‘atmosphere of fear’ after they were among thousands detained on SaturdayHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin DelhiSun 11 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leaders of India’s Cockroach movement accused the Narendra Modi government of declaring “war with its own citizens” and vowed to continue with their protest after being released from police detention, as anti-government unrest rocked Delhi for a second day.The three leaders of the youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) were taken into custody on Saturday when thousands were detained by police as authorities went to extreme lengths to prevent young people taking to the streets to protest.By Sunday morning, a magistrate had ordered that the three CJP leaders, Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, be released on the condition that they would not “breach peace” for a year.View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party, leaves a police station in Delhi after his release on Sunday.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersIn a social media post soon after his release, Dipke, CJP’s founder, pointed his criticism directly at the prime minister. “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said.Saturday’s protest was called by the CJP alongside student groups and civil society leaders to demand the resignation of India’s election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused ofan “assault on democracy”by overseeing an exercise that has deleted 130 million names from India’s electoral roll.‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdownRead moreKumar is accused of implementing the voter roll revision to help Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) entrench its power and to disenfranchise minority groups such as Muslims who are not traditionally part of the BJP’s voter base.Those who attempted to take part in Saturday’s demonstration were ruthlessly obstructed by a security crackdown, in which more than 25,000 police barricaded roads and the internet and public transport were shut down. More than 7,000 people were taken into police custody, many before they had even reached the protest site in the centre of the capital.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel and police detain a journalist during a protest in Delhi on Sunday.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersDespite the heavy-handed police response, it was still an unprecedented display of dissent against the powerful Modi government, which has been notoriously intolerant of any political opposition or criticism over its 12 years in power. Several senior opposition leaders were among those who tried to protest and were detained.By Sunday, the centre of Delhi still resembled a high-security fortress, with roads blocked by barricades and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary still deployed. Supreme court judges have ruled that the government must restore internet and reopen the capital’s metro stations.Small groups of students and Cockroach supporters, many freshly released from police detention, again attempted to demonstrate in Delhi and were detained.Among those taken into custody for a second time was the student leader Neha Bora, whose repeated defiance in the face of the police crackdown has made her a figurehead of the movement.View image in fullscreenNeha Bora, centre, taking part in a march on Sunday.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesIn a video she posted on social media after she was picked up by Delhi police, Bora showed a detention bus with metal grilles over its windows and four small “jail-like” compartments secured with latches.She said six to eight protesters were crammed into each of the compartments, leaving little room to breathe, and that male protesters were subjected to verbal abuse and physical violence.“So many troops, so much police presence, so much violence, abuses targeting mothers and sisters, caste-based slurs – why?” Bora said in the video. “Simply because you want to protect a thief, Gyanesh Kumar.”Marching alongside Bora was Surbi Yadav, 20, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, who said police detained her on Saturday morning. She accused police personnel of dragging her, injuring her arm and leg.“They treated us like animals. They pushed us into a bus and took us to a sports facility that had been turned into a detention centre,” Yadav said, while showing scars on her arms. “The police kept misbehaving with us on the way and warned us against taking part in the protests.”Yadav was released on Saturday evening. By Sunday afternoon, she was back on the streets with other students, holding a placard She vowed to return the following day and keep protesting until their demands were met.“We are not afraid any more. The government and the police will have to understand that,” she said. “They can use as much force as they want to silence us, but it will be futile. In fact, it will only backfire. Every day, more people are turning against this government because of the way it is treating protesters.”At a press conference on Sunday afternoon, the CJP leaders Das and Ranka condemned the police and government for turning Delhi into a “war-like situation” and reiterated their message of defiance that “this fight is on”. They added that it was no longer just about Kumar but also targeted at Modi and his home minister, Amit Shah.View image in fullscreenProtesters who tried to demonstrate in Delhi on Sunday were again detained by police deployed in the city.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters“The state is at war with its own citizens,” Das said. “An atmosphere of fear has been created in country, it’s clearly being done to save one person. We want to ask Modi and Shah, why are you trying to save Gyanesh Kumar?”There was no response from Modi to the accusations by the protesters. However, the BJP’s spokesperson, Gaurav Bhatia, said earlier that the voter roll revision was a legitimate exercise to remove dead and illegal voters and refuted any political interference.“These are baseless allegations being levelled by an irresponsible opposition,” Bhatia said. “The claim that democracy is being destroyed and that the constitution is being undermined has no basis and not an iota of evidence.”The weekend’s protests had drawn support from the leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, who has accused the Modi government of “vote chauri” or vote cheating through the voter roll revision. Gandhi was detained twice last week as opposition parties attempted to hold a protest in central Delhi calling for Kumar to resign.“Mr Modi does not understand that the game is over,” Gandhi said on Saturday. “We will ensure that Modi pays for the crimes he has committed against the country.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsiaShareReuse this content

title: ‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacular | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Welcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of Christmas
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Welcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of Christmas
Content: Halloween trees with pumpkin decorations are a big decorating trend for 2026, says Wilko.Photograph: Elisa Bistocchi/AlamyView image in fullscreenHalloween trees with pumpkin decorations are a big decorating trend for 2026, says Wilko.Photograph: Elisa Bistocchi/AlamyRetail industry‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacularWelcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of ChristmasZoe WoodSun 11 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe tree is up, the wreath is hanging on the front door and you’ve just opened youradvent calendar. All told, it’s beginning to feel a lot like …Halloween.If it sounds like the stuff of nightmares then that’s the point: Britons are increasingly decorating their homes with ghoulish versions of Christmas traditions. Think of it as Halloweenmas.“What was traditionally a single-night celebration has turned into a month-long event mirroring many of Christmas’s traditions, but without the same level of expectation,” said Charlotte Broadbent, the UK general manager for the online wholesale platform Faire.Analysis of thousands of sales transactions on the platform revealed a huge rise in the number of Halloweenmas products available – up more than 500% in the past four years, from 425 in 2021 to 2,632 in 2025. The biggest areas of growth are trees, wreaths and ornaments.According to the budget retailer Wilko, Halloween trees are one of the biggest decorating trends of 2026. It said sales of artificial trees were 200% higher in September than a year ago.“There really aren’t any rules with a Halloween tree,” says Wilko. “You can go all-out or keep it simple with a smaller tree and a few spooky accessories.”View image in fullscreenHalloween isn’t like it used to be.Photograph: Natalia Alkema/AlamyThe lack of rules is clear from social media, where the looks span student party – black tinsel tree shaped like a witch’s hat – to child-friendly cuteness. The arts and crafts retailer Hobbycraft’s website offers “five ways to decorate a twig tree” that include DIY spiderwebs made out of lolly sticks and felt pumpkins.Libby Ewart, who runs the online partyware and gift retailer The Box Party, has bought 40% more stock this year. “Houses are decorated earlier and with way more thought than before,” she said. “Also, this year it falls on a Saturday, so there has never been a better excuse for a party.”Emily Viberg, a senior retail analyst at the research group Mintel, said Halloween was “no longer just about costumes and sweets, it’s about a full season of engagement, gifting and themed activities”.Mintel’s research shows young Britons, in particular, see it as an opportunity to express themselves and experiment with fashion and makeup, with 16- to 34-year-oldsover-indexingin purchases of fancy dress, cosmetics and decorations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Consumers are increasingly buying into the atmosphere and social moments Halloween creates,” Viberg said. “Younger adults are at the heart of this shift, transforming Halloween from a one-night celebration into a broader season of self-expression and experience-led spending.”Viberg said social media had accelerated this shift, with 40% of Halloween buyers using the platforms to buy products directly. “Viral costume trends, makeup tutorials, home decor inspiration and content tapping into popular culture are shaping consumer spending and helping to extend the season well beyond October,” she said.While some people might complain it is all over the top, Broadbent said: “What we’re seeing is people investing into Halloween as a reason to share quality time together ahead of Christmas, with lots of fun and creativity at its heart and without the need to spend big.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryHalloweenShops and shoppingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We look like soft, made-up blokes, but we’re really tough’: Duran Duran on 80s excess, tabloid scrutiny and their Halloween glow-up | Duran Duran | The Guardian
description: They spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying power
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: They spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying power
Content: Wild boys … Duran Duran. Stylist Bea Åkerlund.Photograph: Stephanie PistelView image in fullscreenWild boys … Duran Duran. Stylist Bea Åkerlund.Photograph: Stephanie PistelDuran DuranInterview‘We look like soft, made-up blokes, but we’re really tough’: Duran Duran on 80s excess, tabloid scrutiny and their Halloween glow-upAlexis PetridisThey spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying powerSun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022,Duran Duranwere inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. It felt like a big deal, a sweet moment of acknowledgment for the band’s five-decades-long career, the 100m records sold, the string of bulletproof hits: Save a Prayer, Rio, Hungry Like the Wolf, Girls on Film. They were inducted by actor Robert Downey Jr; Drew Barrymore, Naomi Campbell and Gwen Stefani were on hand to pay heartfelt tribute and, as keyboard player Nick Rhodes points out, “It’s a big national live TV broadcast in America that goes out to millions of people,” so the band booked some warm-up shows. “And it so happened that there was a date that came up in Las Vegas on 31 October,” says Rhodes. “And I looked at everyone and said: ‘Well, we can’t do a normal show. Las Vegas on Halloween – surely that’s the opportunity for a little bit of fun?’”They worked up a set of suitably themed material, including covers of Billie Eilish’s Bury a Friend and Talking Heads’ Psycho Killer. There were, of course, costumes involved, because, as Rhodes drily notes, “When have Duran Duran ever not dressed up?”View image in fullscreenExtraordinary world … Duran Duran at their Manchester Halloween show last year.Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/WireImageHe has a point, although not even in their new romantic pomp had Duran Duran dressed up like this. Replete with the unexpected sight of the band’s heart-throb-in-chief, bassist John Taylor, “with silver hair down to my waist, like some kind of Scandinavian orc”, the show proved such a success that Duran Duran’s Halloween gigs have become an annual event – they performed one at Madison Square Garden in New York in 2024 and at Manchester’s Co-op Live in 2025, while this year’s takes place at the O2 in London – and spawned an album, 2023’s Danse Macabre. Guitarist Andy Taylor, who left the band in 2007 and announced he was suffering from stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction, returned to play on it, while among its covers lurked a version of the Specials’ Ghost Town, an intriguing choice, given that, back in the early 80s, the Specials’ politically engaged social realism was seen as diametrically opposed to Duran Duran’s nakedly ambitious jet-setting glamour.“I remember being in a taxi with John after one of our first rehearsals, talking about stuff,” nods frontman Simon Le Bon. “I’d been in a rock band and a punk band before called Dog Days, and I said: ‘But John, what about street credibility?’ And John said: ‘Simon, Duran Duran’s got about as much street credibility as Chanel No 19.’ And, at that point, I thought: ‘OK, I’ll go with that.’”double quotation markWe survived the cutting of the tall poppies and I think that endeared us to peopleSimon Le BonAlong the way, the Halloween shows have got increasingly elaborate (the Manchester gig had pyrotechnics, dancers and fire-eaters), while even Le Bon, who by his own admission is “not a fan of Halloween – I think it’s become just a sort of marketing thing”, can’t be faulted for his enthusiasm for the whole venture.“At the first one, I was a werewolf, but since then it’s developed. The next one, I was like the ghost of a north Atlantic convoy sea captain. There was a sort of nautical theme which suits me down to the ground.” Readers old enough to remember Duran Duran’s heyday may recall Le Bon’s adventures with his 78ft yacht Drum, which capsized during the 1985 Fastnet race, resulting in the singer being airlifted to safety wearing only his underpants. “Another time I was a kind of cross between Mad Max and a mummy, but I also had this one scene where I was determined to wear antlers, like a druid god. And last time I was sort of aiming for something but it fell a bit short: I was a jellyfish, but it ended up looking like … I was going to say something off RuPaul’s Drag Race, but I’d be flattering myself. This time, I want to do something like Shiva the Destroyer.”View image in fullscreenBoys on film … Duran Duran on Top of the Pops in 1981.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesIt all points to a certain freedom, a desire to do what you want, regardless of whether it’s considered cool. “The thing is, I don’t give a fuck what people think about me,” offers Le Bon, now 67 and a grandfather – or, as he put it on social media, glamfather – of four. “I’m not talking for the whole band – I’m sure some of them do care – but me, I just do what I do, and that’s all it is.”It also suggests a sense of self-deprecating humour that Rhodes thinks might have been overlooked after their 1982 album Rio catapulted them to superstardom, when Duran Duran had fair claim to call themselves the biggest band in the world. In fairness, it wasn’t always easy to spot amid the expensive jet-set videos, supermodel girlfriends and Antony Price suits. “I think it was missed by some people,” he says. “But we grew up with Monty Python and Fawlty Towers and all of those amazing 70s British TV shows and so, inevitably, that was part of what we were doing. It doesn’t mean we were going to put it into songs – I guess we weren’t ever going to write The Laughing Gnome – but at the same time, you know, the videos are filled with humour. Watch A View to a Kill or Rio. It’s there.”Talking to the band’s four members about their heyday is intriguing. It was, all agree, exactly what they’d wanted in the first place. They loved being on Top of the Pops – the video for their recent single Free to Love was a hugely affectionate homage to the show – and clearly relished enjoying themselves in the grandstanding style of the times, palling around New York with Andy Warhol and calling up supermodels’ agents in order to ask their clients to dinner. “Being single was good fun,” smiles Le Bon, when asked what he misses about that era, before his expression changes. “I shouldn’t say that, should I? Being married has been amazing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPop art … Nick Rhodes at Andy Warhol’s birthday party in 1985.Photograph: Patrick McMullan/Paul Bruinooge/Getty ImagesEqually, it’s hard to avoid the sense that the kind of global fame they enjoyed in the 80s – not to mention the unfailing attentions of their diehard fans, the Durannies – was a lot to take on. “It was a mindfuck, actually,” offers drummer Roger Taylor. “I was sitting in my bedroom teaching myself the drums when I was 16; by the time I was 21 we were playing Madison Square Garden. I wasn’t prepared for it in any way. My dad worked in a car factory; my mum worked on the switchboard at a warehouse. I didn’t have any kind of grounding for great success in my life. Five years into it, I thought: ‘I’m not sure I can live with this level of scrutiny.’ The music press was hounding us, the tabloids were chasing us. It was the first time they really wanted to feature musicians as part of their journalism. The fanbase was 12 to 16 years old and very intense. It was definitely time to step away.”He departed Duran Duran and upped sticks to Gloucestershire in 1986. To his delight, the minute he left the band, the fans that had camped outside his house disappeared. “God bless them, but it was a bit of a relief. The only people that tracked me down were the Sun, who banged at my door at six in the morning, then wrote this feature with the headline ‘Roger Taylor: The Hermit of Pop’. But it was great not to be bothered and live a quiet, simple life.”By 1989, the hits had dried up for Duran Duran. “I felt huge anxiety, like water-running-out-of-the-bathtub sort of anxiety,” says Le Bon, who along with Rhodes is Duran Duran’s only constant member since he joined in 1980. They rolled up their sleeves and toughed it out through the band’s lean years, in the company of American guitarist Warren Cuccurullo, the latter a curious character who at one juncture marketed a sex toy modelled on his own penis, but also co-wrote Ordinary World, the 1993 single that briefly returned Duran Duran to the upper echelons of the global charts and remains their biggest streaming hit today. At one juncture, Le Bon wrote a song called Undergoing Treatment that depicted the band “watching others in the news”, while finding themselves “resigned to the mid-price section”. Today, he feels like their wilderness years were the band’s making.View image in fullscreenTheir own way … Duran Duran today.Photograph: Stephanie Pistel“We survived the cutting of the tall poppies and I think that endeared us to people, in a way,” he says. “It proved we’re tough, actually. We might look like a bunch of soft, made-up middle-class blokes, but actually, we’re really tough.”Certainly, you can’t miss a distinct shift in perception of Duran Duran since the original quintet reformed in 2001. The bad reviews that plagued them throughout their imperial phase seem to have been consigned to the past. “I remember coming offstage one night and someone saying: ‘The sound of the crowd has changed,’” says bassist John Taylor. “It had dropped an octave from that shrill treble. Clearly, we’d moved on from that audience that Duran Duran used to get, largely female and teenage, which was fine for us, but the kind of audience that gets pooh-poohed. That felt like, ‘OK, we’re on an even pitch now. We can move forward.’ The guys were done hating us.”If you want evidence of national treasure status, well, they have just been featured on a series of Royal Mail stamps. Everyone from Beck to Brandon Flowers of the Killers to emo band Panic! at the Disco has cited them as an influence. Moreover, they never seem to run out of younger artists to collaborate with: Mark Ronson co-produced 2015’s Paper Gods, Blur’s Graham Coxon turned up on its successor, Future Past, and last summer, Le Bon and John Taylor unexpectedly popped up on stage in Hyde Park with Sabrina Carpenter, belting out Hungry Like the Wolf. Le Bon is hugely enthusiastic about having persuaded the Margate-based band Pigeon to support them on tour, although what the Durannies will make of their “no-wave psychedelic punk” remains to be seen. “We really respect youthful energy. You want to get some of that in the group, some of that in the studio.”That said, there are aspects of 21st-century music they seem very wary of. Rhodes offers some cautious optimism about AI’s impact on music “if you use it as an artistic tool”, but Le Bon says he recently encountered an AI take on a Duran Duran song, and still seems scarred by the experience: “It was absolutely abominable! It was a horrible tune – the vocal was awful. I can’t remember the title but the cover was a girl standing on a yacht, so no cliches there. I do worry that people might just start getting used to it and accepting it in the same way you would accept really bad school dinners, just because you were hungry and it’s food. It’s shocking.”Besides, as he points out, there’s no need for an AI Duran Duran, given that the real deal is still extant and intends to remain so. “I think being in the band gives me the impetus and energy and motivation to try to keep myself mentally flexible, physically strong. I purposely run up and down stairs because I don’t want to suddenly go, ‘Oh, I need to move to a bungalow. My knees have gone.’ I can’t change the age I am, but I can act as youthful as I can and I think that makes you last longer. Until I drop dead on stage? Well, it’s not a bad way to go, to be honest with you.”Duran Duran’s Halloween show is at the O2, London, 31 October as part of their 2026UK and Europe tour.Explore more on these topicsDuran DuranPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d wander through the park all angsty listening to Arctic Monkeys’: Arlo Parks’ honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car, and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car, and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?
Content: Arlo Parks … ‘I love Janet Jackson’s voice – it softens people.’Photograph:View image in fullscreenArlo Parks … ‘I love Janet Jackson’s voice – it softens people.’Photograph:Honest playlistMusic‘I’d wander through the park all angsty listening to Arctic Monkeys’: Arlo Parks’ honest playlistThe singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?As told to Hannah NewtonSun 11 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withI remember listening to Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) by Eurythmics when I was really young. There was something about the line at the beginning that I was completely intoxicated by.The firstdownload I boughtWhen I was about 10 or 11, I would put my headphones on and wander through the park all angsty listening to Fake Tales of San Francisco by Arctic Monkeys, my first download on my iPod Nano. I loved the storytelling, the characters and the gritty tableaux they described: it felt so real, even though it was far away from where I grew up.The song I do at karaokeI inherited a lot of records from my uncle when I was 12 or 13; he let me choose as many as I could fit in my parents’ car. I chose randomly: Sade, LL Cool J, Grandmaster Flash, D’Angelo andPrince. Although I don’t do karaoke, hypothetically I would choose When Doves Cry by Prince. There’s something almost unattainable about the way he sings. I would throw myself at it with passion, but not be able to pull it off!The song I inexplicably know every lyric toThere are so many, but Superstar by Jamelia makes me happy – it’s a kind of a bubblegum pop song.The best song to play at a partyMy parents had a lot of CDs. My dad was into jazz – Miles Davis, Charles Mingus, Duke Ellington – and my mum loved French music and Whitney, Diana Ross, Tina Turner,Janet Jackson. I was playing Janet Jackson’s All for You in my dressing room for my crew and everyone was bopping. I feel like you can never go wrong with her. I love her voice – it softens people.The song I can no longer listen toEven songs tied to painful experiences, I don’t avoid. Fourth of July by Sufjan Stevens is heartbreaking. I have to be careful when I listen to it, because it brings out so much melancholy about grief and loss – it plunges you into certain spaces.The song that changed my lifeThere’s so much space in House of Cards by Radiohead; Thom Yorke’s voice is ethereal. I discovered it a few years before I wrote Collapsed in Sunbeams, it has the same minimalism to it.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateI embrace the music that a lot of people like, because there must be something that brings us towards it collectively. Like Starstruck by Lady Gaga – I blast that shamelessly in the car.The song that gets me up in the morningI’ve been listening to I Care by Turnstile: it’s happy, heart open. It makes me feel like I’m 16, but the drums are, like: OK, time to get the coffee going and start the day.The song that makes me cryGlory Box by Portishead. It’s so piercing, specifically the live version from Roseland theatre. Hearing the little cracks in Beth Gibbons‘s voice, she’s baring herself to the audience, it brings tears to my eyes.The song I want played at my funeralSunday Morning by the Velvet Underground: there’s something so warm about it, it feels soothing, like a new beginning. It’s melancholy but with a glimmer of hope.Ambiguous Desire is out now;Arlo Parkstours the UK and Ireland, 17 to 26 October; tour starts Dublin.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistArlo ParksPop and rockR&BPrinceJanet JacksonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: David Tennant stars in a brutally brilliant prison drama | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Jimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Jimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Completely compelling … Time on BBC OnePhotograph: :BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenCompletely compelling … Time on BBC OnePhotograph: :BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: David Tennant stars in a brutally brilliant prison dramaJimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Priya ElanandAlexi DugginsSun 11 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTimeSunday, 9pm, BBC OneJimmy McGovern’s prison anthology is never an easy watch but the bravery to explore the darkest corners of the British prison system makes it quality viewing. This time, David Tennant is downtrodden prison officer Bobby Bailey at a young offender institute – where wasted youth and potential only add to the gloom. Siobhan Finneran returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise, who joins the YOI. The two get off to a bad start and both have to deal with a tragic event in the tense first episode. Meanwhile, one new inmate is torn between attempting to make amends and fitting in with his violent friends. Once again, the story is harrowing, heart-tugging and completely compelling.Hollie RichardsonThe Reluctant Vampire6.40pm, BBC OneThe gently macabre humour of this comedy, adapted by the Gibbons brothers from a children’s novel by Eric Morecambe, has echoes of Ghosts. Hapless young vampire Val (Lenny Rush) finds himself in the world of humans when a trip to the village leads him into the home of oddball Gertie.Phil HarrisonEva Longoria: Searching for France7.20pm, BBC TwoDesperate Housewife Eva Longoria lands in Bordeaux. Filmed to look a bit like a Nespresso ad and with Eva sounding like a jacked-up Samantha Jones, it’s an enjoyable slice of escapism. That is, if you can stomach lots of one-percenters talking about staggeringly pricey bottles of plonk.Priya ElanApocalypse9pm, Channel 4It’s the Battle of the Bleats, after Eastsider Alix stole the goats from the Westsiders. Celia and Kelly are unimpressed, while Alix and Kiera are planning to play dumb in order to distract from any accusations. But how will they manage to disguise the sound of their four-legged friends when the inevitable confrontation happens?PELater … With Jools Holland10pm, BBC TwoThe ex-Squeeze pianist boogies his woogie all over an impressive lineup of musical guests. The performances include Beautiful South/Housemartins star Paul Heaton, British pop-soul sensation Skye Newman and Mobo-winning Northampton MC DC3. Plus, there’s a chat with Johnny Marr about his new album – and how he recently auctioned more than 80 guitars for charity.Alexi DugginsThe Party11.40pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenUnwanted guests? … The Party on ITV1.Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsSarah Solemani’s moreish take on Elizabeth Day’s novel follows the friendship between two men who went to boarding school together – journalist Martin Gilmour (Luke Evans) and Tory politician Ben Fitzmaurice (Tom Cullen) – and a terrible event that happens at Ben’s 40th birthday party. It opens with Martin in a blood-soaked shirt at the police station, recalling the year he got a scholarship and met Ben …HRLive sportChampionship Football: Southampton v Portsmouth, 11.30am, ITV1At St Mary’s Stadium.Premier League Football: Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest, 1pm, Sky Sports Main EventLiverpool v Man City follows at 4pm. title: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey | Movies | The Guardian
description: The makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governesses
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governesses
Content: ‘A forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale’ … Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) in Wildwood.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale’ … Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) in Wildwood.Photograph: Album/AlamyMoviesReviewWildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odysseyThe makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governessesPeter BradshawSun 11 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an engaging family movie from the Portland-based Laika studio thatcreated Coraline. It is a fantasy adventure in Laika’s distinctively crafted stop-motion animation, written by Chris Butler from the bestseller of the same title by Carson Ellis and Colin Meloy, the latter being a band member ofThe Decemberists, one of whose tour posters we duly glimpse in this film. The director is Laika’s lead animator Travis Knight. It’s a forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale which CS Lewis and JRR Tolkien might have recognised, a story about the mysterious glory of going on a quest and the terrible fear and wish-fulfilment euphoria of being called upon to confront secret forces that the grownups know nothing about.The setting is modern-dayPortland, Oregon, a groovy city whose hipster-ish stores (there’s a coffee shop actually called Dripster) and Woke 1.0 signage are affectionately mocked. But most of all, the film is aware of a huge forest park next to the city, a place here mythologised as the impassable wilderness or “wildwood” where strange creatures, fairytale nobility and wisecracking talking animals reputedly dwell, of which the city-dwelling humans are entirely ignorant. Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is a 12-year-old girl whose parents (voiced by Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) are a couple of amiable hippies who believe in natural forces and benign magic. They have another child, Prue’s baby brother Mac, who Prue has to look after one day, pushing him in his stroller around the city and having to endure a certain classmate of hers tagging along. This is nerdy Curtis (Jacob Tremblay) who has a crush on her.They are stunned when a bunch (or rather a murder) of crows gather with Hitchcockian menace in a kids’ play area, swoop down and carry poor little Mac off to their forest domain. Plucky (and also terrified) Prue and Curtis give chase and enter the dark and trackless forest, and find it is a parallel world, undreamt of by the ordinary human world, populated by all manner of loquacious beasts and oppressed humans.
