Content: ‘A man walked up, put his arm around me and said, “Everything is going to be OK,”’ recalls Steve Askew.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty imagesView image in fullscreen‘A man walked up, put his arm around me and said, “Everything is going to be OK,”’ recalls Steve Askew.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty imagesKindness of strangersLife and styleThe kindness of strangers: In one of my darkest periods, a few compassionate words helped turn my life aroundI was standing at the traffic lights with the weight of the world on my shoulders when a man approached. He will probably never know the impact he had on my lifeRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesSteve Askew as told toKatie CunninghamSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy cousin had recently died in a terrible accident and I had been the one who had to identify the body. It was one of the darkest periods of my life, on seemingly every front: I was in the midst of a divorce; it was during the global financial crisis and the company I worked for was badly struggling, making every day feel heavy with uncertainty and stress. Everything was a mess and I was emotionally exhausted.The kindness of strangers: Two helicopter pilots flew down low to wave to my three-year-old son – he was beside himself with joyRead moreOne morning during rush hour, I stood at the traffic lights waiting to cross on my way to the office. I was lost in my thoughts but must have looked like I had the weight of the world on my shoulders, because something unexpected happened.A man walked up, put his arm around me and said, “Everything is going to be OK.” I burst into tears and by the time I’d pulled myself together he was gone, disappeared into the crowd.There was nothing remarkable about him at all. In fact, I can’t even remember his face. But that brief moment shifted everything for me.I had been dwelling in victimhood and this stranger snapped me out of it. His kindness gave me enough hope to make a change and turn my life around.Soon after, I quit my job. I went travelling around the world, something I had been talking about doing with my cousin, and met the woman who became my partner in Germany. Three children later, we have built a happy and deeply fulfilling life together – a life I could never have imagined standing at those traffic lights all those years ago.That stranger will probably never know the impact he had on me. But a few compassionate words, offered at exactly the right moment, altered the course of my life for ever.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: This is how we do it: ‘At our age we get to wake up and say: What are we doing today? Let’s make love’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A sex podcast opened up a whole new way of communicating for Helen and Ian
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: A sex podcast opened up a whole new way of communicating for Helen and Ian
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘At our age we get to wake up and say: What are we doing today? Let’s make love’A sex podcast opened up a whole new way of communicating for Helen and IanHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toOlivia LadanyiSun 11 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHelen, 71double quotation markI’ve discovered I like to be spanked – my orgasms have become much strongerIan was dating my best friend, Susan, when we met 15 years ago. She invited me around to his house for dinner, and when he opened the door, I thought: oh my god, he’s cute. After they broke up 10 months in and she started seeing someone else, I asked for his contact details and we went on a date. When I called Susan to tell her I was in love, she was totally silent. It was her or Ian. I chose him. It’s one of the best decisions I’ve ever made.Ian is much more sexual than I am: his love language is physical touch, while mine is quality time. I just don’t think about sex as much as he does. Him wanting to do it more than I do has caused tension, but it wasn’t something we spoke about. Then five years ago,while on a road trip, we put on the podcastSex With Emily to pass the time. I’d never heard anyone talk about sex like that before.After that, we’d listen to a sex podcast, pause and discuss it, and now we have a dialogue about sex, which has made intimacy so much better. I’ve become more curious and adventurous: I’ve discovered I like to be spanked, and my orgasms have become much stronger because I’m more relaxed.double quotation markIan has a pass to have sex with men, although he’s rarely used itWe also plan sex now – about twice a week – which gives me time to get in the mood. But I need quality time first: if we’ve been talking and feeling close, I’m more likely to want sex. Ian is the opposite – he needs sex to feel close.Ian has a pass to have sex with men, although he’s rarely used it. Sex doesn’t threaten me, but emotional intimacy does.Ian makes me feel safe and desired, sometimes too much. He’ll pinch my bum in the supermarket or kiss my neck while I’m cooking, and I’ve learned that’s his way of showing affection, not necessarily trying to initiate sex.Because we met in our 50s and our children are grown up, we can focus on being partners to each other. There’s more space and time for exploration. We get to wake up and say: what are we doing today? Let’s make love later. Who cares what we do! We call them “snow days” – where we just hang out and do whatever we want.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreIan, 74double quotation markI blurted out that I wanted to explore my fantasy of having sex with menI’d make love to Helen every day, and twice on Sundays if I could. I’d start and end the day with sex. It’s our glue. But while I use sex to feel close, I’ve learned over time that feeling close has to come first for Helen, so I try to give her what she needs by going to the dog park, grocery shopping, spending time together – it’s like foreplay.If we don’t have sex for a week, I miss the closeness and start to feel defensive and push Helen away. I start to ask myself: why haven’t we had sex? Did we get in a fight? Is one of us sick? But I’ve learned not to take it personally.Fortunately, we rarely go longer than a week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markShe’s got a great body, but it’s the way she is with people that really turns me onThis is how we do it: ‘As a Catholic monk, I was celibate. But sex with Orla feels so natural’Read moreA few years ago, I blurted out that I wanted to exploremy fantasy ofhaving sex with men. Helen is OK with it because it doesn’t make her feel threatened. It’s only happened twice in the last five years, but I feel lucky that we have the kind of relationship where if one of us really wants to try something, we can. We also have a guest room that we call our playground and we’ve explored some kink.When I first met Helen, I thought she was this shiny, bright thing; so light and fun – the total opposite of my ex, who was negative and controlling. I fall more in love with Helen every day. She’s got a great body – she’s 71 but looks 51 – but it’s the way she is with people that really turns me on.Sex has always been validation to me, and it still is, but not to the same degree. I still think about sex all the time, but since I’ve gotten older, I’m a lot calmer about it. Now my body doesn’t respond the way it used to, I’m more patient and sex is no longer so goal-oriented. Now we have more time and fewer stressors, our intimacy has grown.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My partner’s obnoxious conduct at our sons’ football matches is putting me off him | Family | The Guardian
description: His behaviour is certainly inappropriate, but take a quiet moment to try to find out where the anger is coming from
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: His behaviour is certainly inappropriate, but take a quiet moment to try to find out where the anger is coming from
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyMy partner’s obnoxious conduct at our sons’ football matches is putting me off himHis behaviour is certainly inappropriate, but take a quiet moment to try to find out where the anger is coming fromAnnalisa BarbieriSun 11 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy partner and I have been together for 25 years and we have two sons, aged 14 and 16. Both are football crazy and have played since they were very young. My partner’s competitive nature was one of the things I initially found attractive about him (I wanted someone with drive).However, this side of him rears its ugly head when our kids play matches. Heshouts, criticises and, worst of all, swears at teenagers. I’m so embarrassed by itand it’s alsoaffecting the boys. Their teammates hear their dad and it’s creating tension. I’ve tried to speak to him about it but he brushes it off. Our boys and the coaches have spoken to him too, but to no avail.It may sound extreme, but I feel as if I’m falling out of love with him over this. How can I be with someone who shows no respect for his children, their friends and teammates, let alone coaches and referees?I feel he’s being selfish and if he can’t behave decently at matches he simply shouldn’t go.I don’t think it sounds extreme – it’s a really unattractive side to your partner. This isn’t competitiveness, it’s him being an arsehole and I sincerely hope he doesn’t act like this in other areas of his life.I went to UKCP-registered psychotherapist Lucy Fuller. We were both interested in the “why now, why here” aspect of this. You say your boys have played since they were young; has he always shouted at them or is this a more recent, or increasing, behaviour?“Your partner needs to reflect on the suitability of his behaviour,” said Fuller. “I wonder if his experience of being supported/encouraged was by being ‘shouted at’ from the sidelines? Could this be his only model of what support looks like? His own ego and competitiveness are flooding the situation and it’s not appropriate here.”double quotation markIs he a frustrated player? Was his career thwarted? It’s worth digging beyond the behaviour, because all behaviour is communicationHave you tried talking to him away from the sidelines when everyone is calm? What does this bring up in him? What was his adolescence like, specifically when he was the age his sons are now? “When your children reach a certain age, sometimes it triggers feelings in you,” said Fuller. And these feelings may take a little unearthing.We also wondered what he’s like in other areas of his life. “Is this situation a reflection of his attitude to life and his position within it as a whole?” Fuller asked. “He would benefit from some help reflecting on how others perceive him. Maybe this way of behaving has worked for him in other situations?”Fuller also felt that at the heart of this was frustration – but “at what” is the key. Is he a frustrated player? Was his career, perhaps at professional level, thwarted? It’s worth digging beyond the behaviour, because all behaviour is communication. “It’s almost as if he’s so immersed in the game, that he’s angry with himself,” said Fuller. “It’s so loaded with emotion. What is it that’s so important that he has to behave in this way? Does he feel that he can really affect the outcome of the match? I’d question that because being shouted at doesn’t motivate people.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy partner’s sister has published a family memoir that’s unfair to him. Should we cut ties? | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreCan he, in a calmer moment, practise putting himself in the shoes of others? If this sort of behaviour was ever aimed at him, can he remember what it felt like? Can he imagine what it feels like for others?Pick your moment to try to discuss all this with him. Being truly competitive doesn’t have to mean behaving in this way, it’s not sportsmanlike. Mypodcast on projectionmay be worth a listen to try to work out what exactly is being projected on to these football matches.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. title: ‘It’s not just about circling things on a map’: how our journalists use and corroborate satellite imagery | Press freedom | The Guardian
description: From the destruction of Gaza to climate breakdown, satellite imagery has become an indispensable reporting tool. But as a recent Guardian investigation illustrates, a lot of work goes into ensuring its veracity and keeping the focus on the people affected on the ground
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: From the destruction of Gaza to climate breakdown, satellite imagery has become an indispensable reporting tool. But as a recent Guardian investigation illustrates, a lot of work goes into ensuring its veracity and keeping the focus on the people affected on the ground
Content: A composite of satellite imagery of western Myanmar and photographs of Rohingya fleeing and members of the Arakan army.Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / Vantor / APView image in fullscreenA composite of satellite imagery of western Myanmar and photographs of Rohingya fleeing and members of the Arakan army.Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / Vantor / APInside the GuardianPress freedom‘It’s not just about circling things on a map’: how our journalists use and corroborate satellite imageryFrom the destruction of Gaza to climate breakdown, satellite imagery has become an indispensable reporting tool. But as a recent Guardian investigation illustrates, a lot of work goes into ensuring its veracity and keeping the focus on the people affected on the groundGautam MalkaniSun 11 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow to bear witness when you can’t physically go there? Journalists have always grappled with this. Whether it’s because of armed conflict, repressive regimes or prohibitive terrain, some places remain too dangerous or difficult for reporters to access.Enter low-orbit satellites. As the technology has evolved and proliferated, satellite imagery has become increasingly indispensable. But as with all reporting tools, it requires professional judgment and painstaking work to verify things.“When satellite images show that something on the ground has changed, there’s a lot that needs to be corroborated,” says Kaamil Ahmed, a reporter on the Guardian’s global development team who used extensive satellite imagery for aninvestigation we published last weekinto the destruction of Rohingya villages in Myanmar. “For instance, we could see from the images that people had been displaced, but we needed to verify the images, we needed to be sure about what actually happened and who was behind it, and also whether the villages we were looking at were really Rohingya villages. None of that was straightforward.”‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forcesRead more“We have to treat satellite imagery in exactly the same way as any other type of data we look at, or any human source we speak to,” adds Ashley Kirk, the Guardian’s senior editor for visual journalism. “It goes back to basic journalistic principles of second-sourcing and triple-sourcing information. So that might involve checking that we can still see the same thing in images obtained from another satellite provider, or cross-checking things with information from the ground, such as social media posts or witness testimony, and speaking with experts.”Kaamil has been reporting on the persecution of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority group from westernMyanmar, for more than 10 years. Myanmar has been accused of orchestrating an ethnic cleansing of its Rohingya population after a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 led to about 700,000 people seeking refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.Last week’s investigation mapped the more recent destruction of Rohingya villages in western Myanmar since 2024 by a group of insurgents. It also examined the construction of detention camps and labour camps. “We’d heard for a couple of years that things were happening in that particular area, but it was very hard to stand up,” says Kaamil. “Phone lines and the internet have been down for years so there’s so little evidence coming out of the area. Often, we’d have to simply wait for people to go to Bangladesh as refugees before we could hear their testimony. So that’s why satellite imagery has been so useful.”Indeed, it was shortly after Kaamil published another satellite-led investigation back in March – which examinedattacks on a village in Darfuras part of the ongoing war in Sudan – that a source contacted him and suggested he apply the same reporting techniques to a particular area in western Myanmar.View image in fullscreenA composite of satellite imagery from our article about attacks in Darfur and a photograph.Composite: Getty Images / The Guardian“One of the challenges was that this was a very remote area. Satellite providers weren’t passing over it regularly so, to begin with, we were really struggling to get the quality of images we needed. There’d be big gaps in the timeframe, there weren’t images from the right day, or they weren’t the right resolution.”‘Extraordinary cruelty’: images show longterm ‘starvation strategy’ in SudanRead moreAll these things can hamper journalists’ efforts to make informed comparisons.Ashley recalls facing similar issues over the summer when we used satellite imagery to assess the impact of the wildfires across Europe. “We needed to look at historical images to see the burn scars and assess how certain landscapes had changed,” he explains. “But quite often we are restrained by whenever a satellite goes around Earth and captures images of a very specific area. You’ve got to hope that it’s the right time of day and exactly the right area, and also that there are no obstructions such as cloud cover or smoke obscuring the landscape too much – which in the case of the wildfires would often happen.”Even when our data and visual journalists manage to source clear images of a specific area on a specific day at a specific time, there is still a lot of corroboration to be done. Kaamil offers an example from his investigation into the attacks in Sudan: “There’s a lot of destruction in Darfur, but some of the satellite images of burnt landscapes were actually related to agriculture rather than the war, so we have to be very careful about checking and not making assumptions.”Ashley points to another example from his team’s extensive use of satellite imagery to report on thedestruction of Gazaover the past three years. “You would see a circular object and you might think it’s the dome of a mosque. But a circular pattern could also indicate a crater. So then, for example, we’d use images from other times of the day to see if there are any shadows that suggest a building.”View image in fullscreenA composite of a satellite image of destruction in Gaza and a photograph.Composite: Anadolu AgencyFor last week’s story about the Rohingya villages, Kaamil corroborated the satellite imagery using eyewitness testimony from some of the sources he has kept in touch with during his years of covering their plight, as well as other sources of data. “For instance, on top of satellite imagery, we also used fire data from Nasa, which has sensors that detect every fire of a certain size. That helped us to verify that fires actually happened in these villages on the dates that people said that they happened. We also used conflict data because it was very important for us to be sure that these villages were not destroyed as a side-effect of shelling during battles between the insurgents and the military – that they were actually systematically destroyed. The conflict data showed us that there were actually very few battles during the period of destruction indicated by the satellite imagery, because at that point the insurgents had complete control of that particular region.”How war destroyed Gaza’s neighbourhoods – visual investigationRead moreGathering all this supporting evidence isn’t just about corroborating things. Theinteractive articlewe published last week presents some of those eyewitness testimonies, together with photographs and video clips, alongside the satellite imagery. The result is a more immersive experience that gives audiences a fuller picture of what has been happening on the ground.“One of the big limitations of satellite imagery is that it’s literally very distant from the human story on the ground,” says Anna Leach, a visual projects editor who also worked on the investigation. “But of course this is a very human story about the displacement of people, and we always try to show that human element in everything we do.”“We tried to make sure the article remained connected to the people affected,” adds Prina Shah, a senior digital designer on the Guardian’s visual team who also worked on the project. “So we included photos of villagers’ faces and other images to show that people actually live here and it’s not just about circling things on a map.”Ashley highlights another example from our coverage of the war in Gaza. Published in December,the article in question used satelliteimagery alongside on-the-ground photography to chart a woman’s two-year search for safety in the ruins of Gaza. “We tried to show all of the different places that she was displaced to and how each of those places got destroyed, and so she just had to keep on fleeing,” he says. “Combining the satellite imagery with more traditional reporting techniques meant we could tell her story and also contextualize it. We showed the human story, but the satellite imagery allowed us to show, for example, all of the other tents that surrounded her tent and so you immediately see that her story is just one of thousands. Satellite imagery is really effective for giving people a sense of the scale of what’s happening alongside what’s happening to individuals.”View image in fullscreenPhotographs and satellite images from our article about Nour AbuShammala’s search for safety in Gaza.Composite: Nour AbuShammala / The Guardian / Guardian designGiven that our satellite-based interactive articles often contain multiple perspectives and narratives, our visual journalists also put a great deal of effort into honing the experience of scrolling down as you read them and see the visual evidence. “We’re thinking about how we explain quite complex imagery in a digestible way to an audience that might be viewing it on a mobile phone,” says Prina. “This can entail things like ensuring different elements pop up when they’re meant to and fall back when they need to because the audience’s attention needs to be focused on different aspects of the satellite imagery, for example, or on the personal accounts that are presented simultaneously.”What is ‘home’ now? A woman’s two-year search for safety in the ruins of GazaRead moreThis process involves a lot of testing and fine-tuning before the article is published. “Certain issues only come to light when you’re playing with the actual interactive and refining interactive elements and animation and transitions to improve focus or understanding.”Having spent so many years reporting on the Rohingya, Kaamil really appreciates the team’s efforts to bring the story to life: “We’ve tried to go beyond satellite images that just show destruction. People might get immune to that,” he says. “Also, the Rohingya refugee population has existed for so many years now, it can seem like a stagnant situation. Presenting things in a fresh and different way is part of how we try to make people care and ensure that our reporting has impact. So these forms of journalism help us to report on things that aren’t always on the news agenda.”The investigation into the erasure of Rohingya villages was part of the Guardian’sGlobal developmentseries, which is supported bytheguardian.org.Explore more on these topicsPress freedomInside the GuardianNewspapers & magazinesMyanmarfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future? | Christa Pike | The Guardian
description: Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/AP Photo/The Tennessean/Lisa NippView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/AP Photo/The Tennessean/Lisa NippThe Sunday readChrista PikeCapital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlightEd PilkingtonSun 11 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTShareIt took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through whichChrista Pikewould be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”When the team finally achieved what they thought would be a working line, allowing her execution to proceed, Pike, 50, made a point of thanking them. “Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative,” her lawyer Randy Spivey, a witness in the death chamber, said.The world knowswhat happenednext. For reasons as yet not fully understood, the drug did not enter her bloodstream, probably spilling into her arm tissue.View image in fullscreenMedia witnesses leave Riverbend maximum security institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted in Nashville on 30 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APPike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder when she was 18 of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, remained alive. She is the only person ever to survive a full “lethal” injection execution.On Tuesday she remarkably regained consciousness. She is now able to talk and walk around the room, her lawyers have said.In comments to reporters, Spivey said that he was haunted by the harrowing failed execution. “What I saw is not something that should ever happen again. It was done in all of our names.”The events of the past 10 days – starting with Pike amicably assisting her executioners and ending with her waking up shackled to a Nashville hospital bed, her arms grotesquely swollen, facing a long and uncertain road to recovery – has thrown America into a frenzy. If this is the outcome of a punishment carried out in “all our names”, then what are we doing about it?“This is a very big moment,” said Laura Porter, executive director at the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, an alliance of 60 abolitionist groups. “When you see something as horrific as this, the impact is enormous, as it throws attention on the death penalty’s flaws.”Porter has been closely involved in America’s struggle with capital punishment for almost a quarter century, since she became a leader of New Yorkers Against the Death Penalty in 2003. At that time death row prisoners were still being killed at a rate of more than one a week.There were71 executionsthat year in the US (down from the 1999 pinnacle of 98). Since then, Porter has watched and agitated as the number has steadily declined for almost two decades, reaching a low of just 11 judicial killings in 2021.“I believe that the death penalty will die by a thousand cuts,” she said. “Every time there’s a botched execution like Christa’s, or a wrongful conviction, or the execution of an intellectually disabled person, public understanding of the system’s flaws grows.”View image in fullscreenChrista Pike’s attorneys Randy Spivey, center, and Luke Ihnen, right, hold a news conference in Nashville on 7 October.Photograph: George Walker IV/APHow great a difference a few years can make. Six years ago, there was such confidence in the historic fading away of the practice that the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) began itsyearly reportwith the words: “Capital punishment continued to wither across the US in 2019”.But as Mark Twain might have put it, reports of the death penalty’s own death turned out to be an exaggeration. Fast forward to last year, andDPI was recordingthat the 47 executions carried out in 2025 marked the highest incidence in 16 years.No awards for guessing the key individual behind the resurgence. Less than a year after DPI’s “withering” pronouncement, Donald Trump embarked on one of the most concentrated bursts of US state killing of its own citizens in modern times.Toward the end of his first presidency, the Trump administrationexecuted 13federal death row prisoners. They includedLisa Montgomery, a woman with such a shocking history of childhood sexual abuse it bears comparison toPike’s own.Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions. On his first day back he issued anexecutive orderon “restoring the death penalty” in which he said it was “an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes”.The statement was a classic Trump fabrication. The US justice department itself has concluded that there isno proofthat the punishment deters criminals. Many prisoners on death row cannot be described as the most heinous, not least the 4% who byconservative estimationsare innocent.At federal level, Trump has been hampered by Joe Biden, who before he left office commuted the death penalties of all but three prisoners on federal death row. Using his power as commander-in-chef, Trump still managed this week to order the military execution by firing squad ofNidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooter.On Thursday the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth,breathlessly announcedthat Hasan would face a firing squad of soldiers at Fort Hood on 3 December in the first public execution to be staged in the US since 1936. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”The Pentagon’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution prompted a second wave of desbelief that ricocheted around the globe , threatening to drown out even the consternation over Pike’s treatment. US politicians denounced the idea as “disgusting”, while the UN issued the US government with the samestern warningit has given Afghanistan and Iran that the move would be tantamount to torture.When not presiding over an administration that seems determined to turn the clock back 100 years, Trumphas also used his squawk box to exhort death penalty states, where most capital punishment activity occurs, to hit the gas. Many have obliged.First among them has been Florida. The outgoing governor,Ron DeSantis, appears to have been so inspired by Trump’s 2020-21 killing spree that he greenlit a record 19 executions last year.DeSantis will come closeto matching that shattering number in 2026. Florida has already put to death16 prisonersthis year, with two more executions pending, though the governorcancelled a lethal injectionprocedure on Friday without giving an explanation.A bar chart showing that death sentences in the US have been declining since the 2000sNationwide, the US is set to kill up to 38 people this year – the most recent just on Wednesday whenTexas executedconvicted murderer Jamaal Howard. That tally would be down from last year’s high, but still represent a larger display of state killing than in any yearsince 2013.In cheerleading the revival of executions, Trump has been backed by a supporting cast of Christian nationalists. These Bible thumpers have injected their eye-for-an-eye brand of retributive justice into the wider Maga movement.Brooklyn Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville,has studiedChristian nationalist views on justice. She has found them to be far more embracing of retribution, including the death sentence, than other US religious groups.Christian nationalist leaders frequently invoke Old Testament notions of punitive justice “as part of the idea of creating a social order, and then requiring people to fit within it,” Walker said.Doug Wilson, anIdaho pastorwho wants to turn America into a theocracy and has close ties to Hegseth, has pushed for legal appeals to be streamlined. That way death row prisoners could be dispatched more quickly.Joel Webbon, another leading Christian nationalist pastor from Texas,has arguedfor the death penalty to be expanded to include women who make false sexual assault accusations. The day after Pike’s failed executionhe postedto his 120,000 followers on X that “you cannot be pro life without being pro death penalty”.View image in fullscreenLeslie Brown, right, stands with others in the area reserved for people in favor to the death penalty outside Riverbend maximum security institution before the planned execution of Christa Pike.Photograph: George Walker IV/APThe energy blown into capital punishment from such far-right religious pundits is affecting the furious debate that has now erupted in Tennessee over what should happen to Pike. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for Tennessee governor, wants toplug back inthe electric chair.Blackburn’s call for the return of “Old Sparky” speaks volumes about the state of capital punishment. The horrifying scenes at Pike’s attempted execution were part of a wider unravelling of lethal injections, the protocol that has been dominant in the US for almost 50 years.ByDPI’s calculations, there have been 12 botched executions in the past five years alone. Five of the condemned prisoners involved, including Pike herself, survived the procedure meaning that they were rendered immobile while a team of masked strangers failed to kill them for up to several hours.Amid such unconscionable suffering, the claim made on behalf of lethal injections that they are a medicalised and humane form of ending a life has come unstuck. Who would dare to classify what Pike endured as humane?Proponents of the ultimate punishment have been forced to seek alternatives that might avoid some of the pitfalls of lethal injections. But the moment they have introduced such often archaic methods they have run into a whole new set of headaches.Two of the prisoners who survived recent lethal injections, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, were executed by Alabama a year later under the experimental technique, nitrogen gas. The method is regarded by veterinarians as too cruel for the euthanisia ofcats and dogs, and it has now been blocked for human use by afederal court.Other states have tried the firing squad. But when South Carolina took this path last year with Mikal Mahdi, a convicted murderer, the marksmenmissed the targetof the prisoner’s heart, causing him a prolonged and likely agonising death.Such an avalanche of mishaps, spanning botched executions, experimentation, and evendark insinuationsof deliberate miss-targeting, is what Porter means by her “death by a thousand cuts”. It gives her and her army of abolitionists the material they need to sustain a long campaign.As a seasoned abolitionist, Porter knows that she is facing tough adversaries in Trump and the Christian nationalists. But she draws sustenance from the 23 states that have scrapped the death penalty which, if you add the four states that have put the practice on hold, pushes them into the majority.A line chart showing support for the death penalty in the US throughout the decadesThen there is the growing number of young Americans who no longer support the punishment. In the most recentGallup pollthat asked the question, from 2024, only 42% of 18 to 34 year olds approved. (In last year’s poll the overall extent of support had fallen from a 1995 high of 80% to 52%).She also takes heart from the burgeoning ranks of Republican state lawmakers willing to raise objections. And by the increasing unwillingness of juries to mete outnew death sentences.Most of all, she’s buoyed up by the powerful accord she has found from an unlikely source: families of capital murder victims. Amid their grief, some families have had the strength and conviction to join the fight to spare the lives of those who killed their loved ones.“In every campaign I’ve been part of where we’ve ended the death penalty – in Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and many more – victims’ families have been among the lead voices,” Porter said.To those voices we may perhaps, in time, be able to add one more. It would be the most unlikely voice of all – that of a woman whom the modern state, with all its paraphernalia, could not silence: Christa Pike.View image in fullscreenShannon Howard and Ingrid McIntyre hug outside Riverbend maximum security institution on 30 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APHer lawyers tell us that she isangry and confused, her mind foggy. But she is also able to inquire after the well-being of others, including, poignantly, the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer.She is not out of the woods: on Saturday she was released from hospital and returned to the women’s prison in Nashville, where she will still receive medical care.But coming from a state of unconsciousness so profound that even her own legal team feared she might be brain-dead, her reemergence has been nothing short of astonishing.It all leaves so many questions, her lawyer Spivey said ruefully on Wednesday. “We have to ask, ‘How much suffering is enough?’”Spivey directed the question at Tennessee. He might just as well have been addressing America.

title: Thousands without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north | Hurricane Isaias | The Guardian
description: At least four deaths linked to storm amid warnings of flash flooding that could stretch into Appalachians
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: At least four deaths linked to storm amid warnings of flash flooding that could stretch into Appalachians
Content: Downed power lines in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APView image in fullscreenDowned power lines in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APHurricane IsaiasThousands without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves northAt least four deaths linked to storm amid warnings of flash flooding that could stretch into AppalachiansCoral Murphy Marcosand agenciesSun 11 Oct 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs what was left ofHurricane Isaiasmoved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across theFloridaPanhandle and southernAlabamaremained without power.Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts.According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday.Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandleRead moreAt least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes inFloridaandAlabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.Isaias came ashore as a category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. This has been the first hurricane tomake landfallin the continental US in two years, sinceMiltonstruck western Florida in October 2024.Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.Hurricane-force winds in theFloridaPanhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.In Florida’s Escambia county, sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home – and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from four to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.View image in fullscreenCity of Crestview police officers direct traffic after the traffic signals stopped working when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on Saturday in Milton, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesThe first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther intoAlabamawith tropical-force winds.One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, the city’s fire chief, Cory Moon, said. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration forGeorgiaafter the president did the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.The US Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm.The NWS said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.View image in fullscreenA member of Mexico's national guard stands on the Puerto Vallarta boardwalk as waves crash against the shoreline ahead of the potential impact of Hurricane Simon in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco state, Mexico, on Sunday.Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155mph (250kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning on Sunday to parts of south-westernMexicowith life-threatening flooding and mudslides.Forecasters say that conditions brought by Simon are spreading northward along a stretch of coastline that includes Puerto Vallarta. Rain could average 8-16in over sectors of south-western Mexico, with as much as 30in possible in places across Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco through Monday.A woman, a man and their dog in Burke county,North Carolina, were rescued on the Catawba River after their camping trip was overflown by the rising water brought by remnants of Simon that caught them off guard.Tropical storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and southern California. The National Weather Service has issued a flash flood warning in parts of San Diego, Riverside and Imperial counties. Officials issued mandatoryevacuation ordersfor some residents in the Long Beach peninsula through Tuesday.Eight buildings have been red-tagged, or deemed unsafe to enter, and one has been yellow-tagged amid conditions from Rachel. Long Beach officials have provided about 11,000 sandbags for the storm to protect homes from the rising tide.Explore more on these topicsHurricane IsaiasFloridaAlabamaHurricanesWest CoastUS weatherNorth CarolinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in Peru  | Melbourne | The Guardian
description: Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’
Content: Jordan Yap (R) and his partner, Anita. Yap last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range.Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin NguyenView image in fullscreenJordan Yap (R) and his partner, Anita. Yap last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range.Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin NguyenMelbourneMissing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in PeruFamily and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastGuardian staffSun 11 Oct 2026 03.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”Map of PeruTheMelbourneman was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMelbourne hiker Jordan Yap (right), pictured with friend Kevin Nguyen during a hike of Mount Kosciuszko in NSW. Yap was regarded as an experienced hiker.Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin NguyenA spokesperson from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who had died in Peru.“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said.- with AAPExplore more on these topicsMelbournePeruAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities | Panama | The Guardian
description: More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations
Content: The damaged San Atanasio church in La Villa de Los Santos, Panama, on Saturday.Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPAView image in fullscreenThe damaged San Atanasio church in La Villa de Los Santos, Panama, on Saturday.Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPAPanama‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communitiesMore than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuationsAssociated PressSun 11 Oct 2026 02.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePanama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).View image in fullscreenA car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama.Photograph: Enea Lebrun/ReutersThe presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.Map showing epicentre of earthquakePowerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Panama and triggers panic in capitalRead moreAbout 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”View image in fullscreenElodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday.Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPAOfficials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.Explore more on these topicsPanamaAmericasEarthquakesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Oliver Blume says Made in Europe rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Oliver Blume says Made in Europe rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
Content: VW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGView image in fullscreenVW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industryOliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’Jasper Jollyin ParisSun 11 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.The rules are aimed at countering therapid rise of Chinese brands in Europein the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launcheda brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocketRead moreThe proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition fromChina.On Friday,the EU said it had reached a landmark dealwith China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe new all-electric ID Tiguan.Photograph: Volkswagen AGBlume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryChinese economyEuropean UnionChinaAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 13, charged with murder after man stabbed to death in Sydney’s west  | Sydney | The Guardian

Author: Nick Visser
Headline: Second boy, 16, also charged in relation to the stabbing death of a 30-year-old man in Mount Druitt
Content: A 13-year-old boy has been charged with murder after a man was stabbed to death in Mt Druitt in Sydney’s west on Friday.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA 13-year-old boy has been charged with murder after a man was stabbed to death in Mt Druitt in Sydney’s west on Friday.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesSydneyBoy, 13, charged with murder after man stabbed to death in Sydney’s westSecond boy, 16, also charged in relation to the stabbing death of a 30-year-old man in Mount DruittGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNick title: The Australian’s Shadow of Doubt podcast delayed ‘sadistic’ paedophile’s trial, court documents reveal | Australian media | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: As William ‘Rob’ Gilfillan was about to go on trial for sex offences against two schoolgirls, his barrister told a judge his client’s history was easily discoverable online
Author: Amanda Meade
Headline: Exclusive: As William ‘Rob’ Gilfillan was about to go on trial for sex offences against two schoolgirls, his barrister told a judge his client’s history was easily discoverable online
Content: The victim in the case covered by The Australian’s Shadow of Doubt said the podcast had been highly detrimental to her mental health.Illustration: The AustralianThe victim in the case covered by The Australian’s Shadow of Doubt said the podcast had been highly detrimental to her mental health.Illustration: The AustralianAustralian mediaThe Australian’s Shadow of Doubt podcast delayed ‘sadistic’ paedophile’s trial, court documents revealExclusive:As William ‘Rob’ Gilfillan was about to go on trial for sex offences against two schoolgirls, his barrister told a judge his client’s history was easily discoverable onlineFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesSign up for Guardian Australia’s free weekly media newsletter hereAmanda MeadeMedia correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian’s podcast Shadow of Doubt led to a delay of 10 months for the sex offence trial of a“sadistic” paedophilealready serving a 48-year jail term for abusing his daughter, court documents have revealed.William “Rob” Gilfillan, a former physical education teacher, was to stand trial in Victoria in February last year on five counts of indecent assault and sexual penetration of a person under 16, relating to two schoolgirls in his care in Gippsland in the 1980s.Due to the presumption of innocence the jury could not be told about Gilfillan’s convictions for child abuse in New South Wales.Former PE teacher serving Australia’s longest child abuse jail time sentenced for crimes against two schoolgirlsRead moreThe Shadow of Doubt podcast, launched in March 2023, claimed the conviction for the rape and torture of his daughter in 2016 may be a “grave miscarriage of justice”.Gilfillan and his ex-wife, Karen, who was also jailed for sexual abuse,told The Australianfrom jail: “We’re innocent … these things just did not happen.”An editorial in the newspaper in 2023 said the victim’s story was “manifestly implausible”.Neither the podcast nor other reporting named the Gilfillans because there were suppression orders in place until a jury returned a verdict in the Victorian courts.But details such as the family’s involvement in high-level athletics and teaching meant people recognised them.Sign up to get Guardian Australia’s weekly media diary as a free newsletterOn the eve of the empanelment of the jury in the Victorian case last year, the defence barrister, Paul Kounnas, told the court his client’s name and criminal history was easily discoverable online.Kounnas said the reporting of the jail interview by the journalist Richard Guilliatt had sparked feverish speculation on internet forums such as Reddit.“The podcast is the first link that comes up on typing the accused’s name into Google, even though he is not identified by name in that podcast,” Kounnas said.“The podcast is one called Shadow of Doubt … and it details the record prison sentences received in this matter and alludes to the nature of the ‘depraved abuse’ that the trial was subject of.”Kounnas applied for a permanent stay of the trial, arguing the “prejudice is immediate and obvious”.“It has been inflamed to such a degree by the podcast, which I understand was reasonably high profile, that it’s fuelled the internet flames, so to speak,” Kounnas said in court transcripts seen by Guardian Australia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWeekly BeastAmanda Meade's weekly diary on the latest in Australian media, free every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prosecutor, Sandra MacDougall, said the publicity had “created an irredeemable prejudice to the conduct of this trial”.Justice Michael O’Connell denied a stay but ordered the director of public prosecutions to attempt to remove the prejudicial material from the internet before the trial could go ahead. He delayed jury selection until 1 December 2025.“I’m very troubled by the continuing position where these comments remain on the internet notwithstanding that, for weeks now we’ve identified a very significant problem potentially affecting the fairness of the trial and nothing’s been done it seems to resolve the problem,” O’Connell said.When the trial went ahead in December the jury found Gilfillan guilty of “brazen and forcible” sexual crimes and he wassentenced in Juneto seven-and-a-half years in jail, to be served concurrently with his record 48-year term.The Australian did not respond to a request for comment.In April, Corrective Services NSW said itwas investigatinghow Guilliatt had been able to interview the couple in jail.After legal restrictions were lifted, the victim in the New South Wales case agreed to be identifiedby news.com.auand saidthe podcast had been highly detrimentalto her mental health.In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines InternationalExplore more on these topicsAustralian medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens prepare for fight with Labor over social media algorithm reform, with ‘pervert glasses’ in its sights | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: Minor party plans to drive a bargain in exchange for support for digital duty of care legislation
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Minor party plans to drive a bargain in exchange for support for digital duty of care legislation
Content: Sarah Hanson-Young says Australians harmed online must have the right to take big tech companies to court.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPView image in fullscreenSarah Hanson-Young says Australians harmed online must have the right to take big tech companies to court.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPAustralian GreensGreens prepare for fight with Labor over social media algorithm reform, with ‘pervert glasses’ in its sightsMinor party plans to drive a bargain in exchange for support for digital duty of care legislationFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greens will push Labor to dramatically change new laws designed to rein in big tech, calling for individuals to have the right to take platforms to court and win financial compensation.As Labor prepares to introduce its planneddigital duty of care lawsinto parliament this week, the Greens say they will drive a bargain in exchange for support, including pushing for fines by the eSafety commissioner to be levied as a percentage of corporations’ global revenue rather than set amounts.The Coalition is opposed to the duty of care plan, giving the Greens the upper hand in negotiations. Their communications spokesperson,Sarah Hanson-Young, said the laws should do more to address the addictive nature of platforms.“To meaningfully change the behaviour of big tech companies, the digital duty of care laws must include the right for Australians who have been harmed online to be able to take legal action and seek compensation for the damage done,” she said.“Enforcement of the digital duty of care cannot be left to the eSafety commissioner alone.“To really put Australians’ online safety at the heart of this reform, individuals and the community need to have the right to take on big tech through a private right of action.”The negotiations will be the first under the new Greens leader,David Shoebridge.He has flagged a firmer negotiating approach than under his predecessor, Larissa Waters, potentially frustrating the government’s agenda in the second half of the year.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereShoebridge is expected to introduce a bill to stop the importation of so-called “pervert glasses” and other wearable technology this week.Labor wants progress on its remaining budget bills, including moves to make tax treatment for trusts less generous.Last month the government said it would legislate the duty of care and establishing fines of more than A$100m for platforms not protecting users from harm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnika Wells named on Time100 list as one of ‘world’s most influential rising stars’ after social media banRead morePopular platforms as well as online games, apps and AI chatbots will be required to protect against specific harms, including pornography; eating disorder content; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that could cause serious distress, including abuse and bullying.The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to companies, with operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.Users over 16 years of age will also be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content.But Hanson-Young has warned that the proposed fines are too small to change the behaviour of tech giants.“Fines for breaches must be tied to a percentage of global revenue,” she said. “The threat of serious fines and compensation is the only way to force these companies to clean up their act and proactively provide a safe environment for their users.”The communications minister, Anika Wells, will address the National Press Club on Thursday. She has pledged to work constructively with the Greens and any other party to deliver basic safety standards.“We want these platforms to embed safety by design,” Wells said. “Some of them have had 15 years to do it of their own accord. They haven’t, so now we’re going to legislate that they must.”The shadow communications spokesperson, Sarah Henderson, warned on Sunday the duty of care laws could restrict free speech.“At stake is something generations of Australians have fought and died to defend,” she told theConservative Political Action Conference. “Your freedom of speech questions authority, to challenge government, to expose injustice and, above all, the freedom to disagree.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensSocial media banSarah Hanson-YoungAustralian politicsBusinessInternet safetyDavid ShoebridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Content: Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/ReutersView image in fullscreenAftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday.Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/ReutersUkraineTrump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructureLuke HardingSun 11 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consultingVolodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia andUkraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it ifVladimir Putindid the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath on Sunday of a Russian strike on Kharkiv that hit residential homes.Photograph: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy/ReutersThere was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he waslifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraineneeded a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.Map of Ukraine with Russian advances and territoryResponding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, whenTrump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.The Financial Times, citing officials inEurope, reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.The New York Timeshas reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors,the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.View image in fullscreenMedics help a woman injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine on Saturday after overnight strikes.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAOn Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered dronesRead moreThe head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee,Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by theTrump administration– would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official toldthe Kyiv Independent newspaper.On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing StreetsaidBurnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair.
