It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.Luke Harding’sBetrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquestis published by Guardian FaberExplore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyyVladimir PutinJared KushnerUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detained | Poland | The Guardian
description: Polish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Polish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealed
Content: Donald Tusk was told about the threat first thing on Sunday morning.Photograph: Albert Zawada/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Tusk was told about the threat first thing on Sunday morning.Photograph: Albert Zawada/EPAPolandDonald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detainedPolish PM praises police for ‘swift and decisive action’ after threat against him and defence minister revealedAgence France-Presse in WarsawSun 11 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Polish prime minister,Donald Tusk, said on Sunday that a man accused of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister had been detained.“The man threatening an attack has been detained,” Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their “swift and decisive action”.The arrest was also confirmed by the country’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński.The interior ministry had earlier said that Tusk and the defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been targeted.It ordered authorities to take action “in connection with the information received by the police concerning a possible assassination attempt on the prime minister... as well as the deputy prime minister”, who is also defence minister, spokesperson Karolina Gałecka wrote on X.Members of the police, state protection service (SOP) and internal security agency were present at Sunday’s meeting.“We are treating this matter as deadly serious,” a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzyński, told journalists afterwards.“Month by month, year by year, more and more various threats and menacing messages reach the police, SOP, and the services concerningPolandand Poles,” he said. In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out.”Poland, a Nato and EU member, has been on high alert after a series of stabbings in the last week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a “cult of violence”.Explore more on these topicsPolandDonald TuskEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries
Content: Diesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDiesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationAnalysisTrump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts saySimon GoodleyAnalysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineriesTrump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTShareDonald Trump’s deal withVladimir Putinto temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.The US presidentinfuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyywhen he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.The package announced by Trump involves300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately“to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from theUS Energy Information Administration.“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.Graph showing increase in price of US dieselUS prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war,to about $6.30 a gallon, according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of dieselclimbed to a record £2 a litreearlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.”However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, includingEurope.The US Treasurysuspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 Aprilas part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trumpsaid Ukraine neeeded “a new leader”.On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries ifRussiacurbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia andUkraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsEnergy industrySupply chain crisisGlobal economyInternational tradeUS economyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum | Brexit | The Guardian
description: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled
Content: Andy Burnham: ‘We haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham: ‘We haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesBrexitAndy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendumPM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddledAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum fromRussia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote.The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.”He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”The UK is developing a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt hostile state information campaigns aimed at undermining British democracy. Downing Street said it was working with Germany on a new partnership to counter hybrid threats, including hostile activities that threaten both countries’ security and prosperity.A spokesperson said: “National security is the first duty of any government – we are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.“We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies.“We will continue to leave no stone unturned in our efforts to protect the UK from harm.”Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourRussiaEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: People smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis? | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
Content: People run away from teargas fired by police as they try to cross the Channel from Petit-Fort-Philippe in Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople run away from teargas fired by police as they try to cross the Channel from Petit-Fort-Philippe in Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersImmigration and asylumPeople smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis?As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomesDiane TaylorSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time.“I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.”The wind has dropped, the waves are flat and there are no French police in sight. The conditions are perfect as the smuggler rushes everyone into the dinghy as it moves away from the shore.Amad is one of several asylum speakers who spoke to the Guardian this week from the area of northernFranceknown as the Jungle. They were hoping to cross the Channel to the UK in the next few days.“This place is busier than ever,” says another asylum seeker, Omar, from Yemen. “So many refugees and so many smugglers are here. Everyone wants to cross.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers stand guard on the beach in Petit-Fort-Philippe, Gravelines, near Calais.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersSome who have already been forcibly removed from the UK are hoping to return. They were sent to France under the“one in, one out” scheme, where one small-boat arrival is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK.Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?Read moreNow, after moving approximately 1,500 people in both directions across the Channel, the scheme has been brought to an end. Beset with problems, itcould not be effectively scaled up, the British government concluded.NGOs working on the ground with asylum seekers in northern France were unsurprised by the outcome and say the end of “one in, one out” must prompt a wider discussion about how to deal with the crisis in the Channel.The UK government has shown little sign it is contemplating a radical shift in attitude. A Home Office spokesperson pointed the Guardian to anannouncementabout a refugee resettlement scheme that is likely to assist only a few hundred refugees a year and is highly unlikely to stop people crossing the Channel in small boats.The spokesperson said: “Just last week, the home secretary announced the reopening of the UK resettlement scheme for new referrals, providing genuine refugees with a safe and legal route to the UK.”The agencies calling for a different approach hope at least to expand the parameters of the debate.View image in fullscreenPeople sit inside a bus at the port of Calais after three people including a child died while attempting to cross the Channel on 28 September.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersAccording to workers in the Jungle, living conditions there are appalling. Those at Utopia 56, which witnesses police interventions on French beaches where asylum seekers try to board dinghies, say that since the UK increased its funding to France earlier this year on a payment-by-results basis, police violence against migrants has increased significantly.Utopia 56 estimates a 40% increase in police violence from April to August 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. That coincided with an agreement for the UK to pay France£660mover three years to ramp up “stop the boats” initiatives.Sophie McCann, of Médecins Sans Frontières UK, said: “The government’s increasingly brutal efforts to stop people trying to reach the UK by boat are failing. MSF’s medical and mental health teams in Calais and Dunkirk witness the serious physical and psychological harm caused by violence and harassment meted out by French police, largely funded by the UK, on people who have already fled war, persecution and extreme hardship.“People will continue to risk their lives crossing the Channel in search of safety in the UK until the government provides safe and accessible routes.”The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union, which has manyHome Officestaff among its members, has worked with the refugee charity Care4Calais to draw up a blueprint to introduce a refugee visa-to-travel scheme for asylum seekers to travel legally to the UK.The plan would still require asylum claims to be considered on merit and for those whose claims are rejected to be removed from the UK. But they say it would eliminate people smugglers from the equation and save lives. According to the UN’s International Organization forMigration(IMO), at least 225 people have died while trying to cross the Channel since 2018.View image in fullscreenPeople gather after disembarking from a French rescue ship after their boat was caught in the Channel at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 4 August.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/GettyThe scheme would be unlikely to halt irregular arrivals entirely, but Care4Calais says it could dent the smugglers’ business in a way that other initiatives have failed to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCharlotte Khan, of Care4Calais, said: “Consecutive governments have focused on border security measures that have only made Channel crossings more dangerous, resulting in a shocking number of lives lost, while completely ignoring the only solution that will work – safe routes.”The PCS general secretary, Fran Heathcote, called for safe routes to be significantly scaled up. “Our members deal with the human impact of the asylum system on a daily basis and their voices must be heard. The only way to truly undermine criminal smuggling gangs is to remove the demand through a Ukrainian-style visa system, allowing people fleeing war and persecution to travel safely and legally to claim asylum.”The Labour government has arguably made more efforts than any other to try to prevent asylum seekers from reaching the UK in small boats.Previously, people travelled less visibly, in the backs of lorries or on planes, and so attracted less public attention. Images of black dinghies overcrowded with people in orange lifejackets, monetised for social media clicks by far-right agitators, have generated mounting hostility from some who say they are evidence that the government has lost control of its borders.View image in fullscreenA group of people thought to be migrants are brought to a marina in Gosport by the RNLI after a small boat incident in the Channel.Photograph: Trevor Adams/PABut desperate people continue to clamber into dinghies. In the six days between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 peoplearrivedin 23 boats. Along with the now terminated “one in, one out” pilot, which government trumpeted as“groundbreaking”when it announced it in July 2025, the Home Office and the National Crime Agency make regular announcements about smugglers being intercepted and dinghies seized “upstream”.There has been a reduction of more than 40% in small boat arrivals so far this year compared with the same period last year, probably due to a combination of UK government initiatives, windy weather and a drop in irregular migration to Europe overall. According to data published by the IMO, there has beena 39% reductionthis year in these arrivals to Europe – from 98,040 during the same period last year to approximately 60,000.Despite the reduction in arrivals, far-right agitators wearing masks and black paramilitary clothing continue to protest on the streets and try to block small boat arrivals.View image in fullscreenPeople protest against small boats arriving in Gosport near Portsmouth.Photograph: Solent NewsNone of the policy roadblocks appear to have dented the resolve of asylum seekers who want to reach the UK.Two people die trying to cross Channel as anti-migrant protesters clash with police in GosportRead moreSohrab, from Afghanistan, has been sleeping on the streets of Paris and is making his way to the Jungle. “I want to live and I will do anything to save my life from death,” he says. “I have already spent a bad day in jail in France after police caught me trying to get into a lorry heading for the UK. The smugglers are very violent, but there is no other way for me to reach the UK apart than to go to the Jungle.”Despite the failure of “one in, one out” to deter small boat crossings, Emily Graham, of the Future Governance Forum, believes it is the way forward.“The ‘one-in, one-out’ pilot proved cooperation based on responsibility-sharing is right in principle and has the potential to deliver results,” she said. “To reduce the number of people arriving by small boat, the government should build on the previous pilot and seek a new ‘routes for returns’ deal with European partners.”Amad has another idea. “We would much prefer to give our money to the UK government if they allowed us to come here legally, rather than to the smugglers,” he says. “No asylum seeker would pay smugglers who beat and exploit them, or risk our lives on a dinghy, if there was another way.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceMigrationRefugeesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict
Author: William Christou
Headline: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict
Content: Dust and debris inside King Khalid international airport after Saturday’s attack.Photograph: Social media/ReutersView image in fullscreenDust and debris inside King Khalid international airport after Saturday’s attack.Photograph: Social media/ReutersSaudi ArabiaRiyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities sayUnidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflictAnalysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategyWilliam Christouin JerusalemSun 11 Oct 2026 18.28 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.In a post on X, the British embassy inSaudi Arabiaadvised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”The Iran-allied Houthisclaimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300–the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.Regional mapIn response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.Aftermath of strike on Riyadh’s international airportThe Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.View image in fullscreenPeople outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday.Photograph: APIt would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.View image in fullscreenHouthi supporters rally in Sana’a on Friday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAThe Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East crisis: Riyadh airport hit again as Houthis claim attacks, including strike that killed 12 – as it happened | Houthis | The Guardian
description: Houthi military spokesman says Iran-backed group carried out several targeted attacks
Author: Frances Mao
Headline: Houthi military spokesman says Iran-backed group carried out several targeted attacks
Content: 14.03 EDTSummaryFollowing yesterday’s attack on Riyadh international airportthat killed 12 people and injured hundreds,the site was hit againon Sunday. Authorities said an “unidentified projectile” struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport. Air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile” in the vicinity of the airport.An Egyptian flight attendant, a Syrian woman, and an Indian national were among the 12 killedin yesterday’s Saudi airport attack. The Egyptian woman killed was identified as Azza Ramzy, 28. The Syrian woman was identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.TheSaudi General Authority of Civil Aviationsaid in a statement that today’s attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh “resulted in injuries” but did not specify how many.Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for both Saturday and Sunday’s attackson Riyadh Airport. The group said on Sunday they had targeted Riyadh’s airport several times as well as Saudi energy facilities, a day after Saturday’s deadly attack.The United Arab Emirates issued a statement in solidarity with Saudi Arabia, expressing support for “all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability”. The UAE message is significant given the major rupture in relations this year.The Houthis this morning issued a warning to travelers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airportsfollowing yesterday’s attack. A Houthi military spokesman warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”.The attacks on Riyadh airport came just before a major oil summit, the World Petroleum Congress, scheduled for this week. The repeated attacks have temporarily halted oil flows and driven up global oil prices. The CEOs of major companies Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, TotalEnergies had been due to attend the summit but given the attacks, it’s unclear if executives will take the risk.Share

title: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy | Yemen | The Guardian
description: US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable
Content: Donald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty ImagesYemenAnalysisHouthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategyPatrick WintourUS president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainableMiddle East crisis live - latest updatesSun 11 Oct 2026 09.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 15.04 EDTShareThe reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also leftDonald Trumpforced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since theHouthisare firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy.Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blameUkrainefor the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.”The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.”Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics.The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating.So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1bn a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf.The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms.A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances.China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south ofYemenis split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war.So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policyIrananalysisShareReuse this content

title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino’s West End play The Popinjay Cavalier | Stage | The Guardian
description: The production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage, which he will also direct
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage, which he will also direct
Content: Director Quentin Tarantino and actor Sacha Baron Cohen, who will star in the film-maker’s stage debut, The Popinjay Cavalier, on the West End.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenDirector Quentin Tarantino and actor Sacha Baron Cohen, who will star in the film-maker’s stage debut, The Popinjay Cavalier, on the West End.Photograph: APStageSacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino’s West End play The Popinjay CavalierThe production marks the Hollywood director’s first play written for the stage,  which he will also directPress AssociationSun 11 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSacha Baron Cohen will headlineQuentin Tarantino’s play The Popinjay Cavalierwhen it premieres on the West End in London in March 2027.The production marks the Hollywood director’s first work written for the stage – which he will also direct.Premiering at the Phoenix theatre in London’sWest Endon 18 March 2027, tickets go on sale on Monday.Tarantino, 63, who is best known for films including Reservoir Dogs, Pulp Fiction and Once Upon A Time In Hollywood, said he was “keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out”.Please take your seats, the carnage is about to begin: what will Quentin Tarantino’s West End debut look like?Read moreA popinjay is defined as “a vain, foppish or conceited person”, while a cavalier is a cavalryman or courteous gentleman.Baron Cohen added: “Quentin called, I said yes before he even got to say his first ‘motherfucker’. When the best director in the world calls, you don’t ask questions. I am beyond delighted that we will be losing our West End virginity together. I have made him promise not to be gentle.”Set in 1830s Europe, The Popinjay Cavalier has been billed as a “rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen”.It was inspired by the classic swashbuckler genre of old Hollywood, including the writings of George Bruce, Ernst Vajda and Jesse Lasky Jr.Full casting will be announced at a later date.Sony Pictures Entertainment and Sonia Friedman Productions are producing the play.Tom Rothman, the chairman and chief executive of Sony Pictures Entertainment’s Motion Picture Group, and Friedman, said: “It is a joy and an honour to be developing this play with Quentin – and obviously quite an adventure. How lucky we are that one of the great storytellers of our time has chosen to make his theatrical debut.“To see Quentin in action in a rehearsal room is extraordinary. His delight in working with actors, fencers, acrobats, musicians and our creative team is infectious, and there is such pleasure in hearing his delicious language come alive and discovering what his world can become on stage.“And now we haveSacha Baron Cohenat the heart of it all: a fearless, brilliantly inventive actor with the wit, mischief and daring this role demands. We feel immensely fortunate to be producing this show. Audiences are in for a tremendous treat.”Tarantino made his directorial debut in 1992 with Reservoir Dogs, before co-writing, directing and acting in Pulp Fiction, which saw him pick up his first Oscar for best screenplay.He went on to direct Jackie Brown, Kill Bill Volume 1 and Volume 2, Death Proof, Inglourious Basterds, Django Unchained, The Hateful Eight, and Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood.Throughout his career he has won two Academy Awards, two Baftas and four Golden Globes. He has also been nominated for an Emmy and five Grammys.Meanwhile Baron Cohen is best known for creating and playing comic characters including Ali G, Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard.The 54-year-old has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys. He has not yet had a leading role in a major stage production. He trained with the French clown guru Philippe Gaulier.Tarantino first revealed his plans to stage a play in 2025, saying on the Church of Tarantino podcast it was “all written”.“I’m preparing for it to be a success. If it’s a flop, I’ll be done very quickly,” he said.Tickets for The Popinjay Cavalier are on sale from 9am BST on Monday to those who signed up for priority access, with a public sale from 12pm.Tickets start at £25, with more than 16,000 tickets priced at under £50 across the run.Explore more on these topicsStageSacha Baron CohenQuentin TarantinoTheatreWest EndLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Content: Liquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety effortsKanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangersRobert BoothandDan MilmoSun 11 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCompanies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs anAI safety research body, has warned there is a“50% chance”of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has beensignedby leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.View image in fullscreenThe UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesIn one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Fridayrevealedthat when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturdaycalled forAI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Kanishka NarayanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Failure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report finds | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: In first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisis
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: In first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisis
Content: The report said the tagging system was ‘performing poorly and failing to meet demand’.Photograph: Stocksolutions/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe report said the tagging system was ‘performing poorly and failing to meet demand’.Photograph: Stocksolutions/AlamyPrisons and probationFailure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report findsIn first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisisJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 5,000 offenders went unmonitored in the first half of the year because probation staff failed to install electronic tags, while 1,600 tags had no signal for more than two weeks due to faults, a report has found.The Institute for Government (IfG) has revealed the full scale of the crisis in the probation system inEnglandand Wales, concluding that “rationing probation supervision” due to a lack of staff meant sentences imposed by the court had become “essentially a fiction” for most offenders.Once the 2026SentencingAct – which reduces the release point for many sentences – is fully implemented, most offenders will spend the final third of their sentence on licence without any active supervision, the report said.“This risks further undermining public trust in the criminal justice system and making sentences even more convoluted and opaque, including to victims,” the report by the independent thinktank found.UK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been taggedRead moreCassia Rowland, the associate director at the institute and author of the report, said: “It’s hard to set out just how demoralised and unhappy a lot of probation staff are. They feel everything is really chaotic, all of these changes are being flung on to them, they’re worried about their personal safety and the public protection risk of the people they’re managing.”She added: “The sentences courts are imposing are having less and less relevance to the time people are actually serving. The situation we’ve reached now is if you get given a six-year sentence, you’re most likely going to be spending two years in prison, two years on probation and then two years with conditions that no one is monitoring or enforcing. That’s just not a six-year sentence.”The report’s most scathing criticisms of the Probation Service included the electronic tagging of offenders, which the report found was “performing poorly and failing to meet demand”.Between January and April, more than 5,000 people who should have been monitored were not tagged, equating to 15% of all people with an electronic tagging order.Almost 1,600 people were wearing a tag that did not send a signal to the monitoring system for two weeks due to technical faults or the device not being charged.The report highlighted how issues of this kind meant that not a single probation delivery unit inspected in 2024 or 2025 received a rating above “requires improvement”, and two-thirds were rated “inadequate”.View image in fullscreenOffenders leaving HMP Brixton as part of the early release scheme on 1 October.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesThe report, based on public data and interviews with frontline staff, found as well as the increased risk to public safety, prisoners were also being let down, with little action taken to reduce reoffending rates.“People have told me stories of referring prisoners on to substance misuse programmes and their sentence ends before they reach the front of the waiting list. The system is not functioning to try to help people,” Rowland said.The report urged the government to increase the number of probation workers at a steady pace, and reintroduce home detention to help manage the prison population.It also called for a sentencing model that is “transparent and understandable”, and which explicitly sets out time in prison and time supervised in the community, with no licence periods without supervision.The report praised Keir Starmer’s government for taking steps to stabilise the prison population, but said this work may have been “undone” by Andy Burnham, whoannounced a number of exemptions to the early release schemeafter public backlash.At the start of October,the first 700 of an expected 4,500 criminals were released early from prisonas part of emergency measures brought in with facilities just months away from reaching maximum capacity.Some said they expected to quickly return to prison as they had nowhere to live and would breach their licence conditions. The IfG report said administrative recalls for issues not relating to a new offence had “skyrocketed” in recent years.The government said all released offenders would be subject to strict monitoring, including the expansion of electronic tagging, but significant concerns have been raised about whether the overstretched Probation Service will be able to cope.“Tagging more people is also likely to substantially increase the workload for probation practitioners, when they are already short-staffed and struggling,” the report found.Rowland said: “This absolutely raises alarm bells. It’s very frustrating because victims are being made promises which potentially the system can’t meet.”A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a justice system in crisis after years of underinvestment and are taking the steps needed to fix it. This government is overseeing the biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring in British history, making record investment into the Probation Service and community punishment, and recruiting thousands of new probation officers.“We are pulling every lever to better protect victims and tagging is just one tool we use to keep the public safe. Offenders can face being housed in approved premises, curfews, mandatory meeting with probation officers, no contact orders, requirements on where to live and the threat of immediate recall to prison.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceSentencingCrimeEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City  | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling
Content: Andy Burnham said last month he would be ‘really concerned’ if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said last month he would be ‘really concerned’ if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester CityMove comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach rulingPress AssociationSun 11 Oct 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings withManchester Cityin his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, had urged the prime minister to publish everything related to his work with the club asGreater Manchestermayor and the Liberal Democrats wrote to him asking him to release minutes of meetings and declare all hospitality gifts received from owners of Manchester City.City has been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club has maintained its innocence and appealed against the verdict.Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment was serious and that where wrongdoing was established, those responsible should face the consequences.Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday.He said “the football issues are different from the investment issues”.“But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do.“I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.“None of it is recent … in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting … and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there.“But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.”The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd, which owned the club.The shadow sports minister, Louie French, called for Burnham to also “come clean” about any meetings since becoming prime minister and urged Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, to respond to questions.“The prime minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into No 10, the prime minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamManchester CityManchesterLabourGreater ManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote  | Green party | The Guardian
description: Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article
Content: Polanski also questions whether parties should seek to define what members believe.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolanski also questions whether parties should seek to define what members believe.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockGreen partyZack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism voteRapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian articleZack Polanski: How we’re transforming British politicsAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism.TheGreen partyleader has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation.Writing for the Guardianafter his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion.Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week.He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.”Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction.“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes.His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members.Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged.The controversy intensified last weekend when 1,022 members representing about 0.4% of the party’s total membership voted in favour of a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state.The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution.Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the party must not become vulnerable tocapture by extremists and racists, arguing the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise its policymaking structures.Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.“This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.15:19Did the Zionism row lose it for Zack Polanski? | Politics Weekly“At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up withidentity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.“There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel andPalestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.”The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future.The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership.The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiByelectionsJudaismPalestineIsraelGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad | Pennsylvania | The Guardian
description: Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary
Content: Julius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenJulius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APPennsylvaniaPennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dadFather of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinaryCoral Murphy Marcosand agenciesSun 11 Oct 2026 19.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in amassshooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, theAssociated Press reports.“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in PennsylvaniaRead moreThe 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend toldCleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.View image in fullscreenFirefighters work outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in a mass shooting on Saturday in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty ImagesResponding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at anews conference.“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a1982 massacrein Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in aposton X on Saturday.Explore more on these topicsPennsylvaniaUS crimeGun crimeUS gun controlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece
Content: US secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conductSenior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to GreeceAssociated PressSun 11 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.Trump donor accuses ‘grifter’ Kimberly Guilfoyle of $100,000 quid pro quoRead moreThe official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun.
