title: ‘I lost us that game’: Sirianni rues blunder as Jaguars stun Eagles in London | NFL | The Guardian
description: Cam Little’s last-second 57-yard field goal gave Jacksonville a dramatic win over Philadelphia after Nick Sirianni’s costly late decision at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cam Little’s last-second 57-yard field goal gave Jacksonville a dramatic win over Philadelphia after Nick Sirianni’s costly late decision at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Content: Jacksonville Jaguars kicker Cam Little celebrates after making a 57-yard field goal with one second remaining to seal a dramatic 19-17 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday in London.Photograph: Ian Walton/APView image in fullscreenJacksonville Jaguars kicker Cam Little celebrates after making a 57-yard field goal with one second remaining to seal a dramatic 19-17 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday in London.Photograph: Ian Walton/APNFL‘I lost us that game’: Sirianni rues blunder as Jaguars stun Eagles in LondonLittle hits 57-yard winner as time expires in LondonJaguars snatch 19-17 victory after late Eagles leadSirianni shoulders blame for costly kickoff decisionWeek five roundup: Giants salvage tie, Vikings rollAgenciesSun 11 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCam Little grew up playing soccer and watching Premier League games every weekend. So lining up a game-winning kick for the Jaguars in London was something special.Little connected from 57 yards as time expired and Jacksonville beat thePhiladelphia Eagles19-17 in a wild finish at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.Jaguars stun Eagles in wild finish; Bears v Packers, Raiders v Patriots: NFL week five – liveRead more“It was the coolest moment of my career,” said Little, who wore a Manchester United jersey at his postgame news conference.Little sprinted from midfield into the opposite end zone with his teammates in pursuit and struck a Jude Bellingham-style, arms-wide celebration in tribute to the England and Real Madrid star.The improbable scenario was made possible by Ameer Abdullah’s 53-yard kickoff return that left one second on the clock.The Eagles had taken a 17-16 lead on Jake Elliott’s 48-yard field goal with eight seconds left – after Little’s extra-point attempt went wide left following Parker Washington’s 27-yard touchdown reception late in the fourth quarter.The Jaguars were using backup snapper DaVon Hamilton after Ross Matiscik left the game with an injury.View image in fullscreenEagles head coach Nick Sirianni speaks to reporters after his team’s dramatic 19-17 defeat to the Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Sunday.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APPhiladelphia, who slipped to 2-3 for the first time since 2021, played without leading rusher Saquon Barkley and receiver DeVonta Smith and with a makeshift offensive line. The Eagles rushed for just 22 yards.Trevor Lawrence completed 24 of 39 passes for 331 yards and two touchdowns – both to Washington – along with an interception for the Jaguars (4-1).“One of the craziest games, maybe the craziest game I’ve ever been a part of,” Lawrence said, “and I’ve been in some pretty wild ones. Just how cool is this sport? The game’s never over.”Washington, who caught a 51-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter, had six receptions for 124 yards.Eagles linebacker Zack Baun ensured his team went into halftime with a 14-7 lead by getting past Chris Rodriguez Jr and tackling Bhayshul Tuten for a loss when Jacksonville went for it on fourth-and-goal from the one-yard line with one second left in the half. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni jumped and pumped his fist in reaction.View image in fullscreenJacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence pitches the ball during Sunday’s 19-17 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London.Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty ImagesSirianni was asked about not kicking the ball out of bounds at the end.“I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game,” the Eagles coach said. “That’s what I said to our guys, and what hurts there is that, you know, the guys fought so hard and then I don’t make the decision that, you know, that I should make at the end of the game, and I cost us that game, and I put that fully on me.”The Baltimore Ravens had used some late-game heroics in Rio de Janeiro last month to beat the Dallas Cowboys, who came under scrutiny for their coaching decisions.Earlier, Eagles backup running back Will Shipley scored on a two-yard run and Darius Cooper caught a 62-yard touchdown pass from Jalen Hurts.Hurts completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and one touchdown. Jalen Carter had two sacks and two forced fumbles for the Eagles.Little’s 34-yard field goal in the third quarter made it 14-10.Explore more on these topicsNFLPhiladelphia EaglesJacksonville JaguarsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: NFL today: How to watch 49ers v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 11 October | Seattle Seahawks | The Guardian
description: How will the Seahawks and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Seahawks and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Brock Purdy has looked like an MVP contender in the early stages of the season.Photograph: Kelley L Cox/APView image in fullscreenBrock Purdy has looked like an MVP contender in the early stages of the season.Photograph: Kelley L Cox/APNFL watching and streaming guideSeattle SeahawksNFL today: How to watch 49ers v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 11 OctoberHow will the Seahawks and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerSun 11 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast winter, two games between the 49ers and Seahawks decided the shape of theNFLseason. The two teams played each other in the Bay Area on the last weekend of the regular season, and Seattle’s win secured the NFC West and homefield advantage when the teams met later in the NFC divisional playoffs. Seattle’s advantage only got more lopsided at home, and a 41-6 win proved to be the launching pad that sent the Seahawks flying through the rest of the playoffs, ending with a Super Bowl victory. The Niners watched from home.Now they meet again in one of the most anticipated games of the 2026 season to date. The 49ers take an unbeaten record on the road against a 3-1 Seattle team who have kept the train on the tracks despite Sam Darnold getting hurt early in Week 1 and missing a game. Whoever wins here will claim divisional favorite status as we move into the second quarter of the season, and they’ll also give themselves a good shot to claim a head-to-head tiebreaker that may be important in the league’s most competitive division.49ers at SeahawksTime:4.25pm ET/9:25pm BSTStadium:Lumen Field (Seattle, Washington)How to watchUnited States:Watch on Fox or stream onFox OneorFubo(where the local Fox affiliate carries the game).Canada:Stream onDAZNandFuboUnited Kingdom:Watch onSky Sports NFLor stream onNOWWhat to watch forThe main man to watch for Seattle is the same as ever: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who just had one of the handful of most productive receiving seasons ever and is so far averaging more yards per game (120) than he did when he won Offensive Player of the Year. The Seahawks do not have a clear No 2 wideout and have some running back problems, too, given that Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker now plays for the Chiefs and first-round rookie Jadarian Pricewent to injured reserve this week. But as long as an offense has JSN, it has a chance to put up serious point totals. The Seahawks’ 105 points in four games are tied for sixth in the NFC. They’ll rise up the ranks if non-JSN contributors emerge.The 49ers are a more balanced juggernaut at the moment. Brock Purdy continues to be Brock Purdy, putting up terrific numbers in a maximally supportive system. A large handful of offensive players on the wrong side of 30 have all maintained their access to the fountain of youth: Trent Williams blocking, Christian McCaffrey running and catching, and Mike Evans, George Kittle, and Deebo Samuel as downfield targets. An injured defensive front (currently missing star edge rusher Nick Bosa and tackle James Thompson) has not stopped the 49ers’ defense from giving up the third-fewest yards per play in the NFL. The only trouble is that the two teams ahead of them are the Seahawks and Rams. Will this division put three teams in the playoffagain? It looks that way.Explore more on these topicsSeattle SeahawksNFL watching and streaming guideSan Francisco 49ersNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNuclear weaponsFixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilationSimon TisdallThis is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the daySun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTShareHumankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.Donald Trump’sblanket denialsof the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some asthe latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity –existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating,global proliferation of advanced nuclear weaponsis bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima,how much longer can our luck hold?Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putinrecently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time,Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacksdeep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US isupgrading its nuclear arsenalof 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing alucrative dealwith Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’sstatus as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim,whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit,is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow– which, at this rate, there may not be.Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spendingreached nearly $3tnlast year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paperpublished by the non-partisan Arms Control Association(ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too,is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and othersadvances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSimon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsNuclear weaponsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
Content: Liquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiquid-cooled servers at a datacentre in London. Narayan will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety effortsKanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangersRobert BoothandDan MilmoSun 11 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCompanies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs anAI safety research body, has warned there is a“50% chance”of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has beensignedby leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.View image in fullscreenThe UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesIn one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Fridayrevealedthat when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturdaycalled forAI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Kanishka NarayanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Donations to major parties and an ex-premier as a lobbyist: how datacentres play the political game in Australia | Australian political donations | The Guardian
description: As governments face community backlash for fast-tracking developments, big tech’s financial contributions face renewed scrutiny
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: As governments face community backlash for fast-tracking developments, big tech’s financial contributions face renewed scrutiny
Content: Anthony Albanese speaks to the media at the Seattle headquarters of Amazon Web Services last year.Photograph: Lukas Coch/EPAView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese speaks to the media at the Seattle headquarters of Amazon Web Services last year.Photograph: Lukas Coch/EPAAustralian political donationsDonations to major parties and an ex-premier as a lobbyist: how datacentres play the political game in AustraliaAs governments face community backlash for fast-tracking developments, big tech’s financial contributions face renewed scrutinyFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 21.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 14 June 2025, Anthony Albanese stood inside an enormous sphere of glass and steel, surrounded by 40,000 plants from around the world. His mind was firmly fixed on datacentres. The prime minister was in the Seattle headquarters of Amazon Web Services. He stood alongside the company’s chief executive, Matt Garman, who outlined a $20bn plan to builddatacentres in Melbourne and Sydney.Speaking to a travelling press pack, Garman was emphatic that Australia was “incredibly important and a great market” for the world’s biggest datacentre company.Within days of Albanese returning home, Amazon reported its largest payment to an Australian political party on record. The company’s federal disclosures show a $46,500 payment to the Labor party’s federal branch on 28 June.This was one of 34 payments – totalling $538,000 – thatAmazonmade to Labor and Liberal branches over a six-year period.From boom to bust in five days: how Firmus’s much-hyped Australian stock market listing implodedRead moreWhile the money did not influence the government’s decision-making, it continued a trend of Amazon disclosing payments shortly before or after multibillion-dollar announcements.Payments such as this are legal. But as governments face community backlash for fast-tracking datacentres, these financial contributions are facing renewed scrutiny.So, too, are the well-connected political operatives, from former policy advisers to at least one former premier, who have been paid to lobby governments on behalf of datacentre companies.Transparency International Australia’s CEO, Clancy Moore, says a cutting-edge industry is relying on old methods.“Datacentres are the new extractive industries but [are] using the old techniques of cash for access payments and full-scale lobbying to influence our political system,” Moore says.Access to ministersIn 2024 the Albanese government announceda $2bn deal with Amazon Web Servicesto build three top-secret datacentres to store sensitive information gathered by intelligence agencies.Eight days before that deal was announced, on 26 June, Amazon disclosed a $33,000 payment to Labor, according to Australian Electoral Commission filings. Less than six weeks later, another $33,000 payment was disclosed.The payments were membership fees for the party’s fundraising vehicle,the Labor Business Forum, which facilitates access to ministers and MPs. Amazon has paid more than $200,000 in membership fees to the forum since mid-2021.Under Australian electoral law, such membership or subscription fees to political fundraising vehicles are not technically classed as donations. Instead, they are listed as “other receipts”. But ultimately, the money goes to the same place: the party.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe proximity of these payments to major deals, while coincidental, highlights ongoing concerns about companiespaying political parties for additional access to decision makers.Amazon has also been busy attending state fundraising events.Between mid-2021 and mid-2025, Amazon paid $38,100 to theNew South WalesLabor party and $37,400 to the Liberals. During this period, the company was also pursuing several new datacentres on Sydney’s outskirts.An Amazon spokesperson said its payments to fundraising forums were not related to public investments, including datacentre projects.“Amazon’s participation in these forums is longstanding,” the spokesperson said. “Any suggestion that these payments were timed to coincide with public announcements is incorrect.”The federal government and the ALP national secretariat were contacted for comment.Payments to NSW LiberalsIn his final weeks as prime minister in 2022, Scott Morrison toured a new five-storey datacentre in Sydney’s north-west. After cutting a blue ribbon to declare the facility open, Morrison praised his hosts for keeping Australia at the “leading edge” of the digital economy.Three days before Morrison’s 25 March speech, Macquarie Technology Group disclosed a $3,000 donation to the NSWLiberal party. This came shortly after two separate payments from the ASX-listed company to the same branch worth $15,000 in January 2022.The company had been sending a steady stream of money to the NSW Liberal branch as the IC3 East datacentre was being built in the Macquarie Park innovation district. The money was also flowing as it plotted another larger adjacent datacentre, known as IC3 Super West.Australian Electoral Commission disclosures show Macquarie made six payments to the state Liberals worth $10,700 between 12 November 2020, and 7 June 2021. NSW disclosures show the company also paid the branch $1,500 to attend a boardroom lunch with then Liberal treasurer, Dominic Perrotett, on 15 June 2021.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereWhile there is no suggestion these payments sought to influence planning decisions or had any impact on applications, they overlap with milestones for the company.On 15 July, Macquarietold investors about its plansfor IC3 Super West, which could be fast-tracked by new rules deeming datacentres “state significant developments” that could be approved by a minister, rather than a local council.Government documents show aplanning application was under way by early Augustwith asustainability and emissions report completed on 26 October.Three days earlier, on 23 October, the company paid $1,980 to secure a lunch meeting with Ryde’s then Labor mayor, Jerome Laxale, and the then Labor leader, Chris Minns, at a Parramatta restaurant.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLaxale had no role in assessing the application, as it was before the state government. At the time, he was preparing for council elections on 4 December. In 2022, he stepped down after winning the federal seat of Bennelong.View image in fullscreenA datacentre construction site in Sydney.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPA spokesperson for Laxale said “all donations were reported in accordance with requirements”.The City of Ryde has now become a strident critic of datacentres, despite having 12 existing or proposed facilities within its boundaries. It told a parliamentary inquiry in March this year that it was “deeply concerned” about a “rapid concentration” placing“significant pressure” on electricity and water supplies.According to the AEC, Macquarie has paid $2.2m to state and federal branches of the Liberal and Labor parties since 2000.A company spokesperson said “any suggestion that these activities influence planning outcomes is incorrect”.“Macquarie Technology Group engages with federal, state, and local representatives from across the political spectrum through business forums, industry events and stakeholder engagement activities.“[The group] complies with all state and federal electoral disclosure requirements and does not provide political support in exchange for planning approvals, government decisions, or policy outcomes.”A NSW Liberal spokesperson said the party disclosed all donations in line with its obligations.Former LNP premier hired, $20,000 donatedDatacentre companies are increasingly turning to well-connected lobbyists to further their commercial interests.Viridis Green datacentres, which is proposing a number of small datacentres in regional areas, is among them.Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg JerichoRead moreThe company has paid formerQueenslandNational premier Rob Borbidge to lobby Liberal National party ministers and senior public servants on its behalf.Lobbying records show that, in late August, Borbidge gave two of the state’s most senior planning officials a tour of a Brisbane datacentre built by the company.This followed four meetings with public servants since March, including one arranged after discussions with a minister’s office.Borbidge’s engagement came after Viridis made a $20,000 donation to the Queensland LNP on 20 October 2025. Sources familiar with the payment say it funded an event at the LNP party conference on the Gold Coast in November.Viridis was contacted for comment.‘Legitimate question to be answered’Abigail Boyd, the upper house Greens MP leading a NSW parliamentary inquiry into datacentres, questioned why companies would pay political parties if they didn’t expect a return.“Multibillion-dollar companies don’t make donations to major political parties for fun; they do it to acquire access, influence and good favour,” Boyd says.The independent Australian Capital Territory senatorDavid Pocock, a member of a federal inquiry into datacentres, says he is concerned about technology companies bankrolling election campaigns.“We’ve seen big tech pour huge money into political donations ahead of the US midterm elections,” he says. “While at a smaller scale and in different ways, I’m concerned the same pattern is playing out here.”The Centre for Public Integrity’s executive director, Catherine Williams, says a lack of transparency about federal lobbying activity “heightens community concern” about payments to political parties.“There is a legitimate question to be answered about the purpose of any entity paying for party forum membership, or to attend political party/candidate events, if it is not to obtain access and influence that is beyond the reach of ordinary Australians,” Williams said.Explore more on these topicsAustralian political donationsDatacentres - AustraliaAmazonAnthony AlbaneseLabor partyLiberal partyBusinessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially | Scams | The Guardian
description: Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page
Content: Calendar apps can add invitations automatically.Photograph: grinvalds/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCalendar apps can add invitations automatically.Photograph: grinvalds/Getty ImagesScam watchScams‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentiallyAppointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal pageHilary OsborneSun 11 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at yourGooglecalendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them.Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they arecontacting you from your bank, or another institution.Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.View image in fullscreenFake notifications of an auto-renewal are common to persuade people to respond and hand over personal details.Photograph: Sublime Security“Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.”And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says.Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software.“That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.”If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”.What it looks likeYou will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals.Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says.Sometimes the calendar phishing scam uses fake voicemail notifications.Photograph: SuppliedGannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.”The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number.Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.”Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details.As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”.What to doDon’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link.“My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.”Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted.He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchConsumer affairsCybercrimeData and computer securityInternet safetyGooglefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is right
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is right
Content: ‘Donald Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal.’ The site of a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, 10 October 2026.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal.’ The site of a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, 10 October 2026.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAOpinionInternational criminal courtThe Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifiesEditorialA fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is rightSun 11 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareOn Friday, Donald Trump drove home his belief that might is right and the rule of law is an obstacle rather than an essential foundation stone of international order. First came the escalatedassault on the international criminal court (ICC), sanctioning the body itself. Then he announceda deal with Russiato buy diesel.The US has long chafed at the notion of being bound by the rule of law that it espoused publicly. That hypocrisy now appears as a lesser vice. The president hasdeclaredthat “my own morality” is all that constrains him. His brazen flouting of the law, embrace of dictators and rhetorical attacks all undermine global standards.Weeks before the midterms, Mr Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities for high diesel costs. It is his own unlawful war on Iran that has raised prices.The weekend’s attackson Riyadh’s international airport, suspected as the work of Tehran-backed Houthis from Yemen, underscored that he cannot simply park that conflict when it suits him.The Moscow deal is unlikely to produce significant shipments; the Russian military runs on diesel. But Ukraine is supposed to heed its message to make life easier on Vladimir Putin. It is Mr Putin (for whom the ICC has issued a warrant) who launched the illegal war, and whose troops launched lethal attacks on civilians this weekend. But in a world turned upside down, Mr Trump blamesVolodymyr Zelenskyyfor failing to cut a peace deal and says the democratically elected leader should go.View image in fullscreenNavi Pillay.Photograph: Davide Elias/EPAIt is similarly perverse to wield measures designed to target human rights abusers and war criminals against those who seek to defend their victims. Mr Trump’s attack on the ICC was fuelled first by its Afghanistan investigation – though it has suspended consideration of US actions there – and then the issuing of arrest warrants for Israel’sBenjamin Netanyahuand its former defence minister Yoav Gallant. The court hasbeen preparingfor these  measures. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state,saidthat companies have six months to wind down ties and that US allies must rein in the court: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”In stark (and intentional) contrast, the Nobel committee on the same day announced that this year’s peace laureate is Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and chair of the UN commission which last yearconcludedthat Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. It was not only a recognition of a remarkable career that began in apartheid‑era South Africa, but a reminder that institutions defending universal principles are under increasing pressure, and must be defended. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said.As the ICC says, it cannot stand alone. The UK, EU and others too were right tocriticisethe US decision and declare their commitment to the court; invoking blocking statutes against sanctions would add heft to the rhetoric. They must show similar resolve in standing with Ukraine.The nakedness of Mr Trump’s hostility to the rule of law has one benefit: no one can explain it away, or assume it is narrowly bounded. The war on Iran, kidnapping of Venezuela’s president,extrajudicial killingsof alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and threats over Greenland and Canada have shown how far he will go, and overturned assumptions that allies will be safe. It is clear that the problem is not a “rogue court”, as Mr Rubio has claimed, but a rogue superpower.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsInternational criminal courtOpinionInternational criminal justiceDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: I need smart glasses. How else can I monetize every second of my life? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: They’re the latest technological innovation no one asked for – now with added consent issues!
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: They’re the latest technological innovation no one asked for – now with added consent issues!
Content: ‘Smart glasses have one actual, unique application.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Smart glasses have one actual, unique application.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionLife and styleI need smart glasses. How else can I monetize every second of my life?Dave SchillingThey’re the latest technological innovation no one asked for – now with added consent issues!Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTShareI went to a party recently. A fancy one, filled with expensive people and interesting clothes.You might find this surprising, as I expend hundreds of words a week in this publication bemoaning human interaction, but I love parties. I like free champagne, passed appetizers and forced, go-nowhere small talk.Parties in Los Angeles are even better, because they usually involve at least one celebrity. In the case of this most recent event, the celebrity in question was a Real Housewife of Beverly Hills. Well … technically a “friend of”, Bravo reality TV parlance for a person who isn’t in the main cast and appears sporadically on the show thanks to a social connection to one of the actual Housewives. It’s sort of like being Newman on Seinfeld, or the vice-president of the United States. Easy work, if you can get it.Of course, I had to inform my friends who are reality TV fans that an orbiting celestial body had entered my field of vision. But how to prove this encounter really happened? Could I truly get the reaction I wanted from them without photo evidence?Hegseth is obsessed with increasing testosterone. If anything, the US could use less | Dave SchillingRead moreI began to ponder how to snap a picture without her noticing. Perhaps a reflection in a mirror? Pretending I was taking a photo of the canapes andwhoops, I got you in the corner of the frame. I opted for the clever mirror trick and got thewhoatext back from my friends, which means they were sufficiently gobsmacked by my brush with fame.I was satisfied, but left with the lingering feeling that I was part of a persistent shattering of the few walls of privacy left in our teetering society. I spent actual time from the ticking clock of my life to assess how to take a candid photo of a famous person trying to drink a glass of wine.What the hell is my problem? At that moment, I felt like I was one more LA party away from tossing my morals in the trash and buying a pair of smart glasses.Smart glasses are the latest intrusive technological innovation that no one asked for. Instead of just helping you see better or blocking out the punishing light rays of the sun, smart glasses are essentially computers you wear on your face. They can mirror your phone or laptop screen, send and receive phone calls and text messages, and most importantly for the burgeoning creep economy, capture pictures, audio and video.Smart glasses – from companies like Meta andViture, which cost about $300 to $500, or nearly $1,300 for a high-end variety fromXreal– are one more incursion by technology into what is left of the natural world. Fly some hideous graphics in my face while I tromp through the park, so I might quadruple-task (naturemaxxing, framemogging some unc feeding pigeons, checking in on my Kalshi, and livestreaming the whole thing) and optimize my 30-minute lunch break.I don’t think I actually need more gadgets, and yet the product lines keep expanding. I have a phone, a tablet, a watch and glasses that all connect to the internet and feed me hourly distractions and furiously pump me for data.This is why I can’t imagine any company going to market with a brain implant with wifi capability. Once you’ve stuck a microchip in my head, you can’t sell me anything else to wear.There are still so many more hunks of metal and plastic with touch screens or artificial reality interfaces to shove into my pocket or on my body. A nose ring that lights up when I get a new like on a YouTube video. Maybe a hat that broadcasts my TikToks 24/7. My body is not my own. It is the property of Meta, a vessel for the free flow of information into the company’s willing gullet.But what if that sweet online engagement is driven by videos full of people who never agreed to participate?double quotation markIt seems like almost the entire world thinks smart glasses are primarily for pervertsMany courts have banned smart glasses in their proceedings, butpeople are still trying to bring them in anyway.Cruise lines, movie theater chains and restaurantsare restricting smart glasses, too. And now Norway isplanning a temporary ban for certain public places. Eventually, there won’t be anywhere to use them, outside of an old barn, a closet or anabandoned Hooters restaurant.So, if it seems like almost the entire world thinks smart glasses areprimarily for perverts, why does the tech industry persist in suggesting consumers buy them? Surely the obscene profits that Apple collects from the umpteenth edition of the iPhone have seduced Silicon Valley into chasing another world-changing innovation that no one can live without.Except, we already have the iPhone. And the Apple Watch. And the iPad. I have enough gadgets in my life to pretend like I’m a particularly washed James Bond, engaging in mundane adventures like “creating a shopping list” or “tracking how many times I blink”.When so much of our economy is tied to “content creation”, it makes some corrupted sense to give the workers trapped in the coalmines shinier pickaxes. I can’t just record an explainer video complaining about declining privacy or voracious technocapitalism. I need a fancier Bluetooth microphone, a camera stand for my phone, a ring light, and maybe even a funny prop like an inflatable flamingo to keep people’s attention.I can live with all that. After all, I’m the dope who willingly chose to get into the media.But it’s worse when you use other people to fuel your need for digital attention without asking first. Smart glasses let you do that on a scale, and with an ease of use, that is unparalleled. I could film two people having a domestic spat or a grisly car accident without even having to go into my pocket.Smart glasses have one actual, unique application – monetizing every last second of life, whether you want it to or not. Now, we can all be a “friend of” in the Real Housewives of Wherever the Hell You Are, performing our silly little dramas for an audience that might never be satisfied.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsLife and styleOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA nuclear counterattack training exercise at an undisclosed location in North Korea in April 2024.Photograph: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNuclear weaponsFixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilationSimon TisdallThis is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the daySun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTShareHumankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.Donald Trump’sblanket denialsof the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some asthe latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity –existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating,global proliferation of advanced nuclear weaponsis bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima,how much longer can our luck hold?Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putinrecently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time,Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacksdeep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US isupgrading its nuclear arsenalof 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing alucrative dealwith Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’sstatus as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim,whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit,is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow– which, at this rate, there may not be.Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spendingreached nearly $3tnlast year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paperpublished by the non-partisan Arms Control Association(ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too,is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and othersadvances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSimon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsNuclear weaponsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Yes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politics | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: We must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitism, says Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales
Author: Zack Polanski
Headline: We must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitism, says Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales
Content: Delegates gather around the Young Greens booth during the first day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelegates gather around the Young Greens booth during the first day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Alishia Abodunde/Getty ImagesOpinionGreen partyYes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politicsZack PolanskiWe must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitismSun 11 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTShareWhen Istood for leaderof the Greens in 2025, our party was at a crossroads. The transformative leadership of Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay had taken us to an electoral success we’d never seen before. I knew we had even greater potential – and that the country was crying out for the bold politics we could offer.We have seen unprecedented wins this year – from our first everparliamentary byelection winto our landslide council and mayoral victories in former Labour strongholds.Those victories have moved Labour. Our electoral successes helped topple Keir Starmer, seeing him replaced by a prime minister unarguably to his left. They forced a change in tone in the government’srelations with Israel. The government has evenrowed back onsome of its cruel anti-migrant policies.Our work isn’t done. But the next phase for our party takes place in a landscape that is clearly more challenging for us. Andy Burnham is enjoying a honeymoon phase, and hasn’t yet had to make the “difficult decisions” that will reveal exactly who will lose out under his government – unpopular choices he will probably start making at his fast-approaching first budget.Of course I wanted to win theHolborn and St Pancras byelection. But our result shows, as the polling expert John Curtice has said, that our party represents agreater threat to Labourin places like this than ever before. Wetripled our vote sharein a seat that Labour has comfortably held since 1983 and forced it to campaign hard in a constituency it would once have taken for granted.We have transformed the electoral landscape and, as the first nationwide serious threat toLabouron its left in modern political history, we are here to stay.The result also came at a difficult moment for our party. A motion voted through at our conference, “Zionism is racism”, hasstirred up strong feelingsamong many members and the wider public too. And I know there have been questions about my approach to the motion.I’m a Jewish man who grew up in a Zionist household. The story I was told about Israel was one of destiny and safety: a land without a people for a people without a land. But since then I have learned about the people whodidlive on that land – and what has happened to them. The Palestinians driven from their homes; slaughtered en masse; and those who remain, living underan apartheid systemthat denies them fundamental rights, including that of self-determination.It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up withidentity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with – such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone theGreen party– to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.Before the vote, I made it clear thatthere were amendmentsI would like to see made, and I am disappointed that those did not pass.I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party. I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John HarrisRead moreMy responsibility now is to bring our party together to achieve our full potential. This starts with an assurance from me: under my leadership, I will not tolerate antisemitism. No one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith or where they worship. I will meet any group within our party that fears victimisation to understand exactly what they need in order to feel safe and welcome.Second, our party has grown to a size none of us could have anticipated when I became leader. Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible.Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better. This government is on course to preside over theworst parliament for living standardsin modern times. Energy bills are expected to rise again this winter; rent increases are forecast to speed up. Meanwhile, Burnham is offering no concrete support for bills and ruling out any controls on rents, and Reform UK is still using cost of living pressures to stir up division in our communities.The Green party’s bold, principled ideas have never been more needed. From an emergency brake on rents to full public ownership of water companies, we are offering solutions that this government won’t go near unless we force it to. We have work to do – and I will bring my party together to get it done.Zack Polanski is the leader of the Green party of England and Wales and a member of the London assemblyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
