title: Finally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: There is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t work, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: There is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t work, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionMental healthFinally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy?John HarrisThere is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t workSun 11 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTShareBack in late 2025, when Keir Starmer’s grip on the Labour party was loosening and Reform UK was still in its pomp, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, commissioned what the government called its “Independent reviewinto prevalence and support for mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”.Here, it seemed, was not just an inquiry into England’sever-extending waiting listsfor the diagnosis of mental illness and neurodevelopmental conditions, and the dire lack of support for people who experience one or both of them. The review would also dovetail with two other huge issues: mounting claims of “overdiagnosis”, which Streeting hadappeared to partly endorse, and the government’s drive for the reform of so-called welfare. An apparentlywell-briefed piece in the Timesseemed to speak volumes: work led by the renowned psychologist Peter Fonagy, it said, was commencing just “as Labour seeks a fresh crackdown on welfare spending” amid diagnoses “which have become the most common reason for a sickness benefit claim”.Last Friday saw the publication of the600-page final reportFonagy had co-authored with Gillian Baird – a specialist in paediatric neurodisability – and the psychiatrist Simon Wessely. And, as so often happens with such inquiries, its interpretation suggested the media’s equivalent of a Rorschach blot. One of theGuardian’s headlineswas “No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real”. The Mail, by contrast, yelled out arather different message– “Rush to diagnose ADHD and autism can damage children” – while theTelegraph went for“ADHD surge fuelled by benefits, report warns”.Such are the perils of producing a very nuanced mixture of analysis and recommendations. When he appeared on Radio 4’s Today programme,Fonagy saidthat Streeting had been “completely wrong” to agree with suggestions of the common overdiagnosis of mental health disorders. When it comes to autism and ADHD, he and his colleagues’ report says that “if present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing, from previous merited concerns with under-recognition and underdiagnosis towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis”. But it also insists that right now, “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”, and points out that any data that might settle this festering argument “largely do not exist”. This is not the kind of stuff that suits a world that craves simple binaries and polarised shouting, but it speaks an undeniable truth.For the most part, in fact, it is hard to disagree with what the review points out. But among its conclusions lies one troubling proposal – that provision for both mental illness and so-called neurodivergence can and should often be led by observations of need rather than formal diagnosis. In making that suggestion, I have no doubt that Fonagy and his colleagues’ intentions are benign. But our systems of power and politics and the government’s increasingly anxious view of public spending could yet make it very dangerous indeed.First, though, the undeniable positives. In a very elegantly written and often moving introduction, Fonagy – who is 74 – completely rejects the popular idea of a new generation of wilting wimps falsely claiming to be suffering from mental ill-health. “The cacophony of voices now available to a young person – most of them digital, many of them confident, few of them accountable – has made the ordinary developmental process of understanding oneself far harder than it was for me,” he says. He goes on: “Young people today are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”These are mental health issues. When it comes to autism and ADHD, Fonagy and his two colleagues’ insistence that overdiagnosis is currently not happening “at scale” and that “the evidence does not show that people presenting today are less impaired than those presenting previously” is very important indeed. When Streeting commissioned the review, among the most in-vogue books was The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist and epilepsy specialist Suzanne O’Sullivan, whichmade the absurd suggestionthat the overdiagnosis of autism might have reached the point where it was partly to blame for rising rates of anxiety and depression among the young, linked to her claim that “the stigma of autism has been associated with low self esteem among children”. (If autism is still stigmatised, O’Sullivan publicly calling it an “illness” is hardly helpful.)The review, by contrast, is altogether more calm and evidence-based: for a bundle of reasons, it says that overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis may well be a future risk, but we can guard against those dangers by more closely regulating private diagnostic clinics (which are often partly NHS-funded) and stop them advertising their services. These are proposals that many autism and ADHD insiders agree with.On a different subject, Fonagy and his co-authors also do us all a favour by emphasising the correct meaning of the ubiquitous term “neurodiversity”: whereas O’Sullivan says that it “has a biologising, pathologising effect”, the report rightly understands that the word means the complete opposite: it crystallises the plain fact that “variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour is part of natural human diversity rather than pathology or disorder”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Read moreBut what do we do when faced with genuinely diagnosable conditions that are debilitating and entail intensive support? One bit of first-person testimony in the report is heartbreaking. “When she was 12,” says an unnamed parent, “our daughter was put on ADHD medication, which lowered her mood, leading her to self-harm. She was referred to CAMHS [child and adolescent mental health services] who turned her down. Within the next month we ended up in A&E due to taking an overdose. She was then finally accepted by CAMHS, who suggested an autism assessment.“Two years later, after receiving an autism diagnosis, little changed. School would not make any adjustments until an EHCP (education, health and care plan) was accepted, and social care said she did not meet their threshold for support because she did not have a learning disability. Our daughter was broken and unsupported and was admitted to inpatients at 15 years old.”Herein lies one of the review’s few dangers. By way of lessening an increasingly frightening crisis that is partly centred on pitifully long waits for formal diagnoses that can easily be ignored, it suggests moving towards a more “needs-based” approach, which echoes the government’s plans for special needs education. “There should be a fundamental shift from a diagnosis-dependent system to a needs-led plus diagnosis system,” it says. Such a change, the report says, would require “increased capacity, transformation through digitally enabled care, clearer national standards andsustained investment”.They are my italics, with very good reason. The governmentresponded to the reportby saying that the health and social care secretary, Yvette Cooper, “has asked NHS leaders to urgently examine how people can access advice, assessments and treatment more easily”. But without sufficient money, “needs-based” help is likely to amount to very little at all. Coincidentally, the Fonagy review arrivedon the same day as reportsthat the prime minister and the chancellor had rebuffed Cooper’s requests for money to fund a pay rise for NHS staff including nurses, porters and midwives. So what chance of a huge cash injection to tackle what the report so starkly highlights?Meanwhile, the Department for Work and Pensions still has a culture built around crackdowns and pushing people into work. Councils repeatedlyfail to meettheir responsibilities for the care and education of neurodivergent people. And, in the absence of properly funded change, both they and people suffering mental illness only stand even a faint chance of pushing their way through an almost impossible mess of bureaucracy and obstruction if they have pieces of paper confirming that their condition – or conditions – are real and true.This is what makes politicians whotalk of “overdiagnosis”look so crass, and the likely fate of such a definitive and in-depth report so tragic. It is an all too familiar story, indicative of our current defining national predicament: the government simply cannot afford what it proposes, so one of our cruellest modern crises looks set to grind on.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMental healthOpinionAutismHealthNHSAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderNeurodiversityYoung peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: The most successful people I meet are often the ones struggling most | Darren Lee | The Guardian
description: Sometimes the behaviours that helped us survive become so embedded that they mask our past traumas and adversity
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sometimes the behaviours that helped us survive become so embedded that they mask our past traumas and adversity
Content: Outside work, things were beginning to unravel. She was struggling to sleep and increasingly used alcohol to switch off at night, writes Dr Darren Lee.Photograph: kieferpix/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenOutside work, things were beginning to unravel. She was struggling to sleep and increasingly used alcohol to switch off at night, writes Dr Darren Lee.Photograph: kieferpix/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe modern mindMental healthThe most successful people I meet are often the ones struggling mostDarren LeeSometimes the behaviours that helped us survive become so embedded that they mask our past traumas and adversityThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 11 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTShareSome of the most successful people I meet as a psychiatrist are also some of the most dissatisfied with life. They don’t necessarily look unwell. They are executives, entrepreneurs, doctors, lawyers and high achievers. They run companies and families. They are the people others depend on when something goes wrong. Often, they are exceptionally good at coping. Until they aren’t.Holly* came to see me after years of depressive symptoms and worsening substance use, both of which she had largely managed to conceal from family, friends and colleagues. Her GP recommended a residential treatment program. In her early 40s, she held an executive position in a demanding organisation. She was ambitious, respected and known for her extraordinary work ethic. She was also exhausted.Outside work, things were beginning to unravel. She was struggling to sleep and increasingly used alcohol to switch off at night. There were periods of profound sadness and numbness. But Holly kept working.When a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships? | Bianca DennyRead moreIn fact, work was the one place she still felt energised. She would often be in the office 12 hours a day. She told me that when she was busy, she didn’t have to think. There was always another meeting, deadline or problem to solve. Achievement gave her a sense of control and, temporarily, a sense that she was doing well in her life.Holly’s story is something I see regularly – often the characteristics we celebrate as resilience in society can also be ways of coping.In therapy, we began to understand why achievement had become so important to Holly. Her childhood had been unpredictable. She learned early to monitor the moods of the adults around her, avoid causing problems and become fiercely independent. Academic success brought praise and, crucially, higher self-esteem. So she became very good at succeeding but this meant being harder and harder on herself when she failed.None of this meant her ambition wasn’t genuine. Nor does being ambitious mean someone has experienced trauma in their life. But for Holly, achievement had become tangled up with something deeper.double quotation markWithout the next deadline or accomplishment, difficult emotions may have more room to surface, and the person can feel flat or depressedShe told me in one of our earlier sessions: “If I am successful enough, useful enough and busy enough, I know I will feel better about myself.” This can be one of the more difficult manifestations of unresolved trauma to recognise because, from the outside, it can look remarkably functional.Fear of failure can contribute to perfectionism. Difficulty resting can be mistaken for drive. Becoming highly attuned to other people’s moods can make someone appear very emotionally perceptive.Nobody stages an intervention because you’re answering emails at 1am or volunteering for another project. In fact, you may be promoted for precisely the behaviours that are exhausting you. The difficulty comes when achievement stops being something you pursue and becomes something you need. For some people, slowing down creates an uncomfortable silence. Without the next deadline or accomplishment, difficult emotions may have more room to surface, and the person can feel flat or depressed. So they keep working. Until a relationship ends. A parent dies. There’s a redundancy. A child is born. The body simply becomes exhausted. Or the strategies being used to manage the feelings – alcohol, drugs, compulsive exercise or relentless work – begin creating problems of their own.This was where Holly found herself.Treating her depression was important but so was understanding what sat beneath her relentless productivity. Over time, she began recognising that some of the qualities that had once helped her cope earlier in life were also masking deeper difficulties with self-esteem, safety, intimacy and identity.Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughRead moreThe goal of our sessions wasn’t to strip her drive or trace every achievement back to childhood pain. Ambition can come from curiosity, passion, purpose, competitiveness and genuine enjoyment. Instead, I raised questions such as: what happens when you stop? Can you rest without feeling guilty? Can you fail without feeling worthless? Can you say no without fearing rejection? Can you feel valuable when you aren’t achieving anything? For Holly, these questions were surprisingly difficult.After starting to address her depression and substance use, she began creating space in her life that had previously contained almost none. She learned to sit with her feelings rather than immediately working through them or suppressing them. This helped her separate her sense of worth from her role and productivity. She remained successful. But success was now less determined by external factors.Sometimes the behaviours that helped us survive become so embedded that they mask our past traumas and adversity. The challenge isn’t necessarily to give them up. It’s to understand what drives them – and realise we are more than them.* All clients discussed are fictional amalgamsDr Darren Lee, MBBS BMed Sci FRANZCP FAChAM,is the acting medical superintendent atSouth Pacific Private, a trauma, addiction and mental health treatment centreExplore more on these topicsMental healthThe modern mindHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Pumpkin-spiced latte is a con. It’s time to put an end to Big Autumn  | Chloë Hamilton | The Guardian
description: The aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter days, says journalist Chloë Hamilton
Author: Chloë Hamilton
Headline: The aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter days, says journalist Chloë Hamilton
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onAutumnThe hill I will die on: Pumpkin-spiced latte is a con. It’s time to put an end to Big AutumnChloë HamiltonThe aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter daysSun 11 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s getting earlier every year, that first meme about golden leaves and pumpkin-spiced lattes. This year, I swear, I spotted one in early August, while we were still sweltering under our fourth heatwave of the summer.Because, of course, for those that like crisp mornings, Halloween and glasses of red wine in front of roaring fires, the arrival of autumn brings with it something else: the incessant need to tell everyone just how much they love this perfectly pleasant, if perpetually damp, season.I call it BigAutumn. The idea that liking autumn is enough to sustain an entire personality. I don’t know when it first happened but my instinct is that it’s been driven by an almost entirely brown-and-orange aesthetic pushed out via Pinterest and Instagram, and not by the often grim realities: grey drizzle, shorter days, the sense of impending Christmas.It’s not that I have an issue with the season itself. Sure, my partner and I refer to it as “mud season” because we have a spaniel and two young children, and our house won’t feel truly clean again until the end of March. But I’m partial to a roast dinner and a fairy light, I like oversized jumpers and, although I avoid Halloween, I find Bonfire Night quite magical, even if I do always over-layer and end up sweaty and overstimulated.No, it’s not the season I take issue with but rather our need to define ourselves by our preferences. It’s a trend that has been perpetuated by social media. See also: being a cat person or a boy mum. It smacks of Christian Girl Autumn, a viralmemefrom 2019 that emerged as an antidote – one in knee-high leather boots and an oversized scarf – to Hot Girl Summer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it all | Elle HuntRead moreTo me, it merely highlights our modern-day compulsion to construct and curate personalities rather than simply inhabit them. It’s as though the internet has encouraged – nay, forced – us to paint ourselves with broad brush strokes rather than with the nuance and intricacy that a human life calls for. It demonstrates a terminal lack of imagination, although perhaps lives spent juggling always-on jobs, constantly popping WhatsApp groups and the astronomicalcost of literally living have left us so burned out we haven’t the time or the energy to add more detail.I suspect my irritation lies in the fact that liking autumn has not only become a personality, but – because spending and social media go hand in hand – a way of getting us to part with money we don’t have. A pumpkin-spiced chai latte doesn’t come for free and, go on, you definitely need that new-season chocolate-brown knit. Autumn has become a lifestyle, a commodity, not just the passing of the baton from one season to the next.Maybe my frustration with the people for whom a love of this meteorological phenomenon becomes their defining characteristic is that I fear they are unknowingly playing into the hands of Big Autumn. Or maybe I really do just hate drizzle.Chloë Hamilton is freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsAutumnThe hill I will die oncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘We look like soft, made-up blokes, but we’re really tough’: Duran Duran on 80s excess, tabloid scrutiny and their Halloween glow-up | Duran Duran | The Guardian
description: They spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying power
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: They spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying power
Content: Wild boys … Duran Duran. Stylist Bea Åkerlund.Photograph: Stephanie PistelView image in fullscreenWild boys … Duran Duran. Stylist Bea Åkerlund.Photograph: Stephanie PistelDuran DuranInterview‘We look like soft, made-up blokes, but we’re really tough’: Duran Duran on 80s excess, tabloid scrutiny and their Halloween glow-upAlexis PetridisThey spent their heyday on yachts, then rolled up their sleeves in the wilderness years. Ahead of a Halloween show at the O2, pop’s great survivors explain their staying powerSun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022,Duran Duranwere inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. It felt like a big deal, a sweet moment of acknowledgment for the band’s five-decades-long career, the 100m records sold, the string of bulletproof hits: Save a Prayer, Rio, Hungry Like the Wolf, Girls on Film. They were inducted by actor Robert Downey Jr; Drew Barrymore, Naomi Campbell and Gwen Stefani were on hand to pay heartfelt tribute and, as keyboard player Nick Rhodes points out, “It’s a big national live TV broadcast in America that goes out to millions of people,” so the band booked some warm-up shows. “And it so happened that there was a date that came up in Las Vegas on 31 October,” says Rhodes. “And I looked at everyone and said: ‘Well, we can’t do a normal show. Las Vegas on Halloween – surely that’s the opportunity for a little bit of fun?’”They worked up a set of suitably themed material, including covers of Billie Eilish’s Bury a Friend and Talking Heads’ Psycho Killer. There were, of course, costumes involved, because, as Rhodes drily notes, “When have Duran Duran ever not dressed up?”View image in fullscreenExtraordinary world … Duran Duran at their Manchester Halloween show last year.Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/WireImageHe has a point, although not even in their new romantic pomp had Duran Duran dressed up like this. Replete with the unexpected sight of the band’s heart-throb-in-chief, bassist John Taylor, “with silver hair down to my waist, like some kind of Scandinavian orc”, the show proved such a success that Duran Duran’s Halloween gigs have become an annual event – they performed one at Madison Square Garden in New York in 2024 and at Manchester’s Co-op Live in 2025, while this year’s takes place at the O2 in London – and spawned an album, 2023’s Danse Macabre. Guitarist Andy Taylor, who left the band in 2007 and announced he was suffering from stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction, returned to play on it, while among its covers lurked a version of the Specials’ Ghost Town, an intriguing choice, given that, back in the early 80s, the Specials’ politically engaged social realism was seen as diametrically opposed to Duran Duran’s nakedly ambitious jet-setting glamour.“I remember being in a taxi with John after one of our first rehearsals, talking about stuff,” nods frontman Simon Le Bon. “I’d been in a rock band and a punk band before called Dog Days, and I said: ‘But John, what about street credibility?’ And John said: ‘Simon, Duran Duran’s got about as much street credibility as Chanel No 19.’ And, at that point, I thought: ‘OK, I’ll go with that.’”double quotation markWe survived the cutting of the tall poppies and I think that endeared us to peopleSimon Le BonAlong the way, the Halloween shows have got increasingly elaborate (the Manchester gig had pyrotechnics, dancers and fire-eaters), while even Le Bon, who by his own admission is “not a fan of Halloween – I think it’s become just a sort of marketing thing”, can’t be faulted for his enthusiasm for the whole venture.“At the first one, I was a werewolf, but since then it’s developed. The next one, I was like the ghost of a north Atlantic convoy sea captain. There was a sort of nautical theme which suits me down to the ground.” Readers old enough to remember Duran Duran’s heyday may recall Le Bon’s adventures with his 78ft yacht Drum, which capsized during the 1985 Fastnet race, resulting in the singer being airlifted to safety wearing only his underpants. “Another time I was a kind of cross between Mad Max and a mummy, but I also had this one scene where I was determined to wear antlers, like a druid god. And last time I was sort of aiming for something but it fell a bit short: I was a jellyfish, but it ended up looking like … I was going to say something off RuPaul’s Drag Race, but I’d be flattering myself. This time, I want to do something like Shiva the Destroyer.”View image in fullscreenBoys on film … Duran Duran on Top of the Pops in 1981.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesIt all points to a certain freedom, a desire to do what you want, regardless of whether it’s considered cool. “The thing is, I don’t give a fuck what people think about me,” offers Le Bon, now 67 and a grandfather – or, as he put it on social media, glamfather – of four. “I’m not talking for the whole band – I’m sure some of them do care – but me, I just do what I do, and that’s all it is.”It also suggests a sense of self-deprecating humour that Rhodes thinks might have been overlooked after their 1982 album Rio catapulted them to superstardom, when Duran Duran had fair claim to call themselves the biggest band in the world. In fairness, it wasn’t always easy to spot amid the expensive jet-set videos, supermodel girlfriends and Antony Price suits. “I think it was missed by some people,” he says. “But we grew up with Monty Python and Fawlty Towers and all of those amazing 70s British TV shows and so, inevitably, that was part of what we were doing. It doesn’t mean we were going to put it into songs – I guess we weren’t ever going to write The Laughing Gnome – but at the same time, you know, the videos are filled with humour. Watch A View to a Kill or Rio. It’s there.”Talking to the band’s four members about their heyday is intriguing. It was, all agree, exactly what they’d wanted in the first place. They loved being on Top of the Pops – the video for their recent single Free to Love was a hugely affectionate homage to the show – and clearly relished enjoying themselves in the grandstanding style of the times, palling around New York with Andy Warhol and calling up supermodels’ agents in order to ask their clients to dinner. “Being single was good fun,” smiles Le Bon, when asked what he misses about that era, before his expression changes. “I shouldn’t say that, should I? Being married has been amazing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPop art … Nick Rhodes at Andy Warhol’s birthday party in 1985.Photograph: Patrick McMullan/Paul Bruinooge/Getty ImagesEqually, it’s hard to avoid the sense that the kind of global fame they enjoyed in the 80s – not to mention the unfailing attentions of their diehard fans, the Durannies – was a lot to take on. “It was a mindfuck, actually,” offers drummer Roger Taylor. “I was sitting in my bedroom teaching myself the drums when I was 16; by the time I was 21 we were playing Madison Square Garden. I wasn’t prepared for it in any way. My dad worked in a car factory; my mum worked on the switchboard at a warehouse. I didn’t have any kind of grounding for great success in my life. Five years into it, I thought: ‘I’m not sure I can live with this level of scrutiny.’ The music press was hounding us, the tabloids were chasing us. It was the first time they really wanted to feature musicians as part of their journalism. The fanbase was 12 to 16 years old and very intense. It was definitely time to step away.”He departed Duran Duran and upped sticks to Gloucestershire in 1986. To his delight, the minute he left the band, the fans that had camped outside his house disappeared. “God bless them, but it was a bit of a relief. The only people that tracked me down were the Sun, who banged at my door at six in the morning, then wrote this feature with the headline ‘Roger Taylor: The Hermit of Pop’. But it was great not to be bothered and live a quiet, simple life.”By 1989, the hits had dried up for Duran Duran. “I felt huge anxiety, like water-running-out-of-the-bathtub sort of anxiety,” says Le Bon, who along with Rhodes is Duran Duran’s only constant member since he joined in 1980. They rolled up their sleeves and toughed it out through the band’s lean years, in the company of American guitarist Warren Cuccurullo, the latter a curious character who at one juncture marketed a sex toy modelled on his own penis, but also co-wrote Ordinary World, the 1993 single that briefly returned Duran Duran to the upper echelons of the global charts and remains their biggest streaming hit today. At one juncture, Le Bon wrote a song called Undergoing Treatment that depicted the band “watching others in the news”, while finding themselves “resigned to the mid-price section”. Today, he feels like their wilderness years were the band’s making.View image in fullscreenTheir own way … Duran Duran today.Photograph: Stephanie Pistel“We survived the cutting of the tall poppies and I think that endeared us to people, in a way,” he says. “It proved we’re tough, actually. We might look like a bunch of soft, made-up middle-class blokes, but actually, we’re really tough.”Certainly, you can’t miss a distinct shift in perception of Duran Duran since the original quintet reformed in 2001. The bad reviews that plagued them throughout their imperial phase seem to have been consigned to the past. “I remember coming offstage one night and someone saying: ‘The sound of the crowd has changed,’” says bassist John Taylor. “It had dropped an octave from that shrill treble. Clearly, we’d moved on from that audience that Duran Duran used to get, largely female and teenage, which was fine for us, but the kind of audience that gets pooh-poohed. That felt like, ‘OK, we’re on an even pitch now. We can move forward.’ The guys were done hating us.”If you want evidence of national treasure status, well, they have just been featured on a series of Royal Mail stamps. Everyone from Beck to Brandon Flowers of the Killers to emo band Panic! at the Disco has cited them as an influence. Moreover, they never seem to run out of younger artists to collaborate with: Mark Ronson co-produced 2015’s Paper Gods, Blur’s Graham Coxon turned up on its successor, Future Past, and last summer, Le Bon and John Taylor unexpectedly popped up on stage in Hyde Park with Sabrina Carpenter, belting out Hungry Like the Wolf. Le Bon is hugely enthusiastic about having persuaded the Margate-based band Pigeon to support them on tour, although what the Durannies will make of their “no-wave psychedelic punk” remains to be seen. “We really respect youthful energy. You want to get some of that in the group, some of that in the studio.”That said, there are aspects of 21st-century music they seem very wary of. Rhodes offers some cautious optimism about AI’s impact on music “if you use it as an artistic tool”, but Le Bon says he recently encountered an AI take on a Duran Duran song, and still seems scarred by the experience: “It was absolutely abominable! It was a horrible tune – the vocal was awful. I can’t remember the title but the cover was a girl standing on a yacht, so no cliches there. I do worry that people might just start getting used to it and accepting it in the same way you would accept really bad school dinners, just because you were hungry and it’s food. It’s shocking.”Besides, as he points out, there’s no need for an AI Duran Duran, given that the real deal is still extant and intends to remain so. “I think being in the band gives me the impetus and energy and motivation to try to keep myself mentally flexible, physically strong. I purposely run up and down stairs because I don’t want to suddenly go, ‘Oh, I need to move to a bungalow. My knees have gone.’ I can’t change the age I am, but I can act as youthful as I can and I think that makes you last longer. Until I drop dead on stage? Well, it’s not a bad way to go, to be honest with you.”Duran Duran’s Halloween show is at the O2, London, 31 October as part of their 2026UK and Europe tour.Explore more on these topicsDuran DuranPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashes | Rachael Stirling | The Guardian
description: When the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us all
Content: Rachael Stirling with a portrait of her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachael Stirling with a portrait of her mother, Diana Rigg.Photograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianRachael Stirling‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashesWhen the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us allRachael StirlingSun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been headlines of late that make me out to be an ash-guzzling savage nightly devouring her mother’s charred remains. “Rachael Stirling eats mother Diana Rigg’s ashes before going on stage” declared a dozen news outlets last month, while others referred to the “strange habit only she really understands” and “Dame Diana’s daughter admits eating her ashes in bizarre tribute”. I’ve written a book about our relationship, All About My Mother, in which I do confess to nibbling a grain or two, but I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a matricidal cannibal by the press.My mother wasDiana Rigg, an iconic actor with a 60-year career. Young ’uns will know her as the Queen of Thorns from Game of Thrones, be-wimpled spouter of the best verbal roasts on television: “I’ve known a great number of clever men. I’ve outlived them all. You know how? I ignored them.” Old ’uns, meanwhile, go dewy-eyed at the memory of her leather-catsuited telly triumph as Emma Peel in The Avengers from the 60s, the first woman to perform kung fu on western television. She was also the only woman ever to marry James Bond. She appeared in The Great Muppet Caper because I was profoundly in love with Miss Piggy, and her child-murdering Medea was the toast of Broadway. She won an Emmy and a Tony, and had countless honours bestowed upon her for her many stage performances. She was a complete original and very witty to boot.I missed her so intensely, I wrote the book to bring her back to life. Mum never wanted a biography in her lifetime, having been put off by a couple of limp jobs that managed to make her seem a bit dull or, worst of all crimes, earnest. My mother was not earnest. She was honest, sometimes eye-bleedingly so.View image in fullscreenStirling as a baby with her mother.Photograph: Chris Barham/Daily Mail/ REX/ ShutterstockI was her only child, and followed her into the acting profession. She strongly disapproved of my career choice, and this caused some rumpuses, I can tell you. We ran the gamut of emotions from A to Z and eventually we made our way back to the love we’d had in the early years. In the end, the love bits between us did conquer all the awful bits, though there are some joyful and some jaw-dropping stories to share.Which brings us neatly back to the subject of ashes and my ingesting of them.Groucho Marx wished to be cremated, with one tenth of his ashes to be “given to my agent, as written in my contract”. Dying in the Covid lockdown, my mother wished to be cremated, too, but with no ceremony, and scattered in places she loved. Pragmatic to the last, she even made sure we’d paid for the cremation on her bank card before she died. However, we never thought to decide what receptacle her remains would be returned in, so it wasn’t until after her death that I found myself browsing the selection of “scatter tubes” on offer.Scatter tubes are cardboard containers of varying sizes. Some are plain, others have images printed on them. These are pretty unoriginal, pictures of doves and sunsets – or was it a sunrise – and images that felt to me a bitsurle nez.It turns out most things are quite on the nose when it comes to death. There isn’t much of a market for irony. Not many skull and crossbones, or red stilettos, or tubes with “I told you I was ill” written on them. In the end I settled for a variety of receptacles in a variety of sizes, with the least offensive floral decorations on them. I needed quantity, as my mother had many places to go. She was to be scattered from the air across the green fields of England from a biplane by her aviator friend Tracey Curtis-Taylor; she was to be scattered in her garden in France and mine in London; and on the site of the actors’ church in Covent Garden.double quotation markI did not expect human ashes to be so heavy. But they are very heavy. I discovered this when my mother’s mortal remains were returned to me one bright September morningI did not expect human ashes to be so heavy. But they areveryheavy. I discovered this when my mother’s mortal remains were returned to me one bright September morning. The cremation company had told me, when organising delivery, that taking receipt of the ashes could be an emotional event. Certainly, the carbonised corpse of my beloved Ma was the strangest delivery I’d ever expected, and not one to be left on the porch or with a neighbour. So I sat waiting, like an obedient dog awaiting her mistress by the front door.My mother was delivered to me by the gentlest of gentlemen from the cremation firm in Yorkshire, where my mother was born. He pulled her out of the boot in a box wrapped in plain cloth. With kind eyes searching my face, presumably to see if I was going to start bawling and drop her, he handed her to me with the tenderness with which one might hand over a newborn babe.While cremation frees the family to celebrate the life of a loved one in the great outdoors and away from the stuffy formality of funerals, things don’t always go to plan. Everyone has seen a movie where the ashes are scattered and the wind picks up and blows them into the faces of the grieving party. The best story of an ashes mishap took place at a scattering of my father-in-law, Donald Garvey, Dad to seven glorious children, the sixth of whom is my husband, Guy Garvey. There we were to celebrate the greatly missed Don with his huge family at the Great Orme in Llandudno, the site of many a Garvey family holiday. Don had stated he wanted the day to emulate a painting by Jack Vettriano where a woman in a red dress dances with her partner in tails on a stormy day at the beach. Words were spoken on the clifftop, and an intrepid few descended to the shore. Granddaughter Lucie, in a scarlet off-the-shoulder dress, hoicked up her skirts and waded into the unusually clear and calm blue sea to scatter her beloved grandad, as per his specific wishes, in the Welsh tide. Job done, as Lucie solemnly made her way back to her family on shore, she piped up with the now immortal line, “I think I’ve got some of Grandad in mi’ knickers.”The tiniest tube containing my mother was about three inches tall. I’d like to point out that I think scatter tubes are really badly designed. They open exactly the opposite way to the direction they look like they should, so you can easily scatter a loved one’s ashes by mistake. The contents of this tube had – mostly – gone where they were supposed to go, though it still contained the odd grain or 20 of my mother, so I couldn’t possibly throw it away. Plus it was conveniently pocket-size, so I took to carrying what was left of her with me everywhere I went. So far, so normal.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Felicity McCabe/The GuardianThe next play I did was at the same theatre I had last performed at pre-Covid. It was the last show my mother ever saw, Love, Love, Love at the Lyric in Hammersmith. The new show, Scandaltown, was by the same writer, Mike Bartlett, and also at the Lyric. Everything felt eerily similar, yet between the two plays Ma had died and the whole world had turned on its arse. Now, here I was going to rehearsals in the same room, with some of the same people, but without Ma to chat to about how the play was going at the end of the day. Strange new world.As I placed her tube in my rucksack on the first day working on the show, I remember thinking how thrilled she’d be, back in a rehearsal room once more. Nearer opening night, I decided she’d enjoy a permanent stint in my dressing room. My mother had used this same dressing room in 1985, when she was performing in Little Eyolf, a grim Nordic drama from 1894 by Henrik Ibsen. It is the “Number One” dressing room, the room nearest the stage, and here she was once again, sitting in front of a Hollywood mirror with its necklace of blazing bulbs, although this time in a tube. The only thing she missed out on was actually going on stage with me. That was her happiest place, after all, but I could not hide the tube anywhere in my tight-fitting gold lamé suit without having a very peculiar lump in my costume. So there she stayed, in her dressing room, waiting for the call to the stage that never came.double quotation markI licked my finger, picked up the few spilt cinders, and popped her on my tongue. Grainy, in case you were wondering, but it didn’t feel wrong, it felt completely rightActors are an emotional tribe at the best of times and come opening night I was a wreck. My maiden first night with no mother in the crowd made me sad, but this was a high-energy Restoration-style comedy so I had to pull myself together quick-smart. I looked at the small tube containing mama residue, and I don’t know what I was thinking, but I found myself opening it. The wrong way round. A few grains fell on to my dressing table and as I panicked and tried to put them back one by one with varying degrees of success, the PA system blared, “Miss Stirling, this is your call to stage.” It was time to make my entrance. The adrenaline started kicking in and now my heart was pounding. It was time to go.In a panic, like a cocaine addict from a movie who can’t bear to waste a grain of the good stuff, I licked my finger, picked up the few spilt cinders, and popped her on my tongue. Grainy, in case you were wondering, but it didn’t feel wrong, it felt completely right. I laughed out loud at myself and the ludicrous situation. And then, just like that, my nerves disappeared.I know this sounds batshit, but it made complete sense to me. After all, quite a lot of people think they are eating the body of Christ on a weekly basis, and at least this way I really could say I took herwith meon stage that night, back on the boards where she belonged.When I told a widow at the party afterwards what I had done, her eyes widened in recognition and she whispered urgently, “I do that, too!”View image in fullscreenRigg in The Avengers circa 1965.Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyThe difference is, she didn’t talk about it.No one talks about it.It’s secret animal behaviour and, let’s face it, most people do a lot worse in private. It’s just they keep shtumm. But it felt much more important to tell the truth – and I love feeling that some of her is on stage with me. She had refused to retire, after all, and this was my way of enabling her to keep on trucking.I have done the same on every first night since then. As the five-minute call hits the PA before every press night, I open the tube – which I have become adept at – stick my finger in and whatever is collected goes in my gob. Some people listen to music before going on; some do press-ups. I eat the last vestiges of my mother. She was on stage with me on the opening night of Noël Coward’s Private Lives in 2023. Just knowing she was there gave me the confidence to play the part that night, to be joyful, to “Go Fly My Girl”, as she used to write in my first-night cards.double quotation markShe’d have adored going on to the Hampstead theatre stage with me. She’s even been back to Broadway, babyShe’d have adored going on to the Hampstead theatre stage with me when I played Sarah Siddons in The Divine Mrs S, a play about the 18th-century actor whose revolutionary realism in performance caused her audiences to scream and faint. Ma used to quote Siddons to me. She’d say, “If it can be found in nature, I know it can be played” so of course she’d want to be with me under the spotlights as I said those exact words. Before the opening night of Giant at the Royal Court in 2024, the smash hit show about Roald Dahl’s antisemitism in which I played his wife, Felicity Crosland, to John Lithgow’s Roald, once more I nibbled on a crumb. I can’t not do it these days, even though there is hardly anything left; it’s the thought that counts.She’s even been back to Broadway, baby. When Giant transferred to New York in March this year, my mother came with me. Oh, there’s no business like show business, and there was one terrible night when I returned to my dressing room post-show to find there had been a huge leak in the roof above my chair and everything was sopping wet. My first thought was,Oh no,Mother’s gone mushy!But in fact the outside of the tube was only a little damp and inside was bone dry.Love is animal, and grief is certainly so. Dogs sniff bums by way of greeting; my mum bit mine on a regular basis and said as much on national television. “I sink my teeth into her flesh! I bury my nose in her stomach!” she declared to a bemused Michael Parkinson. Isn’t that sort of the same thing, and is it really so strange of me to put my mother, whence I came, back in the same mouth she formed in utero? It is my own act of faith. “Ashes to ashes, funk to funky,” as Bowie wrote. “I’ve loved all I’ve needed, love. Sordid details following … ”Love made cannibals of us both. Despite a widow seeing the sense in my actions, judging by the looks on the faces of most people I tell, few others are in agreement. Reactions vary from sour lemon-sucking grimaces to downright disgust. Despite this, I will not be persuaded to give up the habit. I will die on the hill of my ash-eating, and to any who question my sanity, I reply, “It is natural! I’m sure it is, really! I promise I’m not going mad. It’s what she would havewanted!”All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsRachael StirlingDiana RiggBereavementCelebrityShareReuse this content

title: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey | Movies | The Guardian
description: The makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governesses
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governesses
Content: ‘A forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale’ … Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) in Wildwood.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale’ … Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) in Wildwood.Photograph: Album/AlamyMoviesReviewWildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odysseyThe makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governessesPeter BradshawSun 11 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an engaging family movie from the Portland-based Laika studio thatcreated Coraline. It is a fantasy adventure in Laika’s distinctively crafted stop-motion animation, written by Chris Butler from the bestseller of the same title by Carson Ellis and Colin Meloy, the latter being a band member ofThe Decemberists, one of whose tour posters we duly glimpse in this film. The director is Laika’s lead animator Travis Knight. It’s a forthright, exuberant, good-natured and old-fashioned children’s tale which CS Lewis and JRR Tolkien might have recognised, a story about the mysterious glory of going on a quest and the terrible fear and wish-fulfilment euphoria of being called upon to confront secret forces that the grownups know nothing about.The setting is modern-dayPortland, Oregon, a groovy city whose hipster-ish stores (there’s a coffee shop actually called Dripster) and Woke 1.0 signage are affectionately mocked. But most of all, the film is aware of a huge forest park next to the city, a place here mythologised as the impassable wilderness or “wildwood” where strange creatures, fairytale nobility and wisecracking talking animals reputedly dwell, of which the city-dwelling humans are entirely ignorant. Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is a 12-year-old girl whose parents (voiced by Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) are a couple of amiable hippies who believe in natural forces and benign magic. They have another child, Prue’s baby brother Mac, who Prue has to look after one day, pushing him in his stroller around the city and having to endure a certain classmate of hers tagging along. This is nerdy Curtis (Jacob Tremblay) who has a crush on her.They are stunned when a bunch (or rather a murder) of crows gather with Hitchcockian menace in a kids’ play area, swoop down and carry poor little Mac off to their forest domain. Plucky (and also terrified) Prue and Curtis give chase and enter the dark and trackless forest, and find it is a parallel world, undreamt of by the ordinary human world, populated by all manner of loquacious beasts and oppressed humans. Their rule is divided between the supercilious and incompetent governor (Marc Evan Jackson) and the evil dowager governess, voiced with relish byCarey Mulligan, who has at her command a redcoat army of coyotes.The dowager governess has a wrenching sadness in her heart, due to an awful loss and a tragic attempt at a cover-up, which the film shows us in the opening section. Prue and Curtis, though separated by the action, are to come together for their big showdown with this wicked witch of the forest and a reckoning also with the Wildwood’s bandit leader and freedom fighter Brendan, voiced byMahershala Ali.The stop-motion animation style has, as with Coraline, a robust and pleasing directness, and results in, for me, a more organic character and physical immediacy than Pixar’s ubiquitous digital look, to which it makes a welcome change. I wasn’t sure that the narrative delivered a satisfyingly clear motive for the governess’s reprehensible plan, and in fact the story itself did not have the scary punch of Coraline, except in the uncanny opening sequence. Then again, it’s not that kind of story.Wildwood screened at the London film festival; it is out on 22 October in Australia and 23 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFilm adaptationsThe DecemberistsAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsFamily filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Haunting of Hill House review – a slick and spooky fright night | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Jump scares, flying furniture and psychological unravelling hurtle towards a climax as a trio of guests investigate supernatural goings on at an abandoned mansion
Author: Lucinda Everett
Headline: Jump scares, flying furniture and psychological unravelling hurtle towards a climax as a trio of guests investigate supernatural goings on at an abandoned mansion
Content: Unsettling … Robin Morrissey (Luke), Sophie Lenglinger (Theo) and Clancy Ryan (Eleanor) in The Haunting of Hill House.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenUnsettling … Robin Morrissey (Luke), Sophie Lenglinger (Theo) and Clancy Ryan (Eleanor) in The Haunting of Hill House.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewThe Haunting of Hill House review – a slick and spooky fright nightRichmond theatre, LondonJump scares, flying furniture and psychological unravelling hurtle towards a climax as a trio of guests investigate supernatural goings on at an abandoned mansionLucinda EverettSun 11 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere aren’t many productions that have the audience screaming within seconds of curtain up. But this is an adaptation of Shirley Jackson’s chilling 1959 novel, whichStephen King deemed“as nearly perfect ­­­a haunted-house tale as I have ever read”. It has some seriously spooky shoes to fill.There is certainly the heart-quickening rumble of threat throughout (even terror, for some – the person in front of me spent the whole performance clutching their neighbour, muttering “No, no, no, I do not like thisat all”). This is largely thanks to slick, inventive stagecraft from director Martin Constantine. As a trio of guests arrives at the abandoned Hill House ­– invited by Dr Montague to investigate its rumoured supernatural affliction ­– a soundscape of unsettling music, creaky hinges and unidentified thuds accompanies an intensifying stream of jump scares. Bulbs blow, blankets hover, menacing scrawls appear on walls, and furniture slides about unaided – a disquieting suggestion that even the set changes are the work of ghosts.Excellent lighting and video projections (from Chris Davey and Duncan McLean respectively) on a panelled backdrop conjure the many rooms of the troubled mansion, and ratchet up the fright-factor as events hurtle towards their climax.View image in fullscreenJasper Britton as Dr Montague and Jemma Churchill as Mrs Montague in The Haunting of Hill House.Photograph: Pamela RaithBut the real horror of Jackson’s novel lies in the psychological disintegration of Eleanor, who joins Theodora (here, a slinking, seductive Sophie Lenglinger) and the house’s heir Luke (Robin Morrissey, cocksure yet brittle) after 11 years caring for her bullying and recently deceased mother. Clancy Ryan captures Eleanor’s giddy freedom, gnawing insecurity and yearning for a place in the world. And Stef Smith’s adaptation makes a strong stab at exploring the complexities of Eleanor’s unravelling: her conviction that the house is both haunted by her mother, and the home she has craved; her growing dejection as she is accused of orchestrating events.But it’s a tall order without the novel’s access to Eleanor’s inner world. And a tweaked ending and added twist on the mother-daughter theme take things in a less nuanced, albeit enjoyably creepy, direction.For those coming to the story fresh though, this technically impressive production offers a transporting fright night at the theatre.At Theatr Clwyd, Mold, from 13 to 17 October,then touring.Explore more on these topicsTheatreShirley JacksonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The crime fiction I’m interested in is political’: Ian Rankin on his new novel about the super-rich | Ian Rankin | The Guardian
description: The bestselling writer talks about leaving Edinburgh for London in his latest mystery, and what the future holds for Rebus
Author: Alex Clark
Headline: The bestselling writer talks about leaving Edinburgh for London in his latest mystery, and what the future holds for Rebus
Content: Ian Rankin.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIan Rankin.Photograph: Robert Ormerod/The GuardianIan RankinInterview‘The crime fiction I’m interested in is political’: Ian Rankin on his new novel about the super-richAlex ClarkThe bestselling writer talks about leaving Edinburgh for London in his latest mystery, and what the future holds for RebusSun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSirIan Rankinrarely watches television. Certainly, there’s no gleaming flatscreen in the corner of the apartment in Edinburgh where he writes, listens to music and constructs elaborate Lego models (all four Beatles, their Yellow Submarine and, once, a 6ft version of the Eiffel Tower). Did he not see the most recent incarnation of his most famous creation, Detective Inspector John Rebus, this time played by Richard Rankin (no relation), in the wake of previous performances by Ken Stott and John Hannah? “I did,” he concedes. “They gave me them on DVD, so I could play them on my computer.”Ah, his computer – it’s had its screen and hard drive replaced, and there are grooves in the keys. It sits on top of a plain, compact trestle-table desk he bought on London’s Charing Cross Road in 1987 and lugged back to his Tottenham flat on the tube; both have accompanied him from London to rural Dordogne, in southwest France, where he lived for a few years with his wife, Miranda, in the 1990s, and back to Edinburgh, where the couple and their two sons have been ever since.But if all this makes him sound doggedly attached to the past, wary of change and of modernity, his work stands in stark contradiction. Across 26 Rebus books, a smaller series involving the detective Malcolm Fox, and a number of standalone novels and plays, Rankin has shown himself to be fiercely attentive to the most serious aspects of contemporary life. “The crime fiction I’m interested in,” he tells me, “is the crime fiction that’s looking at society and the mess we’re in and how we got there, and it’s predominantly political.”His new novel, The Heights, takes on the challenge in dramatic and glittering style. Its title refers to a Knightsbridge apartment building aimed squarely at the highest end of the property market, its inhabitants the rich and famous who take as read that their residence will include a cinema and a luxury spa, and that visitors will pass by Chapman brothers artworks in its marble entrance hall. They are perhaps not expecting that their concierge will be discovered with his head bludgeoned, and that DS Gillian Gish will quickly appear on the scene to quiz them as to their whereabouts.One of the influences feeding into Gish, a brand-new lead character, is 1970s American TV detective Columbo, whom Rankin – back in his TV-viewing days – found captivating. “I didn’t realise it when I was watching as a teenager, but he’s a socialist figure,” Rankin says. “He comes into these very rich people’s lives and tears them apart, and they don’t know he’s doing it until he’s already done it. I just thought that was extraordinary. It’s to do with class: he’s the underclass, they’re the overclass, and he’s going to bring them down. Rebus has done that in quite a few of the books. And Gish, I think, secretly really enjoys the idea that she’s going to upset them by asking the wrong questions and by interfering in their very comfortable, cosseted world.”Gish has the kind of hinterland that Rebus lacks; she’s embedded in her own neighbourhood, in Rankin’s previous stomping ground of Tottenham, and after work she goes home to care for her mother. Her off-duty life contributes to the portrait of London as a series of wildly disconnected locations and social milieux. I ask him whether it was nerve-racking to leave the Edinburgh setting that he’s written about for so long? “I didn’t feel any trepidation,” he replies. “In some ways it can be a wee bit stifling. You get an idea for a story, you say, ‘Well, could that be contained in Edinburgh? And if it can’t be contained in Edinburgh, can I write it?’”And he’s convinced that his story of the ostentatious performance of wealth combined, paradoxically, with the obsession with privacy of the ultra-rich, wouldn’t have worked in Edinburgh. A prosperous city it may be, but “You’re not going to see a Rolls-Royce or a Bugatti Veyron. The wealth here is discreet.”The success of his novels has, of course, made Rankin himself a wealthy man, even if it did take him until his 60s – he’s 66 now – to get an office of his own. Over the years, he’s worked in a succession of spare rooms, attics and even next to a juddering washing machine, a clothes airer over his head. He is, he says, glad he didn’t make it big when he was young: “I was stupid. I’m sure I would have bought a Lamborghini and a pinball machine for every room in the house.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKen Stott as Rebus in the ITV series.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockNow, he and Miranda live a few minutes’ walk away from the writing flat, and take trips to far-flung places. “Miranda decided a few years ago that, now the kids have left and we’ve got money in the bank: before we get too old and we lose the use of our limbs and our brains, we should travel. I am holiday agnostic. She’s the one who tells me, right, you’re going here and you’re going there. So we do a lot of travelling, just in the last three or four years maybe. She’s booking through to 2028 at the moment.”When he’s away, he researches but can’t actually write. On a recent cruise around South America, he hadn’t even taken the ancient laptop and was making notes in longhand when a fellow passenger offered him the loan of a computer – which explains the message of gratitude at the end of The Heights. But when he does come back to base, he writes quickly, and determinedly, although he bats away being described as unusually productive. At the couple’s house in Cromarty, “if the weather’s nice, I get no writing done. If the weather’s bad, I get a lot of writing done because there’s nothing else to do. I’m the laziest, hard-working author I know.”But aside from buying vinyl, seeing the odd live band – seated gigs only these days, he concedes ruefully – Lego and holidays, Rankin has another use for his earnings. Each year, between 30 and 40% of his net income goes into the charitable trust that he and Miranda set up, for which their older son, Jack, also works. “I’ve got more money than I can spend. Once you’ve bought a nice hi-fi system and you’ve got a nice car, what are you going to do?”The trust’s focus is on smaller charities, often those supporting young people and adults with special needs – people like the Rankins’ younger son, Kit, who has Angelman syndrome, a genetic condition that means he has severe learning difficulties, and has also experienced epilepsy and vision problems. Now in his early 30s, Kit lives in a care facility nearby, and all four of them meet up every Sunday. “Any money that we leave behind when we shuffle off this mortal coil will get channelled to him to make sure that he’s always looked after. And our older son will be part of that process of looking after him financially.”I feel that I can’t leave without asking about Rebus, whom we last saw behind bars, following the death of his old adversary, gangster “Big Ger” Cafferty. Rankin is tight-lipped on his next project – back to Rebus, or perhaps another outing for Gillian Gish? – but does shed some light on Rebus’s future. After all, I say, you left him in a pretty parlous state. “Everybody says that, but it’s not true,” he protests. “At the end of the book, his lawyer says, ‘You’ve got some very good news.’ So he’s obviously getting out. You know the appeal is going to be heard and he’s going to get out. I have no doubt in my mind that’s the happy ending.”And with that, Sir Ian Rankin is off to do a bit of writing before an evening out. Possibly he’ll drop into the Oxford Bar, where the locals’ only acknowledgment of his elevated status is to ask, “Where’s your horse”? And you sense he wouldn’t have it any other way.The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
