title: ‘What could be discovered? What is new there?’: blockbuster exhibition celebrates Roy Lichtenstein | Roy Lichtenstein | The Guardian
description: The often-criticised pop artist is the focus of a monumental new survey including rarely seen pieces and ambitious new restagings at New York’s Whitney Museum
Author: David Smith
Headline: The often-criticised pop artist is the focus of a monumental new survey including rarely seen pieces and ambitious new restagings at New York’s Whitney Museum
Content: Installation view of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New.Photograph: Jason Lowrie/Estate of Roy Lichtenstein. Photograph by Jason Lowrie/BFA.comView image in fullscreenInstallation view of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New.Photograph: Jason Lowrie/Estate of Roy Lichtenstein. Photograph by Jason Lowrie/BFA.comRoy Lichtenstein‘What could be discovered? What is new there?’: blockbuster exhibition celebrates Roy LichtensteinThe often-criticised pop artist is the focus of a monumental new survey including rarely seen pieces and ambitious new restagings at New York’s Whitney MuseumDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the American artist Roy Lichtenstein created his monumentalGreene Street Muralin 1983, he took inspiration from the Bayeux tapestry for its serial storytelling technique. But whereas the embroidery depicting the Norman conquest continues to delight after nearly 1,000 years, Lichtenstein’s site-specific mural was destroyed after six weeks, in accordance with his wishes.Beyond the canvas: celebrating Lichtenstein’s lesser-known sculpturesRead moreMore than four decades later, however, the monumental Greene Street Mural is to mesmerise art lovers once more. This week a 96ft (29-metre) recreation of the work will span the entire entryway toRoy Lichtenstein: Like New, the first major New York retrospective of the pop artist’s work in 33 years, at the Whitney Museum of American Art.“He was very interested in the Bayeux tapestry,” guest curatorAlex Da Cortesays via Zoom. “This was a huge part of his research, and how he was thinking about his early work pre-pop in that the tapestry contained a serial storytelling, a comic-style frieze or broadside, which is essentially what Greene Street Mural becomes. It’s tied to this idea of the frame-by-frame and a kind of serial mode of storytelling that we understand very well now through scrolls and so many photographs.”The exhibition boasts more than 130 works spanning six decades, from early 1940s studies to unfinished canvases that Lichtenstein left in his studio at his death in 1997. The museum’s connection to Lichtenstein dates back to 1965, when his work was first featured in a Whitney annual exhibition.It was the artist’s widow, Dorothy, who championed pairing an in-house curator,Meg Onli, with an active contemporary artist, Da Corte, to conceive a contemporary retrospective that would innovate beyond a mere conventional survey.View image in fullscreenInstallation view of Greene Street MuralPhotograph: Jason Lowrie/Estate of Roy Lichtenstein. Photograph by Jason Lowrie/BFA.comKnown for his immersive installations that critique visual media and consumer culture, Da Corte had a long interest in pop art. He recalls: “You ask yourself, what do you think of an artist so ubiquitous as someone like Roy? Where is there a gap? What could be discovered? What is new there?”If the public remembers Lichtenstein primarily as a cool ironist who lifted images from romance comics and chewing gum wrappers, Like New exposes a more rigorous and complex artist. At the heart of the exhibition’s thesis is Lichtenstein’s lifelong obsession with an obscure academic mentor:Hoyt Sherman, a professor at Ohio State University.Lichtenstein studied under Sherman in the 1940s before returning to teach alongside him. Across his career, until his death in 1997, Lichtenstein repeatedly cited Sherman as his single greatest influence. Yet Sherman’s radical teaching methods had been underplayed in previous museum retrospectives.To understand Lichtenstein’s mechanics, Onli and Da Corte travelled to the Ohio State University archives to examine Sherman’s curriculum and psychological experiments.Sherman was a pioneer in optics and visual perception, building specialised laboratory environments known as “flash labs”. In these pitch-black classrooms, mechanical devices would flash images of still lifes or geometric forms for fractions of a second. Sherman instructed students to draw what they had seen in complete darkness, training their minds to process spatial form, figure-ground relationships and visual memory holistically rather than sequentially.View image in fullscreenGirl in Window (1964) – Roy Lichtenstein.Photograph: Photograph by Filip WolakDa Corte explains: “Hoyt Sherman’s teaching methods were eccentric and not to be overlooked. He employed a whole bunch of optical theorists who were working at the time, curious about how we see things – going all the way back to Aristotle and [Leonardo] da Vinci, as well as early 20th-century contemporaries.”This casts Lichtenstein’s output in a fresh light: rather than simply copying mass media, he was exploring sophisticated questions of optics and perception through popular imagery. Da Corte says: “We are used to seeing the pop of it and taking it for what it is – recognising that it’s an appropriated image – and then not wanting to excavate a meaning beyond that.“But Roy spoke about a very conceptual practice born out of Hoyt Sherman’s teachings on optics and perception. How curious that you go 50 years citing one professor over and over again? There must be more than meets the eye.”This challenges the persistent criticism that dogged Lichtenstein throughout his career: accusations of plagiarism, uncredited copying and lazy appropriation. During the height of pop art in the 1960s, critics frequently questioned whether Lichtenstein’s practice constituted legitimate fine art or commercial theft. Life magazine ran an article in 1964 asking: “Is He the Worst Artist in the U.S.?”For Onli and Da Corte, these critiques are narrow and fundamentally misunderstand Lichtenstein’s practice. In Like New, visitors can peruse original sketchbooks, source clippings and preliminary drawings alongside comic book panels by illustrators such asTony AbruzzoandWilliam Overgard, showing how often Lichtenstein reworked rather than simply reproduced his sources. He created complex visual composites, re-engineering line weights, cropping compositions and shifting colour fields to agitate the viewer’s eye.Onli reflects: “When we look back, there have been critiques lobbed not only at him, but at people like Warhol as well – quite a few pop artists who used appropriation as a strategy in the 1960s. There’s been critique of how much Lichtenstein could shift his images.“You get a chance to see in this exhibition, through his sketchbooks and clippings, original drawings from comic book artists he referenced. Roy was often making composites. It’s quite reductive to say he just lifted an image directly from a comic book; oftentimes, many different sources went directly into one composition.”View image in fullscreenRoy Lichtenstein, Artist’s Studio ‘Foot Medication’, 1974.Photograph: Elyse Allen/Art Institute of Chicago; Gift of Edlis Neeson CollectionOnli notes that Lichtenstein’s citational habit extended across the entire trajectory of art history. Early studies from 1942 show him copying historical paintings, a habit that evolved into major series referencing ClaudeMonet’s Rouen Cathedral, Pablo Picasso’s cubist figures, Henri Matisse’s interiors and PietMondrian’s grids.Onli emphasises: “All of us who go to art school begin our training through copying. Every single person begins their training through looking at the great masters and making riffs on that. Lichtenstein really plays with that throughout his entire career.”Da Corte draws a direct parallel between Lichtenstein’s techniques and traditional printmaking or comic production, noting that visual art has always been fundamentally collaborative and iterative.“From the Renaissance or before, this idea of tracing and making a cartoon is part of art practice. Anyone who works in comics knows no one does it alone; it’s a collaborative process. The ways in which he’s altering things becomes the real focus of the work. The subject of the work is not about what it appears to be or that it has been lifted, but how it’s been changed, what has been lost or actually erased.”Da Corte adds that Lichtenstein’s subtle adjustments embedded a quiet, personal humour into the work. He says: “Every painting requires analysis from the viewer. In his familiar images, he’s embedding himself with the kind of humour you would have if you were keeping a diary.“The way he engages with the found object or ready-made is not dissimilar to [Marcel] Duchamp, taking something and adjusting it slightly. It appears both completely banal and also agitates. Roy was a humorous guy, known to be funny and deeply liked, but a funny guy.”One of the most spectacular curatorial feats in Like New is the historic reconstruction of Lichtenstein’s landmark 1962 debut exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery on East 77th Street, a moment that helped herald the arrival of pop art. The Whitney has constructed an architectural facsimile of Castelli’s intimate gallery space, scaled up by 15% to accommodate contemporary museum crowds while preserving the impact of the original hanging.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jason Lowrie/Estate of Roy Lichtenstein. Photograph by Jason Lowrie/BFA.comTwo of the paintings in this ensemble have not been viewed by the public for more than 30 years. Onli comments: “What you have a chance to see is the sheer ambition of Lichtenstein early in his career. These paintings are huge for that room – it’s not a contemporary hang. We studied historical photos to understand how he was hanging these works, what the eye level was.”The curators hope that reassembling the Castelli show will remind contemporary viewers that what now seems universally accepted was once considered profoundly radical and dangerous to the art establishment.Onli notes: “It was a very controversial show. Lots of people hated it; some people loved it. WhenIvan KarpandLeo Castellimounted that show, collectors were saying to the gallery: ‘If you continue showing that work, we’re not coming here any more; this isn’t real painting, it’s not on the level.’ Even though we look back and see it as something celebrated, it wasn’t easy. That choice to continue in the face of criticism, to home in on something deeply conceptual and seemingly simple, took a lot of guts.”The 1962 suite showcases works such asLook Mickey (1961), Masterpiece (1962), and Girl with Ball (1961) – canvases where Lichtenstein threw down the gauntlet to abstract expressionism, replacing painterly angst with flat, commercial clarity.It is also the first Lichtenstein retrospective to include his murals. Greene Street Mural was originally painted in 1983 forCastelli’s 142 Greene Streetspace in Soho. Lichtenstein stitched together a vibrant assemblage of his own artistic lexicon: Ben-Day dots, cartoon hands, pyramids, composition notebook covers, tropical folding screens and references to Picasso and Matisse.Onli says: “We used aspects of Lichtenstein’s deadpan humour throughout the show. When Leo Castelli originally asked him to paint for the Greene Street space in 1983, Roy said: ‘Leo, I don’t really know what I would do.’ Then he thought about it and said: ‘Well, I’m going to have to use every image I’ve ever worked with before.’”She adds that the show has four murals in total. Every inch of them, including the outdoor presentation ofGirl in Window (1964), has been painted entirely by hand by Da Corte’s studio team, preserving the crucial tactile tension that defines Lichtenstein’s work.View image in fullscreenRoy Lichtenstein, Blam, 1962.Photograph: Estate of Roy LichtensteinOnli emphasises: “One thing we wanted to stress is that Roy’s work was so emphatically handmade. When you see it in photographs, it looks super slick and machine-made. Even in 1965, Roy joked, oh, the reason my work has been successful is because it translates well into fax machines. But throughout the entire show, all of these works have been done by hand. It has a very, very different feel than how we understand images today through AI or digital processes.”Indeed, in 1968, as mass media expanded rapidly across television, print and advertising, Lichtenstein was already talking about his famous Ben-Day dots in relationship to data. He had been reading Scientific American magazine, fascinated by how visual information could be broken down into discrete units, transmitted across distances and reassembled in the viewer’s mind.Onli says: “When we think about where he looked in time, we think about him so tethered to print culture. But by 1968, he’s already talking about his dots in relationship to data. He’s reading Scientific American, interested in how his dots could represent ideas of transmission and data. A lot of that had been papered over.”Onli notes that younger visitors coming to the Whitney today arrive without mid-century debates around commercial art versus high culture. “Younger generations are coming to the show without the baggage that was brought to this work in the past regarding appropriation.“I remember saying at one point to artistLouise Lawlerthat we all live in a moment now in which the provenance and authorship of an image no longer matters. What does it mean to approach someone like Lichtenstein today for people who are deeply interested in how an image can be decontextualised from its source and recontextualised in art space? His practice feels incredibly young, fresh and – as our title says – like new.”Da Corte sees Lichtenstein’s work as a crucial survival guide for contemporary artists overwhelmed by the endless deluge of digital media. “Right when he was making these works in the 1960s, the world as he knew it was being inundated with images, products and objects. Pop artists were trying to make sense of how they were being advertised to and what it looked like.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Photograph by Filip Wolak“If you ask any young artist now what their dilemma is, the dilemma is that there’s too much stuff. There are so many images in the world, so much to contend with. How do you participate meaningfully? What do you make of all these things? Roy echoes that exact puzzle of images. He shows young people that you can actually take those images that wash over you every day and make something meaningful out of them.”Asked to speculate on how Lichtenstein – who died in 1997 just as the internet was entering mainstream culture – would react to today’s world of smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence, the curators offer a nuanced picture of an artist always intrigued by technological advancement.Da Corte suggests: “I feel like he would have been a peer ofDavid Hockneyand embodied this way of being in the spirit of advancement. He existed in a sweet space right between television becoming normative and the advent of the internet. He accepted technology but he also never loved the subject matter he was dealing with. Comic books were not his actual love; he was attracted to things he had distance from.”Onli concurs, pointing to Lichtenstein’s 1990s experiments with virtual holograms, early computer design and influences from Italy’s avant gardeMemphis Group. “Whether he would like where we are today, I have no idea, but Lichtenstein would absolutely be responding to the visual culture of the moment. When you’re making a show for a person you’ve never met, you hope there are moments that speak to the humour of his work. Alex and I wanted something that is incredibly elegant and serious, while maintaining that deadpan sense of humour.”Roy Lichtenstein: Like New is on display at the Whitney Museum in New York until 10 May 2027Explore more on these topicsRoy LichtensteinExhibitionsArtDesignMuseumsWhitney Museum of American ArtNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Richard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’ | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the series
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the series
Content: Richard E Grant: ‘I can only imagine the faces of the producers.’Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenRichard E Grant: ‘I can only imagine the faces of the producers.’Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe TraitorsRichard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the seriesMatthew WeaverSun 11 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard E Grant has said his early exit from The Celebrity Traitors was due to his failure to realise his fellow contestants would take him seriously.The Withnail and I actor was voted off as a traitor after brazenly admitting his status to other contestants.Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Grant said revealing his true identity so early was a mistake. “I never thought they would take me seriously,” he said.“It was a completely catastrophically idiotic thing to do. I can only imagine the faces of the producers looking at each other and mouthing ‘he said what?!’. The strategy of no strategy is the strategy, clearly.”He revealed that his daughter told him before filming that he would be “slaughtered” as he was “incapable of hiding what you feel about people or anything”.During the first episode, Grant appeared to be thrilled to be selected as a traitor. His enthusiasm for the role appeared to get the better of him when he was asked by his fellow contestant Joe Lycett which side he was on.When Grant confessed to being a traitor, Lycett said: “I think you’ve done something that’s never been done in the game. It’s a bold strategy.”View image in fullscreenGrant (right) with Rob Beckett on The Celebrity Traitors. The actor says he has chosen not to watch the series.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAGrant said he now realised he should have made a joke of his admission. He said: “What I should have done in retrospect is go round everybody and say ‘are you a traitor? Yeah. I am a traitor, I am Spartacus. I am a traitor,’ to try and make light of it, but that may have dug my grave even deeper.”Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic | Stuart HeritageRead moreExplaining the context, he suggested contestants were treated like children and prisoners. He said: “You are so institutionalised in that thing within 24 hours, because you are isolated, kept in a room, there is a guard outside your door, your food is delivered and there’s no internet access, so you are kind of shut down.“You are also not told what time it is and are also prescribed on a daily basis what you are going to wear. So, you are kind of infantilised and institutionalised at the same time.”He said he had chosen to avoid watching the series. “It’s a weird thing because as an actor it is very uncomfortable to watch yourself, and if you watch yourself unscripted – which Traitors is – there’s no place to hide. That is unequivocally you.”Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsRichard E GrantnewsShareReuse this content

title: There’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayor | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space
Content: Liam Gallagher and Noel Gallagher of Oasis on stage in Chicago in 2025.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher and Noel Gallagher of Oasis on stage in Chicago in 2025.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesGreater ManchesterThere’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayorBev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production spaceHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheManchestermayor, Bev Craig, has said the city’s music scene is about more than just Oasis, as she announced funding to nurture a diverse range of local artists, be they “guitar bands or not”.Craig pledged the £2m investment funding inGreater Manchester, as the city region hosted a conference for the creative industries at MediaCity in Salford.She said there was a “real intentionality” to what Manchester was doing, in terms of growing its own music industry and attracting international events.Earlier this year, Manchester’s Co-op Live arena hosted the Brit awards and the Mobos, Europe’s biggest and most influential celebration of Black music and culture.“I wanted to have a major event that celebrated black music, culture and creativity,” Craig said, “and so that’s why we said, just after the Brits, we’d host their 30th anniversary, because we knew it would be the last one that theMobos founder Kanyawould be able to come to.”“I think there’s a real intentionality around what we’re doing with our music scene,” she added. “We’re known, I think, over the world for the influence that some of our indie guitar bands have had on Greater Manchester music, but there’s more to Greater Manchester’s music scene than justOasis.”View image in fullscreenBev Craig was addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit.Photograph: Marieke Macklon/The Guardian“I’m struck by the diversity, the creativity, the talent that we see,” Craig said. “And the job, as I see it, is making sure that that next generation of talent in an industry that’s becoming more and more middle-class, more and more London-centric, and a world where it’s more and more expensive to be able to break through, that we’re giving our local artists the hand up that they need to be able to be the next big thing, guitar band or not.”Addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit on Friday, Craig set out her plan for diversifying opportunities in the music industry. She also outlined commitments to support AI literacy for music professionals, and to monitor the impact of new technologies on employment, income and diversity in Greater Manchester’s music sector.The festival that accompanied the summit featured performances from up-and-coming black and minority ethnic artists including Bawo, JayaHadADream and Alt Blk Era.The final day of the conference was convened by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, whose love of Manchester guitar bands is well known.The culture minister Ian Murray told the conference: “With a prime minister who picks up his guitar to murder Smiths tracks, we have a passion from the very top.He added, joking: “That’s probably a career-limiting sentence for me.”“We’re living and working at a time of considerable change, particularly with technology,” Murray said, “but the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by the choices we make today, and how we support talent, how we reward creativity and how we embrace that innovation.”The £2m of funding Craig has set out is in addition to the £4m Culture Fund investment announced earlier this month, which will fund music projects from grassroots venues to world-renowned institutions.The additional funding is aimed at improving access to rehearsal and production space across the city region, providing practical support and ensuring there are jobs for musicians in their communities.Although the Manchester music scene may be about more than Oasis, the newly elected Manchester mayor did say she would be going to see the band on their sellout tour next year, which includes 11 nights at Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium.“I will, and thankfully the price of pints are much too expensive and the clientele have aged [which] means that you’re not as cautious as to what’s travelling through the air as historically you once would [be],” she said.But she added that “as somebody who loves all forms of music” she was “as excited about seeing [Merseyside band] the Ks at Beyond the Music as I am about seeing Oasis”.“I’m a little bit more into my dance music than the previous mayor as well,” Craig added. “So maybe a bit more varied in my tastes, shall we say.”Explore more on these topicsGreater ManchesterBev CraigManchesterSalfordOasisArts fundingArts policynewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: David Tennant stars in a brutally brilliant prison drama | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Jimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Jimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Completely compelling … Time on BBC OnePhotograph: :BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenCompletely compelling … Time on BBC OnePhotograph: :BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: David Tennant stars in a brutally brilliant prison dramaJimmy McGovern’s incredible series Time returns. Plus: The Party is a moreish new thriller based on Elizabeth Day’s hit novel. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Priya ElanandAlexi DugginsSun 11 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTimeSunday, 9pm, BBC OneJimmy McGovern’s prison anthology is never an easy watch but the bravery to explore the darkest corners of the British prison system makes it quality viewing. This time, David Tennant is downtrodden prison officer Bobby Bailey at a young offender institute – where wasted youth and potential only add to the gloom. Siobhan Finneran returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise, who joins the YOI. The two get off to a bad start and both have to deal with a tragic event in the tense first episode. Meanwhile, one new inmate is torn between attempting to make amends and fitting in with his violent friends. Once again, the story is harrowing, heart-tugging and completely compelling.Hollie RichardsonThe Reluctant Vampire6.40pm, BBC OneThe gently macabre humour of this comedy, adapted by the Gibbons brothers from a children’s novel by Eric Morecambe, has echoes of Ghosts. Hapless young vampire Val (Lenny Rush) finds himself in the world of humans when a trip to the village leads him into the home of oddball Gertie.Phil HarrisonEva Longoria: Searching for France7.20pm, BBC TwoDesperate Housewife Eva Longoria lands in Bordeaux. Filmed to look a bit like a Nespresso ad and with Eva sounding like a jacked-up Samantha Jones, it’s an enjoyable slice of escapism. That is, if you can stomach lots of one-percenters talking about staggeringly pricey bottles of plonk.Priya ElanApocalypse9pm, Channel 4It’s the Battle of the Bleats, after Eastsider Alix stole the goats from the Westsiders. Celia and Kelly are unimpressed, while Alix and Kiera are planning to play dumb in order to distract from any accusations. But how will they manage to disguise the sound of their four-legged friends when the inevitable confrontation happens?PELater … With Jools Holland10pm, BBC TwoThe ex-Squeeze pianist boogies his woogie all over an impressive lineup of musical guests. The performances include Beautiful South/Housemartins star Paul Heaton, British pop-soul sensation Skye Newman and Mobo-winning Northampton MC DC3. Plus, there’s a chat with Johnny Marr about his new album – and how he recently auctioned more than 80 guitars for charity.Alexi DugginsThe Party11.40pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenUnwanted guests? … The Party on ITV1.Photograph: Rob Youngson/ITV/World ProductionsSarah Solemani’s moreish take on Elizabeth Day’s novel follows the friendship between two men who went to boarding school together – journalist Martin Gilmour (Luke Evans) and Tory politician Ben Fitzmaurice (Tom Cullen) – and a terrible event that happens at Ben’s 40th birthday party. It opens with Martin in a blood-soaked shirt at the police station, recalling the year he got a scholarship and met Ben …HRLive sportChampionship Football: Southampton v Portsmouth, 11.30am, ITV1At St Mary’s Stadium.Premier League Football: Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest, 1pm, Sky Sports Main EventLiverpool v Man City follows at 4pm. Coventry v Newcastle is on Mon at 6.30pm.Prem Rugby Union: Exeter v Newcastle, 2.30pm, TNT Sports 1Sale v Harlequins is on TNT Sports 5 at 2.45pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie review – Muriel Spark’s extraordinary heroine made more extraordinary still | Stage | The Guardian
description: Gayle Rankin is funny, sharp-tongued and sexually forthright as Vicky Featherstone’s production ditches 1930s starchiness for the bohemian avant garde
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Gayle Rankin is funny, sharp-tongued and sexually forthright as Vicky Featherstone’s production ditches 1930s starchiness for the bohemian avant garde
Content: Impossible to ignore … Gayle Rankin as Miss Jean Brodie.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenImpossible to ignore … Gayle Rankin as Miss Jean Brodie.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianStageReviewThe Prime of Miss Jean Brodie review – Muriel Spark’s extraordinary heroine made more extraordinary stillRoyal Lyceum, EdinburghGayle Rankin is funny, sharp-tongued and sexually forthright as Vicky Featherstone’s production ditches 1930s starchiness for the bohemian avant gardeMark FisherSun 11 Oct 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJean Brodie has entered the classroom of Mr Lowther (Brian Ferguson). She tells the music teacher she will not be a distraction. “Proceed as if I wasn’t here,” she says.Yeah, right. Nothing can proceed as if Jean Brodie was not there. Played by Gayle Rankin in a drape-sleeved top and figure-hugging leather skirt, she is impossible to ignore. Chloe Lamford’s dust-pink set is a little bit lecture theatre, an awful lot neo-classical staircase; Rankin floats across it like an exotic moth: colourful, distractable, ever present.Pupils and teachers loathe or love her. You never doubt why. She is compellingly herself.In a re-defining performance, Rankin makes Muriel Spark’s extraordinary heroine more extraordinary still. In Vicky Featherstone’s production for the Royal Lyceum and theNational Theatre of Scotland, she is funny, sharp-tongued and sexually forthright. Out goes 1930s starchiness, in comes the bohemian avant garde. She slips off her zebra-striped heels and walks in bare feet.Her singularity comes at a cost. Headteacher Miss Mackay (Maureen Beattie) is worried about educational attainment: today, we would be more concerned about child protection. Brodie’s approval of the predatory art teacher Mr Lloyd (Dyfan Dwyfor) is only one of her contradictions.View image in fullscreenContradictions … Maureen Beattie and Gayle Rankin in The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThose contradictions keep us guessing. To be enamoured of Italian art and European fashion is one thing; to admire Mussolini is another. Her elitism would be at home in an Ayn Rand novel were it not for Spark’s political nous and ironic wit, crisply captured here in David Harrower’s adaptation.On the one hand, we might like her rationality and reason, her desire to create “young heroines of the future” and her amusing distaste for team spirit. On the other, we worry about an individualism that threatens not only this prim school, but society at large. She is at once inspirational and messianic.Only the teenage Sandy Stranger (Bobby Rainsbury) sees through her. The younger woman brings her down as if Brodie were a Shakespearean hero – an obstinate King Lear or Coriolanus, too damaged by her private losses to see her own flaws. She wants to shape a generation in her likeness; her tragedy is to end up just another teacher. In our age of charismatic leaders, Featherstone’s bold, free-flowing, sometimes overstated production has lessons of its own.AtRoyal Lyceum, Edinburgh, until 18 October; on tour until 7 November.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreMuriel SparkNational Theatre of ScotlandVicky FeatherstonereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d wander through the park all angsty listening to Arctic Monkeys’: Arlo Parks’ honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car, and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car, and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?
Content: Arlo Parks … ‘I love Janet Jackson’s voice – it softens people.’Photograph:View image in fullscreenArlo Parks … ‘I love Janet Jackson’s voice – it softens people.’Photograph:Honest playlistMusic‘I’d wander through the park all angsty listening to Arctic Monkeys’: Arlo Parks’ honest playlistThe singer shamelessly blasts Lady Gaga in the car and is brought to tears by Portishead – but which song does she have to be careful listening to?As told to Hannah NewtonSun 11 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withI remember listening to Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) by Eurythmics when I was really young. There was something about the line at the beginning that I was completely intoxicated by.The firstdownload I boughtWhen I was about 10 or 11, I would put my headphones on and wander through the park all angsty listening to Fake Tales of San Francisco by Arctic Monkeys, my first download on my iPod Nano. I loved the storytelling, the characters and the gritty tableaux they described: it felt so real, even though it was far away from where I grew up.The song I do at karaokeI inherited a lot of records from my uncle when I was 12 or 13; he let me choose as many as I could fit in my parents’ car. I chose randomly: Sade, LL Cool J, Grandmaster Flash, D’Angelo andPrince. Although I don’t do karaoke, hypothetically I would choose When Doves Cry by Prince. There’s something almost unattainable about the way he sings. I would throw myself at it with passion, but not be able to pull it off!The song I inexplicably know every lyric toThere are so many, but Superstar by Jamelia makes me happy – it’s a kind of a bubblegum pop song.The best song to play at a partyMy parents had a lot of CDs. My dad was into jazz – Miles Davis, Charles Mingus, Duke Ellington – and my mum loved French music and Whitney, Diana Ross, Tina Turner,Janet Jackson. I was playing Janet Jackson’s All for You in my dressing room for my crew and everyone was bopping. I feel like you can never go wrong with her. I love her voice – it softens people.The song I can no longer listen toEven songs tied to painful experiences, I don’t avoid. Fourth of July by Sufjan Stevens is heartbreaking. I have to be careful when I listen to it, because it brings out so much melancholy about grief and loss – it plunges you into certain spaces.The song that changed my lifeThere’s so much space in House of Cards by Radiohead; Thom Yorke’s voice is ethereal. I discovered it a few years before I wrote Collapsed in Sunbeams, it has the same minimalism to it.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateI embrace the music that a lot of people like, because there must be something that brings us towards it collectively. Like Starstruck by Lady Gaga – I blast that shamelessly in the car.The song that gets me up in the morningI’ve been listening to I Care by Turnstile: it’s happy, heart open. It makes me feel like I’m 16, but the drums are, like: OK, time to get the coffee going and start the day.The song that makes me cryGlory Box by Portishead. It’s so piercing, specifically the live version from Roseland theatre. Hearing the little cracks in Beth Gibbons‘s voice, she’s baring herself to the audience, it brings tears to my eyes.The song I want played at my funeralSunday Morning by the Velvet Underground: there’s something so warm about it, it feels soothing, like a new beginning. It’s melancholy but with a glimmer of hope.Ambiguous Desire is out now;Arlo Parkstours the UK and Ireland, 17 to 26 October; tour starts Dublin.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistArlo ParksPop and rockR&BPrinceJanet JacksonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Healing waters: 10 of the best spa towns in Europe for a restorative autumn break | Spa breaks | The Guardian
description: From Alpine valleys to belle époque towns, dip your toes in the therapeutic waters and steaming mineral pools at spa hotels offering centuries-old healing treatments
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Alpine valleys to belle époque towns, dip your toes in the therapeutic waters and steaming mineral pools at spa hotels offering centuries-old healing treatments
Content: A spa trip back in time … Nové Lázně hotel in Mariánské Lázně, Czechia.Photograph: Jan PrerovskyView image in fullscreenA spa trip back in time … Nové Lázně hotel in Mariánské Lázně, Czechia.Photograph: Jan PrerovskySpa breaksHealing waters: 10 of the best spa towns in Europe for a restorative autumn breakFrom Alpine valleys to belle époque towns, dip your toes in the therapeutic waters and steaming mineral pools at spa hotels offering centuries-old healing treatmentsFiona KerrSun 11 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMariánské Lázně, CzechiaIn 2021,Unesco designated 11 historic spa townsacross Europe as one transnationalworld heritage site, recognising their “exceptional testimony to the European spa phenomenon, which gained its highest expression from around 1700 until the 1930s”. This was the original wellness tourism, and these grand health resorts include Bath in England and the town of Spa in Belgium, as well as the west Bohemia spa triangle of Karlovy Vary, Františkovy Lázně and Mariánské Lázně.Of that trio, Karlovy Vary is the most well known and within a day trip of Prague, but Mariánské Lázně is arguably the prettiest. The town offers three natural healing traditions: mineral springs, carbon dioxide springs known as Maria’s Gas, and therapeutic peloids (mud and clay). Czech nationals are still prescribed weeks-long spa stays to recover from surgery, severe illness or chronic conditions, but anyone can check into theNové Lázně hotel(doubles from €234 B&B, including spa access), a canary yellow neo-renaissance confection built in 1896 that faces the central park.Its spa is a trip back in time: baths surrounded by marble columns and intricately decorated treatment cabins, including one built for King Edward VII, who visited nine times. Join tourists and locals drinking the waters from special porcelain cups while walking along the colonnades, and don’t forget to pair it with a spa wafer – large, thin, crispy confections with sweet fillings such as hazelnut or chocolate. It’s not all virtuous.Bad Kissingen, GermanyView image in fullscreenBad Kissingen in Bavaria is renowned for its architecture.Photograph: Moskwa/AlamyGermany is home to about 350 designated spa towns, including three of the Unesco Great Spa Towns of Europe: celebrity favourite Baden-Baden, quiet riverside Bad Ems and elegant Bad Kissingen in Bavaria. The latter’s striking architecture is arguably the most interesting of the three, much of the central spa district having been rebuilt by star German architect Max Littmann in the early 20th century. This includes the grand fountain hall, with its stained-glass roof, whereBrunnenfrauen(fountain women) dispense different mineral waters from bronze pipes, and the huge basilica-style Wandelhalle, where the town’sspa philharmonic orchestraperforms several times a day.Music has always been part of the spa experience – the Staatsbad Philharmonie Kissingen holds the world record for the most concerts performed in one year (727!) – and the beautiful art nouveau-style Regentenbau houses one of the best concert halls in Europe.The modernKissSalis Therme(from €19 for two hours) on the southern edge of town is the main public bathhouse today, with indoor and outdoor thermal pools, mud treatments and various – clothing-free – saunas.At the more classical end of the spa spectrum, theGrand Hotel Kaiserhof Victoria(doubles from €209 B&B, including spa access) sits next door to the Wandelhalle on the town’sKurgarten. The water used in the spa here is pumped up directly from the brine spring, while the inhalation room has awooden graduation towercovered in knobbly salt deposits, which mimics the healing effects of mineral-rich sea air.Bad Wildbad, GermanyView image in fullscreenA pool at Palais Thermal in Bad Wildbad.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyDeep in the north of the Black Forest, this spa town offers ways of immersing in nature beyond soaking in waters from the thermal springs. Rising above the town, Sommerberg (meaning “summer mountain”) will get pulses racing. Afunicular railwaywhizzes visitors to the top, the starting point for hiking and biking routes. For more heart-pumping views, the accessibleTreetop Walk(€12.50) spirals above the dense pine trees to an observation tower 40 metres up, with a tunnel slide back down the middle for extra thrills, while theWildlinesuspension bridge (€9.50) – with its 380-metre walkway – arches over the Enz valley for maximum views.Back in town, there are two thermal baths to dip into: the modernVital Therme, where those with joint and back problems are prescribed movement therapy and spa treatments (€14 for three hours); and the historicPalais Thermal, where the pools are surrounded by marble pillars, statues of Venus and Moorish tiles (€21 for three hours).Mokni’s Palais Hotelis connected to the Palais Thermal building, meaning guests can pad over in their bathrobes (doubles from €183 B&B, including access to the spa).Bagnoles-de-l’Orne, FranceView image in fullscreenChâteau du Gué aux Biches at Bagnoles de l’OrneLocal legend has it that, after many battles, the medieval lord Seigneur Hugues de Tessé freed his faithful warhorse Rapide in Normandy’s Andaines forest to live out the rest of its days in peace. Much to the nobleman’s surprise, the horse later returned to him stronger and full of life, then led his master to the warm, sulphurous waters of Bagnoles’ spring. Centuries later, a spa resort sprang up so the Parisian bourgeoisie could also tap into this fountain of youth, with belle époque villas laid out on the shores of a lake in the middle of the forest (today, it’s also handily less than an hour and a half from the ferry at Caen for British wellness seekers).That belle époque quartier was the vision of local politician Albert Christophle, whose former hunting lodge on the edge of the village is now the very lovely five-bedroomChâteau du Gué aux Biches(doubles from €195 B&B).This summer, its Danish owners, Klaus Bentin and Soren Rasmussen, added a new restaurant in the old kitchen, serving upsmørrebrød(open sandwiches).The hotel has a partnership with the nearby spa atB’O Resort, meaning Klaus or Soren will line up your treatments, and there are bicycles to borrow so you can pedal a couple of kilometres over for that clay body wrap or hydromassage.The surrounding forest is crisscrossed with hiking, biking and trail running routes. In autumn, take things more meditatively by going mushroom foraging among the more than 1,700 varieties sprouting from the Andaines forest floor.Bad Gastein, AustriaView image in fullscreenFelsentherme thermal spa at Bad Gastein, Salzburg province.Photograph: AlamyThis genteel town in the Hohe Tauern Alps was built on water; indeed, a roaring waterfall cascades right through the middle of it. The healing reputation of its radon-rich waters, which bubble up from the town’s thermal springs, saw grand hotels built in the 19th century to house the emperors and aristocrats, writers and thinkers (Sigmund Freud among them) who came to be cured of their ills.The fashion for “taking the waters” trickled away, but in recent years there’s been something of a revival, with a clutch of new hotels opening. TheCōmodo(doubles from €188 B&B) is one of them, a slick spot refashioned from a 1960s sanatorium. Bedrooms look out over the valley and mountains, as does the thermal water-filled indoor pool.There are several public fountains where you can still drink water straight from the source (warm, slightly salty and metallic tasting), but perhaps more palatable is to soak at the brutalistFelsenthermepublic bath complex with its numerous pools (€40 for a day pass).Just as warming – but with fewer health benefits – is a bowl ofKaspressknödelsuppe(beef broth with cheese-infused dumplings) at the cosy cabin ofSchafflinger Alm(soups from €4.50, mains from €17) after a bracing hike through the forest or carving up the Schlossalm-Angertal-Stubnerkogel ski area, where the season kicks off in late November.Piešťany’s Spa Island, SlovakiaView image in fullscreenIrma Balneotherapy House in Piestany.Photograph: Piestany tourism boardJust before crossing the Colonnade Bridge to get to Piešťany’s Spa Island, there’s a statue of a man breaking his crutch, symbolic of the healing powers of the town’s thermal waters and sulphurous mud, harnessed on this enclave of wellness in the Váh River. The first simple wooden bathhouses were built on the island in 1778, but the opening of theThermia Palace hoteland its Irma Balneotherapy House in 1912 turned it into a health resort.Further hotels and spas are dotted between the trees and become increasingly concrete and functional as you get further from the bridge.The Thermia Palace is still the fanciest option, with a raft of treatment programmes in the spa, from extensive diagnostics and lab tests to mud packs and pools (doubles from €210 half-board, including spa access). The blue-black goop is applied all over the body at a toasty 45C and left for about 10 minutes before being unceremoniously hosed off.Outside, the spa park also feels restorative, with lily ponds, fountains and free-roaming peacocks.In town,Elektrárňa Piešťanyis a former power plant turned cultural centre that feels surprisingly vital, with film festivals and rock concerts, while the strikingly brutalistHouse of Artshosts chamber orchestras and tango music trios.Rogaška Slatina,SloveniaView image in fullscreenThe Grand hotel at Rogaška.Photograph: Andrija Majsen/AlamyThis town in eastern Slovenia is famed for Donat Mg, one of the world’s most magnesium-rich mineral waters, traditionally consumed for its digestive benefits. The company now sells millions of bottles of the stuff each year, but here at the source you can sip it for free from the fountains in thePivnica Drinking Hall– although its salty, fizzy, metallic flavour is something of an acquired taste.Like other towns of its ilk, Rogaška attracted the great and the good of Europe in the 19th century, and its confection of architecture is testament to that. A short stroll away from the drinking hall, through immaculately clipped gardens, the butter-yellowGrand Hotel Rogaškais straight out of the town’s golden age (doubles from €198 half-board include spa access). Bedrooms are traditional, but the spa has all the bells and whistles, from carbon dioxide baths and mineral water inhalations to reflexology and magnetotherapy.Somewhat fittingly for a town famous for its drinking water, Rogaška is also known for its glassware – and visitors can tour theRogaška crystal factory(€12) to see the glass-blowing in action before buying glasses for their Donat Mg from the on-site shop. The surrounding wooded hills are the place for autumn walks.Salsomaggiore Terme, ItalyView image in fullscreenTerme Berzieri in Salsomaggiore, Emilia-Romagna.Photograph: Elena DallariIn Emilia-Romagna’s so-called “food valley”, not far from Parma, this small spa town will help balance out some of that indulgence. Last year, the Italian thermal brand QC Spa of Wonders reopened the beautiful art deco-styleTerme Berzieri, where the gilded interiors – all frescoes, mosaics, majolica and stucco – are as much of a draw as the salty spring waters, rich in iodine and bromide (five-hour spa sessions from €62). There’s the usual thermal attractions, as well as a sauna cinema and infinity rooftop pool, while treatments in wooden barrels nod to the area’s winemaking.Try some of those wines at theCantina Il Poggiovineyard in the hills outside Salsomaggiore, which produces a range of styles including the local sparkling Malvasia di Candia Aromatica (tastings from €30). Continue the tastings with a visit to a parmigiano reggiano producer, such asCaseificio Ugolotti(tour and tasting €23), before picking up some ham from Parma’s famousLa Prosciutteria. Stop for a roast pork sandwich at legendary panini placePepèn, before feasting your eyes on thePilotta Palacecomplex with the Galleria Nazionale, Palatine Library and Farnese theatre, while the opulentTeatro Regiohosts the annualVerdi festivalin October. The organicagriturismoCase Zucchi, about a 10-minute drive from Salsomaggiore, makes a suitably foodie base, with bedrooms named after herbs and the breakfast table piled with fresh bread, eggs, ham, cheese and fruit each morning (doubles from £104 B&B).Caldas de Monchique, PortugalView image in fullscreenThe terraced fields of Serra de Monchique near Fóia, the highest mountain in the Algarve.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyHigh in the Serra de Monchique mountains, surrounded by cork oak and eucalyptus forests, the whitewashed hill town of Monchique offers a slower-paced autumn escape than the nearby Algarve coast. Its cobbled streets are lined with craft shops, ceramic workshops and simple taverns servingchouriço(smoked sausage) with a small glass ofmedronho(fruit brandy). In a wooded valley below town, the spa village of Caldas de Monchique is little more than a handful of 19th-century buildings around a shaded square and park, where you can drink slightly warm spring water from the public fountain.Wallow in the alkaline waters a little longer atCaldas de Monchique Villa Termal Spa Resort(doubles from €84, thermal water circuit £17 for 90 minutes).The spa offers hydro rituals including a Vichy shower, massage and bath, or thermal water circuits around the pools, sauna and Turkish baths, before a dip in the outdoor pool.Afterwards, the 1692 restaurant, with its stained-glass windows, dishes upbacalhau à Monchique(salt cod stuffed with chouriço and ham). It’s not far from here to Fóia, the highest mountain in the Algarve at 902 metres. It’s worth the walk to the summit for the views, or hike on a further 2½ miles (4km) to the Barbelote waterfall, which cascades over a rocky cliff face in the wetter months.Chaves, PortugalView image in fullscreenEco cabins at Pedras Salgadas Spa and Nature ParkThere’s a little run of spa towns in the north of Portugal near the Spanish border, a curative route through Pedras Salgadas, Carvalhelhos, Vidago, Carlão and Chaves.In Chaves, the waters are some of the hottest in Europe, coming out of the ground at a scorching 76C. The Romans built a large therapeutic bathing complex here, that was only rediscovered by accident in 2006 when work began on an underground car park. Now, the freeMuseu Termas Romanas de Chavesallows visitors to explore the pools and soaking baths, perfectly preserved thanks to an earthquake in the 4th century that sealed them for millennia.To take the waters today, head to theAquae Salutem Thermal Complex(€30 for 90 minutes), a circuit of outdoor pools, saunas, steam and showers that opened in 2025.About half an hour down the road, thePedras Salgadas Spa and Nature Parksits on the fringes of one of the other small spa towns. The owners have built 18 eco-houses and treehouses on stilts (doubles from £171 B&B, spa access additional £17 per room) among the pine trees at the source.Guests can do a spot of forest bathing before dipping into the spa – redesigned by one of Portugal’s most famous architects, Álvaro Siza – for a thermal water hydro-massage, or wander between the pink spring pavilions in the park. Pedras Salgadas is also a popular, naturally sparkling mineral water brand.Explore more on these topicsSpa breaksEurope holidaysCity breaksShort breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make pumpkin soup – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A smooth and satisfying soup in nine easy steps
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A smooth and satisfying soup in nine easy steps
Content: Felicity Cloake’s pumpkin soup.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s pumpkin soup.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make pumpkin soup – recipeA smooth and satisfying soup in nine easy stepsFelicity CloakeSun 11 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePumpkin soup, so delicious in theory – sweet, velvety, lightly autumnal – is so often disappointing in reality. Thin in flavour and consistency, thanks to squash’s high water content, it’s likely to make even the most conscientious cook regret not chucking those Halloween offcuts on the compost heap when they had the chance. This, I hope it goes without saying, is notthatsort of pumpkin soup.Prep20 minCook1 hrServes4-6About 1½kg pumpkin or winter squash(eg, crown prince, sugar pumpkin, kabocha), washedOilSalt2 litres light chicken stock, or vegetable stock1 large red or yellow onion, peeled and chopped1 celery stick, cut into small dice2 small carrots, peeled and cut into small dice1 small red chilli, chopped, or a sprinkle of chilli flakes (optional)Sugar(optional)2 tbsp butter(optional)4 sage leaves, roughly torn, or the leaves from 2 thyme sprigs (optional)1 handful grated parmesan, or gruyere or similar (optional)Nutmeg(optional)1 A note on the pumpkinThe single most important step here is your choice of pumpkin. Look for something that feels heavy for its size. I like the dense, fudgy crown prince or a nutty kabocha, but, if all else fails, a butternut squash will do nicely. Asian, African and Caribbean grocers often stock a wider variety than supermarkets, as will your local greengrocer or farmers’ market.View image in fullscreen2 Skin the pumpkinPumpkins can be as much as 90% water, so it’s worth roasting the flesh to concentrate its flavour. Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Wash the pumpkin, then cut off some skin from one end so it will sit firmly on a board. Use a Y-shaped peeler or sharp knife to remove the rest of the skin and put the trimmings in a medium saucepan.3 Deseed and chop the pumpkinCut the pumpkin into quarters, then remove the seeds (and the flesh around them). Add all but a spoonful of the seeds to the pan with the skin, and set aside the rest for now. Cut the flesh into large, evenly sized cubes and put these on a baking tray (use a second tray if there are too many to fit comfortably in one layer).4 Roast the pumpkinView image in fullscreenDrizzle the cubes with a little oil (olive is nice, but anything not too strongly flavoured will do) and toss with a little salt. Bake for about 40 minutes, until soft and beginning to brown. If the cubes are colouring unevenly, turn around the tray halfway and remove any that look as if they might burn before the rest are done.5 Roast the pumpkin seedsView image in fullscreenWash the reserved spoonful of pumpkin seeds, if necessary, to remove any flesh clinging to them, then blot dry with a clean tea towel or kitchen paper. Put the seeds on a fresh tray and toss with a little oil and salt, then put them in the oven for the last 10 minutes of the pumpkin cooking time. Set aside to crisp up.6 Boil the pumpkin offcutsView image in fullscreenWhile the pumpkin is cooking, put the stock in the peelings pan – a good fresh chicken stock is my favourite, because it’s richer and more neutral than vegetable stock, but most varieties will do, as will plain water. Bring to a boil, then turn down the heat and simmer gently for 30 minutes.7 Start the soup basePut two tablespoons of oil in a large saucepan on a medium-low heat, then add the onion, celery, carrots and a good pinch of salt, and fry, stirring regularly until soft but not brown. Stir in the chilli, if using, and fry for another minute or so (if the soup base is ready before the pumpkin is roasted, take the pan off the heat).8 Add the roast pumpkinView image in fullscreenStir the roast pumpkin cubes into the soup base, then strain in the pumpkin-skin stock (discard the trimmings). Bring to a simmer and cook for about 10 minutes, or until the pumpkin is very soft. Puree with a stick blender or in a jug blender (if using the latter, let the soup mix cool slightly first), then taste and adjust the seasoning, adding a little sugar or diluting the soup with water, as necessary.9 Finishing touchesIf serving with browned butter (a drizzle of cold pumpkin oil is a good vegan alternative), heat the butter until golden, stir in the sage and decant immediately into a heatproof bowl or jug. Serve the soup topped with cheese, if using, a grating of nutmeg, a drizzle of the brown butter and sage or oil, and a few roasted seeds.This article was amended on 11 October 2026 to swap the images for step six and step eight which had been put in the wrong place.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassSoupVegetablesStarterAutumn food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Indian Cafe Racer, Birmingham B5: ‘A good news tale for the local food scene’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The cooking is sometimes bang on, sometimes a little slapdash, but then piques your interest all over again
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The cooking is sometimes bang on, sometimes a little slapdash, but then piques your interest all over again
Content: Indian Cafe Racer, Birmingham B5: ‘Elegant with small dashes of eccentricity.’Photograph: Jack Spicer Adams/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenIndian Cafe Racer, Birmingham B5: ‘Elegant with small dashes of eccentricity.’Photograph: Jack Spicer Adams/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewIndian Cafe Racer, Birmingham B5: ‘A good news tale for the local food scene’ – restaurant reviewThe cooking is sometimes bang on, sometimes a little slapdash, but then piques your interest all over againGrace DentSun 11 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndian Cafe Raceron Bristol Street, Birmingham, spent its fledgling years tucked behind a curtain at the back ofthe Wellington pubjust a few doors up from its fancy new home. There was a Royal Enfield motorcycle, chequerboard floors and a psychedelic Indian soundtrack, but this small, homespun spot from Azad Kayes quickly became culty, then oversubscribed, then in need of a bigger home. It’s a good news tale for the Brum food scene.For those who remember it, south Birmingham’s Balti triangle once ran to 30 bustling restaurants along Ladypool Road and Stratford Road. Only two now remain. Something has gone amiss with supply and demand. Indian Cafe Racer, meanwhile, has enough fans for a new, 65-cover, grown-up restaurant, serving an ever-changing menu that, when we visited, featuredshaktimanandsalad (named after an Indian comic-book superhero),gol gappa(crisp shells filled with chickpeas and potato), chicken pepper fry and grilled aubergine and portobello mushrooms, known as farzi steak.View image in fullscreenIndian Cafe Racer’spapdi chatis enough to feed the hordes, as well as ‘excite the desi-food disciple’.Kayes dips into Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata, with a scattering of Indo-Chinese small plates:gobi manchurian(fried cauliflower in sweet-and-sour sauce) and chilli chicken, say. The cocktail bar serves cold, potent liveners with names such as Angry Young Man, Red Carpet and Tiger Rides Bike, alongside endlesskarak chai, a heavily spiced, very sweet, milky tea brewed strong with cardamom and condensed milk. Jump on our Cafe Racer, the menu says, and let us give you amasttaste of India. No visa required.double quotation markThere’s a fine line between extreme pleasure and being legally waterboardedIn fact, the new Indian Cafe Racer has about it a sprinkling ofDishoom: paper menus with faux-olde font, wipeable tables and functional rather than fancy-pants hospitality. The room is elegant with small dashes of eccentricity, and there’s a sense that, in its expansion, some of its silliness has been tidied away. The large glass windows face on to the realities of a dual carriageway, and the room errs on the dark side. Still, the welcome is warm and we kick off with a round ofdahi puri: crisp, plump, puffed flour shells filled with potato, sweet yoghurt, tamarind and mint chutney. We know the drill: eat them in one, though these ones are so large and so liquidy that there’s a fine line between extreme pleasure and being legally waterboarded.Recovering, we move on to chicken 65, named, depending on who you ask, after its position on a Chennai hotel menu in 1965 (other origin stories are available) – fried with curry leaves, green chillies and arguably a little too much mustard seed. A round of spiced lamb chops – two cutlets a portion, marinated overnight and finished in the tandoor – are genuinely succulent.View image in fullscreen‘Crowd-pleaser’: Indian Cafe Racer’sgulab jamun.The tandoori king prawns in house masala are lovable, zinging with crushed ginger and sticky with honey, while the Rajastani lamb is a standout: slow-cooked and finished with smoked charcoal and butter. The increasingly ubiquitous dal makani arrives deeply and sweetly rich in its creamy tomato sauce, but the naans are a bit thin and functional. Indian Cafe Racer’s cooking is sometimes bang on, sometimes a little slapdash, but then the likes ofgobi manchurianpique your interest all over again. If cocktails feel too much by this point, there’s always a cold Bombay Bicycle IPA.Cafe racers were the lads who raced motorbikes such as thatRoyal Enfield, which was once made in nearby Redditch, between roadside cafes in the 60s. Today, Royal Enfield is made in Chennai. The bike went from the edge of Birmingham to India, and this restaurant closes the circle. Arguably, with Indian Cafe Racer’s mature new home, some of the spirit of foot-to-the-pedal mayhem has been lost. Still, it opens every day (including Monday), if you have a horde to feed it will make a huge fuss of your group, and there’s enough choice to excite the desi food disciple who wants Rajastani lamb and mangomachli, without spooking the horses if you’re with Sheila who “doesn’t do” spice – she can have the paneer makani.
